2h ago 04.00 EST Grealish offers Everton apology Jack Grealish has issued a public apology to Everton fans after he made his comeback in a behind-closed-doors match with Derby. Grealish has missed four matches and not played for the Toffees since 17 October following a breach of club discipline. Boss David Moyes has been reluctant to discuss any finer details and the club only confirmed the 31-year-old former England winger was “not match-fit” ahead of a trip to Newcastle on 2 November but Grealish featured in a friendly at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday in the strongest suggestion yet that a line has been drawn over the issue. “Nice to be back out there with the boys today after a few good days training,” Grealish wrote on his Instagram story. “I want to apologise to the fans and everyone at the club for not being able to help the team the last few weeks. I love playing for this club and can’t wait to be back playing in front of you guys in an Everton shirt. See you all soon.” Grealish spent the first half of the 2025-26 campaign on loan at Everton before injury curtailed his spell on Merseyside, but he returned on another temporary deal on transfer deadline day. Sports.title: It’s Happy Harry Kane day as England’s finest seizes his moment in style | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Happy Harry Kane day! And many happy Harry returns. There is a process in clinical psychology known as semantic satiation. Subjects are asked to repeat a word or phrase so many times that it loses any kind of meaning. Suddenly “daffodils” is just an absurd, empty set of sounds. So it was in the buildup to Harry Kane’s record-breaking 126th cap, at the end of Harry Kane Ballon d’Or fortnight, as Harry Kane’s England were led out by top scorer Harry Kane, climax to a week of Harry Kane tributes, Harry Kane montages, 26-page Harry Kane … wait. Where were we?

This was that kind of occasion from start to finish, a night where you expected to look up from your desk mid-match to see Kane’s head looming helpfully over your shoulder, to enter the Wembley toilets at half-time and find him silently offering you a breath mint and a scented tissue.

Football loves its rankings and ratings. England loves a formal march-past. The Harry Kane moment was always going to come at Wembley. And it duly arrived with 61 minutes gone and the score 1-1 in a meandering game of mid-November England product.

There may be less satisfying ways to decide a game of football than a VAR-screen penalty awarded for an overly prolonged grab of the collar on a player who wasn’t going to get the ball. But it’s hard to think of many right now.

View image in fullscreen Kane calmly strokes his penalty beyond Dominik Livakovic. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

It was enough here. There was a gathering roar from the Wembley crowd, luxuriating in the prospect of a Kane penalty sequence: the pre-kick close-up, the jaw, the stare, the iconic hairline. Kane delivered, rolling the ball into the centre of the goal. There was a leap, a punch of the air, an embrace in front of a billowing George Cross flag.

At times like these it is hard to remember a time when Kane wasn’t exactly here doing exactly this, to accept that he won’t just be out there doing it for ever. Although the good news is he now gets to re-break the caps record every time he plays, thereby ensuring more ceremony, more pomp, more of that sweet, sweet, neural fatigue.

No doubt the haters will say: typical Kane. A low-key Wembley. A cheapish penalty kick. The numbers ticking over. But that’s the haters for you, as relentless in their own way as Kane himself. The goal made it 92 in 126 games, which really is mind-boggling in its focus and longevity, the sheer will to keep doing this. Imagine not thinking Kane is England’s best player since Bobby Charlton. What else are you supposed to do out there?

Wembley had been cold and crisp at kick-off, gripped with the familiar echoey, midweek chill, the booming PA, the thin air, like being present at a vast corporate presentation or the opening of a mega-sale in the world’s largest out-of-town DIY warehouse.

The military personnel wobbled the massive flag. Tongues of fire leapt around the perimeter. And as the teams lined up there was a surprise appearance from the real star of this stage, the Ballon d’Or itself, wreathed in event glamour and star-flash.

Kane drew the ballon from its stone in Arthurian fashion, then held it a little sheepishly in one hand. Prince William walked out and gave him a massive framed shirt, which seemed weird in the moment, like the chief area sales manager presenting the prize from the Christmas raffle. Has Prince William ever been asked to carry anything before?

A little earlier a vast Harry Kane tifo had appeared at one end, showing Kane in full roaring lion mode. It carried the tagline “England’s finest”, which sounds like a type of cheddar cheese you can buy at the airport gift shop. But it’s also a good compromise. He is indeed very fine.

It was a striking coronation for a player who made his debut here 11 years ago as a promising other-guy under Roy Hodgson. There is still a similar element of double-take about that Ballon d’Or. Kane has always seemed like one of those sports people destined to be reaching for something, constantly in search of a final validation. This has been his strength and his energy. Well, we’re here now. Kane has his notch on the forever tree. Ultimacy arrived on a London stage dressed in a shiny tuxedo.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane is captured with a huge England flag in the background. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

This does change something. Kane’s entire professional life is now divided into two parts. Everything up to 26 October 2026. And then the last 17 days. How does it feel now? Is the air pressure different, the noise in his head, the tension in his ears?

Here the whole team started slowly. In the opening four and a half minutes Croatia had 92 per cent possession and England made one pass. Thomas Tuchel was up early in his puffy winter coat, tight black slacks and black business shoes, like an actuary going sledging. Kane lurked in some strange deep position and played one or two overambitious passes.

Is this something new? Arrogant Kane. Big-shot Kane. Has he become our Ronaldo? Maybe he should have angrily retired straight after the game and promised to speak his truth on a YouTube chatshow.

Instead Kane helped to make the opening goal for Morgan Rogers, set up with a lovely floated diagonal pass and an expert cutback from Jude Bellingham. England faded a little and were pegged back around the hour. Lewis Hall played well. Trent Alexander-Arnold was fun to watch. They have now definitively qualified for the Nations League knockouts, which is certainly a thing. But in the end this was always going to be Harry’s day.

Sports.title: Morgan Rogers says ‘it’s a lie’ that Cole Palmer does not want to play for England
Sports.content:
Morgan Rogers has said accusations that his Chelsea teammate Cole Palmer is not committed to playing for England are “a lie”.

Palmer, who was left out of the squad for this week’s Nations League ties against Croatia and Spain, has faced questions over his desire to play international football since withdrawing from last month’s camp with a groin injury. Thomas Tuchel, who did not take the 24-year-old to last summer’s World Cup, expressed irritation at the time, saying the Chelsea attacker “misses too many opportunities” to play for his country.

Tuchel last week insisted Palmer’s latest exclusion was “not personal” but he has placed plenty of store in players showing up to camp. The German has previously said it was “hard to argue” when it was put to him that Palmer does not want to play for the national team after his fourth withdrawal from a squad. But Rogers, who scored in England’s 2-1 win over Croatia on Thursday, delivered a strong rebuttal to claims his friend and teammate is not dedicated to the national team.

“It’s a lie,” Rogers said. “He wants to be here. He wanted to get called up and he wanted to come and represent his country as he always has done. People just see it as news and say the easy thing.

“We all know he had a difficult year last year with injuries and I know personally he’s been managing them injuries ever since. He was in quite a low place with his injuries last year and didn’t feel 100% himself on the pitch, so he wants to be here and he wants to be the best version of himself. Of course he does, who wouldn’t? But he also has to look at his body. He wants to play for 10 to 15 years, he also has to manage himself.

“If he has to manage himself in the short term for the greater good then he has to do that and you have to fully support it. It has nothing to do with England or not wanting to play with England. It’s a nonsense really that people are questioning someone that wants to play for England. You see the joy and smile on his face, how much he loves the game, so I honestly don’t get it and he doesn’t get it. But it’s something he has to deal with but I can assure you he wants to be here and he wants to play for his country.”

Tuchel had no issue with Rogers’s defence of Palmer. “It’s totally fine, it’s his teammate and friend,” England’s manager said. “I was very happy with the emotional commitment and physical commitment of Morgan. He was our standout player today.”

Tuchel is not short of options at No 10 and has selected Eberechi Eze, Rogers and Josh King as cover for Jude Bellingham. Rogers played on the right against Croatia and opened the scoring as England secured the win that secured England’s place in the Nations League quarter-finals next March.

England were pegged back by Petar Sucic’s equaliser but they restored their lead thanks to Harry Kane converting a penalty on the night when the captain became his country’s most capped player. Tuchel’s side will win Group A3 if they beat Spain in Madrid on Sunday. But the occasion was slightly overshadowed by Ben White being booed when he came on in the second half. Some fans are yet to forgive White for his self-imposed exile after his early departure from the camp at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

“I didn’t hear the boos,” Tuchel said. “I thought we were past it. I hope it doesn’t happen again. He is a player for us. Since I came in he is desperate to be in the group. He hasn’t put a foot wrong since I am in charge. He is part of our group and I will protect our group. He deserved to be with us and I hope to open a new chapter for him.”

Sports.title: Arsenal dig deep to earn WCL draw in face of Barcelona dominance
Sports.content:
Arsenal continue to be a sharp thorn in the side of the European champions, Barcelona, and they dug deep to hold on to a draw at the Camp Nou on Thursday night. Frida Maanum put the Gunners ahead despite a hugely dominant performance from Barcelona, but Caroline Graham Hansen’s equaliser ensured the spoils would be shared.

Barcelona have been formidable when playing at the club’s main stadium, winning nine and drawing twice, against Chelsea in the semi-finals in 2023 and now Arsenal.

“Grit, resilience, discipline, clarity, communication, leadership, bravery – that’s a lot of words,” said Renée Slegers, whose side now lie fourth in the standings. “There’s a lot of really good things in this performance that we definitely want to build on.”

The last time these two teams met, Arsenal lifted the Champions League trophy at Barcelona’s expense after the most perfect defensive performance and a Stina Blackstenius goal in Lisbon in 2025. It was a far less perfect defensive performance this time but Arsenal showed the guts they have been missing at times this season, against the team that retook their crown last season, and showed they can play ugly when needed.

There was one change to the team that earned a 2-1 win against Liverpool on Sunday, but it was a significant one. Olivia Smith was replaced by Maanum and the Norwegian slotted into the No 10 role with Alessia Russo, who has scored 12 goals in nine games for club and country, moving into the centre-forward position.

It was the England forward’s play on the left that set up the shock first-half goal that temporarily silenced the crowd. She beat two and worked the ball to Maanum. Barcelona got the ball away but Russo was there again and delivered a perfect cross across the face of goal for Caitlin Foord. The Australian forced a close-range save from Cata Coll only for Maanum to power in the loose ball.

The pocket of travelling fans behind plexiglass in the upper tier were jubilant. About 1,000 had travelled despite the late switch of the match to Thursday due to a 24-hour general strike in Spain on Wednesday.

Quick Guide Benfica bounce back to see off Austria Vienna Show Benfica rebounded from their humbling defeat by Arsenal last time out to claim a second Women’s Champions League victory of the season by seeing off struggling Austria Vienna 3-1. Beaten 3-0 at Meadow Park a fortnight ago following Alessia Russo’s hat-trick, Benfica had the ideal opportunity to get back to winning ways against a Vienna side who had picked up one point in three games. They went ahead at Lisbon’s Estadio da Luz through Andreia Norton in the fifth minute before Carina Wenninger levelled after half-time when Valentina Potzl was upended in the area by Lena Pauels. But Vienna goalkeeper Jasmin Pal’s 73rd-minute red card proved a turning point as Caroline Møller headed home before she teed up Nycole Raysla to score in time added on. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

The goal came decidedly against the run of play but Barcelona struggled to capitalise on their first-half dominance. Ewa Pajor and Graham Hansen were particularly threatening as Barcelona targeted Arsenal’s left, made up of the less experienced Taylor Hinds and Lisa Baum.

The scoreline at the break was a little unfathomable based on the run of play and the domestic fortunes of both sides. While Arsenal languish in sixth in the WSL, 12 points behind the league leaders, Manchester City, Barcelona have won nine of their 10 games in Liga F, having scored 41 goals and built a five-point lead over their nearest rivals, Real Madrid.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal’s Alessia Russo shows her dismay after a missed chance. Photograph: Álex Caparrós/Uefa/Getty Images

Arsenal’s gameplan felt familiar. It was as if they had studied the blueprint religiously followed by teams that have sat back in a low block and frustrated them week-in, week-out in the WSL this season.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Aitana Bonmatí, the three-time Ballon d’Or winner, was surprisingly relegated to the bench but her arrival shortly before the hour elevated Barcelona’s threat, causing Arsenal’s defending to look even more calamitous at times, and lifted the mood in a frustrated stadium.

Three minutes after her arrival they were level. Esmee Brugts found an unmarked Graham Hansen on the right and she cut inside and swept in past Misa Rodríguez.

It was no surprise that Baum and Hinds, who had been run ragged, were removed soon after, with former Barcelona player Ona Batlle and Smith, Arsenal’s record signing, replacing them.

Arsenal were better after the goal and the changes, occasionally breaking free of their prison of a final third. At the end they were clinging on, but cling on they did.

“If we were to do it again, we’d try to stay on the ball for longer and play our game even more,” said Slegers. “Definitely there were moments in the first half and in the second half where we were really, really dangerous and created big chances, open chances. I’m just really pleased with the way we played the game tonight because it’s a very different game to what we usually play and that we can do it this way is a big boost for us as a team and that’s what we’re going to take with us going forward.”

Sports.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
Sports.content:
It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player. You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball.

These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Association launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wanderers’ then home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country and the FA secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, said he hoped it would finally break the barrier between those two worlds.

Reader, it did not. But it did set a precedent that is being enthusiastically revived. It’s even possible that, after several decades of hurt, the world’s favourite sport may finally be getting its artistic due. There have been three iterations of the Football Art Prize in the past 20 years, and the latest arrives at the National Football Museum this month (from the Sheffield Millennium Gallery) with a breadth of entries that demonstrate how resonant the subject can be.

View image in fullscreen Felix Higham’s Newcastle 2 Barcelona 7, one of many exhibits that focus on football culture rather than the game itself. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

Meticulous still lives – of battered balls, or boots mid-clean – ache with memory. There’s haunting photo-documentary: Bangladeshi youths playing a pickup game in the middle of a rubbish dump, pitches affected by climate change. “You see the whole gamut of footballing experience on display,” says the museum’s exhibitions director, Pip Diment. Her assumptions – she initially imagined herself hanging portraits of famous moments and iconic players – were overturned. “Pretty much every one of the artists is expressing how football matters to them, but they’re responding and reacting in such different ways.”

There are a few famous faces nevertheless. One artist worked in charcoals to create a hyper-realist bust of N’Golo Kanté. Roy Keane appears twice, once proffering a plate of prawn sandwiches to his viewer, another time in a diptych with Micah Richards. The latter is the work of Conor Rogers, whose satirical series of paintings on abandoned betting slips took second prize. They include a poignant image of Sheffield United’s manager, Chris Wilder, head in hands, next to a repurposed bookmaker’s logo asking: “Lad r u ok?”

Diment says football and art are still perceived as almost entirely separate spheres, so it’s interesting that this year’s winning work – a video by Alina Akbar – explores the connection between “high” and “popular” culture. In Footwork, the multimedia artist segues between keepy-uppy skills and the choreographed movements of Kathak, an Indian classical dance style. The combined rhythms and sounds create a mesmerising meditation on identity, related to the northern South Asian community in which she grew up.

View image in fullscreen Kyle King-Jagger ‘s Roy’s Rolls riffs on Roy Keane’s famous ‘prawn sandwich brigade’ comment. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

Football, she says, is a post-migration culture whose value is sometimes overlooked by the very people who adopted it. “Whenever I went to my great-grandparents’ house, football was on TV all the time and I’d be on their street, trying out tricks,” says Akbar. “My grandad and his brothers were really excited when I started playing, because they’d gone through the more racist era of the 70s, and they never went to games.”

For all its social themes, Akbar’s work still expresses the balletic movement and poise that Picasso once pursued in the flowing form of his ceramic sculpture Footballeur. It’s interesting how so much of the art in the show reflects football culture rather than the game itself – watching from the sofa, in the pub, on the touchline of a recreational game. Perhaps it’s hard for artists to compete with the volume of visual content that the games already provide. And we have moved a long way from a classically inspired fascination with athletes’ physiques (for comparison, check out the leaping goalkeeper in Cecil Beaton’s mid-20th-century painting Footballers, with his unashamedly pert buttocks).

Tim Marlow, the director of the Design Museum and chair of the judging panel, points out that “artists today have unashamedly adopted the position of the spectator or the fan” and that it’s rare to find works that try to get inside the experience of the footballer themselves. One of his favourite exceptions is the 2006 film, Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait, which he calls “a great piece of conceptual art”. “It’s a really intimate study of the game, which in the current era, when you’ve got referees with head cams, might feel old hat, but nothing like it had been done before.”

View image in fullscreen Keith Bird’s Full-time at Maine Road depicts Manchester City’s former home. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

And then there’s Tottenham’s stadium gallery, OOF, where exhibitions of football-related work have ranged from Roger Mayne’s 1950s street photography to AC Larsen’s polemic on the FA’s trans ban. This month brought the opening of Trackie McLeod’s celebration of Wag culture. Historic football art, meanwhile, is rocketing in value. Four years ago Lowry’s Going To The Match went for £7.8m at auction, a record price for the Salford artist’s work, and in 2022 one of Nicholas de Staël’s Parc des Princes 1952 abstract series – based on a friendly he watched between France and Sweden – became the most expensive football artwork when it sold for £16.7m.

Money has always been a key element in the art world, and there are notable collectors within the footballing world today, from billionaire club owners to cultured former players. Fabio Capello has a well documented passion for Kandinsky; David Beckham’s collection is said to include Andy Warhol, Banksy and Yayoi Kusama; Michael Ballack is spotted at major art fairs around the world. The whimsically named J St John, who organised Football and Fine Arts, told the Liverpool Daily Post 70 years ago that art needed a new form of patronage, to help people appreciate the painted canvas in the same they understood the artistry of Joe Mercer, Ferenc Puskas and Stanley Matthews. Could his dream finally be coming to pass?

Sports.title: Nations League: Italy roar back to beat France despite Donnarumma’s early howler
Sports.content:
Pio Esposito struck twice to inflict a first defeat on Zinedine Zidane as France head coach as Italy stormed back to win 3-1 at San Siro and go top of their Nations League group.

Michael Olise profited on a Gianluigi Donnarumma error to put the visitors in front after 10 minutes, but Italy hit back through Esposito and Davide Frattesi either side of half-time.

Inter striker Esposito’s second came from the penalty spot after his brother Sebastiano had earlier fired a spot-kick wide, while France were twice denied by the woodwork in an entertaining encounter.

The result sent Italy top of Group A1 on 10 points, level with France but above them on head-to-head record, while Belgium are third on nine points after inflicting a fifth straight defeat on rock-bottom Turkey.

France were without Kylian Mbappé and Ousmane Dembélé through injury, but it did not show as they made an electric start under pouring rain in Milan. Désiré Doué hit the side netting and first-time captain Adrien Rabiot tested Donnarumma before Lucas Da Cunha’s rasping half-volley flew narrowly wide.

However, the opener was gifted to France when Donnarumma passed the ball straight to Olise, who skipped past a defender before firing home his fifth goal in five Nations League games – a record only bettered by England captain Harry Kane’s seven.

The hosts struck back in the 26th minute with their first chance of the game when Nicolò Cambiaghi drove to the byline and cut back a cross, which Esposito converted with a deft touch. The goal brought San Siro to life as the older Esposito sibling, Sebastiano, threatened a quickfire comeback two minutes later when he forced a sharp save from Mike Maignan.

Bradley Barcola came closest to a third goal before the break with a curling shot from the edge of the box that struck the foot of the far post.

The end-to-end nature of the game continued in the second half as Rayan Cherki’s rasping strike was tipped on to a post by Donnarumma before Italy charged up the other end and forced Maignan into a point-blank save from Cambiaghi. Italy had a glorious chance to go in front when Cambiaghi was tripped by Malo Gusto to earn a penalty, but Sebastiano Esposito failed to join his brother on the scoresheet as he hammered his spot-kick wide on the hour mark.

The Azzurri did not dwell on the disappointment for long, taking the lead just three minutes later when Frattesi drilled in a shot from a Federico Dimarco cross moments after the Inter wing-back was brought off the bench. Fellow substitute Antonio Vergara earned the home side another penalty when he was tripped by Dayot Upamecano, and this time Pio Esposito stepped up to drill a shot into the bottom corner.

The result continued a strong start to Roberto Mancini’s second spell as Italy coach as his side stretched their unbeaten run to four matches and notched their first home win over France since 1962.

Belgium are third after Kevin De Bruyne scored in their 2-1 triumph in Turkey.

During a goal-frenzied first half at Gursel Aksel Stadium, Arda Güler put Turkey ahead with a stunning free-kick from 25 yards out before De Bruyne levelled seven minutes after a cutback from Jérémy Doku. Charles De Ketelaere fired in after Diego Moreira’s shot was saved to earn Belgium all three points.

Belgium host Italy and Turkey travel to France in the final round of group games on Sunday.

View image in fullscreen Charles De Ketelaere jumps for joy after scoring Belgium’s winning goal. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters

Álex Baena scored from the spot and Marc Pubill added another seconds from time as Spain beat 10-man Czechia 2-0 in Group A3. The win in Prague leaves Spain unbeaten for 44 competitive games, including five wins in as many Nations League games this season.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Spain, who already secured a quarter-final berth before travelling to Prague, will face England in Madrid on Sunday in their final Group A3 game.

Baena scored on 39 minutes after a VAR check revealed Czechia midfielder Lukas Ambros had handled the ball inside the box. The Atlético Madrid winger blasted his spot-kick past Matej Kovar who touched the ball but failed to clear it.

Home captain Ladislav Krejci was sent off in the 69th minute after bringing down second-half substitute Roberto Fernández on a counterattack. Pubill, another substitute, beat Kovar with a low shot deep into stoppage time after the Czechia back four left him alone facing the Eindhoven goalkeeper.

Luis de la Fuente missed Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo, Rodri and Eric García with injuries while Mikel Oyarzabal was sidelined with flu.

Fabián Ruiz hit a post with a curling right-footer three minutes from half-time, while Dean Huijsen’s header found Kovar’s arms.

View image in fullscreen Marc Pubill makes Spain’s victory safe in the dying moments against Czechia. Photograph: Michal Čížek/AFP/Getty Images

Yéremy Pino, replacing Yamal on the right flank, saw his goal overturned by VAR for offside just two minutes into the second half.

Czechia showed higher spirits after the break, but David Zima put an effort over on 50 minutes and Adam Hlozek’s glancing header landed on the top of the crossbar.

The hosts lost momentum after the red card, but Baena had two efforts cleared by Kovar who also denied Fernández from close range.

The hosts, led by De la Fuente’s long-time collaborator Santi Denia, have lost all their Nations League games this season. They are next travelling to Croatia for a game they need to win to stay in the top tier of the competititon for the next edition.

Sports.title: Pierre Sage’s failure to fix defensive flaws leaves Crystal Palace seeking new solution
Sports.content:
The moment that summed up Crystal Palace’s season under Pierre Sage came five minutes before half-time at Selhurst Park on Sunday. After Palace had gone close to taking the lead on numerous occasions against Liverpool, the Frenchman must have feared the worst when Alexis Mac Allister headed in from a soft free-kick conceded by Jefferson Lerma. The TV cameras immediately panned to Steve Parish in the stands. After the Palace chair removed his hands from in front of his eyes, his expression said everything you needed to know. The only surprise was that Sage had to wait until Thursday before his inevitable fate was confirmed.

Not since the start of the 2017-18 season, after Frank de Boer was appointed as Palace’s first permanent foreign manager and sacked after five matches, have the club found themselves bottom. In their record 14th consecutive season in the top flight, and with preliminary work having started on building a new £200m main stand despite major doubts over funding, Palace cannot afford to be relegated.

Sage has been walking a tightrope since the 5-0 thrashing at Brighton last month when it was made clear to the 47-year-old that he must tighten a defence that had conceded the most goals in the Premier League. Some players are thought to have questioned his training methods, although Dean Henderson, the captain, was among those believed to have pledged their support for Sage after defeats by Newcastle and Tottenham.

There was some evidence Palace’s players were adapting to his desire to play more on the front foot rather than relying on the counterattacking approach that brought his predecessor, Oliver Glasner, so much success. But they have been far too open at the back and Liverpool’s second goal from Florian Wirtz was almost a copy of Hoffenheim’s in Thursday’s 1-1 Europa League draw, when Palace were extremely fortunate to snatch a point in a game Parish did not attend because he was in New York.

Palace have conceded eight goals from set plays in the Premier League, including four in their current run of four straight defeats. Fixing a problem that dates back to Glasner’s spell has to be the priority for Thomas Frank, who looks poised to take over. The Dane met with Palace in the summer but decided he wasn’t ready to return after a difficult spell at Spurs. He is now believed to be very keen for a new challenge and offers proven Premier League experience - a prerequisite for Parish after Sage. Sean Dyche also had his supporters among the Palace hierarchy. The former sporting director Iain Moody, an influential consultant for Palace who was heavily involved in Sage’s appointment after Sage’s success at Lens last season, worked with the former Nottingham Forest manager at Watford and was thought to favour him.

Frank has played with a back three – a consideration that was a major factor in Palace opting for Sage in an attempt to provide continuity from Glasner – more often than Dyche. Palace could benefit, though, from a change of formation, in the short term at least, given the lack of experienced options owing to the long-term absences of Chadi Riad and Takehiro Tomiyasu.

Palace were rescued from the relegation zone by Sam Allardyce in the 2016-17 season and Parish went back to basics again with Roy Hodgson after De Boer’s disastrous spell, and the team finished 11th despite losing their first seven games. That was without the added complication of European football, however.

View image in fullscreen Pierre Sage’s suggestion that Crystal Palace had to invest in the winter transfer window is not believed to have gone down well with Steve Parish (front). Photograph: Daniel Weir/Sports Press Photo/Shutterstock

Palace signed 11 players in the summer and Sage’s suggestion after the Liverpool game that adjustments may be needed in “some positions during the winter transfer window to give more solutions” is not believed to have gone down well with Parish. Last month, the 61-year-old hired the Raine Group to field interest in investment or a possible sale of the club he helped to rescue from administration in 2010. His American billionaire co-owners Woody Johnson, David Blitzer and Josh Harris are understood to have reservations about funding the new stand.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Parish is said to view the squad as too good to be in this position, although Palace failed to adequately replace the key defenders Maxence Lacroix and Marc Guéhi this year, bringing in Tomiyasu on a free and Axel Disasi and the 18-year-old Honest Ahanor on loan. It is telling that Coventry and Hull – Palace’s next two opponents after the international break – have a higher net spend over the past five years despite being in the Championship until this season. Palace broke their transfer record twice last January and providing mid-season funds will be essential.

Much of the blame for the summer’s haphazard recruitment has been pinned on Matt Hobbs, the sporting director brought in from Wolves to replace the influential Dougie Freedman, who moved to Saudi Arabia in spring 2025. Freedman is said still to be a sounding board over transfers and there have been questions over the influence of the agents Unique Sports Group given the large number of players it has, or has had, on Palace’s books, but it is Parish who calls the shots despite owning less than 10% of the shares. His next move will be crucial to their hopes of avoiding relegation.

Sports.title: Robertson pays tribute to Dalglish as he matches Scotland cap record
Sports.content:
Andy Robertson insists his matching of Kenny Dalglish’s Scotland cap record by no means brings reputational parity. Four decades after Dalglish, widely regarded as the country’s finest player, ended his international run at 102 games Robertson will hit the same figure with the visit of North Macedonia to Hampden Park on Friday.

The Tottenham full-back is understandably delighted by his own tally – and should surpass Dalglish in Switzerland on Monday – but paid glowing tribute to the man he got to know well during nine years at Liverpool.

“For how long the record stood, for starters, for what he achieved in his career, for the person he is,” Robertson said.

“Tomorrow is another reason for our country to honour one of the greatest players that has played a game. He’s definitely the greatest from Scotland. I think it’s another reason for everyone to speak about him and realise his achievements in his footballing career. And also the person that he has been throughout his whole life.

“Obviously, in terms of number, I will stand side by side with him but I don’t want people to forget how important this man has been to our country.”

The Liverpool connection between Robertson and Dalglish adds an endearing, personal element. “He reminds me all the time that getting into the 100 caps back then was a lot harder than it is now,” said Robertson with a smile. “I never set myself personal goals. For me it’s always about the team and how I best deal with the team and things like that.

“When I overtook Darren Fletcher, when I was in the 80s, it felt like it took ages for me to get to Jim Leighton [at 91]. Then I thought: ‘I’ve only got one more to go.’

That’s when I started thinking about it a little bit more, starting to believe that it might happen a little bit more, starting to wind-up Kenny a bit more that it was going to happen. Sat here today, if it happens, it’s something I couldn’t be more proud of.’’

Sébastien Pocognoli, the Scotland manager, has said the country is stepping up efforts to convince eligible players born in England to commit their international futures to Scotland. Archie Gray and Hayden Hackney are among those who qualify to play for Scotland but have, thus far, resisted overtures. In conjunction with others at the Scottish Football Association, Pocognoli would like that to change. Gray’s position as a club-mate of Robertson’s may be significant in this context.

“We are on it,” Pocognoli said. “We are always proactive in all of these situations. What is very exciting about those two names [Gray and Hackney] is that they are young players.

“That’s interesting. We have to look and manage the situation. But it won’t be a definitive choice from them because we weren’t proactive. That has to be clear. We are proactive.”

Sports.title: EDDIE JONES - Inside my week in London visiting old haunts, eating fish and chips, inviting Eddie Howe and Dylan Hartley into camp, taking the mickey out of James Haskell... and plotting how my Japan team can conquer England
Sports.content:
EDDIE JONES - Inside my week in London visiting old haunts, eating fish and chips, inviting Eddie Howe and Dylan Hartley into camp, taking the mickey out of James Haskell... and plotting how my Japan team can conquer England

Eddie Jones Daily Mail Sport Columnist

I was impressed by the way England beat Australia. The Wallabies tried to play them at a power game, but Steve Borthwick can call on a big pack and the Wallabies got brutalised.

With my Japan team this week, we need to learn from that and try to play the game quickly. We need to think outside the box. I like innovative tactics, but not things that are against the spirit of rugby.

I don’t look back on Italy’s visit to Twickenham in 2017 with fond memories. That year, the Azzurri caused chaos by not competing at the ruck. That meant there was no offside line, allowing Italian players to stand in the back line of the English team I was coaching.

Rugby’s a competitive game. And by not competing, Italy destroyed the game. That day, James Haskell said to the referee: ‘I just wanted to know what the exact rule is?’ I reminded him about that when I saw him this week. I think he regrets saying that!

You won’t be seeing any funny business like that from my Japan team, not least because the laws on the ruck and offside have changed a lot since then.

I had seven great years as England coach and have brilliant memories from my time at the RFU. That’s why I’ve loved being back in London this week. One of the best things about being here is the fish and chips. On Sunday night, after I watched England beat Australia, I went to a chippy in Teddington, just next to the King’s Head pub, with Nigel Ashley-Jones who is the Wallabies' strength and conditioning coach.

I've had a busy week ahead of leading my Japan side into battle with England on Saturday at Twickenham

I don't look back fondly on Italy's tactics at Twickenham in the 2017 Six Nations - James Haskell (left) had to ask the referee what the rules were!

Nigel was at Saracens with me, so we go way back. We didn’t go to the pub. Nigel doesn’t drink. He’s crazy enough without alcohol, so we just stuck to the fish and chips.

When I’m in Japan, my diet is mainly sushi, sashimi and rice-based dishes, so I enjoy a bit of traditional English stodge when I’m back – bangers and mash and a good cup of tea. A Sunday night chippy was the perfect start to a big week ahead of going head-to-head with my old team England this weekend.

The English are generally pretty kind and I was at Twickenham for the Australia game, so I’m expecting a good reception. I got sacked by the RFU in 2022. Like most things in life, it ended badly. But I don’t harbour any resentment towards Bill Sweeney, the chief executive, or anyone else there.

It’s been like a trip down memory lane this week. We’ve been based at the Lensbury Hotel in Teddington with Japan – a venue where we’d often stay with England when I was in charge.

During Covid, I lived at the hotel for a bit while my wife was in Japan, so I know the place like the back of my hand. That was a funny old time. I’d eat all of my meals in the hotel. The waiters used to know my order, but the staff has changed now. One night during the pandemic I was pretty much the only guest and I got a bang on the door in the middle of the night. The security officer was checking if I was OK as a load of kids had broken in and were running amok around the place.

It’s been a busy week, getting our preparations for England right and catching up with some familiar faces. I saw two of my old players, Haskell and Jonny May, and we retold old tour stories. I haven’t laughed so hard in ages.

Dylan Hartley, the man I appointed England captain, also came into our camp. With Japan, we have a young leadership group, so Dylan passed on a few tips.

Dylan was a rough, tough guy who hailed from Rotorua in New Zealand. Many people were surprised when I made him captain given his poor disciplinary record. But Dylan had captaincy down to a fine art. He would get the team organised and he was very good at delegating responsibility and staying in touch with his fellow leaders. I always try to see him when I’m in England anyway, so it was great he could pass on his tips to my Japanese players.

I met up with my old mate Haskell this week - I haven't laughed so much in ages!

I also had my old captain Dylan Hartley come into camp to give my Japan players some tips

I've had two outstanding coaches - Borthwick is one of them

Over the years, I’ve had two coaches that have really stood out. One is Steve. The other is Ewen McKenzie, my assistant with Australia. Both are highly intelligent and organised.

I remember the first time I met Steve. I’d joined Saracens in 2006 as an adviser and I was doing some recruitment for them for the following season. I asked those in the know who was the best captain in England. The overwhelming response was: ‘Steve Borthwick at Bath.’

So, I met Steve at a hotel somewhere between London and Bath. It was in the days when you could get away with tapping people up!

Steve arrived with a book as thick as my arm and a long list of questions. About an hour in, I had to stop the meeting. ‘Steve, mate,’ I said. ‘Hang on a minute. I’m supposed to be interviewing you, not the other way round!’ That’s Steve: meticulous, driven and very switched on.

He came under some heat last week, but the way his team responded told me a lot about how England’s players see Steve.

When the England and Australia teams ran out, I heard Nick Mullins on ITV saying how important this month is for English rugby. That’s always been the case. When you’re England coach, every campaign is make or break. It’s just the way it goes.

Win and you’re the best thing since sliced bread. That’s what England are this week. Lose, and you don’t have a clue what you’re doing. The margins between the two are very small.

As opposing coaches, I won’t catch up with Steve this week. But I hope to see him during the finals week of the Nations Championship when all 12 teams will be back in London.

Steve Borthwick came under some heat last week, but the way his team responded against Australia told me a lot about how England’s players see Steve

Steve is meticulous, driven, very switched on and one of the best two coaches I've worked with

A visit from Eddie Howe

We’ve had a fair few visitors to Japan training this week. Dylan was one. We’ve had the scrum coach from Toulouse and the head coach of the Sweden rugby team, Alex Laybourne, who is English.

Oh, and there was Eddie Howe too. The former Newcastle United manager came in to experience a rugby environment, and had some really good ideas on leadership. I was hoping he would give some insight into whether he was going to get the Manchester United job, but I didn’t get much out of him! Eddie is a very sincere man, a deep thinker. He reminds me a lot of Sir Gareth Southgate in the way he leads.

Football managers have to get used to being sacked. It’s an occupational hazard. I’ve experienced that in rugby, too. In the past, the jobs I’ve taken next have not been good decisions. I rushed into them, just because I wanted to get back coaching.

I don’t know what Eddie’s plans are, but I got the feeling that because of the good job he did at Newcastle, he can sit back and wait for the right next move.

My experience, albeit in a different sport, tells me that’s the right call. Whoever goes into Manchester United next, it might be fantastic. But it might also be a continuation of what’s been happening there.

There are obviously bigger problems at Old Trafford than just who is the manager. That’s been shown by the club underperforming for a long time now.

Eddie Howe came into our Japan camp this week too. I was hoping he would give some insight into the Manchester United job, but I didn’t get much information out of him!

It's great to see Will back in England fold

I’m delighted to see Will Joseph back in the England team this weekend.

You have to take a punt on young guys. That’s what I did with Joseph when I took him to Australia as an apprentice in 2022, when he ended up winning his lone cap in the second Test victory in Brisbane.

Henry Arundell was another apprentice on that trip. I’m a bit disappointed we’re not seeing more of him but sometimes, talent takes time to develop.

Joseph is a beautiful player with great timing on the ball and good strength. Whether he’s at wing or centre, he’s got the pace to really trouble opposition defences. He runs very good lines. I’m pleased to see him doing well this season and he’s been rewarded for his PREM form with Gloucester. He’s a great kid.

I coached his older brother Jonathan with England, too, and they’re completely different.

‘JJ’ was such an effortless player. He glided over the pitch, so gifted and laidback. Will is more determined, a bit more urgent about things. He’s someone who I want to see do well. Just not this weekend!

Will Joseph (centre) is a beautiful player with great timing on the ball and good strength. Whether he’s at wing or centre, he’s got the pace to really trouble opposition defences

I coached his older brother Jonathan too - they're very different players!

Marcus is a maverick - and mavericks need time to shine

I've got a lot of affection for Marcus Smith. I first saw him at Brighton College and brought him into the England setup at 18. I’m probably a bit disappointed he hasn’t kicked on more, having been the starting No10 in my last campaign with England.

Fin Smith seems to now be the England fly-half. Fin is not yet an established international 10. There has been a lot of chopping and changing in that position with the two Smiths and George Ford.

That’s been the reason for the complaint about the England team not having an established identity. There is merit in that.

But the team’s attacking identity will evolve the more Fin plays. England will likely play more and more like Northampton, the more Fin is guiding the ship.

With Marcus, he just needed a longer run of Tests. If you look at the history of Test rugby, the most talented No 10s take time to develop. It’s the more pragmatic players who adapt quicker.

The same is true in Test cricket. The big stroke-makers don’t always succeed straight away, whereas the more pragmatic batsmen do.

With Marcus Smith, he just needed a longer run of Tests. If you look at the history of Test rugby, the most talented No 10s take time to develop

Marcus is similar to Richie Mo’unga, the All Blacks playmaker. Both have supreme ability. But Mo’unga has more than 50 caps now and he’s still in and out of the team

Marcus is very similar to Richie Mo’unga, the All Blacks playmaker. Both have supreme ability, but Mo’unga has more than 50 New Zealand caps now and he’s still in and out of the team.

In 2021, I compared Marcus to the British tennis star Emma Raducanu, whose performances I felt had been undermined by commercial distractions. Those are the challenges all young sportsmen and women in England face. I spoke to Marcus about them in private.

At the moment, I’m not sure how Marcus gets into England’s starting XV. What I do know is he has become an outstanding utility player.

He can play 9, 10 or 15. He kicks goals. He plays with great energy. He’s a perfect guy for the No23 shirt on the bench and is still really important to England.

Sports.title: Pat Cummins' remarkable 68-minute press conference took a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Usman Khawaja's integrity - Australia are in a civil war with no obvious resolution, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH
Sports.content:
Pat Cummins' remarkable 68-minute press conference took a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Usman Khawaja's integrity - Australia are in a civil war with no obvious resolution, writes LAWRENCE BOOTH

Pat Cummins is either the greatest actor in world sport – or the claim that the whole Australian team knew about the sandpaper plot in South Africa eight years ago is a figment of Usman Khawaja’s imagination.

After Cummins’s remarkable press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, in which he called Khawaja’s various assertions ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship, it was hard to discern any common ground, much less spot a middle way.

According to the blue corner, everyone was in on the scam, sandpaper was used not just at Cape Town but in the previous Test at Port Elizabeth, and there was a team meeting to discuss the question of collective responsibility.

According to the red, those who knew about the plan did not include the bowlers, nothing untoward happened at Port Elizabeth, and there was no meeting.

The only thing that can be said for certain after another tumultuous 24 hours for Australian cricket was that the two corners are now polar opposites, each eyeing the other with suspicion and incredulity. Barring an improbable climbdown, the twain can never meet.

Cummins, it must be said, eased into his work after an emotional start behind a lectern at the Cricket Central venue in Sydney’s Olympic Park. He began by stating his basic position, then invited questions, which for the next hour and a bit he handled with aplomb and a degree of statesmanship.

Pat Cummins held a remarkable press conference in Sydney to address the sandpaper claims

Speaking for more than an hour, Cummins dismissed Khawaja’s various assertions as ‘complete and utter nonsense’ and questioned the validity of their friendship

This will not please those who still find it impossible to believe that Cummins and his fellow seamers on that trip, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc, knew nothing of the scheme that led to bans for three batsmen – Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.

After all, as any bowler will tell you, the idea that the condition of their most prized possession might be altered without their noticing is as absurd as trying to persuade a batsman to walk out without his favourite willow.

And yet. Cummins stuck to his guns, in contrast to Khawaja’s appearance on the ABC on Wednesday evening, when he repeatedly declined to name Cummins as one of the guilty party. And while Khawaja reacted to his TV grilling by cancelling media engagements, Cummins made it clear he would be answering every question that came his way.

Whichever side you believe, and whatever the doubts that remain, his press conference grabbed the momentum from Team Khawaja.

It also made the previous day’s appearance by Mitchell Marsh, Australia’s white-ball captain for the next three weeks against England, all the more bizarre. By refusing to engage with any of the questions raised by Khawaja’s autobiography, Marsh – himself a veteran of South Africa 2018 – did little to dispel the suspicion that Khawaja had a point.

And that in turn encouraged the view that Cummins, who called his own press conference without the knowledge of Cricket Australia, might be about to come clean.

Instead, he doubled down on the denial he and his bowling colleagues had issued in 2021, but now went further, taking a clear-eyed and devastating aim at Khawaja’s integrity.

‘Usman is a friend, but friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations,’ said Cummins. ‘He’s dealt with the way he’s presented his story in a very casual manner and it affects a lot of people. That’s what I’m grappling with at the moment, because I don’t think that’s OK. It’s not what friends do.’

Cummins plainly intended this to be his final word on the matter, but the problem facing Australian cricket is that the sore may never properly heal.

David Warner then hit back at Cummins and accused him of 'throwing Khawaja under the bus'

Only a couple of hours after Cummins finished, Warner – at Perth’s Optus Stadium as a TV pundit for the first ODI between Australia and England – was being asked for his view, and he didn’t hold back, repeating his belief that Khawaja’s version of events was ‘the truth’.

He added: ‘I really, really support him. I actually feel for him at the moment. I feel that the captain today threw Uzzy under the bus and I’m very, very disappointed about that.’

Disappointment. It’s mutual, and it’s everywhere. Cummins provided a brief distraction, but it doesn’t change the fact that this is a civil war with no obvious resolution.

Sports.title: Fury as Formula One bans Daily Mail's award-winning Motor Racing Correspondent over column calling Ferrari driver a 'sneaky little b*****d'
Sports.content:
Jonathan McEvoy, the Daily Mail's long-serving and distinguished Motor Racing Correspondent, has been banned from attending the remaining races of the 2026 Formula One season by the sport's governing body.

In a barely believable attack on press freedom, the FIA today wrote to the Daily Mail to confirm McEvoy's accreditation had been revoked in response to a column he had written about Ferrari driver Charles Leclerc.

McEvoy's comments were made after Leclerc's team-mate, Britain's seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, questioned Leclerc's mentality after the pair were embroiled in a contentious, opening lap clash at last month's Mexico Grand Prix.

McEvoy, who is regarded as the authoritative voice in the paddock, labelled the Monegasque driver a 'sneaky little b*****d' for his behaviour, before revealing details of a tense post-race debrief with Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur.

Thursday's letter, written by FIA general manager Alberto Villarreal, stated: 'The FIA considers that your article falls short of the standards of professionalism expected of media representatives accredited to cover the FIA Formula One World Championship.

'Accordingly, the FIA has decided to exercise its discretion under the 2026 FIA Formula One World Championship Accreditation Guidelines to withdraw your media accreditation for the remainder of the 2026 season, with immediate effect.'

Jonathan McEvoy's column was written after Lewis Hamilton questioned Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc's mentality

McEvoy, pictured with Max Verstappen and Christian Horner in 2021, has dedicated the last 21 years of his working life to travel tens of thousands of miles to cover almost 400 grands prix

McEvoy is held in the highest esteem by the great and good of the sport and has dedicated the last 21 years of his working life to travel tens of thousands of miles to cover almost 400 grands prix for the Daily Mail.

In that time, he has missed only a handful of races.

In such time he has written illuminating, insightful and piercing copy loved by millions of loyal Daily Mail readers.

He has interviewed the sport's biggest names, from Bernie Ecclestone to Sir Jackie Stewart and Christian Horner to Max Verstappen.

Daily Mail head of sport Chris Dean said: 'This is an unprecedented and outrageous attack on the freedom of the Press.

'We are in dangerous territory when the FIA react in such a heavy-handed way to some mild and fair criticism of one driver.

McEvoy's column on the Leclerc and Hamilton situation - which you can read HERE

Mohammed ben Sulayem, FIA President, is pictured at the F1 Grand Prix of United States

'Jonathan McEvoy is a fearless and first-rate journalist who takes readers behind the curtain of F1's shiny exterior. The FIA should reinstate his accreditation immediately.'

F1 supremo Bernie Ecclestone said: 'It's crazy. I don't know why the FIA would ever do that.

'Apart from the fact I like Jon, he is doing a fantastic job.

'I look forward to reading what he's writing. I don't have to, it's my choice to do that. I think it's completely mad.'

Sports.title: Why Man United staff feel treatment of Michael Carrick was 'disgusting' and the comment from Omar Berrada that raised eyebrows as club legend is put out of his misery - and Mauricio Pochettino gets set to take over
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino would have been fast asleep in his hotel room in the quirky American town of Trilith when Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox sat down with Michael Carrick at Carrington Thursday morning and confirmed the worst-kept secret in football. It was time for Carrick to vacate the head coach’s office at Manchester United, and safe to say Pochettino will have his feet under the desk this time next week. Carrick arrived at 7.50am but, unlike the last two days, he was no longer wearing his United training gear. The agonising wait to be put out of his misery was over, and the club’s chief executive and director of football duly administered the last rites before Carrick left at 10.18am. The decision was communicated to staff and Under-21s boss Adam Lawrence took training with the players who have remained at Carrington during the international break. The first reports of Carrick’s sacking broke at 9.30am, but United insisted that they were premature and it wasn’t until 10.37am that the news was confirmed in a 142-word statement. Michael Carrick finally left Carrington on Thursday morning after an agonising wait to be put out of his misery Staff at Manchester United believe that the former club captain's treatment at the hands of their Ineos paymasters has been 'disgusting'

Your browser does not support iframes.

It's understood that his backroom staff - assistant Steve Holland, coaches Jonathan Woodgate, Jonny Evans and Travis Binnion, and goalkeeper coach Craig Mawson - have also gone. When Evans left on Wednesday night with his car piled high with cardboard boxes, it didn't bode well. The treatment of Carrick and Evans, in particular, has upset staff. Two highly-respected figures at United, whose association with the club goes back more than 20 years, have been left hanging while their employers stumble over a succession plan. Members of staff share Gary Neville’s view that Berrada and Wilcox meeting with Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco, and making a move for Pochettino while Carrick had to keep driving past the cameras on his way into Carrington for the last three days, was ‘disgusting’. It has also reignited anger over the 450 job cuts carried out by Ratcliffe and Ineos over the past three years while pouring millions down the drain in compensation. The £10million to buy Pochettino and his staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation, and the pay-off owing to Carrick and Co, will push the cost of hiring and firing coaches in the Ineos era close to £50m. No wonder eyebrows were raised when Berrada spoke at Sir Alex Ferguson’s 40th anniversary dinner at Old Trafford on Friday night and talked about building a culture at the club. The feeling is that changing United’s head coach won’t make a shred of difference if there isn’t significant change higher up the chain. It has once again turned the spotlight on the relationship between Ratcliffe and the Glazer family, who from February can force him to sell his 28 per cent holding to a third party for less than the £25-per-share he paid in 2024 unless he can match the offer and buy the club himself. However, United sources say they had little choice but to sack Carrick with the club in the relegation zone, having decided to give him a stay of execution at the end of last month. Since then, the club had carried out a comprehensive review and come to the conclusion that a record of one win from 10 Premier League games was unacceptable. The sources indicated that the United board shared the frustration and anger felt by fans over the situation, and believe that a change of head coach will bring about an improvement from a squad that is far better than results would suggest. While United praised Carrick for his ‘highest degree of professionalism’, there was only silence from the players on social media. Many of them are on international duty, including Bruno Fernandes whose criticism of Carrick’s tactics after the Champions League defeat to Como proved so damaging. Following the announcement of Carrick's dismissal none of his former players - including Bruno Fernandes - were quick to say their goodbyes publicly Meanwhile, his would-be successor Mauricio Pochettino is set to face the media on Friday Pochettino will inherit this squad of players once he has completed his duties as US national team coach with the upcoming CONCACAF Nations League double-header against Haiti. The former Tottenham and Chelsea boss is due to speak at 2.15pm Friday ahead of the first leg in Miami on Saturday night when he will face questions over the United job for the first time. Pochettino is expected to stay in charge for the second leg in Cincinnati in the early hours of Wednesday morning before flying to Manchester to meet the players and prepare for the crunch clash with Liverpool at Anfield a week on Sunday. The US have been staying in Trilith, near their new training headquarters in Fayetteville south-west of Atlanta, where they were also based before the World Cup. It’s a unique place designed for the film industry and built around the Trilith Studios which are the largest outside Hollywood. The ideal place for Pochettino to prepare for life at Old Trafford. He has embraced the American lifestyle since he was appointed US coach in September 2024, a few months after leaving Chelsea, and will be sorry to leave. Pochettino is said to have developed a love of bourbon whiskey, country music and Nashville, with Ella Langley’s Choosin’ Texas one of his favourite tunes. He has admitted crying over Miracle, the movie about the US hockey team made up of college kids famously beating the Soviet Union to the gold medal at the 1980 Winter Olympics. But the pull of Manchester United was always going to be too great, and very soon he will be swapping Trilith for Old Trafford.
