World.title: Back to sender: Aisha Jumwa returns to UDA
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto welcome former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa has returned to President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA), ending a three-month political fallout with the ruling party that saw her join opposition outfit Wiper Patriotic Front and declare support for the one-term movement ahead of the 2027 General Election.

President Ruto welcomed Jumwa back into UDA at State House, Mombasa, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, in a political reunion that could reshape alignments in Kilifi County and the wider Coast region as parties position themselves for next year's elections.

The reunion comes barely three months after Jumwa dramatically announced her departure from UDA, accusing the party leadership of frustrating her political ambitions and failing to support her quest for the Kilifi gubernatorial seat.

On July 30, 2026, Jumwa announced her resignation during a press conference at her Kakuyuni home in Malindi, saying her attempts to have her grievances addressed by the President had repeatedly been unsuccessful.

Among her concerns was what she described as humiliation and rejection within the ruling party, including an alleged incident in which she was chased out of State House during a meeting between Ruto and Coast leaders.

She also accused sections of the ruling coalition of undermining her gubernatorial ambitions, claiming that the political arrangements being pursued in Kilifi were designed to deny her an opportunity to contest for the county's top seat.

President William Ruto recieve former Cabinet Secretary Aisha Jumwa back to the ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) on November 12, 2026. [PCS]

Jumwa, who was among UDA's founding members and one of Ruto's most vocal mobilisers at the Coast during the 2022 elections, said her loyalty to the people of Kilifi outweighed her allegiance to any political party.

"My loyalty to the people of Kilifi will always be greater than my loyalty to any political party. The voice of the people of Kilifi is louder than the voice of UDA," she declared during her exit announcement.

Her departure marked a significant political shift, particularly given her central role in mobilising support for Ruto in the Coast region.

In August, Jumwa turned to the opposition, where she was warmly received by Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka, who visited her at her Kakuyuni residence on August 14 alongside a delegation of party leaders, including Nyali MP Mohamed Ali, Kitui Senator Enoch Wambua and Wundanyi MP Danson Mwashako.

Kalonzo subsequently proposed Jumwa for the position of Wiper Deputy Party Leader, citing her political experience and influence, while also backing her ambition to contest the Kilifi governorship on a Wiper ticket.

Jumwa embraced the new political alliance, declaring support for the one-term movement and threatening to mobilise UDA supporters in Kilifi to deregister from the ruling party and join Wiper.

"We are the ones who registered UDA members in Kilifi, and we are embarking on a grassroots campaign to deregister them from UDA and join Wiper," she said at the time.

On September 8, she attended a meeting involving Wiper leaders and Coast gubernatorial aspirants, including Mohammed Ali and Danson Mwashako, as the party intensified efforts to expand its influence in the region.

However, the political alliance has now taken another turn, with Jumwa returning to the party she had accused of frustrating her ambitions.

Announcing her return, President Ruto welcomed the former Cabinet Secretary back into UDA, signalling renewed efforts to consolidate the ruling party's support in the Coast region.

"I look forward to working with her to advance the party’s transformation agenda at the Coast and across the country. We remain committed to uniting leaders and Kenyans around our shared vision of a united, inclusive and prosperous Kenya," the President said.

Her return comes as Ruto steps up political mobilisation in the Coast region ahead of the 2027 elections, with Kilifi emerging as an important battleground for competing political formations.

Jumwa's political journey has been characterised by shifting alliances. She previously served under the Orange Democratic Movement (ODM), representing Malindi in Parliament before becoming Kilifi's first Woman Representative between 2013 and 2017.

She later became one of Ruto's key political allies and served in his Cabinet.

World.title: Buxton estate tensions escalate after county officials attacked
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

A dispute over the multibillion-shilling Buxton Point housing project in Mombasa turned violent after county officials were allegedly attacked while enforcing a government order suspending construction over outstanding contractual obligations.

The confrontation came a day after County Executive Committee Member (CECM) for Lands, Housing, and Urban Development Mohamed Hussein ordered GulfCap Real Estate to halt all construction activities pending the resolution of disputes involving the county government and hundreds of former Buxton Estate residents.

The officials were reportedly pelted with stones as they attempted to serve the developer with an enforcement notice, with allegations that individuals linked to businessman Suleiman Shahbal were involved in the confrontation.

Hussein condemned the incident, saying attempts to intimidate government officers would not derail efforts to enforce the law and protect public interests.

"Let them bring goons, machetes, and stones if they want. I am not intimidated. I will execute my duties, and nobody will threaten me. The law must be followed, regardless of who you are or how much money you have," he said.

"We are here for the people of Mombasa, and we will ensure their rights are protected. Nobody is above the law," he added.

The November 10 enforcement notice, issued by County Director of Physical Planning Qassim Ali, directed GulfCap Real Estate to stop further development activities and obtain valid construction permits.

The notice, issued under Section 72(1) of the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, cited construction under a varied development plan without county approval and an ongoing dispute involving the developer, former tenants, and the county government.

The notice was reportedly received by the project's manager, Billy Okendo.

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county government and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units and commercial spaces developed in the first and second phases.

An addendum to the agreement signed on January 15, 2020, outlines the county's entitlement, with the allocation expected to be transferred upon completion of the second phase.

In a letter dated April 30, 2025, the county demanded 10 per cent of the proposed 1,800 housing units, translating to 180 apartments. The demand was renewed in February 2026, with the county seeking details on how the allocation would be implemented.

However, in correspondence dated September 22, 2026, the Department of Lands, Urban Planning and Housing expressed concern over what it described as the developer's failure to provide substantive responses to previous demands.

The county also questioned whether GulfCap had provided performance security equivalent to 10 per cent of the total construction cost for each phase, as required under the agreement.

It further demanded proof of payment of the Project Development Fee, which is payable in instalments as the project progresses.

The county said it had also raised technical and planning concerns during a meeting with the developer on April 15, 2026, including the need to address outstanding issues and resubmit the masterplan application.

But the dispute goes beyond the county's financial and contractual entitlement, with more than 500 former residents accusing the developer of failing to honour promises made when they were displaced in 2019.

John Tsuma, Secretary-General of the Buxton Tenants Welfare Association, said former residents had waited for more than seven years to return to their homes despite assurances that they would be prioritised once construction was completed.

"We are very disappointed by what happened. We had a meeting with the CECM, and he made it clear that all construction activities should stop until the outstanding issues are resolved. We did not go there to fight anybody. We wanted the directive implemented," Tsuma said.

He accused the developer of benefiting from the project while former residents continued to struggle to secure the houses they were promised.

"The developer has benefited from A to Z. He was given land by the county government, and the houses were sold off-plan. Yet, when it comes to fulfilling the promises made to former residents, we are still being taken around in circles," he said.

Tsuma said residents were not demanding free houses but wanted the affordable tenant-purchase arrangement they were promised before leaving the estate.

"We are not asking for free houses. We want the tenant-purchase arrangement that was promised to us so that we can pay for the houses and return to our homes," he said.

He also questioned why the developer had allegedly failed to surrender the county government's 184 housing units under the joint venture arrangement.

Mohamed Mzee Rubea, chairman of the evicted Buxton residents, said the money paid to the families during their displacement was a relocation allowance and not compensation for their homes.

He said the former tenants were given Sh240,000, with assurances that they would rent alternative accommodation for 12 months and return once the houses were completed.

"What we received was relocation money, not compensation for our houses. We were told to take the money and rent houses for 12 months and that we would be the first people to return once construction was completed. But here we are, more than seven years later, still waiting," Rubea said.

He said the original agreement involved 522 former tenants who were promised priority access to houses under the redevelopment.

Rubea added that each household was also promised Sh60,000 as a deposit towards acquiring a house under the tenant-purchase scheme.

"We were promised Sh60,000 as a deposit for those who would take up the houses. The developer later said the money would only be given to those who actually acquired the units. We are still waiting, and many of us have not received anything," he said. At the heart of the dispute is a joint venture agreement between the county and the developer, which provides for the county to receive 10 per cent of all housing units. [Robert Menza, Standard]

He further claimed that the county had written to the developer in 2023, 2024, and 2025 seeking engagement over the outstanding commitments.

Mutua Mutia, another former resident, said the prolonged dispute had left families frustrated, especially after they were promised they would return within a year.

"I have lived in Buxton since I was a young boy. My firstborn child is now more than 30 years old, and the history of Buxton is one that pains us. We were evicted with the promise that we would return after one year, but today it is seven years and we are still struggling," Mutia said.

The former residents are also demanding the reconstruction of an Early Childhood Development (ECD) centre demolished to pave the way for the project, as well as the construction of a promised community social centre.

Hussein said the county had yet to receive either facility or its share of the housing project.

"The county has not received its 10 per cent share to date. There was an agreement that the demolished ECD centre would be reconstructed and handed over to the county, alongside a community social centre, but we have not received either," he said.

The first phase of Buxton Point delivered 584 housing units in 2023, while the second phase is expected to provide between 1,400 and 1,500 additional apartments. Completion had been scheduled for August 2027.

However, GulfCap Real Estate Chief Executive Officer Chris Ochieng defended the developer's position, saying 492 housing units would be handed over to buyers by December.

While urging the county to stop politicising the project, Ochieng warned that the ongoing controversy risks disrupting the project’s completion and affecting hundreds of workers who depend on it for their livelihoods.

He said the county government's 10 per cent share would be transferred upon completion of the project.

He also maintained that the developer had supported displaced residents by providing Sh240,000 for relocation and offering them preferential rates to purchase apartments.

Ochieng said the continued involvement of county officials in the dispute was unfortunate, particularly at a time when 492 homeowners are expecting to take possession of their houses in December.

He noted that the controversy was not only creating uncertainty among prospective homeowners but also threatening the livelihoods of hundreds of people employed directly and indirectly through the project.

“It is very unfortunate that Mombasa County officials are bringing politics into a national project. We have 492 homeowners who expect to take possession of their units by December. Beyond the homeowners, hundreds of people depend on this project for employment and their daily livelihoods,” said Ochieng.

He called on the county leadership to allow the project to proceed without unnecessary political interference, arguing that Mombasa has previously witnessed housing projects that stalled despite significant public interest.

World.title: Sakaja defends Sh43.7b drop in Nairobi County's pending bills before Senate
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja tells Senate that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors. [File, Standard]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has told the Senate that pending bills in the city have been reduced from Sh118.79 billion to Sh75.07 billion through verification and payment.

Sakaja revealed that internal verification established that the Sh43.73 billion reduction was not achieved solely through payments but also involved legal assessments, court-ordered adjustments and the verification of disputed claims.

The governor, who appeared before the Senate County Public Accounts Committee at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi on Monday, said addressing the inherited debt required establishment of a verification committee to scrutinise the entire outstanding amount and establish the validity of the claims.

“The reduction of Nairobi County pending bills by Sh 43.73 billion was not achieved entirely through cash payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court-ordered reductions and disputed claims,” said Sakaja.

He told the Senate Committee chaired by Homa Bay Senator Moses Kajwang that the Sh118 billion in pending bills was inherited from his predecessors and that he had constituted a committee to undertake an internal verification of the entire amount before payments were done.

Sakaja explained that the verification established that the reduction was not solely through payments but also involved adjustments arising from legal assessments, suspended government-guaranteed loans, court decisions and disputed claims.

“I would like to inform Senators that my administration has provided a detailed schedule accounting for the Sh43.73 billion pending bills reduction through adjustments and reconciliations,” he said.

The governor said that of this amount Sh1.63 billion related to legal assessments, while Sh19.14 billion represented government-guaranteed loans whose servicing had been suspended due to a lack of supporting documentation and loan schedules.

Sakaja told Senators that Sh19.2 billion related to LAPFUND interest and penalties which the County said had been reduced following a court consent that brought the claim down to approximately Sh8.2 billion.

He said that they had provided a signed indemnity form, in accordance with County Treasury rules governing misplaced payment documents, alongside a financial memo confirming that the works had been undertaken and payment made.

“The audit further raised concerns over Sh16.04 million in receivables from non-exchange transactions, which lacked sufficient supporting documentation,” said Sakaja.

The governor told senators that beyond the verification of pending bills his administration had also strengthened the county’s legal department to reduce expenditure on external legal services and protect public resources.

Sakaja noted that through the reforms, Nairobi saved approximately Sh8.48 billion in legal costs over two financial years by expanding its in-house legal capacity, handling more litigation internally and negotiating reductions in legal fees claimed by private advocates.

According to the County Assembly’s Justice and Legal Affairs Committee, of the 174 court cases concluded during the period under review, 84 were handled by the County’s in-house legal team, with 47 determined in Nairobi’s favour, representing a 56 per cent success rate.

Kajwang, commended the County for reducing its pending bills but asked the Governor to provide additional documentation supporting the payments and processes undertaken to account for the Sh43.73 billion reductions.

“The Senate County Public Accounts Committee requires further clarification on the verification exercise and the adjustments made to the outstanding debt,” said Kajwang.

World.title: Gachagua dismisses opposition divisions as 'polygamous family' rivalry
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County on November 8, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua has dismissed claims of divisions within the Opposition, describing the disagreements among its leaders as normal sibling rivalry in a polygamous family, while insisting that the coalition remains united behind plans to field a single presidential candidate in the 2027 General Election.

Gachagua said the Opposition leaders were committed to working together to challenge President William Ruto, despite their differing opinions on the timing of selecting a joint presidential flagbearer and occasional disagreements among their political camps.

Speaking during a church service in Isinya, Kajiado County, the former Deputy President likened the political differences to children from the same father competing for attention but eventually uniting whenever an external threat emerges.

“The Opposition is united to a man, and we have agreed that we will have a single presidential candidate. Everybody is committed, and we talk on a daily basis. The only challenge is normal petty problems,” he said.

He added that the disagreements should not be interpreted as a breakdown of the coalition, maintaining that such differences were healthy and expected in a broad political alliance.

“Ile shida kidogo ni ya boma, watoto wengi wa baba mmoja. Watoto huko ndani, oh, baba anakupenda kuliko mimi. Mbona ulinunua kiatu kabla mimi? Si hiyo ni kawaida kwa polygamous family?” he posed.

Gachagua said the bigger threat to Opposition unity was not necessarily disagreements among its principals but the conduct of their supporters, social media influencers and political bloggers, whom he accused of fuelling unnecessary tensions through insults and online confrontations.

He cautioned Opposition leaders against allowing overzealous supporters to dictate their political relationships, warning that unchecked political attacks could eventually weaken the coalition and undermine its common objective.

“If there is anything to separate us, it is our supporters and social media bloggers. Wanawakisha moto hakuna, watu wangu na wa Matiang'i wanatukanana na sisi tunakula breakfast pamoja,” he said.

He further claimed that some political influencers associated with his DCP party had been recruited and allegedly paid by individuals opposed to him to attack his leadership and the party.

Gachagua urged coalition principals to exercise restraint and avoid reacting to every provocation from supporters, insisting that political leaders must remain focused on the bigger picture.

“I want to ask leaders in the Opposition, be careful. Don't listen to overzealous supporters and influencers; they will lead you astray. Remain focused,” he warned.

On the question of selecting a joint presidential candidate, Gachagua revealed that differences remained over the appropriate timing, with Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka proposing that the flagbearer be identified before December, while Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna favoured February and Narc Kenya leader Martha Karua suggested May.

Gachagua, however, argued that selecting a candidate too early could expose the individual to political pressure and possible frustration from the government.

He proposed April next year as a more suitable time, maintaining that the coalition was united on the principle of having one candidate even if its leaders differed on the timing.

The DCP leader also dismissed arguments that academic qualifications, experience or political credentials should determine who becomes the coalition's presidential candidate, insisting that electoral numbers and the support of ordinary Kenyans would ultimately decide.

“As others say they have experience and an agenda in the Opposition, the deciding factor is the numbers. I'm with the people. You say you have capacity, but the person to decide is the voter,” he said.

He added: “Akili nyingi ni nzuri, but bila kura unaweza kaa nayo nyumbani.”

World.title: Mudavadi urges Western Kenya to unite, says region cannot remain on sidelines
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Prime CS Musalia Mudavadi. [File, Standard]

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has urged Western Kenya to unite ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying the region must strengthen its political representation to have a greater say in national decision-making.

Speaking during a UDA delegates' meeting in Shitoto village, Mumias East, Kakamega County, he said Western Kenya could not afford to remain on the sidelines while decisions affecting the country were being made.

"2027 is the moment we must change the narrative. We must make sure that we are at the table where decisions are made. We cannot afford to remain spectators when the future of our country and our region is being determined," he said.

Mudavadi said parliamentary influence depended on numbers, arguing that electing more MPs would give the region a stronger voice in key parliamentary committees, including the Budget Committee.

"Parliament exercises authority in its own right. We want more MPs so that we can have a say in the Budget Committee and other important committees. These positions are secured through numbers, and numbers matter when decisions affecting the country are being made," he said.

Turning to the opposition, Mudavadi described its leaders as divided and challenged them to present clear manifestos outlining what they would offer Kenyans.

He said the divisions within the opposition would work in President William Ruto's favour as he seeks re-election in 2027, expressing confidence that he would win in the first round.

"We want Ruto to win without a petition. We want to thrash them in the first round," he said.

World.title: Family identifies two security officers involved in Abshir Abdi abduction
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

LSK president Charles Kanjama leads members in a protest over the disappearance of lawyer Abshir Abdi. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

The family of Nairobi lawyer Abshir Ahmedsadak Abdi has identified two security officers alleged to have taken part in their kin's abduction, even as his colleagues threatened mass protests to push for his release.

The Law Society of Kenya (LSK) said the two names have been forwarded to the police to aid in investigations and demanded that the office of the Inspector General of Police, Douglas Kanja, speed up the probe into the abduction.

"One is named Siad and the other is Hussein, and we want them released for investigation, arrest, prosecution, conviction, sentencing and imprisonment," said LSK.

The revelation came during a demonstration led by (LSK outside the office of the Deputy Inspector General of Police and other towns yesterday .

Abshir was forcibly taken on November 1 along Muchai Road, his vehicle was pursued and intercepted by armed individuals in two vehicles before he was seized.

While state security agencies have denied holding him in custody, court filings and colleagues suggest his abduction may be connected to his professional work representing clients in high-profile cases involving senior police officers.

Furthermore, the LSK presented additional names of security personnel linked to the incident, demanding immediate legal action against Chief Inspector Vitalis Kibet, Inspector Kennedy Kimani Karanja, Siad Mohammed, Abdurahman of the Anti-Terrorism Police Unit (ATPU), and KDF officer Ali Hussein.

The leadership voiced their frustration over the state's inaction and the alarming pattern of extrajudicial actions targeting officers of the court. Representatives insisted that lawyers must be allowed to execute their duties without fear of intimidation, torture, or abduction.

"We demand that the officers involved be handed over, arrested, prosecuted, and convicted. We will stand in the courts, in the streets, and in the boardrooms until abductions come to an end," they said in a statement.

The LSK has issued a stern ultimatum to the police command, including the president, DIG Gilbert Masengeli, Inspector General Douglas Kanja, and senior commanders. If Abshir is not released safely and the identified suspects are not formally charged in court by Monday, the LSK warned it will initiate private prosecutions itself.

Furthermore, the society threatened to bring activities to a complete shutdown and demand the immediate resignation of Kanja, Masingeli and Minister for Security Kipchumba Murkomen, carrying their demonstrations to Parliament and State House if necessary.

As court proceedings continue under a habeas corpus application at the Milimani High Court, the legal fraternity remains resolute: the protest at Jogoo House is merely the beginning of an unyielding campaign for justice and the rule of law.

In Nakuru, lawyers protested within the Law Courts, calling for his production.

“It is shocking that one of our colleagues was picked and today we do not know where he is. Unless we voice our concern, there will be complete lawlessness in the country,” said LSK member Ekaterina Handa. “Our lives matter and silencing lawyers is silencing justice. we will not relent until we get justice.”

Rift Valley LSK Chair Wangari Mwangi said it was shocking that the alleged abduction was captured on CCTV.

She rubbished the narrative that the missing lawyer was involved in a crime syndicate, maintaining that he should have been arrested and charged in court. [Additional reporting by Daniel Chege]

World.title: Goon financiers should be cursed and sent to hell, Chief Justice Koome says
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Chief Justice Martha Koome said goonism falls under serious organised crimes that goes against the Rome Statute and humanity. [Phares Mutembei, Standard]

Chief Justice Martha Koome now says those mobilising and financing goons should be cursed and thrown to hell.

Koome on Thursday said goonism falls under organised serious crimes that go against the Rome Statute and humanity.

She spoke at Kieganguru, Maara constituency, where she presided over the opening of the Maara law courts.

While calling on police to focus more on arresting the mobilisers and financiers, Koome said a time has come for the country to plead with God to protect the country and rescue the youth who are being misused and misled into organised gangs and goonism.

“Nobody gives birth to a child to be called a goon. Those organisers will go to hell, we curse them,” Koome said, adding, “If they will not go to hell they will meet God's justice. These are our children, and we reclaim them in the name of our Lord Jesus.”

According to her, the last time she checked, people are charged at the International Criminal Court with Organised crime.

She maintained that the best solution to the current goonism that wreaked havoc, especially in political meetings, is to arrest the organisers.

Koome said the courts cannot hold arrested goons without bail, yet the constitution grants them the right to bail or bond.

“When we arrest small people with petty crimes of causing disorder, the law allows us to release them on bail and bond, but when you bring the organisers, we will charge them under the Serious Crimes Act,” she said.

Koome said currently, the judiciary has gazetted a serious crimes division at the High Court to support Magistrates handling the cases.

“Let us look at the root cause of goonism across the country and rehabilitate those involved by getting them gainful employment,” she said.

Her sentiments, however, differ from those of Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen, who on Wednesday told the National Assembly that the judiciary was the weakest link in the fight against the menace.

Tharaka Nithi Governor Muthomi Njuki, in his remarks, supported Koome’s view of arresting the planners.

Njuki, who doubles up as the Council of Governors Chairperson, said politicians have had their time and organising goons against their opponents should not be condoned.

Using the analogy of a dog, Njuki said ‘every barking dog has an owner ’, and it is time serious action was taken against such characters at whatever level they are.

The county boss said CoG will work closely with county security teams to arrest the fast-rising menace and report all cases.

Security agencies have been under scrutiny regarding goons, with calls for their arrest and prosecution.

Earlier on, Koome and DCI boss Mohammed Amin differed on how to handle the goons during a National Council for Administrative Justice meeting as with the DCI boss also accusing the Judiciary of laxity and granting minor bail to arrested goons.

But Koome maintained the issue must be addressed lest it becomes a thorn in the flesh ahead of the 2027 elections.

World.title: Egypt tops foreign getaways for Russian tourists in November
World.content:
Fueled by warm autumn weather and strong demand for Red Sea resorts, Egypt has claimed the top spot as the most sought-after international destination for Russian travelers this November, outpacing major rivals Turkey and Thailand.

According to data reported by the Russian state news agency RIA Novosti, Russian vacationers are willing to pay a premium for Egyptian getaways compared to competing markets.

The average trip to Egypt currently stands at approximately 274,000 rubles, edging out Thailand at 271,000 rubles and sitting well above Turkey’s average package cost of 221,000 rubles.

World.title: Egypt faces Malawi Friday in crucial 2027 AFCON qualifier
World.content:
Egypt’s national football team faces a crucial test against Malawi in Matchday 3 of the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers.

Cairo International Stadium will host the match at 9:00 PM on Friday, marking the Pharaohs’ second home appearance of the qualifying campaign following their previous clash against Angola at the same venue.

The fixture carries significant weight, as it marks the national team’s first match under newly appointed head coach Ali Maher, who recently took over from Hossam Hassan.

Expected Egypt lineup vs. Malawi

Goalkeeper: Mostafa Shobeir

Defenders: Ahmed Fatouh, Rami Rabia, Hossam Abdelmaguid, Mohamed Hany

Midfielders: Mohanad Lasheen, Nasser Maher, Marwan Attia

World.title: Slight rise in temperatures across Egypt on Friday
World.content:
On Friday, the Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) released its weather forecast and rainfall map, announcing a slight rise in temperatures across most regions.

Mild to warm autumn weather will prevail during the day across most areas, turning hot in southern Upper Egypt, while becoming cool to cold at night and during the early morning hours across most parts of the country.

Temperatures in Cairo are forecast to reach a high of 26°C with an overnight low of 16°C.

There are chances of light to occasionally moderate rain (approximately a 30 percent probability) at intermittent intervals over parts of Halayeb and Shalateen, alongside weak chances of light rain (around a 20 percent probability) over parts of the Northern Coast and northern Lower Egypt (Delta).

Low-lying clouds will also form over scattered areas of southern Lower Egypt, Greater Cairo, and the Suez Canal cities.

Satellite imagery detected intermittent wind activity reaching speeds of 30 to 35 km/h across most regions.

World.title: Republicans’ lame-duck dash to confirm judges is already hitting speed bumps
World.content:
The Democrats’ coming takeover of the Senate has kickstarted a scramble to confirm two dozen of President Donald Trump’s judicial nominees before Republicans turn over the gavel in January.

The mad dash included a November 4 call from Republican Sen. Ted Cruz to a top lawyer in Trump’s Justice Department to solicit the lawyer’s interest in filing a seat in Texas, after the state elected James Talarico, a Democrat who will have veto power over district court nominees. Trump formally announced the nomination of T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel, less than a week later.

But the compressed timeline has also heightened clashes between the White House and Republican senators over the president’s choices.

The stalemates already forced a switcheroo this week of Trump’s choice for an appeals court seat, potentially slowing down the timeline for filling it, while at least one other district court nomination in Oklahoma may be imperiled because of the resistance of a Republican home state senator.

Trump’s remaking of the judiciary – from the Supreme Court on down in his first term – could arguably be the longest-lasting legacy of his presidency. Right-leaning judges could continue to serve as a check on Democrats, by striking down their policies, if they expand their power in Washington in 2028 and beyond.

In his second term, Trump has not been able to match the record-breaking number of judicial confirmations he achieved in his first administration, particularly on influential appeals courts, as he returned to the White House with far fewer vacancies to fill than the start of his first term. Now, Republicans are anticipating the possibility that Democrats won’t allow any of his nominees to be confirmed once they take Senate control, raising the stakes for getting every possible judge approved in the next month and a half.

With little time to spend for negotiation over who the president selects, tensions are flaring within the conservative legal community over how local politics are getting in the way of confirming judges with the bona fides they prefer.

“Trump has set precedents where he will roll over for the state senators,” said Joshua Blackman, a South Texas College of Law professor and a conservative who has written extensively about judicial nomination battles. “And we have the picks who probably are not the best picks as a result.”

Republican leaders are juggling this infighting with the threats of Democratic procedural maneuvers that will jam up the process of confirming Trump’s nominees.

The Senate Judiciary Committee has set an aggressive calendar to push the remaining nominees through the pipeline – prompting Democratic accusations that the GOP is breaking Senate norms – while leadership is charting out a path for moving the nominees along on the Senate floor along with other priorities.

“We’re going to make every second count, and that means all these judicial appointments,” Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the Republican whip, said Tuesday. “We’re going to do everything we can to get every single one of them confirmed.”

GOP infighting over Trump’s choices

The first post-election Judiciary Committee meeting Tuesday kicked off with sparring between its chair, Iowa GOP Sen. Chuck Grassley and Sen. Dick Durbin, its top Democrat, about the lengths Republicans were willing to go to speed Trump’s nominees through.

But soon after, it became clear that the calendar was not the only problem.

Plans to for the committee to vote Tuesday on two nominees to Oklahoma’s federal court were derailed by the opposition that one of the nominees, Zachary West, faces from the junior senator from the state, Republican Sen. Alan Armstrong, according to a source familiar with the nominations process.

Supporting Armstrong in his opposition, according to the source, is North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis, meaning that West would struggle to get out of the committee, which Tillis serves on.

So far, the White House is standing by Trump’s choice, with an official telling CNN Wednesday that the “President has selected two highly qualified nominees for the district court in Oklahoma, and we are confident they will be confirmed.”

But the White House on Tuesday night had to reverse course on a nomination for an Arkansas seat on the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals, after the home state senators balked at the choice over their preferred candidate.

The canned nominee, US District Judge Lee Rudofsky, was widely celebrated by the conservative legal movement for the decisions he has issued from his current perch on the trial-level federal court in Arkansas. Rudofsky had already had his hearing and would have been primed for a vote out of the Judiciary Committee by next week.

The 8th Circuit already has a deep right-lean, but the seat had significance for Trump-aligned legal advocates because filling it will mean that he appointed a majority of judges on that court.

Now, Republicans will go back to square one and schedule a new hearing from the freshly announced nominee, Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland.

“The committee is carefully vetting Hiland’s nomination,” a committee spokesperson told CNN. “As chairman, Senator Grassley has discretion to set the committee’s schedule and is working to efficiently process President Trump’s pending judicial nominees.”

That conservative legal world was already grousing about the current nominee for a Mississippi seat on the 5th Circuit Trump is trying to fill this Congress, who has the support of the senior Republican senator from the state, Sen. Roger Wicker, but is not seen as a reliable vote for the right’s most cherished causes.

According to Blackman, the movement would have preferred a candidate like Mississippi Solicitor General Scott Stewart, who argued successfully at the Supreme Court for overturning nationwide abortion protections. The current nominee, Todd Butler, is a former clerk for the retiring 5th Circuit judge he is set to replace, and according to his application paperwork, he received outreach from Wicker before the vacancy was publicly announced.

“They’re jamming (the White House) up, and I think Trump is just going along with it because he has other stuff he’s worrying about,” Blackman said.

Like Texas, Mississippi flipped a Senate seat, with Democrat Scott Colom projected to beat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Colom, a local district attorney, ran for the seat after Hyde-Smith blocked his nomination to a judgeship by President Joe Biden).

When Trump announced Gaiser’s nomination on Tuesday, he also rolled out nominations for another judicial vacancy in Texas – choosing a Texas Supreme Court justice who just lost his reelection for that seat – and in South Carolina, which elected Democrat Annie Andrews to the Senate.

Democrats have speculated that local politics could get in the way of confirmation of Gaiser, and Texas Sen. John Cornyn, a retiring Republican who also sits on the Judiciary Committee, told the AP he had concerns about how the White House has tried to “air-drop” somebody into the vacancy.

The attorney did not go through the usual process Texas senators use to vet nominees, and Democrats have zeroed in on his limited ties to Texas, which they say amount to just a clerkship in Houston while spending the rest of his career in Ohio or Washington, DC.

Race against the clock

To push through, Grassley has previewed an all-gas-no-breaks approach in his committee – an approach he said Tuesday was justified by signals that Democrats could block any nominee Trump tried to put forward next Congress.

“They’re planning to stonewall a president’s ability to appoint judges – now that is what is unprecedented,” Grassley said at Tuesday’s committee meeting. “So yes, I’m working. I’m going to work hard to get judges confirmed quickly during the lame duck session.”

Under the normal Senate timelines, nominees will need to get their confirmation hearing before the committee by next week if Republicans want to get them on the Senate floor by mid-December, before lawmakers leave for the holidays.

Democrats argue that Grassley is violating procedures in how he is orchestrating that final push. They’ve pointed to norms around having judicial hearings at least two weeks apart (a plan for a November 18 hearing comes after a confirmation hearing on November 10) and giving the Senate committee at least 28 days to review the paper applications – known as Senate Judiciary Questionaries – that are submitted with their nominations.

“Don’t be surprised if some of these violations have now become routine enough to be followed in the future,” Durbin, who is retiring after this year, warned Tuesday.

Grassley countered with examples of Democrats also violating those rules when they held the gavel. Regardless, once Republicans get the nominees out of committee and on to the Senate floor, Democrats have leverage in slowing down the process. Unless Republicans can reach a deal with Democrats, the Senate must devote 30 hours of floor time for appeals court nominees. Only two hours of floor are necessary for district court nominees, but even that could be a burden while the Senate also tries to pass a significant piece of permitting reform legislation.

Thune took a step towards navigating those competing interests on Wednesday, by laying the groundwork for the Senate to stick around through Friday – an uncommon work day for a chamber that usually wraps up by Thursday early afternoon – for opening votes that would start the floor clock on a tranche of district court and appellate nominees.

Democrats have the ability to make the floor process “excruciating” for Republicans, said John P. Collins, a professor at George Washington Law School who focuses on judicial nominations.

Historically, the parties have been able reach deals at the end of a Congress, when senators are eager to get home for the holidays, that allow for the quick confirmation of some nominees in exchange for leaving others behind.

But, Collins said, Republicans have also traditionally been more impassioned about judicial confirmations than Democrats.

“They might be more willing to stay up late in the night to hold all these votes in a way that Democrats were not.”

CNN’s Morgan Rimmer contributed to this report.

World.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills at least six, including doctor and child, Palestinian officials say
World.content:
An Israeli strike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight Wednesday killed at least six people, including a doctor and a child, Palestinian officials say.

The strike on Nasser Hospital shortly after midnight hit the complex’s surgery unit, according to a Gaza Civil Defense spokesman. The attack tore through part of the hospital in the dark of night, Ezz Eddine Abu Sabha said, leaving charred debris scattered across the destroyed unit.

The strike killed 52-year-old Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, Abu Sabha said, as well as a 13-year-old boy who was supposed to have surgery. A total of 40 people were injured in the Israeli strike, including two doctors who are in critical condition.

“They say there is a ceasefire. Where is there a ceasefire? Since the ceasefire, there are more massacres,” said Maryam Abu Hatab, whose brother was killed in the strike. “There are massacres every day in markets, in universities, in the streets. The donkey carts stood by us more than the world’s countries.”

Footage from inside the hospital showed two bombs, one of which failed to explode. A label on the bomb identified it as a US-manufactured GBU-39/B, a 250-pound bomb that has been supplied to Israel.

Munition fragments and an unexploded bomb at Nasser Hospital following an Israeli airstrike. Abed Rahim Khatib/Anadolu/Getty Images

“I was asleep when suddenly I was covered with dust and glass,” said Atiya Abu Basir, an elderly patient at the hospital. “I couldn’t walk because I just had surgery.”

Despite a nominal US-brokered ceasefire signed more than a year ago, Israel has carried out near-daily strikes in Gaza. According to the United Nations, Israeli forces have killed more than 1,400 people in Gaza since the ceasefire, and there is no fully functioning hospital in the devastated enclave.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said they targeted the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade, Muhammad Abu Ismail, as well as “additional terrorists who were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.” The IDF said he planned and advanced attacks on Israeli forces and civilians.

CNN reached out to the IDF to ask if Abu Ismail had been killed in the strike and what measures were taken to reduce the risk to civilians.

Board of Peace chides Israel

Displaced Palestinians clear rainwater from flooded tents in Gaza City on November 7. Ahmad Salem/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Earlier this week, the US-led Board of Peace, which is tasked with overseeing the ceasefire in Gaza, chided Israel for what it called an “insufficient” response to Gaza flooding. Seasonal rains swamped tens of thousands of tents across the coastal enclave, where nearly two million Palestinians are displaced, according to the United Nations.

“The urgent entry and distribution of essential shelter, sanitation, drainage, and other winterization supplies is critical to protecting civilians,” the board said in a statement Monday, calling on Israel to allow more temporary shelters, waste management, and other supplies.

Israel said that more than 91,000 tents had entered Gaza ahead winter, but refused to allow in the heavy equipment needed for large-scale cleanup and rubble removal efforts.

“The reconstruction of Gaza can only begin after Hamas fully disarms,” said Israel’s Coordinator for Government Activities in the Territories.

World.title: The Trump team’s hypocrisy reaches new levels with warning letter to Democrats
World.content:
After years of Republicans going to extraordinary lengths to politicize congressional oversight and target President Donald Trump’s enemies, his administration is now issuing stark warnings to Democrats to not politicize congressional oversight to target Trump and those around him.

Twice in recent days, the administration has offered remarkable initial salvos in the looming investigative battles between it and the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress.

During a CNN interview on Sunday, Attorney General Todd Blanche left open the possibility of the Justice Department prosecuting Democratic lawmakers who threaten to investigate Trump administration officials too overzealously.

And on Wednesday, White House counsel Will Scharf issued a letter cautioning the House Oversight Committee against forthcoming investigations and saying the administration “will not be extorted.”

Both are rather rich, considering the recent history of Republicans leveraging governmental power to target Trump’s foes — in ways with little if any modern precedent.

In the Wednesday letter to incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Robert Garcia, Scharf warns that Democrats’ oversight “must further a legitimate legislative task,” rather than trying to serve the criminal-prosecution functions of the executive and judicial branches.

He cites the possibility of “unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive.” He also cites “abusive and capricious threats” from Democratic lawmakers.

(Garcia, a California Democrat, responded by saying the House “will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the president’s lawyers.”)

Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on September 30. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Scharf’s letter echoes Blanche’s comments from Sunday. After Trump posted on social media that Democrats’ investigative threats amounted to “extortion at the highest level,” Blanche left open the possibility that the Democrats could be prosecuted for it.

Blanche cited Garcia’s two-word statement to the administration on election night: “LAWYER UP.”

“If that doesn’t bother you, if that doesn’t bother your viewers, then we really need to kind of wake up in this country, because it certainly bothers me,” Blanche told CNN’s Dana Bash.

The GOP has explicitly told Democrats to ‘lawyer up,’ too

But Trump and his allies have issued plenty of very similar threats to Democrats in recent years:

Trump has pursued extensive legal retribution

Still, perhaps the bigger point is this: The administration long ago vacated the moral high ground when it comes to “abusive and capricious threats” of investigations “motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred.”

Trump himself has targeted scores of his political foes, often for non-existent or thinly constructed supposed offenses. And he has repeatedly acknowledged he can’t set aside his hatred of his enemies — including in a “60 Minutes” interview that aired this past weekend.

A November 2025 Reuters investigation found that, in less than a year of Trump’s second term, he had targeted at least 470 people, organizations and institutions for retribution.

Tellingly, his administration has investigated people responsible for virtually every major investigation and court case against Trump.

And the president at one point explicitly signaled he was out not for accountability, but for “retribution.”

“For those who have been wronged and betrayed, I am your retribution,” he said in March 2023.

His Justice Department has regularly pursued criminal cases against Trump’s foes based on the thinnest of evidence, often at Trump’s urging.

Several of these cases have fallen apart — either because they didn’t clear the typically very low bar of getting a grand jury to vote to indict, or because those investigating the matter clearly couldn’t produce the goods.

Cassidy Hutchinson, a top former aide to Trump White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, testifies during the sixth hearing by the House Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the U.S. Capitol on June 28, 2022 in Washington, DC. Brandon Bell/Getty Images

That includes:

And despite Trump’s allies having accused the Biden administration of political prosecutions against Trump, there is far more evidence that Trump pushed these probes than there is that former President Joe Biden was involved in getting Trump indicted.

The GOP also politicized congressional oversight, based on little evidence

These are criminal investigations, rather than congressional oversight. But even on congressional investigations, it’s pretty difficult for Republicans to claim they haven’t done what the Trump administration is warning Democrats not to do.

Ahead of an expected 2024 matchup between Trump and Biden, the House GOP launched an impeachment inquiry against Biden that regularly involved overstating evidence of suppose corruption in the “Biden crime family.” One of their central attacks on Biden relied on an unverified claim from an FBI informant who later pleaded guilty to fabricating it.

Republicans ultimately couldn’t even get enough of their own GOP members to vote to impeach Biden, despite not needing any Democratic votes. So the inquiry never served any concrete legislative purpose — the line the Trump administration is now trying to draw with Democrats.

In the same Congress, Republicans also launched a special committee supposedly probing the “weaponization” of government by the Biden administration. It, too, vastly overstated evidence of wrongdoing and went out with a whimper.

Polls show Americans differentiate between the parties’ approaches

Still, the hard-edged front from the Trump administration in recent days at least makes some political sense. Theoretically, the administration could muddy the waters by arguing that Democrats are being overzealous in their intent to scrutinize the administration.

But the polls have suggested that Americans see the difference between how Democrats and Republicans have handled these issues.

While majorities of Americans saw Trump’s indictments as legitimate, polling last year showed Americans said by double digits that the cases against Trump’s foes were politicized and illegitimate.

Americans also took a rather dim view of the Biden impeachment inquiry. And an early 2023 poll showed Americans said by 20 points that the GOP’s “weaponization” committee was mostly “just an attempt to score political points.”

Fast forward to today, and Americans see plenty that’s worthwhile for the Democratic-controlled Congress to investigate.

Recent polling has shown around two-thirds of Americans say that Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself and that he has inappropriately profited. And an AP-NORC poll before the election showed 6 in 10 Americans wanted the next Congress to make investigating the Trump administration a priority.

Of course, it is possible the Democrats could go too far with that — just 36 percent wanted it to be one of the party’s highest priorities — but there is no shortage of real targets that could produce results.

And that’s what the Trump administration seems to fear.

World.title: The $1 trillion question facing Nvidia and Jensen Huang: Who lied to whom?
World.content:
New York —

Nvidia, Jensen Huang, an alleged subordinate and a suspected Chinese spy are at the center of a soap opera captivating Wall Street, Silicon Valley and Washington.

And, like every other soap opera, this one appears to involve at least a dose of deception. Did Nvidia’s rockstar CEO mislead his bosses on the board of directors? Did Nvidia and its board conceal from investors what was really going on?

Unlike a typical daytime drama, the stakes here are epic. Untangling who lied to whom could determine the fate of trillions of dollars.

Huang is viewed as so critical to Nvidia’s success that the chipmaker could lose $1 trillion of market value if the CEO is pushed out, according to estimates from Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.

“Jensen has created a black eye moment for himself and Nvidia and now has created a spider web of complexity that Wall Street, Silicon Valley, DC and the global tech ecosystem are trying to figure out what is next,” Ives wrote in a report to clients on Wednesday night.

Suspected Chinese spy

Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are seen walking around an exclusive golf resort in San Martin, California. CNN geolocated the still to the luxury CordeValle resort. From Social Media

Huang’s enormous value to Nvidia and the AI industry is exactly why Huang would be an obvious high-value target for foreign intelligence as the world engages in an AI arms race.

And that’s where the first, and most obvious deception appears to come from.

Intelligence agencies are known to lure their targets through deceptive schemes like the honey trap suspected in this case.

Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair, and US officials have told CNN that he had a relationship with Alice Huang, who they have concluded is a Chinese spy.

Nvidia’s board is investigating whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

US intelligence concluded in a classified memo issued in May that Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, was a Chinese intelligence asset, according to CNN reporting.

Crucially, Megaspeed was under federal investigation for allegedly diverting highly coveted US semiconductors to entities in China in violation of US export controls.

Did Jensen Huang mislead the board?

But that may not be where the deception stopped.

Gary Gensler, former chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, said that Nvidia’s board investigation must determine if their rockstar CEO was honest with them.

“If he misled the board, it’s likely they remove him from the job even though they don’t have a groomed successor,” Gensler, now a professor at MIT, told CNN Wednesday night.

Misleading the board is no small matter, especially in this case. Failing to disclose an active romantic relationship with a major customer could be viewed as concealing a glaring conflict of interest.

That’s something that could be determined by the independent investigation Nvidia’s board has launched.

If that investigation concludes that Huang deliberately misled his bosses on the board about a massive conflict of interest, the board would have clear grounds to fire him, according to Charles Whitehead, professor of business law at Cornell Law School. And failing to do so could open directors to their own legal exposure.

The alleged second affair

Nvidia shares plummeted Wednesday night after The New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital affair with an employee who reports to him.

Gensler said these allegations raise the question of whether Huang misled the board about this matter, too.

He said board members investigating CEOs typically ask them a “standard” question at the start: “Is there anything else you need to tell us?”

“Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me,” Gensler said.

The imploding corporate defense

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signs a magazine cover for his fans in Taipei, Taiwan January 17, 2025. Ann Wang/Reuters

Another key question is whether Nvidia and Huang were upfront with the public and investors as journalists were digging into this story.

“Did he participate with his staff in misleading public investors?” Gensler asked.

The former SEC chair noted that Nvidia provided an explanation on this controversy that has aged particularly poorly – even though it was delivered barely two weeks ago.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected,” an Nvidia spokesman told The New York Times. “Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

That statement appears to be directly contradicted by the fact that Huang has since admitted to an affair and the board has launched an investigation.

‘You just can’t lie about it’

Of course, it’s now clear that this relationship was anything but routine.

Even though an extramarital affair could be looked at as a personal issue, making a false statement to the public would open up Nvidia to allegations of making a material corporate misstatement.

It would be hard to argue this matter is not material. Nvidia’s share price plummeted by as much as 9% intraday on Monday after Huang admitted an affair and the board launched an investigation.

“The movement in the stock price tells us that this was material information. So that passes one test of law. And the second test is: Did you mislead the public about material information? And it appears that way,” Gensler said.

A shareholder lawsuit, filed Monday in a California court, alleges Nvidia and Jensen Huang deceived investors in their responses to media reports about the affair.

“You can have as many affairs with Chinese spies as you want under federal law, you just can’t lie about it,” said Ann Lipton, professor at Colorado Law School at the University of Colorado, Boulder.

What did the board know and when did it know it?

Another question is whether Nvidia’s board of directors misled investors about this matter.

Federal agents briefed lawmakers roughly a year ago that they suspected Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

What’s less clear is how much the company knew about these suspicions.

But if Nvidia’s board did know, shareholders could argue the board deceived investors by failing to disclose it.

Another major question is whether Nvidia and its CEO knew – or should have known – that Megaspeed was allegedly smuggling cutting-edge AI chips to China in violation of export controls.

“This could, depending on what was said in the bedroom, escalate to a 10b-5 claim (an SEC rule that prohibits securities fraud, material misstatements and deceptive schemes) and potentially even criminal liability to the extent he knowingly aided a violation of the trade restrictions,” said Whitehead.

Nvidia said on Sunday the board has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

‘Very awkward’ spot for the board

This matter is further complicated by how critical Huang is viewed to Nvidia’s success – and the fact he has no heir apparent.

“From the board’s point of view, they have a very tough choice in front of them. They have a founder who is at the heart of this company, no groomed successor,” Gensler said. “What do they do if they find out that he misled the board? What do they do if they find out that he was aware that some information may have been shared with the Chinese inappropriately.”

Nvidia’s board announced on Tuesday it has hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, a prestigious Wall Street law firm, to “conduct a thorough and independent investigation.”

Asked about his experience with boards hiring law firms to conduct so-called independent investigations, Gensler said it’s not clear how fair and balanced this report will ultimately be.

“Oftentimes, boards of directors would like the lawyers to do a report that doesn’t escalate the problem but helps resolve the crisis at the moment,” Gensler said.

Lipton, the Colorado professor, said the board is in a “very awkward” position right now.

“It’s weird for them because even if they want to investigate it with all appropriate thoroughness,” Lipton said, “the worse things they uncover, the more they’re opening the company and Huang up to shareholder fraud lawsuits.”

World.title: Awqaf minister discusses cooperation on promoting Prophet Muhammad’s biography
World.content:
Minister of Awqaf Osama al-Azhari met with Sheikh Nasser bin Musfer Al-Qurashi Al-Zahrani, Chairman of the Board of the International Exhibitions and Museums of the Prophet’s Biography and Islamic Civilization, to discuss ways to strengthen scientific, cultural and intellectual cooperation.

The meeting explored joint initiatives to promote the Prophet Muhammad’s biography, highlight his character and teachings, and present his biography’s human and civilizational values through projects combining scholarly research with modern exhibition methods.

At the end of the meeting, Zahrani presented Azhari with a scientific work titled “The Prophet’s Daily Routine Chart,” illustrating aspects of the Prophet’s daily life and teachings.

The meeting was attended by representatives of the international group and senior officials from the Ministry of Awqaf.

World.title: Liberia: Seven Charged And Forwarded To Court Over Assault on Police Officer in Sinkor
World.content:
Officer Reportedly Suffers Eye Injuries as Attackers Allegedly Seize Police Radio, Cap and US$150

Monrovia-The Liberia National Police, LNP, has arrested and forwarded seven individuals to court over the alleged assault of a police officer and obstruction of law enforcement personnel performing their official duties in Sinkor, Monrovia.

By:Willie N. Tokpah

The suspects, identified as Yokie Johnson, Rachel Johnson, Obediah Yorkor, Anthony Hallie, Spencil Z. Gaye, Prince Sackie and Harris Clomo, are facing multiple criminal charges arising from an incident involving officers responding to a situation on 26th Street, behind ERA Supermarket.



According to an official police statement issued Thursday, November 12, the incident occurred when Police Officer Sedeke K. Kammara, accompanied by two officers of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, LDEA, responded to a reported situation in the area.

However, the police alleged that while the officers were attending to the situation, they were attacked by a group of individuals from the beachside.

The LNP statement further disclosed that the two LDEA officers reportedly left the scene during the confrontation, leaving Officer Kammara behind, where he was allegedly assaulted.

The officer reportedly sustained injuries to his right eye during the incident.

Beyond the physical injuries, the attackers allegedly took his police-issued communication radio, face cap, and US$150 in cash.

The circumstances surrounding the alleged departure of the two LDEA officers during the confrontation were not immediately explained in the police statement.

Following an investigation, the LNP arrested the seven suspects and forwarded them to court to face prosecution.

Multiple Criminal Charges

The suspects are facing charges of Aggravated Assault, Hindering Law Enforcement, Physical Obstruction of Government Functions, Theft of Property and Disorderly Conduct.

The charges were brought under Sections 14.20, 12.4, 12.1, 15.51 and 17.3 of Liberia’s Revised Penal Law.

If proven in court, the allegations could expose the defendants to criminal penalties under the applicable provisions of the law.

However, the suspects remained entitled to the constitutional presumption of innocence, and the prosecution will be required to establish the allegations against each defendant through the judicial process.

Police Warns Against Attacks On Officers

In its statement, the Liberia National Police condemned violence against police officers and other law enforcement personnel performing their lawful responsibilities.

The police maintained that no individual has the right to assault, threaten, or obstruct officers in the execution of their official duties.

The institution also reaffirmed its commitment to maintaining public order, protecting lives and property, and ensuring that individuals suspected of violating the law are held accountable through due process.

The incident has again drawn attention to the safety of law enforcement personnel operating in communities across Monrovia, particularly when responding to confrontations involving groups of individuals.

Meanwhile, the prosecution of the seven suspects is expected to provide an opportunity for the court to examine the circumstances surrounding the confrontation, the injuries sustained by Officer Kammara and the alleged disappearance of his police-issued equipment and personal cash.

World.title: Liberia: Was Cllr.  Benedict Sannoh A Victim of Chicanery, Betrayal and Ingratitude?
World.content:
Counsellor Benedict Sannoh

MONROVIA – An independent assessment conducted in the case involving Counsellor Benedict Sannoh and two complainants in which a six months’ suspension was recommended against him has uncovered what appears to be a chicanery , betrayal and ingratitude against him.

By Augustus D.R Bortue-augustusd.rbortue@frontpageafricaonline,com

Following a series of hearings, the committee asked that he be suspended for alleged misconduct. But an independent probe has shown a more detailed information about what really transpired, how and why .



Cllr. Sannoh was approached by Madam Jallawleh Kollie to help them receive every benefit for a group policy of her late father, which he held with John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Company when he worked for the Massachusett Bay Transport.

It was established by our assessment that this matter dates back to 2002 and was initially looked into by the Ministry of Justice.

On July 19, 2024, Madam Kollie again built a 160 thousand dollars case against Cllr. Sannoh, claiming he had negotiated on their behalf to receive such amount .

However, this was on the contrary again when Madam Kollie drew in Cllr. Varnie Sherman who she said had promised to give her 50 thousand on behalf of some relatives against said amount but she declined. It is not known whether the issue of the 160 thousand was taken before the committee.

A statute of limitation in the law says once a matter is not brought before the court after three years such matter is barred from being heard especially when those involved are in the country. It is more than twenty years since this issue came to the fore, our investigation has established.

World.title: Liberia’s City Streets in Limbo
World.content:
MONROVIA, Liberia — In Liberia’s county capitals, paved streets have been promised many times. This year, the money was finally set aside. The pavement has not followed.

By Rodney D. Sieh

By September 30, the government had recorded more than $10 million against 15 city street projects, in towns from Buchanan on the Atlantic coast to Zwedru near the Ivorian border. The figures appear in the Ministry of Public Works’ pages of the draft national budget for 2027. On Thursday, the ministry said not one contractor had been paid.



The money, it said, is caught in the paperwork of the Ministry of Finance, at the purchase-order stage, a step short of the vouchers that release cash. Contractors will not move equipment onto sites until advance payments arrive. The ministry expects the work to be substantially complete by March 2027.

In Liberia, public money passes several gates before it reaches a contractor.

The Legislature approves it. The PPCC, the procurement regulator, clears the contract. The Finance Ministry releases an allotment, a purchase order commits it to a named firm, and only a payment voucher releases cash. The ministry says most city streets money is stuck at the fourth gate.

The budget book suggests the money may run out before the asphalt arrives. Liberia’s fiscal year ends December 31. In the draft budget for 2027, every city streets line under Public Works is blank.

For a country of about 5.5 million people, where most roads outside the capital are unpaved and many turn to mud in the rainy season, city streets are among the most visible promises of President Joseph Boakai’s government. Public Works Minister Roland Layfette Giddings has called November and December critical months, as the dry season opens the best window to build.

A statement, and numbers that match

The ministry’s statement, headlined “MPW Sets the Record Straight,” followed local media reports that $10.1 million had been disbursed. It urged the public to do due diligence before publishing information about its work.

On its central claim, the government’s own figures support the ministry. Fourteen projects, it says, have cleared Liberia’s procurement watchdog, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC). All 14 show money recorded: $9.12 million of $13.2 million budgeted. The 11 projects still waiting for the commission’s sign-off, known as a “No Objection,” show nothing.

Most of the cleared projects sit close to 70 percent of their budgets.

That is the pattern of a fixed tranche set aside, not of bills paid for work done.

Where the account frays

Not every figure fits. Two projects are recorded in full: $300,000 for streets in Ganta, a trading hub near the Guinean border, and $200,000 for a road to the Duport Road/Soul Clinic community outside Monrovia. The ministry describes all of its allotments as partial. It did not explain the difference.

Then there is Kakata, a market town about 50 kilometres from the capital. The full $950,000 budgeted for its streets is recorded. The ministry says Kakata is a separate, older contract on which paving has begun, but did not say how much the contractor has received. In March, residents complained that work had stood still since November 2025.

Buchanan, the port city that carries the largest allocation at $2.5 million, raises a sharper question.

At a November 3 briefing, Giddings listed it among projects already underway. Nine days later, his ministry said the Buchanan contractor had not been paid and would mobilise only after an advance.

The delays are not new.

In October, Giddings acknowledged the programme was behind schedule. It had been drawn up with legislators, he said, so engineers had to gather data in the field before tendering could begin. He expected the contracts to be finalised with the Finance Ministry within about a month. Six weeks after the September tally, the money still had not moved.

A race against the calendar

The deeper problem is time. Roughly $4.1 million budgeted for the cleared projects has not been set aside at all. The 11 projects still awaiting clearance, worth $4.35 million, range from Greenville and Cestos, whose tenders closed only on October 23, to Sanniquellie, Yekepa, Tappita and the Gibi road in Margibi County. None has a line in the 2027 draft.

Unless unspent balances are carried over, or lawmakers restore the lines before passing the budget, towns could be left with signed contracts and no money to honour them. The same budget page raises wider questions about the ministry’s spending.

A programme to buy road-building “yellow machines” had recorded $8.57 million against a $5.97 million budget, $2.6 million over, and the 2027 draft proposes $14.2 million more. Street lights and two other lines show money recorded with nothing budgeted at all.

Larger projects fared better than the streets. The $26 million St. Paul Bridge and Bo-Waterside roads and the $5 million ELWA–RIA road are recorded in full. Across all its capital projects, the ministry had recorded $80.65 million of $115.4 million, or 70 percent, by September 30.

It is unclear whether the budget’s “year to date” figures record cash paid or money set aside, and whether unspent balances will carry into 2027. It also raises questions as to how much the Kakata contractor has received, and why Ganta and Duport Road are recorded in full.

The ministry closed its statement with a rebuke to its critics: the call for accountability, it said, must come from a position of transparency. In a dozen county capitals, residents will judge that by what is on their streets when the rains return.
