World.title: What Benoni Urey’s Role on Dangote’s ECOWAS Business Council Means for Liberia
World.content:
MONROVIA – Three decades ago, Liberia needed West Africa’s soldiers to help end its civil war. Today, it has a chance to help shape the region’s economic future.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Benoni W. Urey, a Liberian businessman best known as a founding shareholder of the mobile network Lonestar Cell MTN, has been named Liberia’s representative on the ECOWAS Business Council. The council is a new advisory body chaired by Nigerian industrialist Aliko Dangote, Africa’s richest man, and is meant to give the private sector a direct line to the presidents of West Africa.



The appointment comes at a delicate moment. The regional bloc has lost three members, its trade ambitions have stalled, and its energy map is being redrawn by one giant Nigerian oil refinery.

Whether Liberia’s new seat delivers anything for ordinary people — cheaper fuel, easier border crossings, steadier electricity, a bigger market for Liberian goods — will depend on how the council works, whose interests it serves, and how hard Liberia’s representative fights for a small country in a room full of giants.

A Bloc Under Strain

The Economic Community of West African States, or ECOWAS, was founded in Lagos, Nigeria, in 1975. Liberia was one of its founding members.

For many Liberians, though, ECOWAS means peacekeeping more than trade. Its military force, ECOMOG, entered Liberia’s civil war in 1990, and ECOWAS mediators helped broker the 2003 peace agreement in Accra, Ghana, that ended 14 years of conflict.

Fifty years after its founding, the bloc’s economic promise remains largely unfulfilled.

It has also shrunk. In January 2025, the military-led governments of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger formally walked out and formed their own Alliance of Sahel States. That left ECOWAS with 12 members and cost it roughly a fifth of the levy revenue that funds its institutions. In October 2026 the two blocs agreed to set up working groups to manage their relationship, but there is no sign of a reunion.

Trade among members remains thin. Less than 15 percent of the region’s trade happens between ECOWAS countries, held back by tariffs, red tape, roadside checkpoints and poor roads. A long-promised single currency, the Eco, has been postponed again and again; leaders now say it will launch in 2027, starting with the countries that meet its economic targets.

The bloc also has new leadership. General Birame Diop of Senegal now heads the ECOWAS Commission, succeeding Dr. Omar Alieu Touray of The Gambia.

For Liberia, a country of about five million people, the stakes are practical. It trades heavily with neighbouring Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire, imports almost all of its fuel, and depends on regional power lines and road links that ECOWAS helps plan and fund.

Long Promised, Just Starting

The ECOWAS Business Council is not quite as new as it appears. ECOWAS ministers created it on paper in 2021, and its launch slipped from December 2024 to September 2025. Dangote was finally named its first chairman by the bloc’s foreign ministers in Abuja in December 2025, and West African heads of state later endorsed him.

The council’s job is to advise ECOWAS leaders on trade, investment and industrial policy, and to help clear the barriers that stop people, goods, services and money from moving freely across the region’s borders.

Each member state gets one representative, and Nigeria, the region’s largest economy, gets two more. Regional business associations also have a voice. Dangote’s team says his two-year term will focus on energy corridors to ease the power shortages that choke business, as well as ports and logistics, with funding to be sought from lenders such as the African Export-Import Bank and the Africa Finance Corporation.

The council is still finding its feet. By mid-2026 only a handful of national representatives had been confirmed, and its first meeting was planned for late October or early November, with further approvals due at a ministerial meeting in December.

The risk is familiar. Business councils across Africa have often become talking shops. This one will be judged on results — fewer roadblocks, faster customs clearance, power projects that actually get built — and on whether its members speak for market traders and young companies, not just the region’s biggest conglomerates.

Dangote at the Helm

Choosing Aliko Dangote sends a clear signal about how ECOWAS sees its future: industrial, energy-driven and led by large regional investors.

No single business has done more to change West Africa’s fuel market in recent years. Dangote’s refinery outside Lagos, built at a reported cost of about US$20 billion, reached its full design capacity of 650,000 barrels a day in February 2026 and is aiming for 700,000. It now supplies most of Nigeria’s fuel, and according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, Nigeria’s fuel exports to other African countries rose to nearly 120,000 barrels a day in the second quarter of 2026. Analysts estimate the refinery has cut West Africa’s imports of refined fuel from outside the region by close to a quarter. When the conflict involving Iran disrupted supplies from the Gulf and Europe this year, Dangote stepped in with more gasoline exports across the continent.

The company markets its cleaner, European-standard fuel as an end to the days when West Africa served as a dumping ground for low-quality imports.

For Liberia, which imports nearly all its fuel and where pump prices have often run higher than in neighbouring countries, a major refinery a few days’ sail away could mean shorter supply chains, more reliable deliveries in a crisis, and cleaner fuel.

But there are real concerns.

The first is concentration. A region that trades its dependence on Europe and the Gulf for dependence on one private refinery gains proximity but may lose competition. And the council advising presidents on energy and trade policy will be chaired by that refinery’s owner.

The second is conflict of interest. Dangote’s empire spans cement, sugar, fertilizer and petroleum — all sectors shaped by tariffs, import rules and industrial policy. Dangote has long argued that Africa should produce what it consumes and has championed protection for local manufacturers. Regional protection can help West African industry grow, but small, import-dependent economies like Liberia can end up paying more for everyday goods.

The third is Nigeria’s weight. With three seats and the chairmanship, Nigerian business interests will carry outsized influence in the council’s decisions.

None of this means the council cannot serve the whole region. Dangote has publicly urged governments to protect private investment, back local investors and keep their policies consistent — messages that resonate with business owners in Monrovia. The real test is whether the council produces rules that open markets or rules that protect those already on top.

The Record Urey Brings

Urey’s career spans several of the sectors the council has made its priorities.His biggest business success is in telecommunications. Through his company PLC Investments, he was a founding shareholder of Lonestar Communications Corporation, which launched in 2001 in partnership with South Africa’s MTN Group. Lonestar grew into one of Liberia’s two main mobile networks and a major provider of mobile money. That experience matters: ECOWAS wants payment systems that work across borders, and cross-border mobile money may be the most direct way regional integration reaches traders and families who send money to relatives in neighbouring countries.

He also knows shipping. From 1996 to 2003, Urey headed Liberia’s Bureau of Maritime Affairs, which oversees the country’s international ship registry. Liberia, despite its size, flags one of the largest merchant fleets in the world, making the registry one of the country’s few globally significant economic assets. With ports and logistics high on Dangote’s agenda, that background could prove useful.

On energy, Urey once served as a deputy director general at the state-owned Liberia Electricity Corporation. Power is the council’s headline priority, and Liberia remains one of the least electrified countries in the region. Urey could press for faster completion of the regional power lines linking Liberia with Côte d’Ivoire, Sierra Leone and Guinea.

He also runs commercial farms in Konola and Careysburg, outside Monrovia, that supply the local market — relevant in a country that still imports much of its staple food, rice.

And he knows politics. Urey served as mayor of Careysburg and founded the All Liberian Party, running for president in 2017. That gives him a feel for how policy plays out on the ground, but it also raises a question: how will a political party leader keep party interests separate from a regional business role?

What Liberia Should Ask For

A well-connected representative could push hard on the issues that matter most to a small economy. Among them: ending harassment and illegal fees at busy border crossings such as Bo Waterside, on the Sierra Leone border, and Ganta, on the Guinea border; securing regional fuel supply on fair terms; speeding up power links; making mobile payments work across borders; and opening regional financing to Liberian small businesses.

Urey has said he wants Liberia’s entrepreneurs and young companies to have a clear voice in regional policy. That promise is the yardstick by which his tenure should be measured.

What to Watch

Three questions will shape how this appointment is judged.

Business interests. The council will advise on telecoms, digital finance, agriculture and trade — sectors in which Urey has commercial stakes. Lonestar’s competition with rival Orange Liberia is one example. The council should publish a clear conflict-of-interest policy for all its members.

Selection. The press statement announcing the appointment says Urey was chosen after consultations across the region and that membership is by invitation. It is not clear whether Liberia’s government, its Chamber of Commerce or its business associations had a say.

Accountability. Liberian businesses will need a way to bring their concerns to their representative, and a way to hear back from him.

The Bottom Line

Liberia has gained a voice in a body that, if it works, could influence how fuel, power, money and goods move across West Africa. Dangote’s chairmanship gives the council financial muscle and direct access to presidents. It also concentrates influence in the hands of the region’s most dominant industrialist.

For a small country with limited bargaining power, the value of Urey’s seat will be measured in concrete results: lower costs at the border, reliable fuel and electricity, and real opportunities for Liberian entrepreneurs. Anything less, and the appointment will be just another title.

World.title: HANDS International Brings Hope to Patients, Eyes Lasting Healthcare Partnership In Liberia
World.content:
Dr. Reynold Agard, President of HANDS International, said the mission was initially targeting more than 2,000 patients before concluding on Saturday, November 14. But some of the cases encountered have already prompted discussions about interventions that could extend well beyond scheduled outreach.

MARGIBI COUNTY – For some patients arriving at the 14 Military Hospital in Margibi County, the opportunity to receive medical attention is more than a routine hospital visit. It is a chance to confront illnesses they have lived with for years, conditions they could not afford to treat, and medical problems for which specialized care has remained difficult to access.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Since Monday, November 9, a team of 62 medical professionals from the United States and the Liberian Diaspora has been providing free medical services to members of the public through the HANDS International Medical Mission.



The outreach, now in its third day as of Wednesday, November 11, has brought together specialists in cardiology, obstetrics and gynecology, internal medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, dentistry, ophthalmology, dermatology, physical therapy, occupational therapy and wound care.

For the visiting professionals, however, the mission is revealing something deeper than the immediate demand for medical consultations: the extent of the country’s unmet healthcare needs and the financial difficulties that prevent many Liberians from obtaining treatment.

By the first three days, the team had recorded more than 700 patient encounters. Its president, Dr. Reynold Agard, said the mission was initially targeting more than 2,000 patients before concluding on Saturday, November 14.

But some of the cases encountered have already prompted discussions about interventions that could extend well beyond the scheduled outreach.

When a Medical Diagnosis Becomes a Lifeline

Among the cases that particularly concerned the visiting team is that of an eight-year-old girl suffering from a congenital heart condition known as Ebstein anomaly.

According to Agard, the child has experienced breathing difficulties and poor physical development, appearing considerably younger than her actual age because of the condition.

Mrs. Christine Lawrence Nayor, a Liberian based in the United States who serves as the mission’s lead planner. Nayor said she had spent years encouraging Agard to bring HANDS International to Liberia, having witnessed the organization’s medical interventions in other parts of the world. For her, 2026 presented an opportunity to turn that longstanding appeal into reality.

Ebstein anomaly is a rare congenital heart defect involving the tricuspid valve, which affects blood flow through the heart. Depending on its severity, the condition can cause breathing difficulties, heart enlargement and other complications.

Agard said the girl’s condition had reportedly gone undiagnosed, raising concerns about the consequences of limited access to specialized cardiac services.

The team is exploring arrangements to facilitate her treatment, potentially through a cardiac program in Nigeria.

For Agard, the case illustrates why the medical mission cannot be limited to treating patients during a few days of outreach.

He said the team had encountered several conditions that could be treated but remained difficult to address because of limited medical resources and access to specialized services.

HANDS International is therefore considering how it could help connect patients with appropriate treatment facilities and explore longer-term healthcare collaboration in Liberia.

The organization’s experience in Nigeria offers one possible model.

Born in Trinidad and Tobago, a twin-island nation in the Caribbean, Agard migrated to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where he began pursuing his dream of becoming a medical missionary.

He studied Biology at Cheyney University, completing his undergraduate studies in two and a half years with highest honors and graduating as class valedictorian.

The outreach, now in its third day as of Wednesday, November 11, has brought together specialists in cardiology, obstetrics and gynecology, internal medicine, family medicine, pediatrics, dentistry, ophthalmology, dermatology, physical therapy, occupational therapy and wound care.

He subsequently attended Penn State College of Medicine before completing a residency in Internal Medicine at the Medical Center of Delaware, now known as ChristianaCare Health System.

Agard currently operates his own medical practice, Premiere Physicians PA, serving patients in Delaware through medical care aimed at helping them improve and maintain healthy lifestyles. He is also a member of the medical and dental staff of the Department of Internal Medicine at ChristianaCare Health System.

Agard explained that a previous medical mission by HANDS International in Nigeria helped lay the foundation for a specialized healthcare initiative led by Dr. Adeleke. The initiative has since expanded to include three hospitals and training institutions for medicine, pharmacy, nursing and allied health.

He said the Nigerian experience demonstrated how medical outreach could develop into sustainable healthcare infrastructure and help reduce the need for patients to travel abroad for treatment.

“We have even spoken with Dr. Adeleke, who was here. We will try to work in coordination with the medical team here and the government to see if we could establish a program,” Agard told FrontPage Africa.

He said there was potential for a similar initiative in Liberia, although discussions and arrangements would still be required.

A Mission Years in the Making

Behind the arrival of the medical team is Christine Lawrence Nayor, a Liberian based in the United States who serves as the mission’s lead planner.

Nayor said she had spent years encouraging Agard to bring HANDS International to Liberia, having witnessed the organization’s medical interventions in other parts of the world.

For her, 2026 presented an opportunity to turn that longstanding appeal into reality.

She believes the mission could become the starting point for a more enduring partnership between Liberian healthcare institutions and medical professionals in the Diaspora.

Nayor said discussions were already taking place about bringing back a specialized surgical team to address cases that the current group of professionals could not handle.

One of her aspirations is to help establish a cardiac center of excellence in Liberia.

“The need here is so great, and that is just the start. If this mission can lead into perhaps a school of nursing or anything else that could come from it, how wonderful would that be for our people?” she said.

She believes such an initiative could improve access to specialized treatment while strengthening the country’s medical workforce.

However, she acknowledged that establishing such a facility would require sustained collaboration, resources and commitment beyond the current medical outreach.

Nayor also expressed appreciation to members of the Liberian Diaspora communities whose contributions and collective efforts helped make the medical mission a reality.

She acknowledged their support in planning and coordinating the initiative, noting that the successful arrival of the medical team was the result of sustained collaboration and commitment from Liberians abroad.

Nancy Witherspoon, the Mission’s media and communications lead and a resident of Delaware, also expressed delight at being part of the mission, describing its realization as the fulfillment of years of planning.

Witherspoon thanked Agard and his team for their dedication and the medical services they are providing to Liberians.

She said she was pleased to see the long-awaited initiative finally materialize and commended the visiting professionals for their commitment to bringing healthcare services to communities in need.

The Cost of Being Sick

Beyond the complicated medical cases, Nayor said the mission has exposed the financial barriers that prevent many Liberians from accessing even relatively affordable procedures.

She recalled meeting a man who had reportedly lived with a colostomy for more than 12 years and needed a reversal procedure.

A colostomy is a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the abdomen to allow waste to leave the body into an external bag. Depending on the patient’s condition, a subsequent operation may be required to reverse it.

The visiting team could not immediately perform the procedure because the surgeon expected to participate in the mission had been involved in an accident shortly before the trip.

For Nayor, the case demonstrates how a medical problem that might be manageable under the right circumstances can become a prolonged burden when patients lack the financial means or access to specialized treatment.

She said some patients require procedures that might cost a few hundred dollars but remain unable to afford them.

“Someone needed a surgery that’s going to cost $250. In my mind, that is not a lot. But to someone who doesn’t have the means, that is a whole lot,” she said.

For Families, Free Medical Care Brings Relief and Gratitude

For families who have brought sick relatives to the 14 Military Hospital, the medical mission represents an opportunity to receive treatment that might otherwise be difficult to afford.

Francis Paygar, who brought his father to the hospital, described the outreach as a rare opportunity for struggling families to access healthcare without paying consultation and treatment fees.

“This is an opportunity for most of us. Healthcare is costly for us who are struggling. To get this access free of charge is just once in a lifetime,” Paygar told FrontPage Africa.

He said his father was receiving medical attention from the visiting team and expressed appreciation to HANDS International and the Liberians whose efforts helped bring the mission to the country.

Paygar also encouraged other Liberians with sick relatives to take advantage of the outreach before it concludes.

“I want to call on other Liberians who are sick to come and make use of this opportunity, or those whose relatives are sick to bring them. I brought my father, and he is being treated,” he said.

For Lorpu Kpadeh, a mother who also brought her child to the hospital, the experience has been one of gratitude and hope.

She told FrontPage Africa that her child was receiving medical attention while she waited for the consultation to be completed.

“I brought my child. He is seeing the doctor. I’m here waiting for him,” she said.

Kpadeh offered prayers for the visiting medical professionals, acknowledging their journey from the United States to provide healthcare services to Liberians.

“I pray that God bless the doctors and all those who came from all the way America to bring free healthcare to us. We are grateful,” she added.

High Blood Pressure Among Recurring Concerns

Another concern emerging from the outreach is the number of patients presenting with elevated blood pressure.

Nayor said medical practitioners had repeatedly encountered patients with high blood pressure, with some readings sufficiently elevated to warrant additional checks and follow-up.

The medical team has been prescribing medications where appropriate and developing follow-up plans for patients requiring further attention.

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major risk factor for heart disease, stroke and kidney complications. It can remain undetected for years because many people experience no obvious symptoms.

The team’s observations are preliminary and do not constitute a nationwide assessment of hypertension in Liberia. Nevertheless, they underscore the importance of routine screening, early diagnosis and continued access to treatment.

More Than Medical Supplies and Consultations

HANDS International describes its work as extending beyond the immediate treatment of illnesses.

Based in Loma Linda, California, the organization brings together medical professionals and volunteers to provide healthcare services and health education in underserved communities.

Agard said the organization has completed more than 35 medical missions globally, served over 50,000 patients and facilitated more than 5,000 surgeries.

Its interventions also include the distribution of personal hygiene supplies and educating communities about preventing illnesses.

He described the organization’s approach as delivering assistance directly to the people who need it.

“We just don’t send relief; we hand-deliver it with care and compassion,” he said.

Agard praised the visiting medical professionals for their commitment, noting that members of the team worked for more than 12 hours on some days to attend to patients.

He also commended the reception from Liberians, saying the patience and respect shown by people waiting for medical attention had left a positive impression on the visiting team.

Diaspora Engagement Beyond Remittances

The medical mission is being undertaken as part of the Diaspora Annual Return 2026 initiative, under the theme “Many Roots, One Home,” with support from the Office of Diaspora Affairs.

The office, headed by Erasmus Williams, has welcomed the participation of Liberians abroad, describing the initiative as an example of how diaspora engagement can contribute directly to national development.

In a statement, the office said the contributions of Liberians abroad should not be measured solely by financial remittances but also by their professional expertise, knowledge transfer, networks and direct services to communities.

It said the mission reflects President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr.’s call for Liberians in the Diaspora to contribute actively to national development.

The office also acknowledged the importance of partnerships between the government and Liberians abroad in strengthening healthcare delivery, professional collaboration and investment.

Meanwhile, Nayor praised the 14 Military Hospital’s leadership and personnel for their cooperation.

She recalled that a major storm destroyed the team’s tents shortly before the commencement of operations on Monday. However, she said the military personnel worked quickly to restore the arrangements and ensure that the outreach could proceed.

She also acknowledged the support of the Ministries of Health and National Defense and officials in the Office of Diaspora Affairs.

An Opportunity Beyond November 14

Although the current mission is scheduled to end on Saturday, November 14, its organizers say the possibilities emerging from the outreach could extend much further.

A return surgical mission is being considered, while discussions about a possible cardiac center and broader medical training opportunities remain under exploration.

For patients, the immediate opportunity is to receive consultations, treatment and selected surgical services from the visiting specialists.

The organizers have encouraged members of the public to take advantage of the remaining days of the exercise. Doctor consultations and surgeries under the mission are free, although patients remain responsible for laboratory tests and other related medical fees.

Ultimately, whether the outreach develops into a lasting healthcare partnership will depend on the resources, institutional cooperation and follow-through that come after the visiting professionals leave.

For the eight-year-old girl whose heart condition has drawn the team’s attention, the man who has lived for more than a decade with a condition requiring surgery, and hundreds of others seeking medical attention, those longer-term possibilities carry real significance.

The HANDS International mission may last only a few days. But for its organizers, the larger ambition is to help create a healthcare system in which fewer Liberians have to wait for a visiting medical team to receive the specialized care they need.

World.title: Liberia: Parents of Children With Severe Disabilities Are Still Searching for a School That Will Say Yes
World.content:
A teacher uses picture cards to regain the attention of students during a lesson at the Arthur and Zwannah First Autism Classroom in Paynesville. Teachers often use visual cues, repetition, and one-on-one support to help students refocus and stay engaged in class.

Summary:

Nearly eight years after Liberia adopted its “Inclusive Education Policy”, parents say schools still turn away children with the more severe end of the autism spectrum disorder, a developmental condition that affects communication, social interaction, and behavior, and other developmental disabilities.

Liberia has no data on how many children live with the disorder. Applying an African research estimate suggests about 11,600 Liberian children aged five to 14 could be on the spectrum.

A privately funded autism classroom in Paynesville offers free education but cannot meet demand. Despite lawmakers’ calls for action, government funding and nationwide support remain limited.

By Joyclyn Wea, gender correspondent with New Narratives

BASSA TOWN, Gardnersville: Anita watches children in neat uniforms walk to school. Her daughter watches too, but she can’t follow them.



For years, Anita has carried the girl from one school gate to another, hoping someone would finally give her daughter a chance to learn, but all refused. Sometimes that makes her cry.

Her daughter has not been clinically diagnosed, but Anita believes she is on the severe end of the autism spectrum. She has difficulty following instructions, frequently flaps her hands, reacts to bright lights, speaks only a few words at a time, often so softly that others struggle to understand.

Despite these challenges, Anita believes her daughter can learn if a school provides the support she needs.

“I want Mourine to go to school,” Anita s aid. “I know she can learn.”

Experts say Anita is right. In many settings, children with autism are helped to thrive. Nearly eight years after Liberia adopted its Inclusive Education Policy promising children with disabilities equal access to school, many children on the autism spectrum (often shortened to ASD for Autism Spectrum Disorder) are still being turned away.

Adopted in 2018, the policy said children with disabilities should learn alongside other children and that schools should adapt to their needs rather than exclude them. It called for teacher training, early identification of disabilities, county resource centers, classroom support, and closer coordination between the education and health sectors. But implementation has lagged.

Mourine attends an informal home study class in Gardnersville, where a neighbor has taught her the alphabet for the past two years. Her mother arranged the lessons after schools refused to admit her daughter.

Parents and advocates say schools lack trained teachers, classroom support, and resources to meet their needs. The only specialized classroom identified by New Narratives relies on private donations.

Autism occurs on a spectrum. In some children, the signs are so mild they are almost impossible to notice, and they can do well in a regular classroom. Elon Musk, the head of SpaceX, which runs Starlink, and the electric car company Tesla, and the world’s richest man, has said he has Asperger’s syndrome, an older name for someone on the milder end of the spectrum.

At the more severe end, children may not speak at all, may struggle to understand others, and may become very upset by noise, light, or changes in routine. In a classroom, they may need a teacher’s aide working with them one-on-one, a quiet space, and lessons designed just for them.

Liberia has no national count of children with autism. A 2026 review of seven studies in four African countries found that about one percent of participants had autism confirmed by a clinician. Another four percent screened as being at high risk of disorder but had not necessarily been diagnosed. If that one-percent rate applied to Liberia, 11,600 children aged five to 14 could be on the spectrum.

Parents interviewed by FrontPage Africa/New Narratives said many schools still refuse to admit their children, and families are largely left to navigate the system on their own. Some move from school to school searching for one willing to accept their child. Others keep their children at home after repeated rejection. For most families, inclusion remains more of a policy promise than a reality.

Anita said finding a classroom has been one of the hardest parts of raising a child on the spectrum. She has endured years of rejection. Some principals told her they did not know how to teach a child like hers.

One school, Rev. Phillips Academy in Logan Town, eventually admitted her daughter after an American visitor intervened. But constant bullying and mistreatment drove the family to Bassa Town, Gardnersville. Neighbors called her a witch and stopped her from playing with their kids.

Schools in their new community also refused to accept her, forcing Anita to search again. Desperate to see her daughter learn, she asked a boy in their neighborhood to help teach the girl at home, where she receives basic lessons.

“It breaks my heart when I tell parents I can’t take them,” says Agnes Fallah Kamara, founder of Straight from the Heart International, which provides the only support and free educational care for children on the more severe end of the autism spectrum in Liberia and Sierra Leone.

Kamara’s facility is the Arthur and Zwannah First Autism Classroom in Bernard Farm, Paynesville. Created through a community initiative, it operates largely on private donations from Kamara’s friends and supporters. She does not charge fees.

But the classroom has limited space, funding, and trained staff. Although four teachers support the program, only two work regularly because she cannot afford to pay the others full-time. Kamara also helps cover transportation for families who cannot afford the journey.

Kamara says supporting these families should not be left to private citizens.

“The policy already exists,” Kamara says. “What we need now is the commitment to make it real.”

Inside an Autism-friendly classroom

Inside the classroom, learning here looks different. Individualized instruction allows teachers to work at each child’s pace and gently redirect students when they lose focus. One little girl asks to use the bathroom by handing her teacher a picture card instead of speaking. Another spends the morning sorting blocks by color.

Nearby, a teacher patiently repeats the same instruction until a boy who once struggled to remain seated completes a simple task by himself. Success is measured differently. For one child, it may mean saying a first word. For another, it may mean eating independently or learning to use the bathroom without help.

“We are not asking the children to learn the same way every other child learns,” Kamara said. “Every child has a different goal.”

A child participates in an art activity at the Arthur and Zwannah First Autism Classroom in Paynesville. The classroom uses individualized learning to help children develop skills that many parents say they struggle to access elsewhere in Liberia

This classroom began when Kamara, a former UN radio broadcaster, became good friends with a woman from Kenya during a women’s fellowship in South Africa. The woman’s eight-year-old son with the disorder, Arthur, could not speak. She could not find a school to take him. After visiting the family in Kenya and witnessing their struggles, Kamara decided to help. She studied autism and gained practical experience working with children on the spectrum in the United States. When Arthur began communicating through pictures during a program she helped arrange, Kamara saw what similar support could mean for children in Liberia.

In 2017, she organized an autism awareness discussion on ELBC, the national broadcaster. Within three days of the broadcast, about 60 parents contacted her for help. Their stories convinced Kamara that awareness alone was not enough. Their children needed somewhere to learn.

With help from an American friend, she secured space inside an existing school and obtained renovation support from former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor. In March 2018, she opened the Arthur and Zwannah Autism Classroom, named after the Kenyan boy who inspired her work and a Liberian child whose family she encountered while researching autism.

But advocates said it also exposes the limits of relying on private support. Every week, parents arrive hoping to enroll their children. Many leave disappointed.

Operating the classroom costs about $US6,000 a month, funded largely through Kamara’s own salary and donations from friends and supporters abroad. Parents are not charged tuition or other fees. Without stable funding, she said, expansion

Kamara said she has repeatedly engaged officials from the Ministry of Education’s Division of Special and Inclusive Education about teacher training and has also held discussions with the Ministry of Health about expanding autism awareness nationwide. Those discussions, she said, have not resulted in government funding.

Learning materials, sensory toys, and visual teaching aids sit ready for students at the Arthur and Zwannah First Autism Classroom in Paynesville.

Advocates say Liberia’s small government budget is not an excuse. Other African countries are taking steps to address similar barriers. In Ghana, UNICEF has supported teacher training, disability screening and assessment centers to help children with disabilities enter and remain in school. Ghana has also introduced inclusive teaching methods into teacher professional development . Kenya’s 2018 education policy for learners with disabilities provides for early assessment, teacher training, specialized learning materials and educational support. However, these policies do not mean every child can access the services.

A June 2026 UNICEF global report found that making education inclusive requires governments to train teachers, identify children’s learning needs, provide adequate resources, and strengthen accountability.

New Narratives also sent WhatsApp messages to Maxim Bleeten, public relations officer at the Ministry of Education, the government arm responsible for implementing the inclusive education policy, but he did not respond by the deadline.

But the gap has begun drawing political attention.

Late last year, representatives Prescilla Cooper of Montserrado County and Ellen Attoh-Wreh of Margibi County introduced a “communication” urging the House of Representatives to establish autism-safe classrooms and summon the Ministry of Education to explain what progress had been made in expanding educational services for autistic children. Such requests are presented to lawmakers for consideration and may be debated, referred to a committee, or approved for further action. Neither lawmaker responded to requests for comment on whether the House took action on the communication.

For Liberia, which adopted its Inclusive Education Policy in 2018, advocates said the challenge is turning that promise into services available nationwide. Kamara’s classroom demonstrates what targeted support can offer children, but its limited space, staffing, and funding show why private initiatives alone cannot meet the demand. Kamara and parents like Anita say it must become a model the government can replicate rather than a charity project dependent on donations.

World.title: Liberia: Nimba Community Celebrates New Seven-Classroom School Funded Through ArcelorMittal Social Development Fund
World.content:
The new facility in Yokopa is expected to ease years of overcrowding and poor learning conditions, as residents credit ArcelorMittal Liberia’s social development funding and their own contributions for advancing the project.

YOKOPA, Nimba County — Residents of Yokopa and neighboring rail communities in Nimba County have welcomed the construction of a modern seven-classroom school building, describing it as a major step toward improving access to education for children in the area.

Located near Duo and along ArcelorMittal Liberia’s (AML) rail corridor, Yokopa has struggled for years with inadequate educational facilities. The community’s existing wooden-plank structure accommodates 165 kindergarten and elementary pupils but is plagued by overcrowding and a shortage of seating. Some children are forced to sit on the bare ground during lessons or bring benches from home.

The new school, which began construction in July last year, is the first direct development project Yokopa has received through the Social Development Fund (SDF), according to community representatives.



Community Chairlady Betty Yoko said the project would provide much-needed relief to families and create a better learning environment for children.

“We are grateful to ArcelorMittal Liberia for its contribution to social development, which has made our new school building possible,” Yoko said. “Our children will soon move into a better learning environment, and we hope the relevant stakeholders can complete the project soon.”

Yoko also highlighted the challenges facing children who need to attend higher primary grades. Those seeking such opportunities must walk to nearby Duo, exposing them to road safety risks, including speeding motorbikes, as well as bullying.

Melvin Divine Ziamo, ArcelorMittal Liberia’s Community Relations Officer for the rail communities, said residents had played an active role in advancing the project, with women particularly involved.

Community members have voluntarily provided locally available materials, helped fill the building’s foundation and clear the construction site, and offered food and accommodation to workers without charging the contractors or project sponsors.

The completed facility is expected to include seven classrooms, administrative offices, a teachers’ lounge and modern restroom facilities.

The project is financed through AML’s annual US$1.5 million contribution to the Nimba County Social Development Fund. Under the fund’s arrangement, 20 percent, or US$300,000, is allocated to the Community Development Fund (CDF) for communities directly affected by the company’s operations.

Schoolteacher Isaac Meneyengehn described the conditions at the existing facility as “deplorable and unbearable,” saying pupils often return home covered in dust after sitting on the dirt floor during lessons.

He said the new building would provide a more suitable environment for teaching and learning.

Local resident E. Karwah Slaipeh also commended the company’s financial contributions to rural development but urged the Government of Liberia, through the Ministry of Education, to assign qualified, government-supported teachers to the school when it is completed.

He said additional trained teachers would strengthen the work of the community’s current volunteer educators and help ensure that pupils receive the instruction they need.

The project highlights the role of the Social Development Fund in supporting infrastructure in communities affected by mining and related operations. However, residents say the benefits of the new building will depend not only on its completion but also on the availability of qualified teachers and other resources needed to sustain quality education.

For Yokopa, the school represents an opportunity to move beyond years of overcrowded and inadequate learning conditions. Residents are now looking to the relevant stakeholders to complete the facility and ensure it becomes a fully functioning school for the community’s children.

World.title: Court Summons Justice, Gender Ministers Over Government’s Failure to Support Rape Survivor
World.content:
Monrovia-More than a year after a man pleaded guilty to statutory rape and was sentenced to five years in prison for sexually abusing a 14-year-old girl, the Liberian government is now facing judicial scrutiny over its failure to provide the survivor with the educational and social support contemplated in the court’s ruling.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

The matter has taken a new turn, with Criminal Court ‘E’ at the Temple of Justice summoning the Ministers of Justice and Gender, Children and Social Protection to appear before the court on Monday, November 16, 2026, to explain the government’s handling of its responsibilities toward the survivor and her child.



The summons, issued on November 11 by the Clerk of Criminal Court ‘E’, Abraham Richards, was made at the directive of Assigned Circuit Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr.

The two officials summoned are Acting Minister of Justice and Attorney General Betty M. Lamin-Blamo and Gender Minister Gbeme Horace-Kollie.

According to the court’s communications, the conference, scheduled for 10:00 a.m., concerns the provision of support for the rape survivor and her child in keeping with the court’s ruling in the case involving the Republic of Liberia and Victor Eze.

The court’s intervention comes amid concerns that the survivor, who was supposed to benefit from educational assistance and other support, is reportedly still out of school despite the reopening of schools across the country.

For a child whose education and childhood were disrupted by sexual violence, the failure to secure continued schooling raises troubling questions about the effectiveness of Liberia’s protection system for survivors of sexual and gender-based violence.

A Conviction, But What Happened To Survivor?

Court records show that Victor Eze, then 35, was arrested on December 9, 2024, and subsequently indicted for statutory rape in violation of Section 14.70 of Liberia’s New Penal Law.

The indictment alleged that in October 2024, in Jallah’s Town Community, Montserrado County, Eze sexually assaulted a 14-year-old girl.

According to the indictment, the defendant lived in the same yard as the survivor and allegedly entered the room where she slept, threatening her with a knife before sexually abusing her.

The court records further stated that the survivor sustained injuries and was taken to the JDJ Memorial Hospital for medical examination and treatment.

The case took a major turn on June 11, 2025, when Eze pleaded guilty to the statutory rape charge.

During the court’s inquiry into his plea, the defendant acknowledged that the survivor had given birth to a child as a result of the sexual abuse and expressed a willingness to support both the child and the mother.

The court subsequently adjudged him guilty after satisfying itself that his plea was made voluntarily and with an understanding of the charge.

On October 7, 2025, the court sentenced Eze to five years’ imprisonment, inclusive of the nine months he had already spent in pretrial detention.

The court consequently ordered that he serve the remaining four years and three months in a correctional facility within Liberia.

The Government’s Responsibility

Beyond the criminal sentence, the proceedings also brought the government’s responsibility toward the survivor and her child into focus.

The court’s sentencing records referenced support of US$50 provided through the Ministry of Justice’s Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Crimes Unit.

The records also referenced an additional intervention by the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, including the provision of seed funding for a small business and support under an initiative involving SOS.

These interventions reflected the need to address the survivor’s circumstances beyond the conviction and imprisonment of the perpetrator.

However, the latest court summons suggests that questions remain about the implementation and continuity of the support contemplated by the court.

At the center of the present controversy is the survivor’s education. With schools now in session, the reported absence of the teenage survivor from school raises a fundamental question: What happens to a child whose education is interrupted by sexual violence when the very institutions expected to help rebuild her life fail to deliver the necessary support?

A prison sentence may punish the offender, but it can not, on its own, restore the survivor’s education, provide for her child’s welfare, or guarantee her economic security.

Those responsibilities require sustained institutional commitment.

A Test for the Ministries

The appearance of the two ministers before Criminal Court ‘E’ could become an important test of accountability for institutions responsible for protecting women and children in Liberia.

The Ministry of Justice, which oversees the prosecution of criminal cases and the government’s legal responsibilities, and the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, which has a central mandate to promote the welfare and protection of vulnerable persons, are now expected to address the court’s concerns.

The November 16 conference will provide an opportunity for both ministries to explain what measures have been taken, what support has reached the survivor and her child, and what concrete arrangements are in place to ensure that she returns to school.

It also raised questions about whether the assistance referenced during sentencing was intended as a one-time intervention or part of a sustained rehabilitation and protection arrangement.

For the survivor, the issue is not simply an administrative disagreement between government institutions and the court.

It is about her future.

She is a young person who, according to the prosecution’s case, suffered sexual violence at an age when she should have been concentrating on her education, personal development, and childhood.

She now has a child to care for, while the government is being called upon to account for the support expected to help her rebuild her life.

When Justice Must Go Beyond The Courtroom

Liberia has made legal and institutional commitments to combat rape, protect children, and support survivors of gender-based violence. But the effectiveness of those commitments cannot be measured solely by arrests, prosecutions, and prison sentences.

The true measure of justice must also include what happens to survivors after their cases are concluded.

A conviction without meaningful rehabilitation risks leaving victims to confront the consequences of sexual violence alone.

The situation involving the survivor, therefore, presents an important question for the country’s justice and social protection systems, as to whether Liberia claims to have delivered justice when a survivor’s education and welfare remain uncertain after her perpetrator has been convicted.

The court’s decision to summon the two ministers signals that the matter is not being treated as a closed criminal proceeding but as an issue requiring further attention to the welfare of the survivor and her child.

On Monday, November 16, the attention will shift from the courtroom conviction to the government’s response.

For the teenage survivor, however, the most important outcome will not be another official explanation or promise.

It will be tangible support, a return to school, protection for her child, and a genuine opportunity to reclaim the future that sexual violence threatened to take away.

World.title: Nkomeshya underscores the role of resettlements in the GZA
World.content:
Permanent Secretary for Resettlement in the Office of the Vice President, Mavis Nkomeshya has underscored the critical role resettlements have to contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Government is implementing the HOPE 2 project which seeks to build productive and resilient communities in Meheba resettlement in North-western Province and Mwayukwayukwa in Western Province with market – oriented agriculture, practical skills development and Local Area Plans.

Ms Nkomeshya has described the HOPE 2 project as a practical vehicle through which the Grow Zambia Agenda reaches people such as those in resettlements and surrounding communities.

She has since called on the private sector, financial institutions and other stakeholders to invest in resettlements, guided by the Local Area Plans, in order to enable them contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The Permanent Secretary said this during the second Joint Coordinating Committee (JCC) meeting held under the theme “Growing Zambia From the Household Up – One Plan, One People, One Zambia,’’ in Lusaka today.

“A clear, approved plan is what gives an investor confidence. It tells them where land is available, what infrastructure is coming, and for whom,” Ms Nkomeshya said.

She welcomed plans to finalise a dry-season version of the HOPE 2 Approach for 2027, combining technical training with farm planning for five-hectare plots, household food and cash management.

And the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) has commended Zambia for its long-standing support to former refugees and integrated settlers, describing it as a true example of human solidarity.

Speaking at the same meeting, JICA Senior Representative, Yamamoto Koichiro acknowledged Zambia’s commitment to offering protection and opportunities to former refugees and integrated settlers, further expressing his organisation’s pride to support such.

Mr Yamamoto said HOPE 2 reflects the shared commitment between Zambia and Japan to Human Security and Sustainable Self-Reliance, with a goal to help build productive, resilient and inclusive communities in Meheba and Mwayukwayukwa.

He noted that since the inaugural JCC held in February this year, the collaboration between Japanese experts and their Zambian counterparts has recorded notable transformative interventions.

Mr Yamamoto explained that some of the interventions include strengthening the capacity of government extension staff to support former refugees and host communities.

“Let us continue working together to ensure that former refugees and host communities have the knowledge, opportunities and support they need to build prosperous and resilient livelihoods”, he urged.

The HOPE 2 project is being supported by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

The Project builds on the first HOPE Project, with two clear outputs: strengthening the institutional capacity of Government and councils, and promoting livelihoods for former refugees, refugees, Zambian settlers and host communities.

World.title: Nkandu calls on Stakeholders to fight digital piracy
World.content:
Ministry of Information and Media Minister, Elvis Nkandu has called for practical recommendations to fight digital piracy in the country.

Mr Nkandu said this when he officiated at a stakeholders’ engagement forum on digital piracy organised by Independent Broadcast Authority (IBA) Lusaka’s quorum hotel.

He said the Government wants to see the creative industry grow into a significant contributor to national economic growth.

Mr Nkandu said if well harnessed, the creative industry can contribute enormously to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

He cited countries such as South Africa and Nigeria where the creative industry is a major contributor to economic growth.

“Government wants to see more investment in production facilities, more opportunities, more innovation in digital platforms and more significant products for both indigenous and international markets,” Mr Nkandu said.

He however said such growth will only be sustainable if intellectual property is respected and protected.

The Minister said investors must have confidence that their investments will be secure and that they will fairly benefit from their hard work.

Mr Nkandu said the forum should therefore produce practical recommendations to end the criminality of digital piracy.

The Minister said he is a firm believer that when the economy grows, more opportunities are created for citizens.

Speaking earlier, Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA) Director General, Webster Malido, called for a collaborative approach to fight digital piracy.

‘’No single institution can address the challenge alone,” Mr Malido said.

Mr Malido said the IBA remains committed to playing its part in addressing the challenge.

World.title: Economic growth essential in mining sector- Dr Musokotwane
World.content:
Minister of Finance and National Planning, Situmbeko Musokotwane, says Economic growth in sectors such as Mining, Agriculture, Tourism and Energy are essential to creating jobs and business opportunities that would enable citizens to earn income and qualify for housing loans.

Dr Musokotwane said economic growth, increased household income and private-sector investment are key to addressing Zambia’s housing deficit and improving access to decent and affordable accommodation.

He noted that the need for sustainable housing solutions has intensified as population growth continues to increase, while low income makes it difficult for many citizens to afford decent homes.

Speaking during the African Union for Housing Finance (AUHF) Conference under the theme “Transforming Africa’s Housing Future: Innovation, Technology and Value-Sharing Synergies” in Lusaka today, Dr Musokotwane said low income remains a major obstacle to housing affordability.

Dr Situmbeko said the Government alone cannot meet the growing demand for housing, as Zambia’s population has increased.

He said the Government is encouraging private-sector participation through public-private partnerships (PPPs) to accelerate housing and infrastructure development.

Dr Musokotwane disclosed that Government plans to construct approximately six Universities in 2027, with the private sector expected to finance student hostels and accommodation for academic staff, while Government will finance core learning infrastructure.

And Minister of Housing, Christopher Kalila, emphasised the need for innovative approaches, stronger partnerships and improved housing-financing systems to address Africa’s growing housing needs.

Dr Kalila noted that housing is fundamental to family security, public health, human development and inclusive economic growth.

Meanwhile, Lusaka City Mayor Chitambala Mwewa said addressing the accommodation challenge requires commitment and collective effort to ensure that cities develop in an orderly and sustainable manner.

World.title: Agriculture central to the Grow Zambia Agenda- Nyambose
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to expanding decent employment and entrepreneurship opportunities for young people through the Pro-Agro Youth Programme, aimed at strengthening agricultural productivity and rural economic transformation.

Speaking during the launch of the ProAgro YOUTH Programme in Lusaka, Minister of Labour and Social Security, Misheck Nyambose, in a speech read on his behalf by Permanent Secretary, Zakaria Luhanga, said agriculture was central to the Grow Zambia Agenda, with five of its eight pillars cent red on the sector.

Mr Nyambose reaffirmed Government’s commitment to ensuring effective implementation of the programme.

He explained that the sector had the potential to create jobs, stimulate enterprise, strengthen food security and increase value addition, particularly among young people in rural communities.

“Our challenge therefore is not simply to train young people, it is to connect skills to jobs, entrepreneurship to markets, investment to employment and agricultural production to value addition,” he added.

Mr Nyambose highlighted that the government will continue strengthening labour market governance, social dialogue, employment services and labour market information to improve the transition from skills development to employment and entrepreneurship.

He disclosed that training programmes should respond to the needs of employers and emerging value chains, urging young people to consider skills in agriculture, mining and other productive sectors instead of pursuing qualifications that might not guarantee employment.

“Training must respond to employers’ needs and we must move from training for its own sake to skills that produce employment, productivity and enterprise,” he added.

Mr Nyambose noted that the success of the Pro-Agro Youth Programme will be measured by the jobs created, enterprises sustained, incomes improved and opportunities opened to young people, rather than the number of people trained or activities undertaken.

Speaking at the same event, International Labour Organization (ILO) Country Office Director for Zambia and Malawi, Wellington Chibebe, in a speech read on his behalf by ILO Employment Specialist, Jealous Chirove, said the ProAgroYOUTH Programme will help address barriers preventing rural youths from accessing decent employment and entrepreneurship opportunities.

“The program will strengthen integrated Agribusiness Hubs in Zambia’s Eastern Province, bringing together training providers, employers, financial institutions, business development services and employment services,” said Mr Chibebe.

Mr Chibebe noted that the initiative will be built on the achievements of its first phase, which demonstrated that equipping young people with relevant skills, business networks and opportunities could enable them establish sustainable enterprises and contribute to local economic development.

Meanwhile, the Zambia Federation of Employers (ZFE) President, Blake Mulala, called for greater private sector involvement in the implementation of the ProAgroYOUTH Programme to ensure sustainable employment and entrepreneurship opportunities for rural youths.

Mr Mulala said this in remarks read on his behalf by ZFE Board Member, Shupa Munkombwe.

Mr Mulala stressed the need for established agribusinesses and other private sector players to support young people through skills development, mentorship, internships and business linkages.

“Training alone is insufficient to address youth unemployment. There is a need to connect young people to financing, appropriate technology, reliable markets and practical business opportunities,” he said.

World.title: Increased child marriages worry Chinsali education authorities
World.content:
Education authorities in Chinsali District, Muchinga Province have expressed concern over increasing cases of early pregnancies and child marriages among school-going girls in Kambwi village.

Chinsali District Education Board Secretary (DEBS) Katele Kalale, says the situation is worrying with some girls reportedly being married off as young as 16 years.

Mr Kalale said the extent of the problem became evident during an engagement with traditional leaders, community representatives and other stakeholders who confirmed that early marriages and pregnancies were prevalent in the area.

He disclosed to the media that at Kambwi Primary School, three Grade 7 girls did not sit for their examinations due to pregnancy, while two others had been married off.

This is out of a total enrolment of 25 grade 7 learners.

“The number is quite disturbing here at Kambwi Primary School, and we feel we can still do more to prevent this vice,” he said.

Mr Kalale stressed that the situation required urgent intervention, adding that the education authorities would return to the area next week in collaboration with the Departments of Community Development and Health to sensitise parents and guardians on the dangers and consequences of marrying off underage girls.

He further expressed concern over learner absenteeism arising from seasonal caterpillar harvesting which has disrupted teaching and learning activities.

Mr Kalale explained that education authorities were working with traditional leaders, the clergy and other community stakeholders to discourage parents from withdrawing children from school to participate in the seasonal activity.

He said communities should not continue treating the practice as normal simply because it had been part of their traditional way of life, emphasising that education remained one of the most valuable investments parents could make in their children’s future.

Meanwhile, Kambwi Primary School Acting Head teacher Frank Mwenda, added that caterpillar harvesting had resulted in significant absenteeism with approximately 150 girls from different classes reportedly leaving school to participate in the activity.

Mr Mwenda said the development was affecting the delivery of lessons as teachers were often compelled to spend additional time helping learners who missed classes catch up with the rest.

“It has really affected the delivery of lessons because when you teach with only a few learners in class, those who have missed lessons lag behind, and you need to find time to help them catch up,” he stated.

He added that the school administration planned to engage parents and guardians to sensitise them on the negative effects of allowing children to miss lessons for caterpillar collection.

World.title: Kafue East MP hands over classroom block
World.content:
Government, through the local authority in Kafue District, has handed over a newly constructed one by three classroom block, furnished with 75 desks, to Shamanjanji Community School in Malundu Ward of Kafue East Constituency.

The project was completed at a total cost of K1,300, 000 under the 2025 Constituency Development Fund (CDF) budget cycle.

Speaking during the handover ceremony, Kafue East Member of Parliament Buumba Malambo, who officiated at the event, said the infrastructure would provide a more conducive learning environment and contribute to the delivery of quality education.

Ms Malambo reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to improving access to education through the construction of new schools and expansion of existing learning facilities.

“The Government remains committed to improving access to education through the construction of schools and expansion of existing facilities,” said Ms Malambo.

Meanwhile, Headwoman Shamanjanji commended the Government for the development, describing the classroom block as the first social amenity her community had received from Government since independence.

“We are more than happy to receive this first-ever social amenity from the Government in this area. This school is indeed a testament to the Government’s commitment to better our lives,” said Headwoman Shamanjanji.

And Kafue District Education Board Secretary, Levy Matongo said his office will deploy qualified teachers to the school.

Mr Matongo disclosed that the community school currently has 85 registered learners.

He further urged the community to take care of the newly constructed infrastructure and teachers who would be deployed to the school.

“We are sending teachers to the school by next week to attend to the 85 registered learners,” said Mr Matongo.

World.title: CPPA urged to resolve boundary disputes in Mumbwa
World.content:
Mumbwa District Commissioner (DC), Namukulo Hayumbu has called on the Central Province Planning Authority (CPPA), to help find a lasting solution to chiefdom boundary disputes in the district to foster development.

Ms Hayumbu, says the district is grappling with the deeply-rooted boundary disputes among local traditional leaders that have adversely affected development in the district.

The DC was speaking when a delegation from the Central Province Planning Authority paid a courtesy call on her in Mumbwa.

“Mumbwa is facing a serious problem of boundary issues among our traditional leaders. We need to hold hands to resolve the problem,” she said.

Ms Hayumbu said boundary disputes have potential to degenerate into a chaotic situation, especially among chiefdoms, if not urgently resolved by the planning authorities.

She said the CPPA and other strategic offices should help the Mumbwa Town Council in addressing land-related issues to unlock Mumbwa’s potential to contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

“Some traditional leaders don’t even want the original 1958 map in resolving boundary disputes,” Ms Hayumbu said.

And CPPA Vice Chairperson, Samuel Ng’ambi said the authority is concerned about the continued boundary disputes in Mumbwa.

Mr Ng’ambi called on stakeholders to embrace constructive dialogue as one of the strategies of resolving the matter instead of fighting through courts.

He said meaningful development can only take place when land-related disputes are resolved in an amicable manner.

The CPPA also had engagements with Mumbwa Town Council Chairperson, Charlie Masumo and Council Secretary Sifaya Mainga in its quest to promote professionalism in land management to avoid unplanned settlements and uncoordinated developments.

World.title: Muchinga Chiefs back removal of illegal miners
World.content:
Traditional leaders in Muchinga Province have called on government to halt all illegal mining activities in the region.

‎Chief Chikwanda of the Bemba people, Chief Mukungule of the Bisa people both of Mpika District and Chief Mukwikile of the Bemba people of Shiwangandu District, said the move will help to restore order in the mining sector.

‎Speaking on behalf of other traditional leaders, Chief Mukwikile bemoaned that illegal mining is causing more harm than good in the province.

‎Chief Mukwikile who was speaking during a stakeholders’ engagement meeting on mineral regulation, compliance and the formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining in Mpika said the vice has had serious negative effects on communities and the environment.

‎The traditional leader said the province had recorded many deaths, crime, water pollution adding the mining sites are also harbouring prohibited immigrants, among other illegal vices at the mining sites.

‎He said the vices were being felt by communities living around the sites and are impacting the environment.

‎The traditional leader explained that the call to stop illegal mining and remove them from sites is in the best interest of the province and the nation at large.

‎”Any sound mind person cannot support the illegalities happening at these mining sites,” he said

‎And Muchinga Province Deputy Permanent Secretary, Grant Chisapa disclosed that all illegal miners had been given up to November 18th to vacate the mining sites in the province or face force removal by the Zambia Army.

Mr Chisapa urged the community not to politicize the removal of illegal miners from the mining sites in the province.

‎”It is sad that some individuals are trying to bring politics at the expense of real development,” he said.

‎Mr Chisapa said government remains committed to restoring order at all mining sites in the province and will not allow lawlessness to take over the operations of the mining sector in the province.

‎The stakeholders’ engagement meeting was aimed at strengthening mineral regulation and compliance and promoting the formalisation of artisanal and small-scale mining.

World.title: Minister orders ZIMDEF to deliver results, not just collect money
World.content:
Local News

Valentine Maya · November 12, 2026

HIGHER and Tertiary Education minister Frederick Shava has reminded the Zimbabwe Manpower Development Fund (ZIMDEF) that its success will be measured by the skills it imparts on students and the jobs it supports, not by the money it collects or disburses.

Officially opening the 2026 ZIMDEF strategic planning workshop in Mutare this Thursday, Shava said, “ZIMDEF must remain focused on interventions that deliver tangible value to the economy, within its statutory mandate and the Ministry’s policy priorities.”

Shava said the retreat must produce a comprehensive assessment of 2026 performance against the strategic plan; clearly defined corrective measures for outstanding commitments and implementation challenges; and a realistic, costed and prioritised 2027 annual work programme and budget aligned with the government’s long-term plans.

He also said the workshop’s outcomes must be an evidence-based assessment that demonstrates what has been achieved, what remains outstanding and what must be done differently to improve delivery.

“Last year, ZIMDEF developed its 2026–2030 strategic plan, aligned with the Second National Development Strategy (NDS2). Our task today is to take stock of implementation during 2026, identify areas requiring improvement and agree on strategic priorities for 2027,” he said.

He urged delegates to approach the exercise with openness, objectivity and a clear focus on results.

The Minister of Higher and Tertiary Education, Innovation, Science and Technology Development, ambassador Frederick Shava, receives a token of appreciation from ZIMDEF vice chairperson colonel Siwinile Tauya at the ZIMDEF 2026 Strategic Planning Review Workshop in Mutare.

Pictures: MHTEISTD Communications and Advocacy Officer Kudakwashe Hunda

On the 2027 budget, Shava said resource allocation must be guided by strategic priorities, available resources, demonstrated needs and the readiness of proposed projects for implementation.

“Particular attention must be given to completing ongoing projects and ensuring that previous investments generate their intended benefits,” he said.

Shava also called for tighter revenue collection.

“I wish to emphasise the importance of strengthening revenue mobilisation and compliance and ZIMDEF must sustain engagement with contributing employers, improve the efficiency of collections and pursue outstanding obligations consistently and professionally, within the applicable legal framework,” he said.

The minister also tied the fund’s work to the ministry’s heritage-based education 5.0 philosophy.

“Within this framework, ZIMDEF has a critical responsibility to support the development of a skilled, competent and productive workforce that responds to the needs of our economy,” he said.

He acknowledged the ZIMDEF board and management’s continued commitment to strengthening the fund’s contribution to skills development and human capital formation in Zimbabwe.
