World.title: Africa: Africa Made It: Turning Africa's Cotton Wealth into Jobs, Industry and Economic Power
World.content:
Africa Made It campaign was launched in Lagos, Nigeria, aiming to drive Africa's industrial sovereignty under the theme, "Power, Protect and Purchase."

Africa produces cotton, inspires global fashion and boasts a vibrant creative industry. Yet much of the economic value generated from these resources is captured beyond the continent. Launched during CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, the Africa Made It campaign seeks to change that narrative by promoting local manufacturing, strengthening Africa’s textile value chain and encouraging consumers to support African-made products.

Africa’s fashion and textile industries hold considerable potential to drive industrialisation, create employment and strengthen the continent’s economic independence. However, despite its abundant natural resources and creative talent, Africa continues to capture only a limited share of the value generated by its cotton and fashion industries.

The Africa Made It campaign, launched during the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) WKND 2026 in Lagos, aims to address this imbalance by encouraging African countries to move beyond exporting raw cotton and invest in a fully integrated fibre-to-fashion value chain.

Built around three pillars “Power, Protect and Purchase” the campaign seeks to mobilise governments, investors, manufacturers, fashion brands and consumers to strengthen local production and retain more economic value within Africa.



The initiative highlights the potential of the sector to contribute an estimated US$34 billion annually to Africa’s GDP through increased domestic textile and garment production.

In an interview with AllAfrica’s Nontobeko Mlambo, Abimbola Ogundairo, Senior Consultant at Africa Practice, discusses the campaign’s ambitions, the challenges facing Africa’s textile industry and the lessons other African countries can draw from Benin’s emerging manufacturing sector.

What inspired the Africa Made It campaign, and why is it important for the continent?

Africa Made It is a movement designed to showcase the investment potential of African-made brands, starting with the fashion industry.

Its significance lies in a challenge we have faced for decades: Africa contributes enormous value to the global economy but captures very little of the wealth generated from its resources.

Take cotton, for example. Thirty-seven of Africa’s 54 countries produce cotton, yet the continent captures less than 2% of the global cotton economy. And cotton is only one example. The same challenge exists in other sectors, including cocoa and gold.

Africa Made It aims to bring these conversations together and address the missing links in our value chains, particularly the lack of local processing and manufacturing capacity. We want to engage policymakers, development institutions, investors, businesses and other stakeholders across the value chain to explore how we can connect these different elements.

The objective is to ensure that more of the value Africa produces remains on the continent rather than being exported for others to benefit from.

How does the campaign align with CANEX’s broader ambition to develop Africa’s cultural and creative industries?

Platforms such as CANEX are incredibly important because the creative industries have long been overlooked as sources of economic value and cultural identity. Across Africa, young people are achieving remarkable things in fashion, music, art and other creative sectors, often despite limited institutional support.

Africa already exports enormous cultural influence and creative talent. Our fashion, music and artistic expressions have a global presence. The question is whether we have the mechanisms in place to capture the economic value associated with that influence.

CANEX provides an opportunity to bring the right stakeholders together. It allows creatives to showcase their achievements while engaging directly with policymakers, investors and institutions capable of providing the infrastructure, financing and policies they need.

What makes these platforms particularly valuable is their ability to move the conversation beyond isolated initiatives towards coordinated, sustainable solutions. We need to institutionalise the support systems that allow creative businesses to grow and ensure that the economic benefits generated by African creativity remain within the continent.

What are the campaign’s main objectives, and what changes does it hope to bring to Africa’s fashion and textile industries?

The campaign aims to unlock the enormous economic potential of Africa’s cotton-to-fashion value chain.

Research estimates that an investment of approximately US$1.8 billion across the continent could help create up to two million permanent jobs and generate US$33 billion in annual household income. For African countries seeking to accelerate industrialisation, increase revenue and create employment, this represents a significant opportunity.

Benin provides an interesting example. Through the development of the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone, the country has begun transforming its cotton industry.

According to the figures we have seen, Benin has moved from exporting approximately 90% of its raw cotton towards processing around 30% locally. The country is also reportedly exporting about 10 million garments annually and aims to create 300,000 permanent jobs by 2030.

These developments demonstrate what can be achieved when investment, infrastructure and industrial policy are aligned. This is why our campaign is built around three pillars: Power, Protect and Purchase.

Power means providing African manufacturers and businesses with the energy, financing and infrastructure they need to operate and expand.

Protect focuses on creating fair trade policies and addressing illicit imports and other practices that undermine the competitiveness of local industries.

Purchase is about encouraging governments, businesses and consumers to buy African-made products.

We must move away from the assumption that foreign products are inherently better. Buying African is not only an expression of cultural identity and pride. It is also an economic decision that supports local businesses, creates employment and strengthens our economies. Ultimately, we want to build a movement that brings all stakeholders together to close the gaps in Africa’s manufacturing value chain.

Why is it important for African consumers to recognise, support and take pride in locally made fashion?

As a Nigerian, I grew up in a society where people take enormous pride in wearing traditional clothing and expressing their cultural identity. For many Nigerians, wearing local styles is already part of everyday life. However, there is an important economic dimension to this conversation.

We may proudly wear African prints and traditional fabrics without realising that some of these materials are manufactured outside the continent. Ankara, for example, is widely associated with African fashion and identity, yet much of the fabric is produced elsewhere.

This raises an important question: when we celebrate our cultural identity through fashion, are we also supporting the local industries and workers who should benefit from it?

Cultural pride should translate into economic empowerment. We need to ensure that the clothes we wear and the products we celebrate contribute to employment, manufacturing and wealth creation within our own countries.

Africa has contributed immense cultural and economic value to the world for generations. We should also be able to capture the financial benefits of that contribution. We do not want to become a continent that proudly wears its cultural identity without benefiting economically from it. We can do both: celebrate who we are and build industries that create prosperity for our people. That is the thinking behind Power, Protect and Purchase.

What specific activities, partnerships or initiatives are needed to turn the campaign’s ambitions into tangible results?

Everyone has a role to play in building a sustainable African fashion and textile industry. The value chain begins with cotton farmers, who need access to agricultural inputs, technical skills and resources to improve the quality and productivity of their crops. It extends to processing facilities, storage, transportation, manufacturing infrastructure and the policies required to attract investment.

Governments have a responsibility to create enabling environments, while investors must recognise the opportunities available across the industry. Fashion businesses also have an important role. They should consider whether they are sourcing materials locally, working with African manufacturers and supporting artisans within their communities. The media and other storytellers can help raise awareness of the industry's potential and highlight successful initiatives. Development institutions and international investors also have opportunities to contribute.

Regional integration is particularly important.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) provides a framework for strengthening trade and industrial cooperation across African countries. For example, cotton could be grown in Nigeria, processed in Benin and transformed into finished garments elsewhere in the region. Different countries could contribute at various stages of production, allowing more of the economic value to circulate within Africa.

We should also recognise that fashion extends beyond clothing. Technology is creating new opportunities, including the use of artificial intelligence to improve garment design, sizing and the consumer experience.

The industry encompasses accessories, innovation, logistics and many other activities. Our challenge is to connect these different elements and ensure that businesses have access to the resources they need to grow.

You have highlighted Benin as a success story. What lessons can other African countries learn from its experience?

Close 

One of the most important lessons from Benin is the value of creating an environment that encourages private investment. The Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone demonstrates how cooperation between the public and private sectors can support industrial development. The government has played a role in facilitating investment and establishing conditions that encourage manufacturing. Such partnerships are important because building a textile industry requires substantial investment in infrastructure, energy, transport and production facilities.

Benin’s experience also shows the importance of moving beyond the export of raw materials towards local processing and the production of finished goods. The country is now reportedly exporting approximately 10 million garments annually. Other African countries can learn from this approach by developing policies that attract investors, encourage industrial partnerships and support local manufacturers. Ultimately, the lesson is that industrial transformation requires coordination, long-term commitment and a willingness to invest in domestic value creation.

How will you measure the success of the Africa Made It campaign?

The campaign is designed to raise awareness, encourage dialogue and connect stakeholders across Africa’s cotton-to-fashion value chain. In the short term, success will mean generating greater recognition of the opportunities available in the sector.

We want to see more conversations involving policymakers, investors, development institutions, manufacturers and fashion businesses. We also want these discussions to lead to practical collaboration. That means identifying where investment is needed, which policies require reform and how institutions can work together to support local businesses.

African entrepreneurs should not have to succeed despite structural obstacles. They should be able to thrive because the right infrastructure, policies and institutional support are in place. In the longer term, success will be measured by tangible economic outcomes. We want to see investment mobilised, manufacturing capacity expanded and sustainable employment created.

The estimated US$1.8 billion in investment and the potential US$33 billion in annual household income illustrate the scale of the opportunity.

If African countries, investors and businesses work together, we can build stronger industrial value chains and ensure that more of the wealth generated by Africa’s resources and creativity benefits African people. That is the transformation Africa Made It hopes to achieve.

World.title: Niger: UNHRC Calls For Millions in Emergency Aid to Fill Critical Gaps
World.content:
Geneva — The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, warned on Tuesday of a deepening crisis that has caused tens of thousands of people to flee from Nigeria to neighbouring Niger and Benin, where problems of malnutrition and disease are surfacing.

Dominique Hyde, UNHCR director of external relations, said at a UN press conference in Geneva that nearly 64,000 people have arrived in Niger fleeing violence in northern Nigeria since the beginning of the year.

“They are adding to the growing humanitarian needs in a country already hosting more than half a million refugees and asylum-seekers, including some 327,500 from Nigeria, alongside people displaced within Niger itself,” said Hyde.



In the past decade, attacks by Boko Haram, Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) fighters and criminal gangs have displaced millions of people fleeing the violence.

“The impact of the violence is also being felt further afield, with several hundred Nigerians seeking refuge in neighbouring Benin,” said Hyde.

“Although the numbers remain relatively small compared to arrivals in Niger, these movements highlight the widening geographical impact of insecurity in northern Nigeria and the increasing distances families are travelling in search of safety.”

UNHCR said that most arrivals have sought safety in Diffa, in south-eastern Niger, and Tahoua, in western Niger, both bordering Nigeria, which are already grappling with insecurity, climate shocks and overstretched services.

The refugee agency said in October alone, around 1,200 people crossed into Diffa and another 3,400 into Tahoua, as violence continued to force families from their homes.

THOUSANDS OF NEWLY-ARRIVED REFUGEES

“Thousands of newly arrived refugees, many of them children, are struggling to survive with limited access to food, clean water, shelter and essential services, as humanitarian resources fall critically short,” noted Hyde.

In Diffa, more than 23,000 people, over two-thirds of them children, have arrived since the beginning of the year.

Many are living in makeshift shelters that offer little protection from the elements, while access to clean water remains a major challenge.

“Refugee women describe having to walk several kilometres to collect water for their families. With no nearby health facilities or schools, families are struggling to meet even their most basic needs,” said Hyde.

The UN agency said that protection concerns are growing and only around 5 percent of Nigerian refugees who arrived this year have been registered, due to limited resources.

Close 

Without documentation, refugees face additional barriers to accessing assistance and essential services, leaving them exposed to heightened protection risks.

“Education is another major concern, particularly for children arriving from Nigeria’s English-language-based education system, with no schools or transitional classes at some locations,” explained Hyde.

UNHCR said an urgent increase in humanitarian assistance, stronger coordination and additional operational partners are needed to address critical gaps in water, food, shelter, health care, registration and protection.

Beyond emergency assistance, greater investment is needed in livelihoods and longer-term solutions.

The refugee agency said it urged the international community to urgently fill these critical gaps while investing in more stable, sustainable futures for refugees and host communities, as it calls for $11.4 million for emergency solutions in Niger, Nigeria and Benin.

World.title: Rwanda: Kigali Wetlands Will Protect 220,000 People From Floods, Says PM
World.content:
Rehabilitation of five wetlands in Kigali will reduce flood risks for more than 220,000 residents while creating public green spaces, jobs and livelihood opportunities, Prime Minister Justin Nsengiyumva said at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

ALSO READ: Prime Minister Nsengiyumva makes case for green industrialisation

With national and international partners, approximately $195 million has been invested in flood-risk reduction, informal settlement upgrading, the construction of access roads and, more recently, the rehabilitation of five urban wetlands covering nearly 500 hectares in Kigali, the Prime Minister said.

ALSO READ: VIDEO & PHOTOS: Inside Kigali Wetlands Park



"These investments are reducing flood risks for more than 220,000 residents while creating public green spaces, jobs and livelihood opportunities. Nature-based solutions can deliver resilience at scale," he said.

Rwanda is committed to extending this model to secondary and satellite cities, in line with the third version of its climate action plan, known as NDC 3.0.

However, he said, achieving this requires financing.

"Developing countries will need more than $300 billion annually for adaptation by 2035, up to 14 times the current support," he noted.

ALSO READ: COP31: What issues are on agenda as UN climate summit begins?

Rwanda has welcomed Türkiye's Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility (SURFF), an initiative introduced under the COP31 Action Agenda.

The facility is intended to help cities turn climate objectives into investable projects, secure financing and deliver investments.

Another model of climate resilience

Prime Minister Nsengiyumva also cited the Green Gicumbi project in Gicumbi District, supported by the Green Climate Fund, which aimed to strengthen the resilience of about 249,000 people, nearly two-thirds of the district's population.

ALSO READ: What's at stake for Rwanda as COP31 approaches?

"Communities terraced hillsides, protected watersheds and moved vulnerable families into climate-resilient homes. Its independent evaluation confirms that climate-smart practices have spread, food security has improved and households are better able to withstand shocks," he said.

Achieving these ambitions requires addressing the barriers that have constrained investment, he noted.

"Good plans do not automatically become bankable projects."

Reducing carbon emissions

Delivering Rwanda's statement at the high-level segment for heads of state and government at COP31, the Prime Minister said national action alone cannot deliver the transformation required.

"Under our third Nationally Determined Contribution, Rwanda has committed to reducing emissions by 53 per cent by 2035, relative to the business-as-usual scenario."

Achieving this target requires $12 billion in investment, 80 percent of which is conditional on international support, he said. Rwanda needs predictable, accessible and adequate financing for adaptation and mitigation to meet these targets.

"We must also remove the barriers that prevent capital from flowing into viable projects in developing countries. As President Kagame observed at the recent Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, the perception that 'there are higher risks for investments in the South than in the North' is misplaced. Investments should be judged on their merits, not on their location."

Close 

He said governments and the private sector must work together to make viable projects investable, deepen markets and mobilise capital on terms that developing economies can afford, without adding to unsustainable debt.

"Rwanda stands ready to cooperate with all nations. As we assume the chairmanship of the G77 and China in 2027, we reaffirm our commitment to strengthening solidarity among developing countries and completing the outstanding work under the climate negotiations, including work on Global Goal on Adaptation indicators relating to financial needs and financial provision," he said.

World.title: Nigeria: 2027 Lagos State Governorship Debate - How the Candidates Fared
World.content:
The Lagos State governorship candidates fielded questions on the economy, housing, transportation, infrastructure, health, flooding, and other areas where the state faces challenges.

The debate among the candidates of the leading political parties for the 6 February 2027 governorship election was held last Sunday. The debate, organised by the Nigeria Debate Consortium, featured Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Obafemi Hamzat of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) who is the incumbent deputy governor of the state, Funso Doherty of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), and Adedeji Doherty of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

The debate, broadcast live on Sunday, 8 November, was moderated by Seun Okinbaloye of Channels Television and Nifemi Oguntoye of TVC News.

The candidates were asked how they would solve challenges affecting Nigeria's economic capital and largest city by population, such as the economy, housing, transportation, infrastructure, health, and flooding. PREMIUM TIMES monitored the debate and here is our review of how each of the candidates fared at the debate.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Gbadebo Rhodes-Vivour

Due to the alphabetical arrangement of the names of the candidates' political parties on the podium, Mr Rhodes-Vivour of the ADC was asked most of the questions first. Dressed in a plain while kaftan with a hat to match, Mr Rhodes-Vivour, who was the runner-up in the 2023 governorship election when he ran on the platform of the Labour Party, started by saying that his desire for Lagos was one that is better, safer, cleaner and economically viable. He explained that his desires are the same as those of every Lagosian.

He stated that the misgovernance of the ruling APC is the reason the state is bedeviled with a lot of seemingly insurmountable problems. (The political hegemony that makes up the APC in Lagos has been in power in the state since 1999, when Nigeria's incumbent president, Bola Tinubu, who is generally considered as the political godfather of the state was elected governor under the banner of the Alliance for Democracy. Since then, his political proteges have governed the state under two other political banners - Action Congress of Nigeria and currently APC.)

He claimed he has a track record of siding with the people unlike the APC, which he claimed is elite-centred. To buttress his claim that his government would be people-centred, he immediately promised to build 100,000 housing units within four years to reduce the creeping housing shortages in the state.

The Lagos State Government estimates a housing deficit of 3.3 million in the state. This acute shortage has contributed significantly to arbitrary increases in rent and other sharp practices in the real estate sector.

During debates, politicians often struggle with the "how" of implementing their promises. Mr Rhodes-Vivour appeared to have thought through his implementation strategy. He said he would achieve his housing plan from funds to be derived from a luxury tax. He, however, did not give details of the nature of said luxury tax.

He said, if elected, his government would pass a law that would require landlords to give tenants at least a six-month notice before increasing rent. He said the law would also peg the percentage rent can be increased within a given time.

He said he would develop the Eastern Foreshore area of the state - around the Ibeju-Lekki axis while decentralising development in the state.

Mr Rhodes-Vivour plan of developing the Ibeju-Lekki area of the state leaves one wondering about his claim of decentralising development in the state.

The Ibeju-Lekki area is already one of the fastest growing areas of the state with a growing residential and industrial hub championed by facilities like the Dangote Refinery, the Lekki Free Trade Zone and the Lekki Sea Port.

With the pace at which developments in Ibeju-Lekki are moving, it is near impossible for other areas of the state such as Badagry, Ojo, and the densely populated Alimosho to keep up with that axis in the nearest future.

He promised to adopt a private sector driven approach to solving some of the persistent problems of the states such as transportation. Mr Rhodes-Vivour said he would ensure that the state is safer by removing street urchins and prioritising skill acquisition.

He said he would solve the perennial flood problem of the state by adopting a wetland policy. He said instead of just sand filling wetlands, which blocks the absorption of excess water he would introduce and encourage the adoption of technology that would not hinder the right of way of water.

When asked to respond why the state appears to be rich while its residents are poor, Mr Rhodes-Vivour admonished the government for being elite-focused rather than people-focused. He said during the campaign towards the 2023 election, Mr Hamzat promised the inhabitants of Makoko, a sprawling slum in Yaba, of developing their community only to turn around to demolish their homes and forcibly evict them.

He said while Lagos is wealthy on paper, most residents are not benefiting from that wealth.

On traffic management, Mr Rhodes-Vivour said urban planning should be decentralised. He said he would depart from the approach of building long and expensive bridges to connect parts of the state and would rather use short bridges of a few kilometres to connect communities within the state. He said he would revisit the proposal of using cable cars, improve water transportation, create cycle lanes and develop inner roads within towns and local governments.

On the metro rail, he chided the government for building the project on its balance sheet rather than welcoming private sector investment for the speedy completion of the project that has been on-going for more than 20 years. He alleged that corruption and avoidance of transparency were the reasons the project is being built on the state's balance sheet rather than through private investment.

On health, he promised to create emergency rehabilitation centres across the state to reduce the travel time of patients in need to critical and urgent care.

He also said if elected, his government would depart from what he claimed is the current pick-and-drop waste disposal policy of the state, which he blamed for the foul smell in many parts of the state. He said he would encourage capable private sector participation in waste management that would prioritise recycling and creating wealth from waste.

VERDICT: Mr Rhodes-Vivour displayed a relatively deep understanding of the problem facing the state and his responses showed that he had thought through the solutions to the problems. In many cases he explained how these problems will be solved and how his approaches at tackling the problem differ from what the incumbent administration is doing. His ideas are fresh, innovative, and in many cases reasonable alternatives to the approaches of the incumbent administration.

However, his idea of decentralising Lagos appears to be contradictory and heavily focused on the provision of transportation infrastructure without considering other means of decentralisation such as expanding of commercial and industrial hubs to other parts of the state, provision of recreation centres and entertainment facilities, which will reduce the travel time and distances across the state.

SCORE CARD: 8/10.

Obafemi Hamzat

He started by saying he considered the debate a job interview and Lagosians as his employers. He said he would bring his experience as a seasoned administrator in the United States and in Nigeria (he was the state's commissioner for science and technology under the administration of the then-Governor Bola Tinubu and was retained in the position by Mr Tinubu's successor, Babatunde Fashola).

He listed the Lekki-Ikoyi Link Bridge, the first cable bridge in West Africa and the second in Africa as one of his achievements as the commissioner for science and technology. He said his plan for Lagos will be hoisted on seven pillars, which he said formed the acronym PROMISE. He said P stands for the people, R for renewal, O for opportunities, M for machinery of government, I for inclusion, S for system and E for economic development. When asked why many Lagosians are poor but the state is rich on paper, he did not answer the question directly but went ahead to reel out some of the achievements of the incumbent government and his plan if elected as the governor of the state.

Mr Hamzat said that his government would work toward completing the metro rail line therefore creating a better and hassle-free connection of parts of Lagos. He said his government would prioritise mass movement of people by providing 4,000 CNG-powered BRT buses. He said BRT lanes would be created to connect major towns in the state like Badagry. He also promised to introduce electric ferries to improve water transportation.

He listed the housing projects that are being built by the government in areas like Ajara in Badagry. He said the government already enacted a law - the Lagos Real Estate Registration Agency Law, to deal with sharp practices in the housing sector and encourage Lagosians to report erring landlords and realtors for better enforcement of the law.

He acknowledged that the housing shortage in the state is more severe in lowbrow areas of the state, saying he intends to solve that by encouraging developers to build in less desirable parts of the state as they build expensive houses in highbrow areas like Ikoyi and Lekki. He however did not explain how this will be done.

He blamed perennial flooding in the state to increase rainfall and climate change. He acknowledged that the state is demolishing structures built on wetland or obstructing the flow of water. When challenged about the flooding in communities along the coastal roads, which was blamed on the lack of environmental impact assessment before the road was constructed, he said that contrary to the claim, an environmental impact assessment was done during his tenure as commissioner for science and technology.

On healthcare, he said, the government intends to expand the Ilera Eko health insurance programme to capture more users. Mr Hamzat said the state government is building or expanding several general hospitals across the state and that it plans to establish a university of medicine.

VERDICT: As expected, Mr Hamzat put up a spirited defence of the policies of the incumbent administration, while trying to also project that he was his own man. Refreshingly, he did not use the word "continuation" as many potential successors of ruling parties in the country are wont to do. He tried earnestly to explain the policies of the current government and what has been achieved. His responses suggested that he was aware that the job is nowhere near being done and that some of the policies require fine tuning and expansion.

However, some of his responses are hard to understand and he did not bother to explain how they would be achieved. For instance, his suggestion that property developer would be made to build houses in cheaper areas of the state sounded strange as he did not explain how he would go about doing this, the incentives to make developers or private businesses whose aim is to maximise profit use resources to develop properties in poor areas where such properties would not bring the same profit as those built in highbrow areas.

His claim about the flooding along the coastal road and how helpless the state government was with demanding that a proper impact assessment was done by the federal government sounded unconvincing. There are several areas where state governments have collaborated with the federal government for a proper development of infrastructure.

SCORE CARD: 7/10

Funsho Doherty

Mr Doherty said Lagos is operating below its potential and blamed this underperformance on bad governance. He said bad governance has made life increasingly difficult for many Lagosians. He said residents of the state are not getting the worth of the taxes they pay. He said it was time to change the political hegemony that has governed the state for the past 27 years because they have had all the time to fix the problem but have failed to do so.

He said he would prioritise affordable housing and plans to build 150,000 housing units in the first four years of his tenure, if elected. He promised to create an ombudsman to deal with sharp practices and arbitrary increases in the rent in the state, saying a situation where Lagosians use a large chunk of their salaries for rent is not sustainable.

He added that the government has to be the driver of social housing. He berated the state government for stepping back and allowing the sector to be almost fully run by the private sector, a situation, he said, is bad for many Lagosians.

The NDC governorship candidate promised to focus his attention on other areas including small businesses and the environment, while also vowing to run an honest and accountable government.

He also said his government will be people-centred as he drew a connection between the wealth of the place to the wealth of the people living therein.

He stated that, if he is elected, his government would be more involved in the provision of affordable social amenities such as transportation, healthcare and education.

He promised to make education truly free and that, if elected, his government would provide one affordable meal to children in schools. He said his idea is to enable people to prosper.

On the recurrent flooding in the state, he said, the problem is a symptom of a long failure in governance. While admitting that Lagos is a coastal state thus, exposed to flooding, he said, the government should raise the bar in tackling the problem as seen elsewhere. He advocated for the protection of wetlands. He said the practice where people are allowed to build on wetland for such properties to be demolished years later is not the solution that Lagos needs.

He claimed that no environmental impact assessment was done on the coastal road before it was constructed, hence, the unprecedented flooding experienced in the corridor this year. He said even if the road was a federal road, it was the responsibility of the state government to insist that things are done properly.

He also chastised the state government for deliberately refusing to modernise its transportation system. He said the state is stuck with the old transportation system, which is mainly run by rickety buses known as danfo, because persons in the government have vested interest. By this he was suggesting that the state government has no political will to remove street urchins and touts, popularly called agbero, representing road transport unions collecting tolls from commercial motorists. He said it is an eyesore for a city like Lagos to have its transportation system still in the hands of miscreants. He said, if elected, he would modernise transportation infrastructure in the state.

He said healthcare under his government would be made totally free for the poor. He argued that the government-run health insurance scheme, Ilera Eko, was either inadequate or not the way to go and said the government has to play a more participatory role in healthcare provision.

On waste management, he said it was too centralised, and that if elected, he would encourage local governments to play more role in the collection, recycling and disposal of waste.

Close 

VERDICT: Mr Doherty easily picked holes in the shortcomings of governance in the state. He was clear-headed about what needed to be done. However, maybe due to time or the way the questions were structured, he could not explain, for instance, how he intends to fund the one free-meal for school children and his idea of a totally -free primary healthcare provision.

One would have loved to hear how he intends to modernise the transportation infrastructure and system in the state and how he plans to rid the state of agberos.

Score Card: 7/10

Adedeji Doherty

Adedeji Doherty spent the time allotted to him to introduce himself and his plan for the state, talking about how he is a man of the people and a loyal member of the PDP.

Interestingly, he used almost a minute of his allotted three minutes to pay homage to Mr Hamzat, and Musiliu Obanikoro. a former governorship candidate of his party, who has since joined the ruling APC.

He said he has a 10-point agenda but could not list all in the time remaining.

On tackling the housing shortage in the state, he said unlike the other contestant, he has no plan to build 150,000 housing units in the state, saying that he does not control the price of building materials and cannot tell developers how to sell or rent their houses. "There is no government that can control landlords," he said. He, however, mentioned that if elected he would form a research team to look into the housing problem in the state, but again could not fully explain the role of this research team before he ran out of time.

Strangely, he said to end sharp practices in the housing sector and end arbitrary rent increases, the state government will rent houses from landlords and sublet them to Lagosians. He did not explain how this idea would be achieved or how feasible it was.

When asked why Lagosians are not reaping the benefits of its seemingly wealthy government, he blamed it on the debt burden of the state government. He said the government uses N20 billion to service debt.

He, however, promised to run a small government to save up funds for other developmental projects adding that the state currently has over 160 ministries and agencies and maintaining them was not sustainable.

He said there was nothing the state government could do about flooding and blamed the yearly flooding of the state to global climate change and that flooding is experienced all over the world. He said credit should be given to the state government for what it is doing to manage flooding in the state.

On traffic management, he said, if elected, he will build long bridges connecting far-flung parts of the state like from Berger (Kara) to Lagos Island, And another to Badagry. He wondered why the government had yet to build the 4th, the 5th and the 6th mainland bridges to deal with traffic congestion.

VERDICT: Most of Mr Adedeji Doherty's responses were trained towards either excusing the inadequacies of the policies of the incumbent government or to suggest that there was little he would do to change the status quo. This leaves one wondering about his reasons for contesting for the position if all he wants to do was rehash the ways things are being done.

He also proposed some strange policies like how his government would rent houses from landlords and then sublet them to residents. His idea of solving the traffic problem of the state by building long bridges that traverse one end of the state and another appeared not to have been given a proper thought. Of all the contestants at the debate, he was clearly the least prepared.

SCORE CARD: 3/10

World.title: Namibia: MPs Weigh in On Income Tax Amendment Bill
World.content:
Members of Parliament (MP) have backed up the proposed Income Tax Amendment Bill, while raising concerns about its impact on ordinary taxpayers, government revenue and access to tax justice.

During a debate in the National Assembly on Wednesday, MPs welcomed proposed tax relief measures and the establishment of an independent Tax Court but called for improved taxpayer education, transparency and affordable dispute-resolution processes.

The contributions highlighted the need to ensure that the proposed reforms benefit workers and small businesses without compromising Government revenue or making it difficult for ordinary citizens to challenge tax assessments.

Lukato: employee tax deductions

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Martin Lukato welcomed the proposed tax relief measures, including deductions for retirement contributions and education policies, saying they could improve employees' disposable income and encourage long-term savings.

He also supported the proposed reduction of corporate income tax for qualifying small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to 20%, saying it could encourage business formalisation and economic activity.

However, he raised concerns about the taxation of retirement benefits and restrictions on employees offsetting losses from secondary businesses against their salary income. Lukato further questioned the proposed arrangements for employee tax refunds, warning that employers facing cash-flow difficulties could struggle to refund workers following retrospective tax adjustments. He called for more accessible tax services, particularly for workers outside major towns, and cautioned that penalties of up to 200%, together with interest, could place a heavy burden on taxpayers who fail to declare their income or fringe benefits correctly.

Atshipara: clarity on revenue implications

Modestus Atshipara supported the proposed reforms, particularly the establishment of a dedicated Tax Court and tax incentives aimed at supporting businesses and improving Namibia's investment environment. He highlighted several proposed changes, including increasing the tax-free retirement fund lump-sum commutation limit from N$50 000 to N$375 000, introducing an annual cap of N$400 000 on housing benefits and reducing the corporate income tax rate for non-mining companies from 30% to 28%.

However, Atshipara questioned whether government had assessed the revenue implications of the proposed tax reductions.

He warned that reducing corporate tax rates without properly calculating the potential revenue losses could affect Government's ability to fund public services adding that Government must ensure that efforts to attract foreign investment do not discourage local shareholders, pension funds and small investors.

Atshipara also called for adequate funding, judicial capacity and accessible procedures for the proposed Tax Court, stressing that taxpayers outside Windhoek should not be disadvantaged.

Lutuhezi: tax education and affordable justice

Lilian Lutuhezi supported the Bill but called for stronger taxpayer education, particularly among informal traders, young entrepreneurs and small business operators. She focused on three areas, namely taxpayer education, access to justice, independency and transparency of Tax Court.

She said many people operating businesses, including those selling goods through social media, might not understand their tax obligations, record-keeping requirements and customs procedures.

She urged NamRA and Ministry of Finance to provide simplified information through different media platforms and indigenous languages, as well as conduct outreach programmes in rural communities.

Lutuhezi also questioned whether ordinary taxpayers would be able to afford legal representation when challenging tax assessments before the proposed Tax Court.

She raised concerns about provisions limiting appeals to grounds stated in the initial notice of objection, warning that taxpayers without professional assistance could lose opportunities to raise legitimate arguments. She further questioned provisions relating to court costs and the non-public nature of court proceedings, calling for transparency and safeguards to protect taxpayers' rights.

Busch: Tax Court must be operational without delay

Sharonice Busch supported the establishment of an independent Tax Court, describing it as a necessary intervention following the 2021 High Court judgment that declared the previous Special Tax Court arrangements unconstitutional.

She said taxpayers had been left without a specialised court to hear income tax and value-added tax disputes following the judgment.

Busch described the proposed reform as long overdue and urged Government to ensure that the court becomes operational without further delays once the legislation is enacted. She said the institution must be accessible, affordable, efficient and independent, warning that prolonged tax disputes could affect businesses' cash flow, investment decisions and employment.

Close 

She also called for adequate judicial capacity and reasonable turnaround times to ensure that taxpayers receive timely decisions.

Thomas: Calls for relief from the tax burden

Festus Thomas supported the establishment of an independent Tax Court but argued that the Bill should also address the financial pressure taxation places on ordinary Namibians. He described the combination of Pay As You Earn deductions and Value Added Tax as a double tax burden, saying workers are taxed on their earnings and again when spending their remaining income.

Thomas called for an increase in the tax-free income threshold, arguing that the current N$50 000 threshold had not kept pace with inflation and the rising cost of living.

He also proposed zero-rating essential goods and services, including basic food, electricity, water and sanitary products, to provide relief to low-income households.

Thomas further called for a review of taxes affecting employment and small businesses, saying excessive taxation could discourage formal employment and business development.

World.title: Namibia: 10km Pipeline Brings Clean Water Closer to Villages
World.content:
ONGWEDIVA- More than 100 households in three villages in the Omuntele Constituency will benefit from improved access to clean water following the commissioning and handover of the 10-kilometre Onkani-Onakandi water pipeline by the Oshikoto Regional Council.

The project, which includes the installation of three public water points, was constructed at a cost of more than N$600 000 under the Council's Cash/Food for Work Programme for the 2025/2026 financial year.

Speaking during the handover at Onakandi earlier this week, Oshikoto Regional Council Deputy Director of Rural Services Priscilla Lyakwata described the project as a milestone, noting that it was the longest pipeline the Council had constructed in the region so far.

She said that the pipeline would serve three villages and urged residents to take collective responsibility for maintaining the infrastructure, preventing water wastage and ensuring its sustainability.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"It is a milestone and something tangible for the community to utilise now and in the future, and for future generations, as we are speaking about sustainability," she said.

Regional Head of Water Supply and Sanitation Coordination Steven Tuukondjele said that the project had addressed water shortages in the benefiting communities, where residents previously travelled long distances to access clean water.

He said that community members participated in excavating trenches and were compensated for their labour under the Cash/Food for Work Programme, while the government provided pipes and other necessary materials.

"The community met government halfway. The government procured the pipeline and other necessary materials to ensure that the pipeline is completed," he said.

Tuukondjele assured residents that the supplied water was safe for human and livestock consumption. He added that his office would monitor the pipeline and work towards installing tank stands and cattle troughs.

"Community members will also again benefit by getting private offtakes to take and supply water to their households which will bring extra relief to the community," he said.

Meanwhile, Christofina Absalom from Onankazizi village welcomed the development, saying it had reduced the burden of walking long distances to fetch water.

"I am very happy for the clean, safe water that we got in our village, the long walking distances have been cut short," she said.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 13, 2026
World.content:
MSF Warns Ebola Funds Not Reaching Frontline Workers in DR Congo

Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned that funds meant to fight the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo are not reaching frontline workers and affected communities. The charity says health workers remain unpaid, poorly trained and short of essential supplies, while some ambulances have run out of fuel. More than 5,400 people have died, and 11,000 have been infected since the outbreak was declared in May. The warning follows concerns from Africa CDC that $700 million of the $962 million disbursed to response organisations remains unaccounted for. MSF has called for greater financial oversight and accountability as the outbreak continues to spread. The charity also warned that poor surveillance and gaps in contact tracing are allowing infections to go undetected, prolonging the outbreak.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Uganda Probes Suspected Poisoning Deaths of Four Schoolgirls

Ugandan police are investigating the suspected poisoning deaths of four schoolgirls at Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre in Kampala. The pupils reportedly became ill after eating oranges shared by another learner, with five children developing vomiting symptoms. The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital. The school's head teacher has been arrested to assist with inquiries, and post-mortem examinations are being conducted to establish the cause of death. Police have cordoned off the school as a crime scene. The incident has renewed calls for stronger food safety checks, improved hygiene and better monitoring of school feeding programmes across Uganda.

DR Congo Leader Clears Path for Possible Third Term

DR Congo President Felix Tshisekedi has signed a law easing the requirements for holding constitutional referendums, opening the way for possible changes to the country's constitution ahead of the 2028 elections. Opposition parties have blasted the move, accusing him of trying to clinch a third term as president, despite constitutional limits that bar him from two terms. Tshisekedi, who has been in power since 2019, previously said he would accept another term if the people wanted it. The development comes amid growing political tensions and renewed conflict in eastern DR Congo, where former president Joseph Kabila, now linked to a renamed rebel movement, has threatened to end what he calls tyranny, including by force. Opposition groups have rejected any constitutional changes, a third term, or postponement of the 2028 elections.

Sudan Hunger Crisis Worsens as Funding Cuts Worsen, WFP Warns

The World Food Program (WFP) has warned that funding cuts are worsening Sudan's hunger crisis, leaving hundreds of thousands of vulnerable people without food assistance. During his first visit to the country, new WFP Executive Director Luke Lindberg called for an end to the conflict and increased international support. He warned that people facing severe hunger are being forced to choose between fleeing, rebelling, or starving. The agency said that it has reduced assistance from more than four million people to just over three million, with 900,000 losing support. WFP is seeking $520 million to provide emergency food and nutrition assistance to 5.4 million people through April 2027. Insecurity, blocked roads and flood damage are also making it increasingly difficult for humanitarian organisations to deliver aid to affected communities.

Amnesty Calls for Probe Into 23 Deaths in Tunisian Prisons

Amnesty International has called on Tunisian authorities to investigate at least 23 reported deaths in prisons between July and August 2026, amid allegations that extreme heat, water shortages, overcrowding and inadequate healthcare contributed to the deaths. The organisation verified 12 cases. It said that some families were not informed promptly when relatives became seriously ill or died in custody. Tunisia experienced its hottest summer since 1950, while prison occupancy reportedly reached 194% in 2025. Amnesty is also raising concerns about restrictions on independent prison monitoring and has urged authorities to improve detention conditions, ensure accountability and allow independent inspections. The organisation said that independent investigations are essential to establish whether neglect or abuse contributed to the deaths and prevent further loss of life.

Close 

Armed Men Storm Nigeria Opposition's Peter Obi Campaign Rally in Lagos

Armed men have attacked a campaign event organised by Nigerian opposition presidential candidate Peter Obi's Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC) in Lagos, assaulting supporters and journalists ahead of the January 16, 2027 election. The attackers reportedly stormed the venue carrying axes, clubs and machetes, triggering clashes that spilled into the streets before police arrived and dispersed the crowds with tear gas. A journalist was beaten and robbed of his recording equipment. NDC supporters blamed the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), but the party denied involvement, saying there was no evidence to support the allegations. The attack has renewed concerns about political intimidation and election-related violence as campaigning intensifies ahead of the vote.

World.title: Kenya: Kalonzo Takes Ruto Fight to U.S. Congress Ahead of 2027
World.content:
Nairobi — Wiper leader Kalonzo Musyoka is taking the opposition's campaign against President William Ruto to the United States, where he plans to engage American lawmakers and rally Kenyans in the diaspora ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Kalonzo will lead a nine-member delegation on a seven-day US tour from November 18 to 24, combining a meeting with members of the US Congress at Capitol Hill with diaspora town halls and institutional engagements across six cities.

The tour will take him to Washington, Boston, Germantown, Baltimore, Minneapolis and Cleveland.

"He is expected to present the opposition's alternative agenda and mobilise support among Kenyans living abroad," Paloma Gatabaki, the Communications Lead in Musyoka's office said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to a media advisory issued by his office, the visit will begin with a congressional engagement in Washington on November 18, followed by a meeting with the technology and investment community at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Boston.

Kalonzo will also hold a town hall with Kenyans in the Washington, DC, Maryland and Virginia region before travelling to Minnesota and Ohio for further diaspora engagements.

The opposition leader is also scheduled to attend the Somali Hero Awards and Somali Book Fair in Minneapolis, alongside former Kenyan diplomat Mohamed Abdi Afey, and take part in a Kenya-Africa reception in Cleveland.

The tour comes as opposition leaders intensify efforts to build a united political front against Ruto ahead of the 2027 polls.

The delegation is expected to depart the US for Nairobi on November 24.

World.title: Popular snack may help support brain health in older adults, new study finds
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An unsuspecting snack could help support brain health in older adults, new research suggests.

A small study by researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands, published in the journal Food & Function in September, found that eating peanuts regularly may improve how the brain's memory-related regions respond to insulin.

The study involved just 31 healthy older adults, and researchers did not determine whether the changes could prevent cognitive decline or Alzheimer's disease.

POPULAR FOODS AMERICANS EAT EVERY DAY LINKED TO SILENT BRAIN DAMAGE, ALARMING STUDY FINDS

In addition to regulating blood sugar, insulin helps nerve cells in the brain to grow and communicate with each other, which in turn can support overall cognitive function.

Consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts every day positively affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults, the study found.

"This is an interesting study because we're increasingly recognizing that insulin plays an important role in brain health, not just blood sugar regulation," Kellyann Niotis, a New York-based preventive neurologist, told Fox News Digital. "Insulin has important functions in the brain, including supporting communication between brain cells and the processes involved in learning and memory."

"I would not interpret these findings as evidence that peanuts prevent Alzheimer's."

The study involved 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75 who ate 60 grams, or around two servings, of peanuts daily for 16 weeks.

CLICK HERE TO 

Participants could choose what time of day they ate the skin-roasted peanuts, which were provided in premeasured packets.

During a control phase of the study, participants did not eat any peanuts.

Using MRI scans to measure various aspects of brain health, the researchers discovered that eating peanuts every day for 16 weeks led to an approximately 4% increase in overall blood flow in the brain.

Researchers also observed improved insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions, including the hippocampus.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"We know that insulin resistance and metabolic dysfunction are associated with an increased risk of cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease," Niotis said. "What we're still trying to understand is whether improving insulin signaling specifically within the brain can help prevent or delay AD."

The study found that daily consumption of about 60 grams of unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts for 16 weeks may benefit brain insulin responsiveness in older adults.

"I would not interpret these findings as evidence that peanuts prevent Alzheimer's. And it's unlikely that one food will ever have that much power," Niotis said. "The strongest nutritional evidence continues to support overall dietary patterns, rather than any single food."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Because this was such a small study, she added, researchers "don't yet know whether these changes translate into meaningful benefits for memory or long-term brain health."

The research was funded by the Peanut Institute Foundation, which the study reported had no role in its design, analysis or publication decisions.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I would much rather see someone focus on eating a Mediterranean-style diet consistently than worry about whether they're eating enough peanuts," Niotis said.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

Companies that have gotten back to business are doing exactly what the law and their shareholders require of them. Threatening them for following the law and fulfilling their core mission is not legitimate oversight. It is an attempt to reimpose political control.

Corporate directors and officers already operate under clear legal duties. Their primary obligation is to the corporation and its shareholders — not to any political party, activist group or congressional committee that wants to use private enterprise as a vehicle for social change.

TOP DEM ON COMMITTEE FIRES BACK AFTER WHITE HOUSE COUNSEL WARNS AGAINST OVERREACH AMID INVESTIGATION THREATS

When politicians demand that companies ignore those duties in favor of ideological priorities, the correct response is not surrender. It is resistance. Shareholders are not a secondary constituency. Their interests are the reason the company exists. Political bullying does not override that reality or primary obligation. Corporate America has been granted emancipation from the shackles of heavy-handed progressive activism. Why would any company voluntarily be taken captive again?

At 1792 Exchange, we have tracked these trends through our Corporate Bias Ratings and Back to Business resources. The data show a measurable shift: companies are exiting activist frameworks, backing away from political engagement unrelated to their business and refocusing on operational excellence. This is healthy. It reduces legal exposure, improves talent decisions and better aligns corporate activity with the interests of customers and owners. Our work exists to encourage corporations to make decisions and set policies that are enduring and will remain unswayed by changing political winds.

The incoming Democratic majority now faces a choice. It can treat private companies that have rejected progressive activism and adopted greater neutrality as prime targets for investigation, or it can honor the principles of free enterprise and economic freedom to serve customers and shareholders without imposed partisan litmus tests.

This is not routine oversight. It is political retribution dressed up as "accountability." And the hypocrisy is impossible to miss.

The former path will waste congressional resources, chill ordinary business decision-making and confirm that the real objective is the advancement of an ideological agenda. The latter path would leave companies to do what they are supposed to do: serve their shareholders, produce excellent goods and services and treat their employees, customers and suppliers well.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

And that is the path that creates greater opportunity and greater prosperity for all Americans.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Companies that have punted the scorecards and returned to their core missions should stand firm. Their duty is to their shareholders, employees and customers, not to the political preferences of whoever holds the gavel in the congressional committees.

World.title: Democrats won Congress, but their Trump obsession could give it right back
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Very few in Washington saw Democrats taking both chambers of Congress to this extent. The results changed who controls Congress, but they did not change what voters need: lower costs, a stronger economy, and a government focused on the problems families face.

Republicans should take the result seriously and make a clear case for how conservative policies can meet those needs. In the lame-duck session, Congress still has to fund the government and pass the annual defense bill. Republicans should work to finish that business and show voters that governing matters more than scoring points.

The bigger test begins in January. Democratic leaders have promised investigations into the administration, its officials, and companies. That choice could consume the new Congress. It could also repeat a political mistake Democrats have made before: turning their opposition to Trump into the central story, and giving him the chance to cast himself as the target of a partisan campaign.

JAMIE RASKIN CALLS CONCERNS OVER SPENDING TOO MUCH TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP A MEDIA 'NARRATIVE'

That argument helped Trump in 2024. He made the prosecutions and investigations against him a central part of his appeal, and voters returned him to the White House. Democrats should understand the risk. A Congress organized around investigating Trump could once again make him the central figure in the national debate, while leaving less time and attention for the issues voters want addressed.

The stakes extend beyond the administration. Democratic lawmakers have warned that companies, too, should expect investigations. When Congress puts private businesses under a partisan spotlight because of their dealings with the government or their connection to a political dispute, the consequences reach employees, investors, and communities. It can also make businesses think twice about working with the federal government, even when that partnership serves the public.

JEFFRIES LEAVES DOOR OPEN TO INVESTIGATING MAJOR TRUMP ALLY AS DEMOCRATS PREPARE TO TAKE POWER

Republicans should call out that overreach clearly. A congressional majority should not use subpoenas and hearings to intimidate political opponents or companies associated with them. If Democrats spend the next two years pursuing a sweeping investigation agenda, Republicans should press them to explain what it will do to lower costs, strengthen the economy, or improve Americans’ lives.

But Republicans cannot build a strategy around waiting for Democrats to overreach. They need to offer a credible alternative: a practical agenda on affordability and economic opportunity, serious attention to energy and national security, and a willingness to work on solutions that can win support across party lines.

ELAINE PARKER: DEMOCRAT WIN IS A WAKE-UP CALL FOR REPUBLICANS, NOT A VOTE FOR SOCIALISM

In the minority, Republicans will have fewer tools to set the agenda. They will still have a responsibility to represent our constituents, make the case for their ideas, and hold Democrats accountable for the choices they make. That means staying focused on results and resisting the temptation to answer every partisan maneuver with one of their own.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The election handed Democrats control of Congress. It did not give them a blank check to turn the next two years into a campaign of subpoenas, hearings, and headlines. If that is their priority, voters will see the difference between a party focused on governing and one focused on Trump. Republicans should be ready to make that case, and to show voters what they would do with the chance to lead again.

World.title: A spy took out Nvidia’s CEO. Here’s how America still wins the AI race
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

With Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, an accused Chinese spy has taken out the No. 1 player on America’s AI roster. This is worse than a first-and-goal fumble. It’s a body blow that puts the U.S.-China AI race in flux.

Chinese President Xi Jinping knows that if he doesn’t stop the momentum soon, America’s lead in AI will forestall his country’s plans to take over and become a world hegemon.

If Nvidia stumbles without Huang, China has us right where it wants us. Nvidia was the first company to surpass the $5 trillion milestone in market capitalization. Fellow CEOs like Michael Dell lauded him as a "great partner and friend, a true leader and visionary of the AI age" just last spring. Yet reports of Nvidia chip smuggling led Singapore to launch an investigation in 2025.

SOUND OFF ON JENSEN HUANG'S RESIGNATION FROM NVIDIA

Here's what America must do to stop China’s assault.

1. Wake up to the pervasive China threat.

It comes as no surprise that an accused Chinese spy targeted Jensen Huang. Americans have to wise up.

The Wall Street Journal reported back in 2022 on China’s attempts to influence state and local government leaders and officials. Americans in the defense sector already know to steer clear of inquisitive strangers at trade shows.

Sales and market share were not always integral to national security policy. Back in the Cold War, it was enough to ban exports of sensitive items. That won’t work now.

Sad to say, but Chinese citizens should be treated cautiously. Due to China’s national security laws, every Chinese citizen operating abroad, whether a high-flying executive or a student at a U.S. university, is obliged to give the Ministry of State Security information, if asked.

US ATTORNEY WARNS CHINESE ESPIONAGE IS 'EXTREMELY PERVASIVE,' SAYS BEIJING 'PLAYING THE LONG GAME'

2. Encourage the competitors.

Nvidia’s market share is massive, but it is not the only game in town. Top rival AMD — whose processors power El Capitan, the supercomputer that claimed the world's No. 1 spot upon its debut — is a major competitor. Meanwhile, tech giants like Google, AWS, Meta and Microsoft are increasingly deploying their own "custom silicon" in-house and via cloud services, part of a custom AI chip market projected by some analysts to grow from $32 billion in 2026 to $132 billion by 2035. As Google rolls out newer generations of its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) to challenge Nvidia’s dominance, hyperscalers are actively working to reduce their reliance on Nvidia's hardware.

WINNING THE AI RACE MEANS BEATING CHINA ON INNOVATION, COST AND TRUST

"Nvidia is investigating its own CEO. Google is busy building the chips that could take its customers," wrote Jared Blikre at Yahoo Finance on Monday after Google released two new tensor processing units to do battle with Nvidia’s chips.

3. Don’t rock the boat on investment.

The U.S. ability to deploy capital for startups, mergers and other investments is a key advantage over China. Huang was a financial engine for AI. In China, the state invests; here, it takes Big Tech players to fuel the AI ecosystem. One of the scariest aspects of the uncertainty at Nvidia centers on Huang’s financial support for many other customers and partner companies in the AI ecosystem.

THE BIGGEST THREAT IN AMERICA'S RACE WITH CHINA ISN'T BEIJING, TECH EXECUTIVE WARNS

Let’s start with a few examples of how Nvidia uses its cash: a $3 billion purchase of Meta stock and a $105 billion guarantee for OpenAI’s leases for data centers in Ohio. Colette Kress is stepping up from her role as CFO to serve as Nvidia’s interim CEO, so she will have good visibility into these deals. Cash needs to keep flowing, and the U.S. must resist overly restrictive regulations.

4. Win global market share.

Clearly, Huang wanted to fight for China’s AI chip market. The backstory on Nvidia and China is complicated. Nvidia held a 95% market share in China in 2022 until Xi Jinping’s self-reliance policies and U.S. export bans turned the tables. Nvidia’s share fell to 40% in 2025 and is forecast to fall to 8% in 2026, as reported by Fast Company. "If the United States doesn’t want to partake, participate in China, Huawei has got China covered, and Huawei has got everybody else covered," CEO Jensen Huang said in a June 2025 interview with CNBC.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Sales and market share were not always integral to national security policy. Back in the Cold War, it was enough to ban exports of sensitive items. That won’t work now. Chinese companies like Huawei are eager to set up their AI tech stacks and data centers to score market share and boost Chinese innovation.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The AI race is one the U.S. government cannot win by itself. We’ll see if Nvidia can still carry the torch.

World.title: Pence leaves door open to 2028 White House run, issues stark warning to GOP after midterm disaster
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

EXCLUSIVE - Former Vice President Mike Pence isn't ruling out another run for the White House in 2028, telling Fox News Digital that he has heard from people across the country about a potential presidential bid.

The former vice president also delivered a warning to his party following the GOP's severe setbacks in the 2026 midterm elections, arguing that Republicans risk another defeat unless they abandon departures from the traditional conservative principles that have defined the party for decades.

Pence, who unsuccessfully campaigned for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, said at an event in September at the Economic Club of Washington that he had "no plans" to run for president or any other elected office in 2028.

But in his first interview since the midterms, Pence appeared to leave the door open to another White House bid, telling Fox News Digital he's received outreach urging him to consider another White House bid.

ONLY ON FOX NEWS: PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE TO VANCE, TRUMP

"We've been hearing from a lot of people around the country. I've been very humbled by that," he said.

Pence didn't reveal any timeline for making a 2028 decision.

Instead, he repeatedly emphasized that "the most important thing is that we win the presidency in 2028. And to do that, I think it will be essential that we focus first on what we're for before we focus on who we're for."

WILL TRUMP AVOID MAKING AN ENDORSEMENT IN THE 2028 GOP NOMINATION RACE?

Pence, who has seen Advancing American Freedom, his policy and advocacy organization, dramatically expand over the past year, highlighted that he's going to "continue to lean into advocating that broad mainstream conservative agenda that's defined the Republican Party for the last 50 years."

"The truth is, if we don't return the Republican Party to the principles of a strong defense, limited government, fiscal responsibility and the right to life, it won't matter who we nominate in 2028."

Pence partially blames the GOP's midterm shellacking, which saw the Democrats win a large House majority and also regain control of the Senate, on what he argues is President Donald Trump's second term retreat from conservative principles and towards a populist agenda.

Pence, who served as Trump's first-term vice president, claimed that "this version of Republicanism was just rejected by the American people" in what he called "the wreckage of the 2026 midterm elections."

Asked for comment, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital, "Mike Pence’s total and complete lack of courage caused untold damage to our great country. If Republican voters cared what Mike Pence had to say, he wouldn’t have had to drop out of the presidential race months before the Iowa caucuses."

VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS

Looking ahead, Pence said, "I don't know what the future holds, but all of my energies, all of my focus and my calling now is to be a champion and an advocate for the conservative principles that have defined our party, led us to our greatest successes, and always made America strong and prosperous and free."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Asked if he doesn't run, he could support Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio if either seeks the GOP nomination, Pence answered, "What I'm gonna be looking for is men and women who embrace that historic traditional conservative agenda of the Republican Party."

He argued that "there's a lot of folks on the populist right that suggest that people that that hew to that old Reagan tradition don't know what time it is, and I think the midterm elections have given a verdict on their approach to Republicanism."

World.title: Howard Lutnick agrees to testify as bipartisan pressure grows over Nvidia scandal
World.content:
Earlier Thursday, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told reporters that Lutnick should appear voluntarily, though if he doesn’t, “He may need to be subpoenaed.”

Blumenthal said one thing he wants to know is, “Were export controls relaxed?”

Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind., said in an interview with Fox News that he’d like Lutnick to testify before Congress “ASAP,” noting concerns about chips being exported that should not have.

“We have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns about what’s happened over the last year that would allow some of these issues to continue, to chips being exported, it appears, to defy President Trump’s orders for those exports to be stopped,” Banks said.

Huang’s extramarital activity has added to concerns that Nvidia chips may have been smuggled or illegally accessed by AI companies in China. Nvidia has said that it complies with U.S. laws on exports.

Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., told reporters on Capitol Hill Thursday that Lutnick “certainly should” testify before Congress.

“I think he should be given the opportunity and the strong encouragement to do it without a subpoena,” Cramer said. “If a subpoena becomes necessary, that would be too bad. But yes, he absolutely should.”

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement that Lutnick needs to “explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military.”

The White House has defended Lutnick, writing in a statement that the president “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.”

Huang has previously praised Lutnick’s role in uplifting the U.S. efforts to lead in AI.

“Howard is the person I talk to most in the administration — he’s on top of the technology and learning the industry quickly,” Huang said while appearing at a Nvidia panel alongside Lutnick in September 2025.

Reps. Gregory Meeks of New York, Gabe Amo of Rhode Island and Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California — top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee — signed a letter Monday demanding answers from Lutnick over the Trump administration’s “approval of advanced AI chip exports,” noting “concerning links to China” and “alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties” to Huang.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., said Thursday that Huang had agreed to brief lawmakers, though the date and venue were still being negotiated. In a new letter to Huang on Thursday, Mast asked that he appear before the committee on Dec. 1 for a “closed-door, transcribed interview,” adding that a subpoena would be issued if Huang did not confirm the interview by Friday evening.

Some members of Congress said they want answers from Lutnick much sooner than next month, when the Senate Banking Committee has scheduled its hearings.

“Come here before Thanksgiving. Give us the facts,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said Thursday.

Tillis, who is leaving Congress in January, said it would be wise for Lutnick to testify to Congress now, before Democrats take control of both chambers next year, adding the secretary “should recognize right now he’s got a lot of Republicans that are pulling for him.”

“I’m not one of them, but he does,” Tillis said. “So it would seem to me that he would do himself a favor by getting in a room with Republicans, whether it’s a committee hearing or not, and lay out the facts so that he’s got a group of people that are generally going to take at face value what he says.”
