World.title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for majority leader
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., announced Thursday he will run for Senate majority leader, becoming the first to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the position.

“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from Donald Trump’s disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement.

Van Hollen’s move follows attempts by grassroots progressives — and some newly elected Democratic senators — to draft him for the position as some seek an alternative to Schumer.

“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader,” he added.

Schumer, who has led the Senate Democratic caucus since 2017, remains favored to retain the position of Democratic leader. Still, it’s likely to be the most serious challenge he has gotten for the job.

Democratic senators will hold a vote in December to choose their leadership for the next Congress. That vote is held behind closed doors and requires a simple majority of the caucus.

Van Hollen said in an interview with MS NOW Thursday night that more than 10 senators have pledged to support him.

“We have a lot of people, but here’s the thing about an election like this: As you say, I’m the underdog,” Van Hollen said. “I told people I was thinking about it, and so now we are opening up the process, right?”

He added, “Now people will have to make a decision, one way or the other, and they have to decide whether they want to vote for change or whether they want to vote for the status quo.”

Van Hollen plans to run on having the new Democratic majority use every available tool to end the Iran war, starting with the upcoming government funding measure to avoid a December shutdown, according to his team. He’s also proposing to reverse President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” get money out of politics and tackle corruption.

Van Hollen, 67, is newer to Congress than Schumer, 75, but both men have served in Congress for decades. Van Hollen was first elected to the Senate in 2016. Before that, he served in the House for over a decade, beginning in 2003. Schumer was first elected to the House in 1980 and moved up to the Senate in 1999.

Schumer responded on X to Van Hollen’s announcement, saying he has the votes to win.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together—55 seats and counting is an amazing result—and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” he said. “I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people.”

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., said Wednesday that he would support Van Hollen if he decided to launch an official bid for the leadership role. The day prior, Sanders had said he would not back Schumer, saying at a press conference that “in my view, the time is now for change.”

After Van Hollen’s announcement on Thursday night, Sanders wrote in a post on X that he would be supporting his bid to lead Senate Democrats.

“The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families,” he wrote.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan endorsed Van Hollen for the role shortly after his announcement Thursday night, writing in a post on X, “I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience.”

“We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” El-Sayed wrote, adding that to “earn our mandate,” Democrats “will require bold leadership.”

Still, Schumer has maintained support from longtime colleagues who point to his work as minority leader ahead of Democrats’ landslide midterm victories.

“Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” Sen. Angus King, I-Maine, wrote in a statement on Thursday night. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”

King wrote that Schumer “outlined an aggressive plan for the new Democratic majority which is directly responsive to the message we heard from the voters, and he has the experience and unique mastery of the Senate process to make it happen.”

Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., also urged Democrats not to turn their backs on Schumer earlier this week, saying that “no one has put in the time and effort that anyone has put into this cycle than he did.”

Gillibrand, who oversaw Senate Democrats’ campaign arm for the midterms, said Schumer ensured that resources were provided to help 100,000 new voters register in Mississippi, where Sen.-elect Scott Colom just captured a stunning victory.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done, and that’s why you will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position,” Gillibrand said.

World.title: Democrat Cindy Holscher defeats Republican Ty Masterson in Kansas governor’s race
World.content:
Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher has narrowly won Kansas’ race for governor, NBC News projected Thursday, extending the party’s hold on the office in the red state.

Holscher defeated Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, who was backed by President Donald Trump, to succeed two-term Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly.

While Trump carried Kansas — a state where registered Republicans outnumber registered Democrats nearly 2 to 1 — by double digits in the latest three presidential elections, polling had shown a close race down the stretch due mostly to voter frustrations with Trump and his handling of the economy. Democrats also benefited from increased attention on the traditionally conservative state as its Senate race tightened.

Kansas Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher. Evert Nelson / The Capital-Journal / USA Today via Imagn

Holscher’s victory came despite a nearly 3-to-1 Republican ad spending advantage in the general election, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact.

In the general election, Holscher aggressively tied Masterson to Trump, while also maintaining that she’d find areas to work with the administration.

“I think that’s a concern that [Masterson] has the ear of the administration, because the administration also has a hold on him. You won’t see Ty Masterson pushing back against bad policy, like tariffs that are hurting our farmers or the importing of beef that are hurting our ranchers,” she told local news station KMBC in October. She added that will also “work with folks” in the administration “to make sure we bring good things to Kansas.”

Masterson, who was endorsed by Trump, attempted to distance himself from the president on his website and in campaign materials. But his connection to Trump, who faced increasingly lower approval ratings in the traditionally red state, was unmistakable: the president came to Kansas over the last weekend before Election Day to campaign alongside Masterson and the Republican candidate in the state’s Senate race, Sen. Roger Marshall, who lost his re-election bid to Democrat Adam Hamilton.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Ty Masterson. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty

Meanwhile, Holscher also prominently highlighted her opposition to new data center construction throughout her campaign.

“This field of Kansas sunflowers is under threat because big tech wants to build a day out of center. As governor, I’ll hit pause on data centers until we can set up firm guardrails to protect our communities and our budgets,” she said in one spot featuring her standing in a field.

Masterson has opposed a moratorium on data centers and has defended a 2025 law he voted for giving a sales tax exemption for data center investments. Holscher has called for a statewide moratorium on the new data center construction. Building the Future, a pro-data center super PAC, jumped into the race last month to boost Masterson.

Holscher’s win followed a primary that featured Democratic infighting. Kelly, who has maintained strong job approval ratings in the state, had endorsed Holscher’s Democratic primary opponent, state Sen. Ethan Corson, and issued stark warnings to voters about being “very concerned about the direction Kansas will go in” if Holscher were to win.

Holscher had run a more progressive-styled campaign, while Corson ran as a moderate. Kelly endorsed Holscher following the primary.

World.title: FBI recovers $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance
World.content:
Washington — The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange.

The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor.

The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total.

Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.

Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos.

U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program.

"Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities," First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli said in a Justice Department statement. "Today's seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime."

U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro said in the statement that "By springing into action at a moment's notice, we worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks. The North Korean regime may think they are sophisticated cyber criminals, but we have consistently met them head on, as we did here seizing more than $1.2 billion of their stolen assets."

World.title: Microsoft battling major worldwide outage
World.content:
From Asia to the U.S., a Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted many users, companies and some government operations as the technology giant struggles to fix the issue.

Microsoft said in an update early Friday that the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using "a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure."

The company said it didn't have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident "with urgency and priority until full resolution."

More than 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook earlier on Thursday although new reports have since fallen from that peak.

Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue.

In its latest update, Microsoft said, "Recovery actions are ongoing and have progressed in phases across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure. ... However, service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline."

Widespread impact

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.

U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.

In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024.

Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, this could "impact the production timeline," he said.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.

Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.

The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses.

In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that they were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

World.title: Van Hollen will challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader
World.content:
Washington — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.

"In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person – it's about answering that call," Van Hollen said in a post on X. "That's why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

The decision by Van Hollen, who said earlier this week he was in "listening mode" about running for majority leader, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership since it decisively won last week's midterms.

Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont quickly threw his support behind Van Hollen on Thursday. Some other Democrats have not yet committed to voting for Schumer in leadership elections, which are expected early next month, but haven't explicitly endorsed another candidate.

Van Hollen, 67, has been in the Senate since 2017 after representing the state in the House for more than a decade. The Maryland Democrat has gained attention from progressives in recent years. In 2024, he vocally supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticized the Biden administration's posture toward the war in Gaza. Van Hollen also gained attention when he traveled to El Salvador last year to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who lived in Maryland and had been sent to the country's notorious CECOT prison.

Supporters see Van Hollen as someone who's willing to speak to the issues progressives hold most dear. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told NPR in an interview this week that Van Hollen is "willing to take risks when it matters," citing his trip to El Salvador.

Schumer, 75, responded to Van Hollen's announcement in a post on X, saying he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead."

"I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," he wrote. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."

Schumer has led Senate Democrats since 2017, when he succeeded retiring Sen. Harry Reid of Nevada.

Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who chairs the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, defended Schumer at a news conference earlier this week, crediting his "strategic leadership."

"You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position," Gillibrand said. "We are about to win nine Senate seats — that has never happened in my political history."

Democratic Sen. Jacky Rosen of Nevada endorsed Schumer late Thursday, praising his work ahead of the midterms and writing, "I know he has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment."

The challenge comes as Schumer is still widely expected to hold on to the top leadership post, especially after the strong showing for Democrats in the midterm elections. Despite a Senate map that appeared unfavorable for the party heading into the cycle, Democrats flipped at least eight Senate seats — with one race remaining up in the air in Alaska — securing a sizable majority in the new Congress.

With the election results, Schumer has appeared to improve his position with the caucus, following a tumultuous tenure in recent years. The pushback took hold after the New York Democrat maneuvered to avoid a government shutdown in early 2025, prompting frustration from his party's left flank.

Later that year, he changed course and kept Democrats largely united through a record-breaking government shutdown as they sought to prevent the expiration of health insurance tax credits.

In an interview with MS NOW announcing his run for majority leader, Van Hollen acknowledged he is an "underdog," but said he has spoken with caucus members and believes the race is "very much in flux."

Asked what he would do differently from Schumer, Van Hollen suggested the current leader hasn't taken a firm enough stance on using the power of the purse to force the Trump administration to end the Iran war. He told host Jen Psaki that Democrats should use the Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government as leverage, saying it "should not be a finger-in-the-wind issue."

Van Hollen also criticized Schumer for, in his view, moving behind the scenes to back certain candidates in Democratic primaries — a longstanding point of contention for progressives.

"On the political side of the equation, we shouldn't have a Democratic leader who is getting involved in picking sides in open Democratic primaries. … We have two senators right now in the United States Senate who wouldn't be there if the current majority leader had his way," Van Hollen said, referring to El-Sayed and Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan.

Some members of the Democratic caucus — including both progressives like Sanders and moderates like Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas — have called for new leadership.

Sanders endorsed Van Hollen in a social media post late Thursday, writing: "The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families."

Two days earlier, Sanders announced in a news conference he would not support Schumer. Sanders was flanked by the more moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who said she was "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."

"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

World.title: GOP lawmakers press Huang and Lutnick to testify over Nvidia
World.content:
Republicans on Capitol Hill are pressing now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear before Congress early next month about the scandal that has rocked one of the most important companies in the world — as a Senate panel asks Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.

"We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk," the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, Foreign Affairs Committee and Intelligence Committee said in a statement requesting Huang's presence.

The three committee chairs wrote a letter Thursday asking Huang to appear for a closed-door interview on Dec. 1. They said if he does not accept their request by Friday evening, the House Foreign Affairs Committee will issue a subpoena.

The upper chamber has also pushed Huang to appear. Republican Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, asked Huang to testify voluntarily before the panel in the first week of December, but warned the committee is prepared to use its subpoena power if needed.

"The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote on X.

Nvidia, whose chips have fueled the AI boom, announced on Thursday that Huang had stepped down following a scandal over his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang's resignation from the company he co-founded has not dampened calls from members of Congress for answers about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to highly prized chips that are banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.

Moments before Nvidia announced Huang's resignation, Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said on CNBC on Thursday morning that he would happily support subpoenaing Huang. A Cramer spokesperson said he would still support subpoenaing the tech founder.

The controversy has also raised questions about whether the federal government has done enough to prevent Nvidia's chips from being diverted to China — and about the Trump administration's close relationship with Huang.

Scott asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear for a public hearing next month. The House Foreign Affairs Committee also requested testimony from Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler, who leads the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency that oversees export controls.

Some critics have argued Lutnick's Commerce Department should have taken action to prevent Megaspeed from buying chips. The New York Times reported that a Bureau of Industry and Security probe into the firm was halted last year.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told CNN on Thursday he wanted to hear from both Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, saying: "This is serious as an aneurysm."

Earlier Thursday, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China, GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, said lawmakers were "in discussions" with Huang "on a date to come and meet with us." But he added, "If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power."

Moolenaar and two other chairs — Rep. Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rep. Rick Crawford of the Intelligence Committee — first asked Huang to appear in a letter last week. They said the purpose of the closed-door briefing would be to discuss Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset." The lawmakers gave Huang a deadline of Wednesday to respond.

Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Thursday that they received a response. Mast said Huang indicated he's willing to appear. Moolenaar said that Huang's resignation "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony.

"I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune also told CBS News that he expects "there'll be an interest in doing oversight" in the Senate. Asked whether he wants Huang to testify, Thune said, "I think that it would make sense because of the, again, the nature of the association and the governments and the national security interests, what we're talking about here."

Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said Democrats have questions for the Trump administration, too.

"Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer said on X. "The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset."

President Trump, a friend of Huang's, has downplayed the scandal and said he doesn't believe Huang knew the Megaspeed executive was a spy. The president said Thursday that Huang had done a "fantastic job."

"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place — TIM COOK of Apple," the president posted to Truth Social.

World.title: Crews begin excavating site of building collapse in Brooklyn
World.content:
The death toll rose to eight Thursday after a Brooklyn building collapsed and an adjacent building was significantly damaged.

A three-story, multi-use building on Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a nearby construction site just after 4 p.m. Wednesday, tearing off the side of another building.

At least eight people were killed and 17 others were injured as of Thursday afternoon, according to the FDNY. Six people were found dead at the scene, and two died at the hospital.

"We know that this morning they pulled out, I believe a couple of construction workers that were on site last night, which added to the death toll this morning," said Councilwoman Farrah Louis.

The structure was fully occupied by residents, and workers were in the construction pit performing excavation work at the time of the collapse.

Emergency crews worked through the night under floodlights with the help of drones and K-9 units to get through the massive piles of rubble.

Video showed dozens of firefighters at the scene Thursday morning searching for additional victims. First responders also used machinery to excavate debris.

The FDNY completed its rescue operations just after 3:30 p.m. Thursday after searching the entire site and determining there were no remaining victims.

Members of the New York City Fire Department and first responders search for victims in the rubble a day after a building collapsed in Brooklyn. Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images

The building collapse site has now been turned over to the Department of Buildings and the NYPD. Officials are trying to determine what caused the ground to give way.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the incident devastating, praising first responders for executing a grueling, high-risk technical operation.

"Rescue workers have spent the night searching the site of yesterday's building collapse, working under extremely dangerous conditions to find and save anyone who may still be trapped. I am heartbroken that eight New Yorkers have now lost their lives and at least 17 have been injured, including three firefighters. There are no words for a loss of this magnitude," he said in a post Thursday.

Investigators are conducting comprehensive reviews of the conditions at the collapsed building and neighboring construction site. Investigators said developers have active permits for excavation and foundation work associated with a new building project.

Records revealed the site had been cited for violations months before the disaster. Those were corrected, and work was allowed to resume in May.

Investigators have not determined whether that work contributed to the collapse.

A full stop-work order has been issued as recovery operations continue.

The Brooklyn District Attorney's Office is also investigating whether any criminal conduct contributed to the collapse.

World.title: Kratom and 7-OH can feel like 'a miracle.' They can also be addictive
World.content:
Kratom and 7-OH can feel like 'a miracle.' They can also be addictive

toggle caption i Mindy Schauer/MediaNewsGroup/Orange County Register via Getty Images

Tyler's opioid addiction began in his early 20s, and when he decided he wanted to quit, he used kratom leaf powders to help ease withdrawal symptoms.

Tyler, now 38, told NPR he thinks kratom helped him stop using opioids for a decade.

Tyler asked NPR to use only his first name because of the stigma attached to his history with drug use and addiction.

In early 2025, he saw a new product at a gas station called 7-OH. He hadn't heard of 7-OH, but said the tablets were advertised as "kratom products." He decided to try them, since the kratom powders he'd taken in the past "can be hard on your stomach," he said.

Sponsor Message

At first, 7-OH gave him a feeling of euphoria he described as similar to opioids, which "felt like a kind of a miracle," he said.

Nearly a year and a half later, he was in a rapid detox program in Michigan, where he was sedated to sleep through the withdrawals he experienced when he tried to stop taking it.

In the past few years, highly concentrated products with 7-OH — sometimes alongside other semi-synthetic opioids — have popped up online, and at many smoke shops, liquor stores and gas stations. They can come in the form of tablets, gummies, tonics and chocolate.

7-OH, or 7-hydroxymitragynine, is one of the major psychoactive ingredients in kratom, which comes from a tree in the coffee family. It's naturally found in kratom in very small amounts, and seems to act more like an opioid in the human brain than kratom leaf products. Kratom is used by some people with opioid addiction to maintain long-term recovery. Some people say it makes them feel energized or focused. Others describe the effects of kratom like those of opioids, and say it can relieve pain, feel calming or even create euphoria.

"More potent than I imagined"

Some users of 7-OH and kratom show classic signs of addiction, researchers and policy officials say. But the products are not always clearly labeled, so it's difficult or impossible for users to know what quantity of the substances they are consuming.

Sponsor Message

"I did not know at all what I was in for. It was much more potent than I had imagined," Tyler said.

Estimates of how many people use kratom and 7-OH in the U.S. are wide-ranging. Some suggest over 5 million people have used kratom in their lifetime. David Epstein, a senior investigator at the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Intramural Research Program, says he's seen estimates of kratom use as high as 15 million. Those estimates don't usually distinguish between whole leaf kratom, 7-OH or other related products.

In the last decade, the U.S. government has attempted to restrict both kratom and 7-OH products, but strong opposition to those moves by the public and powerful advocacy groups backing the substances have kept them federally legal.

That's started to change in the last few months.

A federal crackdown is likely on the way

No federal actions have been taken against "traditional botanical kratom," but a new federal restriction on some 7-OH products could go into place as early as Friday, Nov. 13, 2026.

The path there has not been straightforward. In August, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) restricted the making and sale of three semi-synthetic opioids derived from 7-OH and other related compounds: MGM-15, MGM-16 and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MGPI). Those compounds were listed under the Controlled Substances Act alongside the most highly restricted drugs, like heroin and LSD.

That caused backlash from kratom advocates who worried the rule would affect products with "trace amounts" of the semi-synthetic opioid, MGPI. One kratom advocacy organization, the American Kratom Association, filed a federal lawsuit on Aug. 26 against the DEA. It asked the DEA to ensure natural kratom products with traces of MGPI would remain legal.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) then issued a new recommendation on 7-OH and MGPI on Oct. 9, and the DEA changed its course. They now plan to restrict a narrower range of 7-OH and MGPI products: ones that contain higher concentrations of 7-OH and/or MGPI.

Sponsor Message

HHS and the DEA say they are not focusing on natural kratom products.

toggle caption i Yanawut/iStockphoto/Getty Images

The research on kratom and 7-OH

Many people who oppose the restriction say kratom and 7-OH products have kept them away from traditional opioids, and helped them manage chronic pain, mood and mental health. Some also point to the fact that opioid deaths in the U.S. are decreasing. In 2023 alone, a KFF report found there were over 79,000 opioid deaths, and in 2024 there were 54,000.

A recent report of data from 53 U.S. poison control centers shows reports of calls related to kratom increased about 1,200% between 2015 and 2025. Chris Holstege, a physician and a professor of emergency medicine and pediatrics at the University of Virginia's School of Medicine, is one of the authors of that report. He said he and the other authors "were a bit stunned" by those findings, which do not distinguish between kratom or products like 7-OH.

The report included 233 deaths associated with kratom during 2015–2025, with 79% of those deaths involving multiple substances. The most severe outcomes were linked to people using multiple substances alongside kratom products, like opioids, stimulants and benzodiazepines.

But Holstege points out over half the reports of calls, 62%, involved people using kratom without other drugs.

The authors used data on kratom from the National Poison Data System (NPDS), which includes calls from the public, healthcare professionals or medical examiners, and medical records.

For some, a "life-changing" dose

Still, there are people who report benefits of using kratom or 7-OH, said Epstein, the NIDA investigator.

NPR spoke to one mom in Delaware, Angela Wilson, 44, who said 7-OH has helped her manage excruciating chronic pain related to endometriosis, and symptoms of depression she's had since she was a teenager.

She said she's been taking 32 to 40 milligrams of 7-OH a day, split into three doses, for the last year and a half.

Sponsor Message

Wilson said kratom powders made her feel anxious and shaky, and 7-OH seems to work for her without those side effects.

"It's been truly life-changing for my family situation, my personal life," she said.

Wilson doesn't have health insurance, and said losing access to 7-OH under new restrictions would be "devastating" for her and her family.

"We're not really sure, you know, what I'm gonna do when it's not available," she said.

"It was game over." Dangers of addiction

Epstein has also heard stories like Tyler's. He said people can become addicted or dependent — and some of his ongoing research suggests that risk is higher with 7-OH products than with whole leaf kratom.

He said for some people, their 7-OH use "seemed to go nicely for the first couple of days, but then they found that they had to keep using to avoid withdrawal," Epstein said. "And some of them, not all of them, but some of them, even said they had to, you know, they couldn't make it through the night. They had to get up in the middle of the night to take more."

He said other people were happy with the effects they got from taking 7-OH and didn't feel like it caused problems for them.

Tyler told NPR that 7-OH tablets gave him more energy at first. He works a job where he's on his feet a lot, and with 7-OH, he said, " I can go, go, go, go, go, you know?"

He began taking around 300 to 400 mg of 7-OH a day, about ten times the dose Angela Wilson takes. In the next year, he said he made a few attempts to stop, but the withdrawals were debilitating.

"The best way to put it, I think, is to imagine having the flu, the worst flu you've had, you know, multiply that by at least three times," he said. "And then just know that all you gotta do is take one pill, and it's gone in seconds."

Sponsor Message

Another former kratom and 7-OH consumer, Brian, 41, told NPR at the height of his use, he was using much more 7-OH than both Angela Wilson and Tyler. Brian also asked NPR to use only his first name because of the stigma associated with drug use.

Brian used 1,200 mg of 7-OH — and estimates he spent around $150 each day — on the substance. He'd quit using opioids in 2016, but found kratom at a gas station in 2022. He said it claimed to help with energy.

"And 'cause literally right next to the register, nothing taboo about it, looks like those 5-Hour Energy shot type things," he said.

Brian said within minutes of taking it, he realized he felt "exactly" like he did when he'd been taking opioids.

"I was like, 'What is this?,'" he said. "'Like, are you telling me I found a legal, you know, healthy opiate that f***s you up and, you know, you feel great and no consequences, like the legality of it and everything?"

"I was like, 'This is it,'" he said.

Brian tried to stop taking kratom multiple times, but couldn't. One day at a smoke shop, he said the clerk offered him a sample of 7-OH. The clerk described it as a "version of kratom" that Brian could take in lower doses to get the same effects.

"Once I found these little tiny tablets — that I had to take one and it felt like I had taken an Oxycontin — you know, that was it," Brian said. "It was game over."

An uncertain future

Researchers say more research should be done to understand the potential benefits of kratom and 7-OH products, including whether they can help treat addiction. On their website, NIDA says, "early studies suggest kratom and kratom compounds warrant further study as experimental treatments for substance use disorders, specifically opioid use disorder."

Sponsor Message

In the meantime, Holstege, at the University of Virginia's School of Medicine, says current marketing around kratom products seems to attract users for other reasons.

"I find it a little hard to believe that all the shops that are popping up around my campus right now are trying to advertise to people who are addicted to opioids," he said. "So the question is, what else are they advertising this product for?"

" I certainly have a growing list of patients in addiction clinics who are addicted to this, and in withdrawal, that we're having to manage," Holstege added.

Brian stopped taking 7-OH in April 2026, when he said he decided to "quit cold turkey." He said he experienced more debilitating withdrawals from 7-OH than he had from quitting opioids. He noted, though, he'd had a much easier time accessing 7-OH, and took it more frequently than he'd taken opioids.

When stopping 7-OH, he said he felt fearful, anxious, and had gastrointestinal issues. He lost the desire to leave his house.

"It was a nightmare," Brian said.

Tyler told NPR he hasn't used 7-OH or kratom since he traveled to the Michigan detox program in March. He said he doesn't think he would have been able to stop using 7-OH without that program.

"There's no chance," he said. "It's just too addictive and too accessible."

He said the road to feeling like himself again has been even longer than when he stopped using opioids. With opioids, he said, it took a few weeks to feel like he had energy again.

With 7-OH, he said the process has taken months.

"Kind of just this week I'm starting to feel kinda great," he said in October. "But it's been a long journey of getting my energy back."

World.title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who chastised him
World.content:
Hegseth awards medal to soldier who chastised him

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

Coming out of the bruising the Republicans suffered in the midterms, this week was bearing up to be a bad one for Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Many thought he'd be the first in the administration to be fired for his support of the Iran war, which proved unpopular with voters.

Then a member of his own party called for a vote to impeach him and, in an embarrassing incident that went viral, he also got chastised for poor decorum when visiting the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

Still, he managed to survive the former – except for Thomas Massie, who sponsored the resolution to impeach him, all other Republicans in the House voted against it – and sought to turn the latter into a PR opportunity.

Sponsor Message

The day after the impeachment effort, an incident occurred at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, one of America's most sacred military sites. It happened when Hegseth, his wife, and staffers went to lay a wreath at the memorial just outside Washington D.C., to mark Veteran's Day on Wednesday.

Someone in the defense secretary's group laughed loudly, prompting a sentinel on duty at Arlington National Cemetery to shout: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!"

As the video spread on social media, there was a flurry of condemnation online, with some dubbing Hegseth "the secretary of offense."

Political opponents, including Rep. Gwen Moore (D-Wis.), as well as former GOP congressman Adam Kinzinger, criticized Hegseth and his group.

"Pete Hegseth continues to demonstrate his utter lack of fitness for his office," said Moore on X . "One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier."

On Thursday, the embattled Defense secretary tried to regain control of the narrative. He invited the soldier who bellowed at him, Spc. Thomas Iglesias, to the Pentagon, where he honored him with the "Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."

Sponsor Message

"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth wrote. "Carry on Patriots."

World.title: Rivers in the sky are raining down on the Pacific Northwest. What are they?
World.content:
Rivers in the sky are raining down on the Pacific Northwest. What are they?

toggle caption i David Ryder/Getty Images

It's the wettest time of the year for one of the wettest parts of the country: the Pacific Northwest.

This week is no exception as heavy rain, high tides and a rising sea level hit the West Coast.

And more storms are on their way.

Two atmospheric rivers, bringing heavy rain, will pound parts of Oregon and Washington state back-to-back on Friday and Saturday. Two other atmospheric rivers already dropped multiple inches of rain on both states earlier this week.

Sponsor Message

"What's really problematic is when you get compounding impacts from multiple atmospheric rivers," said Josh Weiss, a meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Weather Prediction Center. Those impacts include flash flooding, urban flooding and even landslides, he said.

This year's atmospheric river season, which runs from October to March, is off to a fast start, said Weiss.

What do we mean by a river in the sky?

An atmospheric river is a narrow band of water vapor pushed by the wind. Loaded up with moisture, it dumps rain or snow. These rivers can be up to 2,000 miles long and 600 miles wide, said F. Martin Ralph, the director of the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes at UC San Diego's Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

"It's literally a river in the sky," said Ralph, one of the leading researchers on atmospheric rivers. These rivers are a natural climate pattern. In fact, about 50 to 60% of rain in California comes from atmospheric rivers, Weiss said.

toggle caption i Gillian Flaccus/AP

Residents in the Pacific Northwest are used to heavy downpours. But the atmospheric rivers are hitting as El Niño's warm ocean waters contribute to rising sea levels and fuel storm systems. And right now, these natural weather patterns are coinciding with annual high tides, known as King tides . That leaves coastal and inland waterways along the West Coast at risk for flooding.

Sponsor Message

Ralph said that according to 40 years of data from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, 90% or more of all flood damage in the Western U.S. is from atmospheric rivers.

This weekend, Jeff Michalski, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Seattle, said that Washington's coast could be hit by significant 20-foot swells.

Pineapple and rum

People may know atmospheric rivers from their nicknames, such as Pineapple Express or Rum Runner Express. These names describe where the atmospheric river originates. A Pineapple Express, which came across the Pacific Ocean from Hawaii in late October, caused devastating flooding and multiple deaths in the Southwest's Four Corners regions .

Atmospheric rivers aren't just a West Coast phenomenon. Some larger nor'easters on the East Coast can pack a "nasty" atmospheric river, UCSD's Ralph said.

The term atmospheric river is one of a few technical science terms that have gained traction on social media and in the news over the past few years, along with El Niño and Kelvin waves .

But is there a relationship between El Niño and atmospheric rivers? Do the warm ocean temperatures associated with El Niño and the heat those waters release make the rivers stronger? That was Ralph's theory back in 2015, but his research showed the opposite.

"[Atmospheric rivers] don't dance to the tune of El Niño," Ralph said

Climate scientists say there also isn't enough data to connect the weather pattern to human-caused global warming , although a warming world does mean more water vapor in the atmosphere .

"We've got to keep our eyes" for atmospheric rivers, Ralph said. "Whether it's an El Niño year or a La Niña year or a No Niño year."

World.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
World.content:
Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories

toggle caption i Don Ryan/AP/AP

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.

An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.

Many parents do not.

"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."

Sponsor Message

When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom.

But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified, Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.

In a post on X, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.

A baffling move

Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.

Sponsor Message

She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.

Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.

"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."

When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement, where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.

NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.

The "AI or nothing" approach

In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "unacceptable risk" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.

The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.

Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.

Sponsor Message

"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.

Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.

He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.

"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."

The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.

Edited by Nirvi Shah and Nicole Cohen

Google is a financial supporter of NPR.

World.title: Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients
World.content:
Fed up with the healthcare industry, this red state capped insulin prices for patients

YouTube

HILLSBORO, N.D. — The Kritzberger family has farmed in the Red River Valley for more than a century. They once had livestock. Now they grow sugar beets, soybeans and grains.

Like many farmers, they labor to balance the books.

"We're in an incredible amount of debt," Ang Kritzberger said as she walked the farm on a recent fall morning.

For the past 10 years, the Kritzbergers have had another worry. Their daughter Nina has Type 1 diabetes. That landed the family in a national debate about how to protect patients from high insulin costs.

Nina was diagnosed when she was 7.

"I slept by her bedside for the first 60 days," Ang Kritzberger said. "And I had to stick her finger every two hours, 24 hours a day, to make sure that she was OK."

toggle caption i Hannah Norman/KFF Health News

The Kritzbergers also pay a lot out-of-pocket every year for medical care, despite having insurance — at least $8,000 for drugs, supplies and medical appointments.

That's not uncommon. Soaring insulin prices for years forced people with diabetes to pay hundreds, even thousands, of dollars. Many rationed insulin, with sometimes deadly consequences.

But today, there's a growing movement across the country to cap what people with diabetes pay for insulin. That's brought together Democrats and Republicans, tapping an emerging consensus that the government should protect people from high drug prices.

Sponsor Message

"Typically, Republicans are more on the free-market side of things, Democrats are more supportive of intervening," said North Dakota state Sen. Sean Cleary, a Republican. "But in this case, I think there was broad-enough agreement that this market just wasn't functioning for folks."

Cleary co-sponsored legislation last year to cap patients' insulin bills at $25 a month. North Dakota is one of 29 states that have enacted such measures.

The cap limits what patients have to pay out-of-pocket every month for insulin — even if they have a high deductible that might force them to pay thousands of dollars before coverage kicks in for other healthcare, such as physician visits, hospitalizations or other prescriptions.

Patient advocates including the American Diabetes Association began pushing for out-of-pocket caps and other protections amid spiking insulin prices and stories of patients who had died because they couldn't afford their medicine.

toggle caption i Hannah Norman/KFF Health News

About a fifth of the estimated 40 million Americans with diabetes depend on insulin. The drug has been in use for a century. But steep price hikes boosted patients' out-of-pocket costs, which hit an average $470 a year in 2018 for people with private health insurance, according to federal data.

Prices have since moderated as drug companies faced a public backlash. Average yearly out-of-pocket costs for people with private insurance declined to $220 in 2025.

But for many families like the Kritzbergers, the prospect of a government cap offered protection from future price hikes and some relief from the anxiety of a serious disease.

Sponsor Message

Nina Kritzberger, now 17, said she already has a lot to worry about.

"I have to make sure I have insulin, a spare pump, a spare Dexcom," she said, ticking off the equipment that patients with diabetes rely on. "Oh, what if my pump doesn't work, or my Dexcom? Then I have to bring a testing kit. What if I go low? I need Gatorade, glucose."

toggle caption i Hannah Norman/KFF Health News

A missed dose of insulin could land her in the hospital. "My body would start attacking itself and start shutting down," she said. "And then I would die."

The price cap strategy initially caught on with Democrats. In 2019, Colorado became the first state to enact what was called an insulin copay cap. State-regulated health plans there cannot charge patients more than $100 for a 30-day supply of the drug.

In 2022, President Joe Biden signed legislation that capped insulin prices for Medicare enrollees at $35 a month. Biden and congressional Democrats wanted to extend the cap to people with private health insurance, including Americans with employer-provided coverage. But Republican opposition sank that proposal.

In North Dakota, state Sen. Tim Mathern led the effort to enact an insulin copay cap for health plans regulated by the state. For a long time, Mathern struggled to find supporters. He's one of only five Democrats in the Senate. There are 42 Republicans.

"One is very lonely being a Democrat," Mathern said, "especially if you espouse the more progressive end of public policy."

toggle caption i Hannah Norman/KFF Health News

Health insurers and the state chamber of commerce said price relief for people with diabetes would mean higher insurance premiums for everyone else. "We do not make health insurance more affordable by passing coverage mandates," Blue Cross Blue Shield of North Dakota lobbyist Megan Hruby told lawmakers.

The industry tapped into many lawmakers' skepticism about regulation, said Janelle Moos, a state lobbyist for AARP. The nonprofit advocacy group for older Americans supported the insulin bill.

"It wasn't the role of government," Moos said she was told by many GOP lawmakers. "In a state like ours, we hear that all the time."

Sponsor Message

Ang and Nina Kritzberger joined other families driving hours across the state to testify at the Capitol in Bismarck.

It was intimidating at first, Ang Kritzberger said. "It was me and six other lobbyists that were going to be giving their testimony against me," she recalled.

But supporters of the insulin bill showed that a similar measure that limited out-of-pocket costs for state employees with diabetes had little impact on insurance premiums.

It also became clear that many lawmakers, including Republicans, had grown very frustrated with drugmakers, health insurers and others in the healthcare industry.

"Why are folks paying hundreds of dollars a month for a drug that's been commercially available for decades?" asked Cleary, the state senator. "I just kept coming back to the fact that this market seems so broken and these families are having to make impossible decisions about rationing medication or skipping treatment."

State Rep. Carrie McLeod is also a Republican, and a diabetes educator. She said the healthcare system had become too focused on the bottom line. "The insurance companies started out to really help people with catastrophic needs, but things have gotten out of control," McLeod said.

toggle caption i Hannah Norman/KFF Health News

When the insulin bill came up for a vote last year, it passed with overwhelming bipartisan support.

The cap won't suddenly make healthcare affordable. For one thing, states can regulate only some health plans. Health insurance provided by larger employers is typically regulated by the federal government.

But polls suggest government regulation of healthcare prices is drawing Americans together.

About 7 in 10 U.S. adults — including 68% of Republicans and 77% of Democrats — said in a KFF survey earlier this year that there isn't enough government regulation to limit the price of prescription drugs.

Congress is now considering a national cap on insulin prices. Among the bipartisan list of co-sponsors is Sen. Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican.

Sponsor Message

Back on her farm, Ang Kritzberger says the insulin debate showed something else.

"We're very connected in North Dakota," she said, recalling how her neighbors had recently helped a farmer with brain cancer harvest his sugar beets. "It's all about being connected and finding that common ground."

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: Why even a fraction of a degree can escalate climate change impacts
World.content:
Why even a fraction of a degree can escalate climate change impacts

toggle caption i Sirachai Arunrugstichai/Getty Images

Countries have gathered at the annual climate change negotiations at the COP31 summit in Turkey to discuss how to achieve a goal that is increasingly unachievable. A decade ago, countries agreed to limit climate warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit). Now, that goal is out of reach.

Globally, average temperatures are already close to 1.5 degrees Celsius warmer than they were before the Industrial Revolution. Heat-trapping emissions from burning fossil fuels are still rising in the atmosphere, and most countries are not on track to meet their climate pledges to cut emissions by transitioning to cleaner energy.

Sponsor Message

The best-case scenario for the planet is now 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius of warming (roughly 3 degrees Fahrenheit), according to a recent United Nations study . If fossil fuel emissions stay on their current path, the world would be around 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter by the end of the century.

While the difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees Celsius may seem tiny, scientific research shows those increments can produce dramatically different outcomes for the planet. More warming raises the risk of extreme weather globally and could lead to the collapse of some of the planet's most sensitive ecosystems.

Loading...

"The crucial point is that every fraction of a degree matters," says Tim Lenton, climate professor at the University of Exeter. "Every fraction of a degree that we avoid is really able to do a huge amount of limiting harm."

Coral reefs already close to the edge

Corals are architects of an entire ecosystem. As they grow, they create the framework that supports vast numbers of other species, making reefs biodiversity hotspots. They're also vital to hundreds of millions of people who depend on them for food and livelihoods.

Corals are also highly vulnerable to heat. Prolonged marine heat waves cause corals to bleach, turning them white, which can eventually kill corals. Since the late 1990s, there have been four global bleaching events. With a historically strong El Niño now raising water temperatures, scientists say the fifth global bleaching event is likely unfolding.

Even before the previous bleaching event from 2023 to 2025, researchers found that 44% of coral species globally are at risk of extinction.

"These are incredibly worrying statistics, but they also emphasize that time matters," says David Obura, director of the coral research organization CORDIO East Africa, who worked on the study published last month in the journal Nature. "Every ten years, every five years counts."

Sponsor Message

Given their susceptibility to heat, the survival of most coral reefs depends on the difference between 1.5 and 2 degrees of warming. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change found that beyond 2 degrees Celsius of warming, 99% of corals would be lost .

"At 2 degrees of warming, we anticipate most corals just won't survive, not in functional ways to build a reef ecosystem," Obura says. "So you might still find some of the species, but many of them may be so rare or so compromised that they will have gone extinct by then."

With the dire forecasts for the future of coral, conservation groups and coastal communities are working to make reefs as healthy as possible in many areas so they can better withstand climate change. That includes restoring corals, reducing water pollution and even breeding more heat-tolerant corals .

"Most people around the world don't have the luxury of giving up on degraded ecosystems, because that's where they live," Obura says. "That's all they have. So we have to work out how to make them function again."

Millions more exposed to extreme heat

The goal of 1.5 degrees Celsius is an average temperature, measured across the planet. What it masks is the increasingly extreme heat events that are raising the average.

Researchers have found that for every tenth of a degree of warming, an additional 140 million people are exposed to dangerous levels of heat.

Heat waves are already causing heavy death tolls, like in Europe, where an estimated 50,000 people died of heat-related causes this past summer. Heat is particularly dangerous for those with chronic health conditions, as well as for people who are elderly or pregnant. The real toll of heat waves is often hidden, since many heat-related deaths are undercounted .

"You could think of it a bit like a tipping point for the human organism or body," Lenton says. "At some point, our physiology kind of reaches a tipping point and the worst tipping point is death."

Sponsor Message

Powerful storms

Every degree of climate change also affects the intensity of storms. Warmer air can produce heavier downpours because it holds 7% more water vapor for every degree. Rainstorms are already getting more intense in most of the U.S.

Scientific research also shows higher levels of warming could lead to other risky tipping points , like the collapse of Antarctic glaciers. If they destabilize, the melt would add vast volumes of water to the ocean, raising sea levels globally.

"We're never exactly sure where the tipping point is until we cross it, but we can be 100% confident that, for most of them, more warming is a bigger likelihood of crossing them," Lenton says. "Less warming is controlling that risk and that's why we should fight for every fraction of a degree that we can stave off."

At the ongoing climate negotiations in Turkey, countries are not expected to make major new commitments to cut climate emissions. Discussions are focusing on a new goal for electrification, meaning more cars and homes would run on electricity instead of fossil fuels. That would help reduce overall emissions, since a growing share of the world's electricity comes from cleaner sources, like solar and wind.

World.title: The cost of college is confusing. Some schools are trying to change that
World.content:
The cost of college is confusing. Some schools are trying to change that

toggle caption i Oliver Parini for The Hechinger Report

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

MIDDLEBURY, Vt. — Stately buildings of Vermont limestone surround meticulously tended lawns in a village that could be the setting for a Hallmark Christmas movie.

Middlebury College looks … expensive. But like other universities and colleges, it's working hard to persuade people that it's not.

Middlebury has announced that students from families with household incomes up to $175,000 can enroll tuition-free. That makes it one of a growing number of colleges trying to reduce widespread public confusion about what college actually costs.

These offers may seem like generous expansions of financial aid; after all, $175,000 is more than double the nation's median household income.

Sponsor Message

But while it's true that a few additional families will benefit — 35 to 50 in the incoming class at Middlebury, which typically enrolls about 630 new students per year, the college says — most people from families earning $175,000 or less already attend without having to pay tuition.

The real purpose of what Middlebury and other schools are doing, experts say, is to confront a problem that has soured many Americans on higher education: how frustratingly hard it is to figure out what college will cost.

"Let's make it as non-complicated as possible," said Ian Baucom, president at Middlebury: "If your family income is $175,000 or less, at Middlebury, you don't pay tuition." What the school is doing, he said, is trying to "just [be] really clear and get that out of the way, and then let the students decide."

toggle caption i Oliver Parini for The Hechinger Report

This includes low-income students — and young people whose parents didn't go to college — who find the price and the process of financial aid hardest to decipher, admissions officials say.

Nearly 80% of families of all kinds that were considering sending a student to college eliminated a school from consideration based on the price, a survey by the student loan company Sallie Mae found.

Middlebury becomes the latest of a growing number of schools to make tuition guarantees, including Princeton (for most families earning up to $250,000, with typical assets), the University of Chicago ($250,000), MIT ($200,000), Harvard ($200,000), Swarthmore ($200,000) and Davidson ($175,000).

Sponsor Message

Most aren't necessarily lowering their prices — just trying to make them more clear, said Phillip Levine, an economist at Wellesley College who studies higher education finance and is the author of the book Hidden Tuition: An Insider's Guide to College Pricing and Financial Aid.

When families see these pronouncements, they think, "'Oh, wow, the college is cutting the price.' And that's almost a perfect example of the misperceptions of the pricing system," Levine said.

In fact, said Levine, whose research bears this out, at most of the institutions making these tuition-free guarantees, "the college was already free for almost all those kids."

Free tuition guarantees don't cover room, board, books, transportation or other expenses — $24,462 a year at Middlebury — though other financial aid is often available for those.

Most of the growing number of income-based tuition plans take effect next year, as at Middlebury, or began for students who enrolled this fall.

That's not coincidental. Many of these schools have reached or surpassed a listed price of attendance of $100,000 a year; at Middlebury, it's $97,386. And public confusion about how much they actually cost after discounts and financial aid is helping drive a near-record-low confidence in higher education that threatens to exacerbate enrollment and revenue challenges.

Nearly 70% of students and parents think the financial aid process is partly or completely confusing, according to a separate survey by the Strada Education Foundation.

Most Americans also think that colleges are overpriced, with nearly two-thirds saying four-year institutions are unaffordable, a Gallup survey found; among parents who don't want their children to go to a four-year college, it found, the biggest reason was the cost.

Yet more than three-quarters of adults without college degrees couldn't correctly estimate the price of a public four-year institution within $5,000, another survey, by Gallup and the Lumina Foundation, showed. (Lumina and Strada are among the funders of The Hechinger Report, which produced this story.)

toggle caption i Oliver Parini for The Hechinger Report

A culprit for this is colleges' own increasingly self-destructive policy of advertising a high list price that almost no one pays, then giving discounts. It's a strategy that has evolved from a time when the price was intended to signal value and the discounts — which the colleges call "scholarships" — to entice the most desirable prospective students to enroll.

Sponsor Message

So much has that spiraled that, at 445 colleges and universities of all kinds, not a single student now pays the advertised price, according to a Hechinger Report analysis of federal data. At private, nonprofit four-year universities and colleges, fewer than 1 in 5 families pay that amount, an analysis of federal data shows.

Yet consumers appear fixated on that listed "sticker" price.

"The most important problem, I would argue, in college pricing today is the lack of transparency," said Levine, who said that even he had trouble figuring out the prices when he sent his sons to college, despite his Ph.D. in economics.

"If you're going to charge people different amounts of money, you have to provide them with some indication of what that's going to be. Or how are they supposed to make good financial decisions? And for the most part, we don't do a very good job of accomplishing that goal," Levine said.

One reason is that colleges often don't give families a final price until after a student is accepted and submits financial documents.

"I mean, you're waiting till the end to see how it all shakes out, and you won't know until, really, you have your FAFSA filled out," said Liz Mark, a mother from Wisconsin, referring to the Free Application for Federal Student Aid.

Mark, who was making a fall visit to Middlebury with her high school junior, Charlotte, compared it to the pricing system for medical care.

"It's a little bit like going to the doctor, right? You don't know exactly how much a procedure is going to cost until you get all of that information and get your pre-approvals," she said.

Another parent touring Middlebury, Mark Doughty, said he was lucky to have a friend who works in higher education, and who helped him better understand the process.

Sponsor Message

"The price on the menu is not necessarily what you pay," Doughty said he learned.

"If you don't have some guide through the system, then you could walk in and pay way more than you have to," said Doughty, of Massachusetts, who already has a son at Middlebury and a daughter considering applying there.

Free-tuition promises based on family income are at least "creating a very clear ceiling," he said.

There are two even newer reasons to do this than the principal one of making prices more transparent, said Nicole Curvin, dean of admissions and vice president of strategic enrollment at Middlebury: general anxiety about the cost of living and a fast-changing labor market.

"The economy is all over the place. Undergraduates are concerned about their employment opportunities. They are concerned about everything from AI to world dysfunction," Curvin said. "Affordability is the top question that every family is asking us, and we have to be willing to address that."

toggle caption i Oliver Parini for The Hechinger Report

Other colleges are also looking for ways to make their prices more transparent.

A few are simply lowering them, including Prescott College in Arizona, the University of Tulsa and Concordia University, St. Paul in Minnesota.

The University of Pennsylvania, which already makes tuition free for students from families earning $200,000 or less, just debuted a calculator that can tell families — before they apply — how much going to the university will cost them. "Penn is more affordable than most people realize," blares the heading at the top of the Ivy League institution's calculator webpage.

"Higher ed in general is trying to respond to some of those concerns, some of those questions" about what college really costs, said Mariana Valdes-Fauli, the university's associate vice president of student registration and financial services. "This really just kind of opens our door to our financial aid process and what we consider and what we don't, to allow all kinds of students to see that Penn is a real option."

Sponsor Message

Colleges with fewer resources are offering promises of free tuition to more limited audiences.

Earlham College is making tuition free for students from families earning $100,000 or less who live in its home state of Indiana. First-year students in New Hampshire whose families earn $100,000 a year or less will be eligible for free tuition to that state's public universities and colleges.

At North Carolina's private Wake Forest University, starting this fall, in-state students from families earning $200,000 or less pay no tuition. Marist University in New York is capping tuition at $32,000 a year starting next year for new students from that state whose families have incomes of $200,000 or less.

The common motivation, said Baucom, the Middlebury president, is the realization that consumers "are broadly aware that there is financial aid, but often it's just difficult to figure out, 'How does it work? How do I get access to it?'"

The stakes are higher than just whether someone might apply to Middlebury, and who gets to attend there, he said, regardless of their families' incomes.

"The social contract of American life depends upon the idea that everyone can come into the fullness of what it means to live and think and study and work here. And that's fracturing," Baucom said.

The sight of the idyllic campus outside the window of his office, "might convey [that] this is not for your family," he acknowledged. "And I just want to be as simple and clear as possible: We want every family, and families of all sorts."

This story was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization focused on inequality and innovation in education.

Edited by Nirvi Shah and Steve Drummond

Digital story reported and written by Jon Marcus

Audio story reported and written by Liam Elder-Connors
