World.title: Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration
World.content:
Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp says that midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

Nmecha 'does not discriminate against anyone'

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

Felix Nmecha's 'Crowns down' celebration caused much discussion over the past week Image: Madeleine Fantini/HMB Media/picture alliance

Nations League quarterfinal berth up for grabs

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Jürgen Klopp is hoping to keep alive Germany's chances of a Nations League quarterfinal berth Image: Michael Memmler/nordphoto/picture alliance

Just 5,000 children and coaches to attend

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

World.title: EU leaders gather for first ever AI summit
World.content:
The summit comes as worries about the artificial intelligence's global impact mount and Europe seeks a role in its development and regulation.

European Union leaders are meeting in Dublin on Friday at the first ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI). The meeting comes at a critical moment, as the bloc seeks a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology.

"Given the rapid pace of AI development, ​I ‌believe that a first dedicated discussion, at leaders' level, is now needed on the opportunities presented by AI, as well as on its transformative effect on our economies and societies," European Council ‌President Antonio Costa wrote in a letter to EU leaders last week.

The meeting is taking place in Dublin's Convention Center, which was also the meting place of the European Political Community summit this week.

Scrutiny over AI and its leaders grow

French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch, as well as Nobel-prize winner and researcher Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," are expected to speak to EU leaders at the summit.

The summit will take place a time of mounting worries about the emerging technology, which promises to transform ‌industries, labor markets and societies.

It also comes in the wake of a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months and the wider discussion about how the technology could harm humanity.

Tech leaders behind the technology have also fallen under scrutiny. As recently as this week,Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign after it was revealed that he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company.

Finding Europe's role in the AI revolution

During the summit, a discussion about where Europe fits in within the AI movement is expected.

Leaders face questions on how to unlock AI's potential, how to catch up with China and the United States in the race for the technology, but also how to protect against the risks it poses to individuals and businesses.

The governments of Estonia and Finland wrote in a letter ahead of the summit that Europe must "establish EU-level arrangements for responding to serious AI incidents," calling for "developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly."

Meanwhile, Mistral has pushed back on calls to slow down AI development, urging Europe to push ahead.

World.title: Ukraine updates: Second car bomb to hit Russia in two days
World.content:
Skip next section Russia says it wants to "understand Europe's genuine intention" before allowing EU into talks

Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia needs clarity on the European Union's "real intentions" for joining the Ukraine peace talks before making a decision on whether to expand the trilateral format.

US negotiators ‌said on Thursday that ‌President ​Vladimir Putin had agreed to an EU seat at the table, but Peskov's remarks indicate that the Kremlin has not yet agreed.

"Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format," Peskov said.

"If the Europeans really do have someone who is at least authorized in some way to talk, and if the Europeans really do have the desire to do so, then, of course, we will be ready to talk to them," he said.

Speaking after the latest trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, Russia's lead negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, claimed that "Russia did not receive single concrete peace proposal from European countries."

World.title: Humanitarian situation in Gaza worsens amid political deadlock
World.content:
In war-battered Gaza, heavy rain flooded and damaged thousands of tents. Several people died. Could pressure by Trump's Board of Peace on Israel and Hamas help to ease the humanitarian crisis amid stalled peace talks?

This autumn's heavy rain and falling temperatures are exacerbating the humanitarian situation for civilians in Gaza. Torrential rainfall over the weekend killed at least six people, including children, according to UNICEF. Local authorities said at least 70,000 tents were flooded and more than 200,000 people affected.

"Over the past two days, we have been trying to stabilize our tent with sand and rubble to keep water from seeping inside," Rawan Al-Omari, a mother of two, told DW on the phone.

She and her children share a tent west of Jabalia in northern Gaza. "The entire area around us has turned into mud, so even leaving the tent has become difficult," the 33-year-old said. "Everything is exhausting."

The rain also soaked the tent and everything 45-year-old Radi Amin and his three children own.

"For three consecutive days, we have been trying to dry our clothes while my children were shivering in the cold," he told DW. "Only on Wednesday, with the sun finally out and warm enough, our belongings started to dry."

Amin said that "the heavy rain served as a stark reminder of our truly dire state."

Aid teams meanwhile have started to clear blocked sewer lines and stormwater basins at 60 locations, benefiting an estimated 30,000 families, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported on Wednesday.

However, OCHA's humanitarian partners also warned that there is not enough space to relocate people living in flooded areas or war-damaged buildings. "Israeli authorities are restricting Palestinian access anywhere behind the so-called 'Yellow Line,' which means that most of Gaza's land remains off limit," OCHA said.

Following the Hamas terror attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, the ensuing war in Gaza has destroyed most of Gaza's infrastructure and housing. More than 74,600 people were killed in the Gaza Strip, according to figures from Gaza's Health Ministry. Israel controls about two-thirds of the territory, which is marked by a military demarcation line, the so-called Yellow Line.

Hamas continues to exercise governing authority in much of the remaining territory close to the Mediterranean Sea, where most of Gaza's roughly 2 million residents live. Most of them have been displaced several times and live in tents, camps for displaced people or in houses that are deemed unsafe. Hamas is classified as a terrorist organization by Germany, the EU, the United States and others.

Despite the nominal ceasefire from October 2025, Israel keeps targeting alleged Hamas members in Gaza, like here at the Nasser Medical Complex Image: Ramzi Abu Amer/JNA/ZUMA/dpa/picture alliance

Reconstruction stalls amid Hamas-Israel deadlock over disarmament and Israeli presence in Gaza

As part of the US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025, US President Donald Trump established the Board of Peace (BoP) committee to oversee the ceasefire's implementation as well as Gaza's postwar governance and reconstruction. According to a joint assessment by the World Bank, United Nations and European Union published in April 2026,Gaza's recovery and reconstruction will require an estimated $71.4 billion (€64.2 billion) over the next decade.

However, little progress has been made as negotiators have been failing to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its troops from the territory. Despite the ceasefire, Israel continues to carry out airstrikes on Gaza. On Thursday, Israel carried out a strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis against alleged Hamas members.

For Nathan Brown, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University in the US, the current rainfall exemplifies the deadlock of Trump's peace plan for Gaza.

"The failure of the Board of Peace to advance reconstruction, or even secure reliable relief, is fundamentally due to Israeli objections based on the insistence that Hamas has to completely disarm first," he told DW.

Until the recent elections in Israel, the Board of Peace showed little interest in challenging that view, Brown added: "Now it is willing to go public, though not in very confrontational terms."

On Monday, the Board of Peace issued a statement saying that Israel's steps to improve the humanitarian situation ahead of the coming winter remain insufficient. "We call on the leadership of the current Government of Israel to act immediately to authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies."

Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) said the same day that among other equipment, 12 sewage vacuum trucks for the International Committee of the Red Cross arrived in Gaza and that 91,000 tents and more than 8,200 trucks carrying tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothing had entered Gaza in recent months.

In its statement, the Board of Peace also called on Hamas to abide by commitments under the ceasefire, including laying down its weapons and transferring governing authority. Hamas promptly rejected the criticism in a statement and accused Israel of obstructing implementation of the peace plan and withholding urgently needed humanitarian supplies.

The United Nations as well as numerous international agencies have accused Israel of systematically preventing the import of prefabricated shelters into Gaza. The UN said around 150,000 tents were outside Gaza and ready to be dispatched, pending the necessary approvals, a claim Israel rejects.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is serving as caretaker prime minister while a new government is being formed following the October 27 elections, denied that Israel was responsible for the worsening conditions and blamed Hamas instead.

He warned that "as long as Hamas remains in power, it will use every dual-use item entering Gaza to entrench its terror regime and expand its military arsenal."

Most of Gaza's population lives in shelters, displacement camps or houses that are deemed unsafe Image: Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP

Residents bear the brunt of man-made humanitarian crisis

For Gaza's population, this deadlock amid the approaching winter spells ongoing hardship.

"Children and families are facing devastating conditions, with around 1.2 million people, including more than 560,000 children, living in critical or catastrophic shelter conditions," Ahmad Alhendawi, regional director of the aid organization Save the Children, told DW.

The amount of available winter clothing remains critically insufficient in Gaza, he added.

Gaza's children bear lasting scars three years into war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"As available supplies cover less than 1% of needs, hundreds of thousands of children face the winter without adequate clothing, blankets or heating, leaving them exposed to hypothermia and respiratory illnesses," Alhendawi said.

Furthermore, Nestor Owomuhangi, the UN Population Fund's (UNFPA) representative to Palestine , told DW that around 400,000 people in Gaza continue to live in areas at high risk of flooding, including an estimated 10,000 pregnant women.

"For women and girls already enduring displacement and hunger, the rain threatens their health, safety and dignity," he told DW, adding that "with around 180 babies born every day, mothers and newborns urgently need dry, warm shelter."

World.title: Germany news: Parliament agrees on debt-laden 2027 budget
World.content:
Politicians on the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at both ends heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

The session took over 15 hours, and already politicians are talking about areas where they still see room for further improvement or alteration — but the document does at least stand in such a form in which it can take effect without too many complications.

Including all spending plans, in the core budget and from the so-called "special funds" for infrastructure and military modernization, new debt constitutes around a third of total spending plans.

In total, the plan is to take out new debt worth just over €210 billion ($233 billion), while taking in a little less than €400 billion in taxes.

That's the second-highest level of new debt in the post-war history of the Federal Republic of Germany. Even at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021, new debt was only slightly higher, at €215.4 billion.

We'll break down more of the details and cover some of the reactions in later posts.

World.title: Czechia braces for massive protest against cuts to public media
World.content:
A fast-tracked bill to cut public media funding has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is planned for Prague on Sunday.

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.

The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

What's in the bill?

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

Crowds protested outside parliament while inside, the government pushed through the first reading of the controversial media funding bill on the night of October 23/24 Image: Michal Kamaryt/CTK Photo/IMAGO

The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

What are the objections to the bill?

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

The protests continued in the days after the late-night vote in parliament Image: Michael Heitmann/dpa/picture alliance

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.

What has happened since the bill was fast-tracked?

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.

Why has the reaction been so strong?

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

'For you, not for politicians' — Public broadcasters are seen by many in Czechia as cornerstones of democracy Image: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.

How has the government reacted?

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

During the November 3 strike at Czech Television, hosts read the news in front of a darkened newsroom Image: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."

What are the potential risks for the government?

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.

But this could come at a cost.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.

"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

Could things turn violent?

Babis is aware of the danger.

Public opposition to the government's plans for Czech public media are nothing new: this demonstration outside Czech Television in June called for the dismissal of Culture Minister Oto Klempir and expressed support for the country's public media Image: Ondrej Deml/CTK/picture alliance

The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

World.title: After suffering its worst election result, what's next for the ANC — and for South Africa?
World.content:
A crushing local election result across the country has left South Africa's ruling ANC searching for answers. Experts say the vote reflects public frustration with service delivery failures — signaling a political shift.

South Africa's governing African National Congress (ANC) party is forced to confront its worst electoral setback to date after securing under 31% of the vote in the country's significant local government elections; party leaders themselves have described the result as "catastrophic."

This outcome marks a steep decline for the party that had once led South Africa's liberation struggle; the party that had dominated the country's political landscape since the end of apartheid in 1994.

The result reflects growing public frustration about the ANC's lack of performance in key areas such as skyrocketing unemployment, poor service delivery, local governance failures and years of graft and corruption — sometimes at the highest levels of government.

So what comes next for the ANC — and for South Africa?

After years of dominating the political scene, the ANC's future now looks increasingly unstable Image: Leandre Steenberg/Matrix Images/picture alliance

Voters express growing frustration and despair

Tasnim Essop, a researcher at the Society, Work and Politics Institute (SWOP) at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, says it is time for the party to undertake some serious introspection. She believes that the ANC has to confront a long list of difficult questions about governance, leadership and accountability.

"You're talking about issues like water, electricity, housing, public services at the basic municipal level. And those kinds of things have been key issues. And ... research has shown that unemployment is also a big part of what drives people to vote in certain ways" she told DW.

Essop also highlights the fact that the outcome of the vote didn't happen overnight, and that it rather reflects a slow erosion of public confidence in the erstwhile ruling party over a long period.

South Africa election hit by disinformation surge To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DW correspondent Dianne Hawker-Kalubi, who reported from various polling stations during the election, agrees with that observation, stressing that many of the voters she had spoken to expressed "a lot of frustration, a lot of concern about basic services not being delivered" for years.

Mokhiri Phooko, a Cape Town resident, said that "people are losing hope" across the country after over three years of the political landscape being dominated by late President Nelson Mandela's party:

"You promised us jobs, why [are] you not keeping up the end of your bargain right," she told Reuters, stressing that "(t)he unemployment rate went up drastically" in the past few years.

A shifting role for the ANC

The ANC itself meanwhile has acknowledged that things have to change: In a statement , the party announced that its National Executive Committee would convene a special meeting to deal with the "serious political responsibility to listen to the people, confront its shortcomings and provide leadership."

Furthermore, the party also has to prepare a framework for upcoming coalition negotiations at the same time — many times involving some of its biggest rivals, as was the case after the 2024 general elections.

Helen Zille, chairwoman of the DA, has agreed to coalition talks with the ANC before Image: DW

The election results therefore signal a broader shift in South African politics, with voter support increasingly spread across multiple parties rather than being concentrated behind a single dominant force.

While nationally, the ANC remained the country's largest party, opposition parties made significant gains; the Democratic Alliance (DA) managed to strengthen its position across several major urban centers.

Meanwhile the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party, launched by former President Jacob Zuma in late 2023, performed rather strongly in the KwaZulu-Natal provice despite entering the political arena so recently.

At the local level, smaller civic organizations and community-based movements also recorded notable successes.

'Vote fluidity' enters South African politics

Essop describes this trend as a growing sense of "vote fluidity," with voters increasingly willing to move their support between parties instead of remaining loyal to a single political organization.

Some observers have already linked this drift to the idea of South Africans are moving beyond liberation-era loyalties; however, Essop opines: "I would be cautious to say that liberation politics are dead and gone," as many political parties continue to draw ther legitimacy and support from the country's liberation history — even if they no longer operate under the ANC banner.

Essop argues that the political shift does not signify a wholesale rejection of that liberation narrative itself, but rather a growing demand for effective governance and leadership.

A critical test for the ANC

For the ANC, the challenge now is rebuilding trust, with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa saying that the results are a challenge not just for his party but for all political parties to come together and perform better for citizens.

In a statement, Ramaphosa said that "[t]hose who have been elected to councils now need to prove themselves worthy of the trust placed in them by the South African people."

The election results also represent a growing lack in confidence in Preseident Cyril Ramaphosa's leadership Image: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/ZUMA/picture alliance

While the ANC still remains South Africa's largest political party, its latest setbacks at the polls underscore how much the country's political landscape is no longer what it was when apartheid ended.

The era of undisputed ANC loyalty and dominance appears to be over as voters are showing a greater willingness to support alternative parties and punish those they believe have fallen short.

Whether the ANC can reverse this decline will depend largely on how convincingly it can deliver not only improved public services, but effective change throughout.

World.title: Is the TFFF rainforest fund failing due to a lack of money?
World.content:
The TFFF rainforest fund aims to make forest conservation more profitable than deforestation. But a lack of money may prevent it from getting off the ground.

The world's tropical forests play a vital role, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later, logging continues.

In 2024 alone, more than 8 million hectares of forest were lost — an area 30 times larger than the country of Luxembourg. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% between August 2025 and 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

Deforestation in Brazil's Amazon falls to record low To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched last year at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

TFFF aims to protect forests through investments

Because rainforests are so important for the entire world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks or investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for government donors to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors purchasing TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, explained Felix Finkbeiner, founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," said Finkbeiner, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur in the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

Millions in funding — but only for intact ecosytems

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

For every hectare of forest they preserve instead of chopping down, they will receive $4 per year. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website , an independent platform tracking investments launched by Finkbeiner's organization, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive some $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. While it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: if countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

Although land in the Amazon rainforest continues to be cleared for soybean cultivation, the recent rate of deforestation is the lowest it has been in nearly 40 years Image: Larissa Schwedes/dpa/picture alliance

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

Governments may change, conservation will continue

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, also because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] D.C. decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," said Finkbeiner.

At the same time, the TFFF fund is also immune to donor countries backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

TFFF still $2 billion short

However, for the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," said Finkbeiner.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has said it would provide the TFFF with around €1 billion starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he said. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that 10 billion."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: De la España vaciada al futuro digital: las pymes aragonesas que crecen empujadas por los centros de datos
World.content:
La inversión de AWS en Aragón ha abierto oportunidades para empresas locales de sectores tan distintos como las telecomunicaciones, el hormigón prefabricado o la obra civil. Una colaboración que impulsa el empleo, la innovación y la especialización de un tejido empresarial rural que puede encontrar en la economía digital una vía de expansión

Hay pocas cosas que hoy no podamos hacer desde un móvil conectado a internet. Y, para que todos esos millones de operaciones sean posibles, detrás hay una infraestructura crucial: los centros de datos. Edificios que en sí mismos constituyen un prodigio de la técnica: kilómetros de fibra óptica, redes de comunicación interna, sistemas de seguridad de vanguardia para proteger instalaciones así deestratégicas, estructuras de ingeniería tan sofisticadas que son un reto para aquellos con el encargo de construirlos, equiparlos y mantenerlos. Edificios que, además, pueden convertirse en una oportunidad para el impulso del empleo y el crecimiento económico en zonas rurales, como está ocurriendo en Aragón, según las conclusiones del informe de la consultora GfKencargado por Amazon Web Services (AWS) y tal como atestiguan algunas pymes de la zona, como las constructoras Gilva o Giral o la empresa de comunicaciones Gotor.

Desde noviembre de 2022, España cuenta con infraestructuras de servidores y datos de AWS en tres áreas de la región de Aragón, unas instalaciones que, en palabras de Suzana Curic, directora para España y Portugal de AWS, “convierten al país en uno de los centros neurálgicos para la nubeen el sur de Europa”. 33.700 millones de euros. Esa es la cantidad que prevén invertir en España hasta 2035 para ampliar y dar soporte a estas infraestructuras aragonesas, afirma Curic, una inversión que estiman que contribuya al PIB con hasta 31.700 millones y que apoye al empleo con 29.900 puestos a tiempo completo en empresas locales, contando los directos, indirectos e inducidos.

Esa transformación que, dice Curic, “hará que España pueda competir globalmente en la era de la inteligencia artificial” ya está en marcha. José María Alzaga, directorgeneral de Gotor Comunicaciones, define lo que están viviendo como “histórico”. ¿Por qué? “Estas inversiones no solo generan actividad económica y empleo, sino el desarrollo de nuevas capacidades y el refuerzo de la competitividad. El mayor legado será contar con empresas aragonesas más preparadas, innovadoras y capaces de abordar proyectos exigentes dentro y fuera de nuestra región”, cuenta Alzaga.

Gotor Comunicaciones Ingeniería de telecomunicaciones 1989 Fundada en Zaragoza Desde que comenzó a colaborar con AWS en 2022, su plantilla ha crecido un 20% “El mayor legado de estas inversiones será contar con empresas aragonesas más innovadoras” José María Alzaga, director General de Gotor Comunicaciones

Esta empresa de ingeniería de telecomunicaciones zaragozana fundada en 1989 es la encargada de instalar y configurar las redes físicas que conectan los aparatos alojados en esos centros de datos, las que permiten ese tránsito de información. También serán ellos quienes velen por su buen funcionamiento futuro. Tareas nada sencillas para las que necesitaron un periodo de entre seis y ocho meses de homologación de procedimientos técnicos, corporativos y de prevención de riesgos y que les obligaron a tirar de ingenio y sacar lo mejor de sí mismos.

00:50 Así es un centro de datos de AWS por dentro Así luce por dentro uno de los centros de datos de AWS en EE UU. Vídeo: AWS

Más empleo y nuevos negocios

Los datos del informe de GfK son elocuentes: un 60% de los proveedores de AWS ha aumentado su plantilla; uno de cada cinco empleados, de media, dedica sus jornadas a tareas relacionadas con estos proyectos; un 85% afirma que el impacto de los negocios con AWS ha sido muy positivo y dos de cada diez explican incluso que, gracias a su experiencia con AWS, han logrado abrir nuevas vías de negocio o expandirse fuera.

Gilva Constructora especializada en prefabricados de hormigón 1973 Fundada en Calanda (Teruel) Desde que comenzó a colaborar con AWS en 2023, su facturación ha crecido un 23% y ha pasado de 101 a 115 empleados “Hay un efecto que va más allá: estas inversiones fijan población y generan empleo cualificado” Jaime Valimañas, CEO de Gilva

Dice Jaime Valimañas, CEO de la constructora especializada en estructuras de hormigón Gilva, que en lugares donde “cada puesto de trabajo cuenta”, pueblos como “Alcañiz, Calanda y el Bajo Aragón en general, generar empleos cualificados y fijar población” se recibe casi como una bendición.

La suya es una empresa familiar de Calanda con más de 50 años de historia que se enorgullece de contribuir a “la construcción de una de las infraestructuras tecnológicas más exigentes de Europa, con estándares de calidad, seguridad y plazos de entrega al nivel de los mejores del mundo”. Su plantilla —cuentan con ingenieros que diseñan y plantas que fabrican en la zona— también creció, un 15%, y tienen motivos, más allá de “dar empleo en una zona deprimida como la provincia de Teruel”, para presumir de su particular contribución. Fruto de las necesidades de AWS, han diseñado una solución de hormigón prefabricado muy innovadora para las canalizaciones del cableado, un producto que, en sus palabras, “aporta rapidez, porque las piezas llegan terminadas de fábrica; calidad homogénea, porque todo se produce en condiciones controladas; y durabilidad y protección del cableado”.

Trabajos que, además, te hacen mejores

Para Javier Giral, CEO de la empresa oscense dedicada a las excavaciones Giral, con más de medio siglo de historia, su dilatada experiencia no hace menor “el reto que supone una obra de estas dimensiones”. “Hemos aprendido mucho”, cuenta un Giral que explica cómo desde que se implicaron en 2021 en este proyecto han tenido que afrontar cambios importantes dentro de la empresa: “Hemos invertido en maquinaria nueva, hemos incorporado tecnologías con las que antes no trabajábamos y hemos tenido que adaptar nuestros equipos a lo que nos demandaba la obra. También hemos podido contratar a más trabajadores y dar formación a los que ya teníamos. Se trata de una inversión que nos sirve para seguir creciendo en este negocio”.

Giral Constructora especializada en excavaciones 1971 Fundada en Huesca Desde que comenzó a colaborar con AWS en 2021, su plantilla creció un 25% y su facturación un 22% “Creo que lo mejor de todo es lo mucho que hemos aprendido por el camino” Javier Giral, CEO de Giral

Es un valor que todos los testimonios comparten: el aprendizaje que ha supuesto y cómo este les ha preparado para ser mucho más competitivos y valientes a la hora de atreverse a abordar proyectos internacionales. El futuro, dicen, está ahí, en trenes como este “que no hay que dejar pasar”. Sobre todo en zonas como Aragón, donde de los 731 municipios contabilizados, 541 (el 74%) tienen 500 habitantes o menos, según el Instituto Aragonés de Estadística. Una de las regiones donde la incidencia de la despoblación es más grave.

“Nos gustaría que, con los años, estos proyectos ayudaran a crear empleo estable, a fortalecer las empresas que ya tenemos y a dar oportunidades a los jóvenes para que puedan desarrollar su futuro profesional aquí”, asegura Giral, que resume el deseo de todos: que la España vaciada vea por fin ante sí un horizonte próspero.

World.title: “Preservamos las variedades tradicionales de cacahuete. Nos hacen únicos y, a la vez, diferentes”
World.content:
Desde la Granja de la Costera (Valencia), Ana Climent convirtió las semillas centenarias de sus bisabuelos en Ca Climent, un proyecto familiar que apuesta por el origen local, la proximidad y la conservación del patrimonio agrícola. Junto a su padre, se encarga de todo el proceso de forma artesanal, desde el cultivo hasta el envasado

La motivación de Ana Climent fue un puñado de cacahuetes insípidos que probó durante la pandemia. Recordó entonces el sabor único de los que cultivaba su familia en La Granja de la Costera (Valencia) y decidió acercar ese producto a más personas. Junto a su padre, recuperó las semillas centenarias de sus bisabuelos y creó Ca Climent. Querían preservar dos variedades autóctonas, el collaret y la cacaua, y mantener un ingrediente estrella en el acompañamiento clásico del tradicional esmorzaret valenciano.

Climent era comunicadora y combinó su profesión con la aventura de emprender. Sintió la responsabilidad de que, si no lo hacían ellos, nadie lo haría, como explica en el vídeo de Gastronomía para una Inmensa Minoría, un proyecto de Cervezas 1906 que pone en valor proyectos que innovan desde la tradición, defienden el territorio y la identidad propia. Paralelamente, la marca también apoyó a Ca Climent con una máquina para descascarillar cacahuetes, una mejora que les permite vender el producto sin cáscara y facilita su llegada a un mayor número de consumidores.

Climent cuenta con unos 830 metros cuadrados y un obrador. Desde allí se encargan de todo el proceso: cultivan, recolectan, tuestan, envasan y distribuyen alrededor de mil kilos de cacahuete al año. “Preservamos las variedades tradicionales porque creemos que son las que nos hacen únicos y, a la vez, diferentes”, describe en su conversación con la chef Verónica Gómez, formada en el Basque Culinary Center y conocida por su paso por MasterChef. La cocinera reivindica, además, la labor de esta familia como los únicos productores y tostadores de cacahuete de España. La propuesta de Climent gira en torno a ese origen local, la proximidad y la conservación del patrimonio. Persiguen una agricultura sostenible, incluso con envases compostables fabricados con papel y PLA, un material de origen vegetal (maíz) permitido en el uso alimentario.

Algunos restaurantes y chefs, alineados con los valores de esta iniciativa, han comenzado a incorporar el cacahuete valenciano en sus propuestas gastronómicas. Entre quienes respaldan el proyecto figuran (y participan en el vídeo) Pepe Vieira, chef con dos estrellas Michelin y fundador del restaurante homónimo en Raxó (Pontevedra), y Begoña Rodrigo, galardonada con una estrella Michelin y fundadora del restaurante La Salita, en Valencia. Esta cocinera también utiliza el producto de Ca Climent en su restaurante para elaborar vinagre. “Hace falta que haya muchísimas más Anas que vayan a contracorriente”, insiste.

World.title: Voy a comprar mi primera vivienda con mi mujer, dueña de otra casa antes del matrimonio. ¿Puedo obtener el préstamo de 50.000 euros?
World.content:
Dos personas retiran dinero de un cajero automático junto a un anuncio de hipotecas del Banco Santander, en una oficina de Madrid.

Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. Estoy adquiriendo una vivienda de nueva construcción con mi mujer en Madrid. Ella ya era propietaria de una casa previamente a nuestro matrimonio. Sería mi primera vivienda y sería para uso habitual. ¿Podría ser beneficiario del préstamo a interés cero de hasta 50.000 euros del Gobierno? E. Pascual

Respuesta. Si compra la vivienda usted solo, al estar casados bajo el régimen de separación de bienes, sí puede acogerse al préstamo de hasta 50.000 euros. Al existir separación de bienes, su patrimonio y sus condiciones jurídicas son totalmente independientes de las de su esposa. Dado que no tiene ninguna vivienda a su nombre, cumple formalmente el requisito exigido por el Real Decreto-ley de ser comprador de primera vivienda habitual. Si la compra es conjunta, no podría acceder al préstamo público.

Los requisitos obligatorios para la compra individual son los siguientes: la vivienda debe registrarse única y exclusivamente a su nombre. Su mujer no puede constar como copropietaria en las escrituras de compraventa, ya que ella tiene otra vivienda y esta nueva no sería su primera vivienda. La hipoteca bancaria (que cubrirá habitualmente el 80% restante) debe ir únicamente a su nombre y el banco le exigirá las capitulaciones matrimoniales que demuestren que están en separación de bienes.

No obstante, se trata de un caso muy específico, por lo que sería conveniente analizarlo en detalle.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Vamos a setas: seis rutas micológicas para el otoño, haya o no hongos
World.content:
El cambio climático ha retrasado un mes la temporada en España y los expertos no descartan que se alargue. En estos montes podremos saciar nuestro apetito de paisajes

Antes empezaba a tronar y a jarrear a finales de agosto y justo a los 21 días aparecían las setas en el monte. Así ocurría, por lo menos, en la sierra de Guadarrama, a caballo entre Madrid, Segovia y Ávila, donde el que esto escribe vive desde 1995. También antes el veranillo de San Miguel –29 de septiembre– y el de San Martín –11 de noviembre– eran unos pocos días de otoño en los que repuntaba el calor y se podía salir en manga corta a buscar setas, porque las había a patadas. Con el cambio climático, sin embargo, dejó de llover y de refrescar a finales de agosto y llegó el veroño, que comenzó siendo cosa de una o dos semanas y amenaza ya con suplantar al verdadero otoño, para desesperación de los seteros, a los que cada vez nos cuesta más entender y encontrar algo en este mundo al revés.

Pero veamos la botella –y la cesta– medio llena. Quizá todo esté ocurriendo a deshora y solo haya que aguardar. Las lluvias que no cayeron este año en agosto lo han hecho en octubre y algunas setas han salido. Si llueve más en noviembre y las temperaturas se mantienen altas, ¿por qué no podría haber un brote tardío? En ese caso, los siguientes montes serán buenos para salir a buscarlas, pues la experiencia nos dice que en ellos no suelen faltar. Y si no las encontramos, allá penas: disfrutaremos de seis de las excursiones más agradables que pueden hacerse en noviembre en España, con la cesta vacía y en manga corta.

Más información Cómo evitar una intoxicación por setas y por qué no hay que fiarse de las aplicaciones del móvil

1. Las Burbonas del Gorbeia (Álava)

La hayas que pueblan las laderas de las Burbonas alavesas son magníficas, hasta el punto de que en otoño el caminante no puede dejar de mirarlas y fotografiarlas, aun sabiendo que en el suelo se esconden setas deliciosas.

José David Fernández, director del parque micológico de Gorbeialdea –que abarca la cuarta parte del parque natural del Gorbeia, el mayor y más setero del País Vasco–, cree que las setas van con un mes de retraso y que este año se dejarán ver hasta finales de noviembre “con permiso de las heladas”. Recomienda, como es lógico, sacar el preceptivo permiso –10 euros por persona y día– y participar en alguna de las rutas que él mismo guía que él mismo guía todos los fines de semana y en las que se recolectan alrededor de 25 especies distintas.

Una buscadora de setas junto a una haya monumental en las Burbonas del Gorbeia. Andrés Campos

Los boletus aereus y los edulis son dos de los hongos más abundantes y apreciados. Y la ruta favorita de José David y de cualquiera de los seteros que frecuentamos el “corazón verde de Euskadi” es la que asciende desde la casa del parque de Sarria hasta la triple cima de las Burbonas y luego regresa al punto de partida siguiendo de cerca al saltarín río Baias. Subiendo y bajando de las Burbonas, además de setas, se ven hayas majestuosas de melena dorada, cobriza y roja que, por sí solas, justificarían recorrer este itinerario circular de 16 kilómetros y cinco horas de duración, seis si nos paramos a ver qué hay debajo de la hojarasca. Para no perderse, hay que seguir las indicaciones y el track de Wikiloc. Para reponer fuerzas después de la excursión, nada como el cocido de alubias y las habitaciones del Hotel Doña Lola, que ocupa un caserío de piedra del siglo XVI en Izarra.

Al día siguiente podemos ver la cascada de Gouiri –una de las más altas de España, de 105 metros– y comprar el queso de Idiazábal que los hermanos hermanos Basterra elaboran con la leche de un montón de ovejas latxas que pastan arrastrando sus largas guedejas al lado mismo del salto.

Si andamos un lunes por la zona y deseamos profundizar en su riqueza micológica, podemos acercarnos a la Sociedad Micológica Gorbeiako Bazterra, en Murgia, donde ese día hay un servicio gratuito de identificación. Su vicepresidente, Vicente Blasco, es categórico respecto al anómalo comportamiento de las setas este año, que han brotado muy tarde sin que apenas haya llovido en cinco meses: “Han salido por aburrimiento”.

Queseria de los Hermanos Basterra, en Goiuri. Andrés Campos

2. Castañar de los Ojestos (Cáceres)

El Castañar de los Ojestos, en la sierra cacereña de Gata, también es espectacular en esta época, cuando las hojas se vuelven amarillas y caedizas, pero lo de no fijarse en el suelo aquí es más complicado. Además de setas hay castañas, y eso ya es demasiada golosina para no prestar atención. En San Martín de Trevejo, uno de los pueblos más bonitos de España, arranca el sendero PR-CC 184, que atraviesa de abajo arriba este castañar, el más extenso de Extremadura.

A 2,5 kilómetros del inicio, como a una hora de paseo sosegado, se llega a la altura de los Abuelos, dos castaños enormes a los que se les calcula una edad de 600 años. Media hora después se cruza el río de la Vega, que con las lluvias otoñales forma unas buenas chorreras. Y en media más se alcanza el puerto de Santa Clara, donde acaba Cáceres y empieza Salamanca.

La bajada, que es por el mismo camino, toca hacerla –ahora sí– fijándose en el suelo, donde en noviembre suele haber níscalos, lenguas de vaca, parasoles, algún que otro boletus y las últimas castañas llovidas del cielo amarillo. En el restaurante Saboris de Sempris, en San Martín de Trevejo, los boletus edulis se sirven acompañados con unas tostas de torta del Casar. Otros dos comedores serranos donde no faltan en temporada los edulis son el gastrobar Los Portales, en Gata, y la taberna El Buen Avío de Trevejo.

Puesta de sol en el hotel Habitat Cigüeña Negra, en la sierra de Gata. Andrés Campos

El año que viene, porque ya es tarde para encontrarlas, vendremos a buscar la codiciada Amanita caesarea o huevo de rey. Para ello, lo más fácil y gratificante es alojarse a principios de otoño en el hotel Habitat Cigüeña Negra y salir a pasear con la cesta por la dehesa de encinas que lo rodea. Curiosamente, la especialidad del restaurante, que tiene una estrella verde Michelin por su cocina sostenible, no son las setas, sino la carne de Retwagyu, un cruce de vaca retinta extremeña y buey wagyu japonés que pace alrededor del hotel sin mostrar ningún interés por este bocado de césares. Aquí cada cual –los seteros, los clientes del asador y las vacas– van a lo suyo.

3. Sierra de Cebollera (La Rioja)

En la ermita de Lomos de Orios, en Villoslada de Cameros, un lagarto tallado en cuerno de vaca recuerda la historia que cuenta que en 1824, la Virgen salvó a un pastor de ser comido por uno gigantesco. Lino Martínez, que así se llamaba el pastor, lo había criado, hasta que éste que alcanzó un metro y medio de longitud. Un día, la criatura se abalanzó sobre su cuidador, el cual se libró in extremis de ser devorado al entrar corriendo en la ermita y cerrarse milagrosamente la puerta detrás de él, partiendo en dos al lagarto. Grandes como aquel animal y su ingratitud son los boletus edulis que se cogen hasta que empiezan a blanquear las cimas de la sierra riojana de Cebollera. Unos piensan que se llama así por la forma redondeada de sus montes y otros opinan que es por la abundancia que hay en ella de gamones blancos (Asphodelus albus), también llamados cebollanas, cebollinos, cebolletas de monte, cebollas de culebra, cebollas gamonitas, cebolleras moriscas o ceborrinchas.

Además de hermosos boletus, aquí las cestas se llenan de níscalos, parasoles, pardillas, negrillas, trompetas de la muerte y, entrado ya el invierno, pies azules. Algunas zonas de recolección pillan tan lejos que hay que acercarse en coche por pistas forestales de acceso restringido, pagando otro permiso además del que uno ya saca para ver si coge algo: seis euros en total. Para quien no quiere complicarse pidiendo ese otro permiso y metiéndose con el coche por vaya usted a saber qué caminos, existe un cómodo un cómodo sendero circular circular de algo menos de siete kilómetros –un par de horas a paso tranquilo– que lleva desde la misma ermita hasta las cascadas de Puente Ra, atravesando un hayedo precioso. No tiene pérdida: está marcado con trazos de pintura naranja y verde.

Su mayor aliciente, aparte de hallar setas, es ver los saltos de hasta diez metros que pega el arroyo de Puente Ra, afluente del río Iregua, el principal del valle. El premio de consolación para los que acaban con la cesta vacía es comerse unas pochas con boletus o un guiso de jabalí con hongos confitados y salsa de arándanos en el restaurante Corona, en Ortigosa de Cameros. Al lado hay un alojamiento rural que se llama como lo que se acaba de admirar paseando valle arriba: Cascadas de Puente Ra.

Cascadas de Puente Ra, en sierra de Cebollera. Andrés Campos

4. Barranco de la Barbulla y Muela de Cortes (Valencia)

Donde ha llovido bastante en lo que va de otoño es en las montañas del interior de Valencia, que ahora están a tope de rebollones –como allí llaman a los níscalos–, de lenguas de vaca y de seteros con la navaja afilada y el brillo del ansia viva en la mirada. El Rincón de Ademuz y la comarca de los Serranos o del Alto Turia –cuya capital, Chelva, exploramos a fondo recientemente– son dos lugares famosos por su riqueza micológica.

Quien busque otras zonas menos trilladas y otras atracciones, aparte de esa, hará bien en acercarse a Cortes de Pallás. A la entrada de este recóndito pueblo, plantado en un barranco lateral del encañonado río Júcar y al pie de la alta y acantilada Muela de Cortes, un cartel de la oficina de turismo anuncia: “Un mundo aparte”. Y es verdad: más apartado no puede estar. Aquí el coche sirve ya para poco: toca echarse a caminar monte arriba, explorando los manantiales, los saltos de agua, los canales de riego y las balsas que convirtieron el barranco de la Barbulla en uno de los mayores paraísos hortícolas de los moriscos.

Recorriendo la llamada ruta de las Cascadas, veremos en un par de horas media docena de ellas. La mayor de todas, la de El Corbinet, resbala por una cornisa rocosa de ocho metros de altura y cae en una charca amplia, verde y sombría, idónea para comer –hay mesas alrededor– las tortas de sal o de embutido que se compraron en Ca’ la Conchin, frente a la oficina de turismo.

Vista desde el castillo Chirel, al que se llega por un sencillo sendero de tres kilómetros (ida y vuelta). Andrés Campos

Un camino más largo y esforzado, de siete kilómetros y casi cinco horas con paradas contemplativas, es la senda Cavanilles, que sube zigzagueando como una serpiente de escalera a la Muela de Cortes, donde 4.000 de los muchos moriscos que vivían en la comarca se refugiaron en el otoño de 1609 porque no querían ser expulsados de España ni abjurar de su fe.

Otro más sencillo, de solo tres kilómetros –ida y vuelta–, es el que lleva al castillo de Chirel, que fue el cuartel general de las tropas gubernamentales cuando los moriscos se rebelaron e hicieron fuertes en la Muela de Cortes. Desde la ruinosa fortaleza, a 300 metros sobre el Júcar, se ven como desde un helicóptero las aguas color turquesa del río y los barcos que navegan por ellas llenos de pensionistas del balneario de Cofrentes.

Si haciendo estas rutas no encontramos algún rebollón o alguna llanega negra –la seta mocosa típica de estos bosques de pino carrasco sobre rocas calizas, que suele alargar la temporada hasta enero–, solo nos queda subir en coche a la Muela de Cortes y parar por el camino en algún pinar prometedor. Donde haya vehículos en el arcén, habrá setas.

05 Sierra de Aracena (Huelva)

Esta sierra del norte de Huelva, fronteriza con Portugal, Badajoz y Sevilla, es Eldorado andaluz de las setas, donde cualquiera que haya estado en otoño habrá visto por doquier camiones frigoríficos cargando toneladas de ellas para llevarlas al extranjero. Aun así, el tiempo está tan loco, tan trastocado, que “este octubre no se ha cogido ni una”. Jorge Jaímez, gerente y guía de Linxaia, confía en las lluvias de noviembre: “A finales de mes, casi dos más tarde de lo habitual, esperamos estar haciendo rutas micológicas”. Como otras 26 empresas de la sierra, Linxaia participa en Soy Ecoturista, una iniciativa de la Asociación de Ecoturismo en España para proponer experiencias que contribuyan a la conservación de los espacios naturales y al desarrollo local.

Senderista en Alajar, municipio de la sierra de Aracena. Andrés Campos

Las rutas son sumamente respetuosas con el entorno y con los vecinos, a los cuales se pide permiso para hacerlas, no solo por cortesía, sino porque casi todo el monte en la sierra de Aracena es privado. Aunque tarde, este año volverán a salir las tanas (Amanita caesarea) y los hongos negros (Boletus aereus) entre los castaños de Fuenteheridos, Galaroza, Alájar o Castaño del Robledo y en las dehesas que los rodean, y los boletus edulis a alturas superiores a 600 metros.

Más adelante aún lo harán los níscalos en los pinares y los rebozuelos en los castañares y alcornocales más húmedos. El que no volverá a abrir sus puertas –no con Luismi López y Adela Ortiz al frente, por lo menos– es el restaurante Los Arrieros, en Linares de la Sierra, que era un templo de la cocina del terruño y de las setas en particular. Pero en la sierra sigue habiendo dos establecimientos donde las preparan con cariño en otoño: Peña de Arias Montano, en Alájar, y Montecruz, en Aracena. Un comercio de referencia para comprarlas frescas es Sirlache, en la calle Constitución, 1. Y un hotel idóneo para quienes estamos enganchados a ellas es Finca La Fronda. No hace falta ni salir de él para buscarlas: solo pasear por el jardín.

Cogiendo setas en el Pinar de Valsaín. Andrés Campos

6. Pinar de Valsaín (Segovia)

En la sierra de Guadarrama, este octubre ha sido flojo micológicamente, con temperaturas altísimas y la humedad justa para que los seteros locales cogiéramos seis o siete boletus edulis y un puñado de níscalos cada uno. Parasoles (Macrolepiota procera) hay muchos, pero pocos los recolectamos, aun sabiendo que, cortados sus sombreros en cuartos, empanados junto a una loncha de jamón serrano y fritos en aceite de oliva, están muy ricos.

Un lugar donde cabe esperar que con algo más de lluvia se anime la cosa a mediados o finales de noviembre es el pinar de Valsaín, en la vertiente segoviana del puerto de Navacerrada. Podemos dejar el coche en el aparcamiento de más de 30 plazas que hay junto a la fuente de la Canaleja y el puente de la Cantina, al pie de las Siete Revueltas –kilómetro 17 de la carretera CL-601.

La bicicleta es una excelente manera de explorar el pinar de Valsaín. Andrés Campos

Allí mismo veremos un portillo con un cartel que dice “acotado de setas” –habremos pedido permiso antes, claro– y un sendero que se adentra en este magnífico bosque de pino silvestre, ligado a la corona desde tiempos de Carlos III. Subiendo siempre a corta distancia del arroyo del Puerto del Paular, que baja del puerto de Cotos, o de su afluente de las Pintadas, siempre encontraremos veneros y tollas donde, por seco y mustio que esté el resto del pinar, crecen los níscalos. Noviembre es su mejor mes y también el de las capuchinas.

Otra excelente manera de explorar este pinar es en bici, siguiendo la pista forestal asfaltada que lo rodea por completo. Es una vuelta de 35 kilómetros, con salida y llegada en la Granja de San Ildefonso, que se puede hacer en unas tres o cuatro horas, depende del tiempo que se invierta en examinar las muchas zonas húmedas que se atraviesan. Tampoco es mala idea dejar de registrar el bosque a mediodía y bajar al real sitio a probar los famosos buñuelos de setas con foie del restaurante La Fundición.
