World.title: Viktor Orbán says he won’t visit detained brother in prison to avoid giving media a reason to celebrate
World.content:
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has said he will not visit his younger brother Áron in prison following his pre-trial detention in a suspected human-smuggling case, claiming he does not want to give the media something to celebrate.

Speaking in an interview with online channel Ultrahang, the Fidesz leader described the investigation involving his brother as a politically motivated spectacle and insisted that Áron was innocent. A Budapest court ordered Áron Orbán and his partner into pre-trial detention for one month on Wednesday over their alleged involvement in a scheme helping Vietnamese nationals obtain Hungarian visas.

Orbán said he last spoke to his brother by phone around two weeks ago. Áron had called to ask whether he should take his children to Slovenia during the autumn school holidays. According to the former prime minister, he told him that he had done nothing wrong and should continue living as he had before.

Orbán, who said he had known his brother for 49 years, described him as a decent, good-hearted person and said he was 100% certain he was innocent. He added that he would not visit him in prison because he did not want the media to be pleased by the visit.

Orbán calls investigation a political show

The former prime minister accused the government of staging a political spectacle through the detention of his brother and former government officials. He claimed the measures were not part of an ordinary legal procedure and likened their theatrical presentation to methods associated with forced confessions.

Orbán said he had no objection to investigations or official scrutiny in principle, but argued that law enforcement was being used for political purposes. He also claimed that the authorities were sent after people who spoke out against the government.

He repeated his earlier assertion that he himself was the real target and his brother merely a tool in a political campaign. The authorities have not publicly established that the investigation is directed at Viktor Orbán.

Former PM defends his record and criticises government

During the interview, Orbán also defended his time in office, rejecting comparisons between Fidesz’s former government and the current Tisza administration. He accused the new government of acting arbitrarily and predicted that Hungary’s economic situation would worsen in 2027 and 2028, citing what he described as damaging tax increases and austerity measures.

He also guaranteed that investigators would find no wrongdoing among his former ministers, describing their decisions as lawful and appropriate.

Asked about rumours that he could become the next United Nations secretary-general, Orbán declined to comment, saying the question was not timely.

World.title: Eight Key Defendants in Istanbul Municipality Mass Trial Freed From Custody
World.content:
Eight defendants in the Istanbul Municipality trial walked free on Friday after a court ordered their release late on Thursday despite prosecutors demanding that all detained defendants remain behind bars.

Those freed included Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu’s lawyer, Mehmet Pehlivan, and Fatos Pinar Turker, manager of Istanbul Municipality’s media company. The decision brought relief in opposition circles, although Imamoglu and other defendants remain in prison.

“I am happy, of course, but also saddened. My brother and my friends are in prison. I want them to regain their freedom soon,” Pehlivan said on Friday after leaving prison.

Turker also focused on those who remained detained: “My only wish is to reunite with my daughters. My thoughts are with the other friends who remain imprisoned,” he said.

Mayor Imamoglu, who is also the main opposition presidential candidate for the next election, is one of the 46 defendants still in custody after the eight were released. A total of 436 people have been indicted in the case, accused of involvement in corruption. They insist that the charges are politically motivated and false.

During the latest hearing, Imamoglu again denied the prosecution’s claims and criticised its reliance on secret witnesses.

“This pile of rubbish built on a secret witness has collapsed. There is not a single tangible witness,” Imamoglu told the court, demanding his release.

Defence lawyers and opposition figures have challenged the use of secret witnesses in the case and demanded the release of those being held, pending trial.

Over the last few years, dozens of opposition mayors and hundreds of party members have been arrested on corruption and terror charges.

Imamoglu was arrested on March 19, 2025. The prosecutor’s office is demanding a 2,352-year prison sentence for him. Imamoglu denies all the accusations.

Opposition politicians, rights groups and international organisations have said the government is using the judiciary to crush its political rivals in what they call an unprecedented crackdown.

World.title: After the Protests: Bulgaria as a Cautionary Tale
World.content:
“The situation is not better, not worse. It’s just the same,” said Vesislava Tancheva, spokesperson for Bulgarians United for One Goal, the civic association behind the protest outside the Russian embassy and which also demonstrated against the previous government. It goes by the acronym BOETS, which in Bulgarian means ‘fighter’.

One thing is different, however – the scale of the protests.

In November and December 2025, tens of thousands of Bulgarians took to the streets across the country. The collapse of the ruling coalition led by the centre-right GERB party, the dominant party in Bulgaria since 2008, was portrayed in media reports as a success story.

Twenty-two-year-old law student Aleksandar Tanev saw firsthand how quickly Gen Z can mobilise. After a few demonstrations, he and some fellow students founded Students Against Mafia. They were soon inundated with requests from young people across the country to join.

A year on, however, Tanev says “it was not enough”.

“This corrupted management that ruled Bulgaria for more than 15 years is responsible for our cities, our roads, our education,” Tanev told BIRN. “They are guilty, but we vote for them. We need to understand our responsibility.”

He was echoed by Asen Lazarov, 27, another of the young people who took to the streets last year and co-founder of the NGO Active Politics, which aims to make politics more accessible to young people.

“Protests are a way to express your democratic participation, but they should not be the final step,” he said. “We should expect more from the politicians that we’ve elected.”

At a time when social movements in France, Albania, Spain or Serbia are challenging the political establishment, Bulgaria offers an instructive case study.

Governments change, system remains

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary Pick Fight with Berlin Over Ukraine Aid
World.content:
Hungarian PM Peter Magyar also criticised the idea of linking Ukraine’s financial support to the ongoing EU budget talks during a visit to Germany this week. “I would like to express, diplomatically and politely but nevertheless firmly, that I do not consider it a good idea to link the European budget, which is ultimately about the EU itself, in any way to another issue,” he said at a press conference with Merz in Berlin, where he otherwise heralded a new beginning in German-Hungarian bilateral relations after years of frosty ties under his predecessor Viktor Orban. Magyar also delivered the renowned State of Europe speech organised by the CDU-affiliated Konrad Adenauer Foundation. Speaking in German, he did not spare Europe’s governing elites, accusing them of having “lost contact with the people”, nor Brussels, which had detected the problems Europe was facing but had been unable to find solutions in recent years. The PM also warned against radical movements offering easy solutions to problems but, in fact, merely end up dividing and polarizing Europe and serving the interests of outside, often hostile forces. His view of the EU sees a gradual shift back towards nation states, which, in his words, know better what their societies need. He also pleaded for cheaper energy sources – though stopped short of saying they should be Russian – and for strengthening the continent’s industrial fabric and competitiveness, and stepping up the fight against illegal migration and climate change.

Fico’s mood this week was not helped by his government losing its parliamentary majority. The prime minister, who spent years demanding early elections whenever his opponents found themselves in the same position, now seems prepared to govern without one. The numbers became clear on Wednesday, when a controversial amendment to the Criminal Procedure Code received just 75 votes in the 150-seat parliament. Two MPs around the recently dismissed environment minister and lawmaker Tomas Taraba voted against it, while former coalition MP Jan Ferencak abstained. The amendment sought to restrict the use of testimony from cooperating defendants. Prosecutors and anti-corruption groups warned that it could undermine ongoing criminal cases, including the “Purgatory” police corruption trial, in which high-profile Smer politician and former police chief Tibor Gaspar is a defendant. Gaspar denies the legislation was intended to help him personally in his legal disputes. Things went wrong again that afternoon. A bill to abolish postal voting from abroad was derailed because none of its sponsors appeared to present it. Under parliamentary rules recently introduced by the coalition itself, the proposal could now be delayed for six months. Gaspar, who was chairing the session and is also among the bill’s sponsors, wants that interpretation reviewed. Fico once had little patience for governments relying on independent MPs. He accused former PM Mikulas Dzurinda of buying support and demanded early elections when Iveta Radicova and Eduard Heger struggled with their majorities. In 2006, he described opaque deals with independent MPs as one of the gravest attacks on parliamentary democracy since 1989. His own coalition now has 75 dependable MPs. Fico says he will negotiate with Taraba’s group and accepts that some bills may fail. Smer still insists this is not a minority government.

World.title: High Bank Fees Hamper Albania’s Crackdown on Cash
World.content:
In Tirana’s 9-Katëshet neighbourhood, people queue for ice cream at 100 lek a scoop.

Previously, the ice cream parlour only accepted cash, but the growing number of tourists among their clientele, many of whom don’t carry cash, has forced the business to start taking bank cards too.

If you pay by card, however, the price is 125 lek.

“We don’t make any extra profit from this,” the woman behind the counter said. “It’s the fee charged by the bank that provides us with the card payment service.”

World.title: On a Bosnian Mountainside, a Quiet Exodus Leaves Only the Elderly Behind
World.content:
As All Saints’ Day approached, Dubravka Jurisic sat down in her home in Straza and counted its residents.

She ran a finger down the handwritten pages where for years she has kept a record of births, deaths and who lives where in this village on the slopes of Mount Majevica, in the far northeast of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Reaching the end, she declared: “Seventy-one people currently live in the village.”

That’s less than half the number counted the last time Bosnia held a census, in 2013. Then, authorities registered 188 residents of Straza, part of Srebrenik municipality, though census totals can include Bosnian citizens who have lived abroad for years. In January 2017, Jurisic made her own count: 138.

Between 1991 and 2013, the population of Srebrenik municipality as a whole shrank from 40,882 to 39,678. The town of Srebrenik itself grew by roughly 1,400 residents. The villages, in other words, are emptying faster than the town.

Those who remain are, by and large, elderly. While Srebrenik municipality is majority Bosniak, Straza is Catholic Croat. Many of its residents hold Croatian passports, easing their departure since Croatia joined the European Union in 2013.

“Before the war, there were about 100 unmarried young men in the village,” said Jurisic, 52, referring to the 1992-95 war in Bosnia during the collapse of federal Yugoslavia. “Today we don’t have a single one.” According to Jurisic, the youngest resident is already a teenager.

World.title: Bosnian Court Convicts Three of Wartime Abuses of Civilian Prisoners
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp



Bosanski Novi. Photo: BIRN.

The Bosnian state court on Thursday sentenced Mira Bosancic to 17 years in prison, and Simo Licina and Zarko Kalinic to 12 years each, for crimes against civilians who were detained in the fire station building in Bosanski Novi during the Bosnian war in ​​1992.

In the first-instance verdict, the court found Bosancic, Licina and Kalinic guilty of committing crimes against humanity – persecution by murder, enforced disappearance and physical abuse.

They committed the crimes while serving as military policemen with the Bosnian Serb Army’s Light Novograd Brigade.

“The judging panel has determined that during the relevant period, a widespread and systematic attack by the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, now Republika Srpska, took place,” presiding judge Halil Lagumdzija said.

Bosancic was found guilty on three counts of participating in the beating of detained civilians in the basement of the fire station building, as well seizing several people who have been missing ever since.

Licina and Kalinic were found guilty of tying up and stripping a prisoner, cutting him with a knife and then pouring salt on him. The prisoner died of his injuries.

“His body was taken away and has not been found to this day,” said Lagumdzija.

However, the judges found that it had not been proven that Bosancic participated in the forced disappearance of two civilians and the killing of another. Due to lack of evidence, the defendants were acquitted of beating and taking away two men.

Four other defendants in the trial – Nedjeljko Pilipovic and Bogdan, Zarko and Jovan Grab – were acquitted of all charges.

The verdict can be appealed.

World.title: Greek Deputy Minister Quits Over Allegations About Daughter’s University Admission
World.content:
Deputy Minister of Development Lazaros Tsavdaridis. Photo: Greek Ministry of Development .

Deputy Minister of Development Lazaros Tsavdaridis has resigned following allegations that his daughter only nominally joined a handball team, without actually participating, in order to secure extra points for her university admission requirements.

A report by MEGA TV on November 11 alleged that 17-year-old registered with the youth handball team of Pylaia, Thessaloniki, and travelled to the Panhellenic Youth Championship with the team, but did not actrually play.

Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis accepted the Deputy Minister’s resignation on Thursday morning. Pavlos Marinakis, the government spokesperson, said that the explanations provided for the incident “were not sufficient”.

Marinakis said the government was reviewing the system for awarding academic points to athletes, with an emphasis on actual participation and the duration of their involvement in sports, adding that the Ministry of Education will re-examine the current framework in place since 1999.

Tsavdaridis denied wrongdoing. “My daughter never made use of additional points to gain entry into any Greek university department,” he stated on November 11.

He said his daughter sat for the entrance exams and gained admission to the School of Agriculture in Larissa on her own merit, without using any points derived from the handball team she played for.

He also noted that she did not attend the School of Agriculture, choosing instead to pursue her studies at a university in Cyprus.

The Greek Handball Federation in a press release issued on November 11 said no competition regulations had been violated.

“According to official competition records, [the teenager] had a valid athlete registration card and was physically present on her team’s bench during the matches for which she was registered,” it stated.

“There is no evidence of any violation of competition regulations that would constitute an unlawful or irregular participation of the athlete in the tournament,” it added.

The government said Deputy Interior Minister Vasilis Spanakis is taking on the position of Deputy Minister of Development.

World.title: North Macedonia Opposition Accuses Govt Over Subsidiary of Failed Serbian Bank
World.content:
Venko Filipce, head of North Macedonia’s main opposition Social Democrats, SDSM. Photo: SDSM.

The opposition Social Democrats, SDSM, on Thursday accused the government of trying to silence it and protect the local subsidiary of Serbia’s failed Alta Banka.

The claim came after North Macedonia’s National Bank filed criminal complaints against four senior SDSM party officials over their statements about the bank’s condition.

The SDSM said the bank’s criminal complaints against party leader Venko Filipce and three others were intended to put pressure on the party, accusing Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski of acting “in a panic to protect Alta Banka”.

Filipce wrote on Facebook that his party would file its own criminal complaints over Alta Banka’s entry into North Macedonia and its handling of citizens’ and public enterprises’ funds.

On Wednesday, North Macedonia’s National Bank confirmed that it had filed criminal complaints over statements made by senior SDSM members containing “serious and unfounded accusations” about Alta Banka Bitola, the North Macedonia subsidiary of the recently bankrupted Serbian Alta Banka. The National Bank did not specify the alleged criminal offences.

On November 5, Mickoski called for prosecutors to investigate the SDSM for the “criminal offence of sabotage”, accusing it of spreading lies and putting citizens in a state of unjustified insecurity and fear.

Serbia’s central bank revoked the operating licence of Alta Banka in Belgrade on October 31, citing the deterioration in its financial position. Bankruptcy proceedings followed.

Its North Macedonia subsidiary, in which the Belgrade bank holds a 95.17 per cent stake, was placed under temporary administration by North Macedonia’s central bank on November 1.

This was intended to protect the local bank’s assets and depositors while its ownership situation is resolved. It has resulted in temporary restrictions on customers’ access to their money, triggering concern among savers and queues at ATMs.

The SDSM has questioned how and why Alta Banka was given a permit to enter the North Macedonia market in 2025, and whether the origin of its capital was properly checked.

Filipce has alleged links between the bank’s Serbian owner, businessman Davor Macura, and Serbian ex-President Aleksandar Vucic’s political and business circles.

He raised suspicions that the bank could have been used for money laundering, involving Russian and other questionable capital. His party has also questioned whether the bank’s reported financial assets actually exist and whether political influence affected the National Bank’s decisions.

Filipce has claimed that as much as 150 to 180 million euros could be at stake, questioning whether customers, including pensioners receiving payments through the bank, would be able to access their money.

On Wednesday, in parliament, Central Bank Governor Trajko Slaveski insisted Alta Banka Bitola was financially sound, and should be offered to another potential buyer.

He refused to disclose how many big corporate clients, including state-owned companies and public enterprises, hold accounts with Alta Banka Bitola, which could shed more light on the extent of the problem, calling it a “banking secret”.

Chief Public Prosecutor Nenad Saveski at the same hearing declined to answer whether the Prosecutor’s Office had opened an initial investigation into the bank, insisting that, too, was confidential.

Despite the political storm surrounding it, Alta Banka Bitola is a relatively small player in North Macedonia’s banking sector.

It ranked in 12th place among the country’s 14 banks in terms of total assets in 2025, with assets of around 11.3 billion denars [about 184 million euros], representing just 1.21 per cent of the banking market.

World.title: War of words follows consumer watchdog action against retail chains in Bulgaria
World.content:
A war of words lasting days has followed action by Bulgaria’s consumer protection body against retail chains in Bulgaria, with the row inevitably also attracting political comments.

As The Sofia Globe reported on November 9, Bulgaria’s Consumer Protection Commission (CPC) said that it had fined supermarket chain Kaufland Bulgaria 75.7 million euro, citing “unfair trade practices towards Bulgarian food producers”.

The regulator announced three violations against suppliers: pressure to reduce delivery prices, unfair deduction of fees for services, and unjustified delay in price increase negotiations. The decision is subject to appeal in court.

The chain rejects the accusations, claims that the total added value they generate for the state is almost 14 billion euro and it is preparing for a legal battle.

Mihail Petrov, CEO of Kaufland Bulgaria: “And if Kaufland goes on a bobsled ride down, then the bankruptcy of Corpbank will seem like a spring breeze to them. Kaufland has a lot of loans, a lot of suppliers, it has 8,800 employees and stop practicing on it. I can’t wait to go to court and turn the CPC’s act into dust”.

The retail chain’s director’s warnings about a possible outflow of investments prompted a sharp response from Economy Minister Alexander Pulev, who described Petrov’s tone as arrogant and said that the government would not give in to such warnings.

“We are not at war with retail chains, we are at war with unfair trade practices,” Pulev said.

The FMCG (Fast Moving Consumer Goods) market is quite profitable, quite liquid, even if there is an outflow in the market position of a chain, this vacuum will be filled literally within a few weeks by their competitors,” he said.

“Before threatening the Bulgarian state, let this gentleman open the statistics and look at the fact that literally the latest data for this year show a 100 per cent growth in foreign direct investment in the country, so I am calm, I have no reason for any concern about this type of arrogance,” Pulev said.

On Facebook, Prime Minister Roumen Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria ruling party said: “No matter how big you are, you are not above the law.

“When he (Petov) makes an analogy with CorpBank, the Kaufland manager confuses the law with lawlessness,” Progressive Bulgaria said.

“No one is stronger than the state when it applies the law to protect the rights of its citizens. Such declarations only confirm the correctness of the control bodies. Instead of arguments, we hear threats,” the ruling party said.

The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions in Bulgaria (CITUB) also expressed serious concern about the public statements by the management of Kaufland Bulgaria .

CITUB said that it does dispute the company’s right to defend its interests through legal means, but it is unacceptable for the jobs and fate of employees to be used as an argument to exert pressure on state institutions.

“Every company has the right to defend its interests in court. At the same time, CITUB considers it unacceptable for the jobs and fate of workers to be used as an argument for putting pressure on state institutions in connection with the exercise of their legal powers,” the trade union organisation said.

Ivailo Mirchev, an MP for opposition coalition Democratic Bulgaria, said that Petrov’s statement was arrogant and unacceptable.

Instead of scaring with catastrophic scenarios, the management of Kaufland should think about whether it has always been fair to Bulgarian producers over the years and whether it has had unacceptable commercial practices, Mirchev said.

Milena Dragiyska, chief executive of Lidl Bulgaria – a Lidl shop in Vidin was shut down temporarily earlier this week by the Bulgarian Food Safety Agency over alleged violations – described to the media how the pressure was affecting the daily work in the shops.

Dragiyska said there have been cases where seven, eight or nine inspectors have arrived at employees who are on their own shift.

She alleged that inspectors had apologised to staff, explaining that they were ordered to find grounds for a sanction.

“Actually, the big question is what is the goal? That is not clear to us,” Dragiyska said.

She warned that the consequences of this pressure could affect thousands of jobs and Bulgarian producers who rely on the chains for the sale of their goods. According to her, Lidl alone works with over 300 Bulgarian producers, and the volume of joint work is growing.

Dragiyska insisted that the conversation with the state focus on irrigation, labour, financing and the competitiveness of Bulgarian production.

Bulgarian food producers and processors have said that state pressure on large retail chains is also threatening their own production.

Zhivka Grozdeva from the Association of Fruit Growers in Bulgaria believes that the voice of producers who have been working successfully with the chains for years remains silenced in the public conversation.

At a conference of the Association for Modern Trade – an association of which most major retailers in Bulgaria are members – Grozdeva said that large retailers provide a market for significant quantities of Bulgarian fruits and vegetables.

” Without them, part of the production would remain unsold or even unpicked ,” said Grozdeva, who is also a fruit producer.

She said that no one is obliged to work with chains if they prefer another option.

Asked to comment on the average markups on Bulgarian fruit, she estimated that they amount to about 10 per cent-15 per cent, unlike small shops, where, according to her, it reaches 50 per cent.

Grozdeva described the relationship with the chains as a direct negotiation process: the manufacturer sends an offer, the retailer responds, and both parties specify the terms and deliveries.

According to her, the main obstacles to Bulgarian production lie elsewhere – in insecure access to water for irrigation, as irrigation systems cover 1/7 of the country’s territory, the shortage of workers, and the growing administrative burden.

“They increase costs and make it difficult to compete with producers from other countries,” Grozdeva said.

“I see a partner in the large chains,” Vladislav Mihaylov from the National Association of Dairy Processors said during the Association for Modern Trade conference.

Mihaylov described the pressure on foreign chains in recent weeks as an “undeclared war”.

“Nobody wins from any war. Neither the state nor the consumers. We, the producers, are between a rock and a hard place,” Mihaylov said.

Nikolai Vulkavnov, executive director of the Association of Modern Trade, said: “Progress is not measured solely by the price of cheese in the shop”.

He said that constant changes in rules, unpredictable enforcement and huge sanctions could lead to investments being frozen or withdrawn, with consequences for jobs and incomes.

“There will be no new jobs, existing ones may be cut, salaries may fall,” Vulkanov said.

On November 13, GERB leader Boiko Borissov sharply criticised Kaufland Bulgaria’s Petrov’s statement.

Borissov described Petrov’s words as absolutely unacceptable: “They will certainly fire him and all this has to happen, because no one will like such a statement, no one will allow it”.

The GERB leader said that he was wondering whether the government wanted to take Bulgaria back to the time of the communist-era state-owned shops.

Borissov said that he suspects that those close to the government are interested in the properties of Kaufland and other large retail chains.

“I guess because communists never do anything for their own sake, and the best properties in big cities are in these chains,” Borissov said.

In my opinion, one of Radev’s oligarchs has looked around in the chains and now they will do everything possible to expel them. They are worth chasing, I emphasise, with such behaviour, but they do nothing for their own sake,” he said.

(Photo: Bartosz Wacawski/ freeimages.com)

World.title: Bulgaria supported ‘with reservations’ declaration in Dublin on European security
World.content:
Bulgaria has supported with reservations the French initiative on key principles of European security, presented at the Ninth Summit of the European Political Community in Dublin, the government government information service said on November 13.

Radev expressed written reservations to the preamble of the declaration, requesting that the political messages be adapted to the current stage of the peace negotiations in Ukraine, the statement said.

The statement followed media reports that Bulgaria was alone among European Union member states to not have signed the declaration.

Bulgaria supports the achievement of a just and lasting peace in Ukraine through negotiations, the new round of talks in Abu Dhabi with the mediation of the United States is an important step in this direction, according to the statement.

“European positions must support this process, and the language of the common documents must reflect the dynamics of the processes and expectations from the peace negotiations,” it said.

The preamble of the document speaks of “the unprovoked full-scale Russian aggression against Ukraine and the growing threats to the stability of Europe”.

It also says that the signatories “reaffirm their firm support for the independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders”.

They emphasise that Russia’s hybrid campaigns and attempts to undermine support for Ukraine will only strengthen their commitment to Ukraine and their resolve.

The signatories recall that the path to peace in Ukraine must be decided together with Ukraine and that any issue affecting European security must be resolved together with Europeans.

It is emphasised that Ukraine’s security is an integral part of Euro-Atlantic security and that the future development of European strategic stability will be conditioned by the end of the war in Ukraine.

This is the full text of the declaration, as posted on the website of the President of France:

Committed to peace and upholding international law, and in the face of unprovoked full-scale Russian aggression against Ukraine and growing threats to Europe stability, the signatory states, gathered for the 9th Summit of the European Political Community in Dublin on the 12th of November 2026, consider strengthening European security and defending their security interests as their common objective.

The signatory states reiterate their firm support for the independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognised borders

They underline the necessity to provide robust and credible security guarantees to Ukraine and reiterate, for those concerned, their intention to do so, in order to prevent the recurrence of aggression in Europe in the future.

They underline that Russia’s hybrid campaigns and attempts to undermine support to Ukraine will only strengthen their commitment to Ukraine and their resolve.

The signatory states recall that the path to peace in Ukraine should be decided with Ukraine and that any matter affecting European security should be decided with the Europeans.

They consider that the following key principles of European security can contribute to provide a path to a just and lasting peace for Ukraine, which will be of utmost importance for stability in Europe

They emphasize that Ukraine’s security is an integral part of Euro-Atlantic security and that future developments in European strategic stability will be conditional upon the conclusion of the war in Ukraine.

I. General Principles

The signatory states reaffirm the following general principles related to European security :

International law and the Charter of the United Nations are the cornerstone of this Declaration. In addition, the signatory states reaffirm the rules and principles upon which European security is and must remain founded, notably where applicable to the relevant signatory states, the North Atlantic Treaty (1949), the Statute of the Council of Europe (1949), the Treaty on the European Union and the Treaty on the functioning of the European Union (1950, 1957, 1986, 1992 and sq.), the Helsinki Final Act (1975), the Charter of Paris for a New Europe (1990), the Agreement on the European Economic Area (1992), and the Istanbul Charter for Security in Europe (1999). Common objectives contained in this Declaration are rooted in these fundamental documents and the signatories which are parties to them aim to ensure their effective implementation In this regard, the signatory states underline the importance of the following principles, which form the foundations of peace and stability on the European continent : respect for the sovereign equality of states and the rights inherent in sovereignty, such as the territorial integrity, the inviolability of borders, non-interference in domestic affairs, and the right of states to freely determine their relations with other states, and to choose whether or not to participate in treaties, alliances, or international organizations ; the refraining from the threat of or the use of force, including irresponsible nuclear rhetoric and coercion, and the peaceful settlement of disputes, in accordance with international law and good neighbourly relations ; the right to individual or collective self-defence in the event of an armed attack ; and the respect for the international law, including the international law of the sea as reflected by UNCLOS. The signatory states recognise that European states bear a primary responsibility and are assuming greater responsibility for the security of Europe, which will also contribute positively to global and transatlantic security. The signatory states reaffirm their commitment to human rights, and fundamental freedoms for all, without distinction of any kind, including on the grounds of race, sex, language, or religion, including in the digital realm, as well as the right of all nations to freely determine their political status, in accordance with international law. Democracy, rule of law, human rights and respect of the humanitarian international law are essential elements of comprehensive security and contribute to resilient societies capable of resisting both internal and external pressures. Enhanced participatory democracy, transparency and enabling civic space, including media freedom and freedom of expression, are indispensable safeguards of democratic resilience and long-term security. International law also applies to the global commons we share. Free, safe, autonomous and unhindered access to these spaces must be ensured within the limits of international law, in the air, on the seas, in outer space and in cyberspace. This declaration and the associated common objectives are in line with international mechanisms and the missions of existing multilateral organizations and forums in Europe (NATO, EU, OSCE, Council of Europe). Signatories who are members of NATO reaffirm that NATO is the foundation of their collective security and that the Alliance remains the cornerstone of their collective defence. They recall their ironclad commitment to collective defence under Article 5 of the Washington Treaty. They reaffirm their unwavering commitment to the transatlantic bond and to the Euro-Atlantic security. They recall their determination to build a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO, working together with the United States and Canada which continue to play an essential role in NATO and assuming greater responsibilities for the Alliance’s collective defence. Signatories who are members of the European Union reaffirm their commitment to a stronger and more capable European Union that is better equipped to act and deal autonomously with immediate and future challenges and threats with a 360° approach, while recognizing the challenge and threats on the Eastern Flank. Enlargement of the European Union, anchored in a merit-based process and as a geostrategic investment in peace, security, stability and prosperity, also contributes – together with the European Neighbourhood Policy – to the security of the continent. In this global context, the security of the continent depends on strengthening both national and collective defence capabilities in the appropriate forums to address threats with a 360° approach, with the aim of deterring any aggressive actions and being able to defend against them. It also relies on strengthening the resilience and robustness of our democracies, as well as human rights and rule of law. International cooperation, to complement and deepen European and transatlantic frameworks, should always be pursued with a 360° approach. Diversifying partnerships with countries that are committed to upholding the principles of international law and the UN Charter, and that offer balanced and mutually beneficial relationships under the principle of good neighbourly relationships contributes to security and stability in Europe and to address shared challenges and advance common interests.

II. Common objectives

With the aim of strengthening security in Europe, the signatory states support the following common objectives in accordance with their respective international commitments and constitutional laws :

Security – the signatory states will uphold security, peace and stability in Europe in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations and their respective international commitments, including through bilateral agreements between them and for the states concerned by further strengthening the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union, which are cornerstones for our security. National security and Defence efforts – in accordance with their respective international commitments, security and defence policies and constitutional obligations, the signatory states reaffirm their commitments to strengthening their capabilities in order to respond to their legitimate security needs, enhance their security and ensure the defence of Europe. To this end, and according to their respective commitments, they will make the most effective use of their resources and continue to develop cooperation among themselves and with relevant organizations, as each of them deems appropriate. Collective resilience – in the face of destabilizing actions conducted below the threshold of armed attack, including through cyber and hybrid activities and coercion, and the expansion of conflict into new areas, the signatory states will work in order to develop the tools necessary to prevent, deter and respond to these challenges, to strengthen the protection of their critical infrastructure, to enhance their resilience, and to cooperate on a voluntary basis to improve the detection and attribution of these attacks, with the aim of discouraging the threats and providing a coordinated response and holding to account those responsible. Risk management and reduction– the signatory states support discussions on further risk management and reduction mechanisms that contribute to stability in Europe, once the conditions are met and peace is restored in Europe. This could address particular risks, be it military or coming from actions conducted below the threshold of armed aggression, aiming at ensuring the stability of the entire continent. Operational Planning – the signatory states will continue to strengthen their collective working practices and their joint operational capabilities for the defence and security of Europe, notably through NATO for those being members of it, as well through other cooperation mechanisms and inclusive coalitions. Industrial cooperation – the concerned signatory states will continue to strengthen their defence industrial production capacity and cooperation across Europe to develop resilient, secure and more independent supply chains and infrastructure for their defence equipment, without prejudice to cooperation with trusted partners. They will promote, as appropriate, cooperation projects between all European actors and foster a competitive European defence equipment market across Europe. They will actively work to create the necessary conditions to mobilize private capital, and support the growth of European defence companies Strategic Dialogues – the signatory states will continue deepening their exchanges and dialogues on strategic issues related to European security, complementing and benefiting from existing collective security frameworks for those participating in them and bilateral arrangements. Democratic integrity – Human rights, rule of law and democratic systems, upon which European societies are fundamentally based, and must be protected and strengthened, to ensure their integrity and resilience in the face of growing deliberate campaigns aimed at undermining those values, including Foreign Information Manipulation and Interferences (FIMI). The signatory states will continue to promote solidarity, cooperation, and the use of the necessary mechanisms and institutions to achieve this goal. Fight against terrorism – the signatory states reaffirm their commitments in the fight against terrorism. In this framework, they condemn terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, including state-sponsored terrorism in the strongest possible terms and will continue their cooperation to respond collectively to this threat, in accordance with international law. Response to illicit drug and human-trafficking and migrant-smuggling as well as organised crime networks in Europe – the signatory states reaffirm that illicit drug and human-trafficking as well as organized crimes networks are a major threat to the security, safety and health of the citizens in Europe. They remain committed to fighting illicit drug and human-trafficking and organised crime networks in accordance with international law with the strongest determination and to safeguard the integrity of European societies. Security of supply – the signatory states will continue to work towards the reduction of their dependencies as well as regarding supply chains for critical components or materials. By diversifying and setting up new trade partnerships, they will enable Europe to better respond to the challenges it faces. Protection of global commons – the signatory states will contribute to the protection and security of global commons, ensuring, within the limits of international law, safe, autonomous and unhindered access to these areas, and taking greater responsibility when European interests are involved. In accordance with international law, the protection of freedom of navigation on international waterways, in particular, requires upholding the high seas as a space of freedom, cooperation, and law. These same principles apply, as appropriate, to other shared global commons. Contribution of Europe to Global food security – building on the principles of protecting global commons, the signatory states reaffirm the necessity of the freedom of navigation and of the safety of commercial shipping, notably in the Black Sea, and that the uninterrupted functioning of all maritime routes is essential for global food security.

The above is without prejudice to the specific character of the security and defence policy and interests of the signatory states, and their respective constitutional laws and international commitments.

The Signatory States :

Republic of Albania, Principality of Andorra, Republic of Austria, Kingdom of Belgium, Republic of Bulgaria, Republic of Croatia, Republic of Cyprus, Czech Republic, Kingdom of Denmark, Republic of Estonia, Republic of Finland, French Republic, Georgia, Federal Republic of Germany, Hellenic Republic, Hungary, Republic of Iceland, Ireland, Italian Republic, Republic of Latvia, Principality of Liechtenstein, Republic of Lithuania, Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, Republic of Malta, Republic of Moldova, Principality of Monaco, Montenegro, Kingdom of the Netherlands, Republic of North Macedonia, Kingdom of Norway, Republic of Poland, Portuguese Republic, Romania, Republic of San Marino, Slovak Republic, Republic of Slovenia, Kingdom of Spain, Kingdom of Sweden, Ukraine, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

World.title: November 15 is the statutory deadline to fit vehicles with tyres suitable for winter conditions
World.content:
From November 15 to March 1, motor vehicles in Bulgaria must by law be fitted with tyres suitable for winter conditions.

According to the law, approved by Bulgaria’s Parliament in 2016, cars must have tyres designed for winter conditions or that have a tread depth of no less than or equal to four millimetres, the Interior Ministry said.

The Road Traffic Act allows the use of all-season or even summer tyres if they meet the grip requirement, but experts strongly recommend winter tyres for better safety in cold weather.

The traditional Interior Ministry “Winter” campaign, which aims to increase drivers’ attention to preparing their cars for the upcoming winter season, started on November 1.

(Photo: Clive Leviev-Sawyer)

World.title: Bulgaria issues weather warnings over strong winds forecast for November 13
World.content:
Bulgaria’s national meteorological bureau has issued the Code Orange warning of dangerous weather for several districts for November 13 because of forecast strong winds.

The districts subject to the Code Orange warning are Montana, Vratsa, Dobrich, Varna, Bourgas, Shoumen, Yambol, Stara Zagora and Haskovo.

All the remaining districts, with two exceptions, are subject to the lesser Code Yellow warning of potentially dangerous weather, also because of forecast strong winds.

The exceptions are the districts of Blagoevgrad and Smolyan, which are classified Code Green for November 13, meaning that no weather warning is in place.

In Bulgaria on November 13, minimum temperatures will be between 11° and 16° Celsius, in the Sofia region, about 12°.

There will be variable cloudiness on Friday. In the evening, from the northwest, the cloudiness will increase and thicken, and rain will begin.

It will be warm for the period with maximum temperatures between 20° and 25° Celsius, in places subject to southerly winds up to 27°-28°, and in Sofia, about 21°.

In the mountains, light rain will fall in places. A strong, stormy wind will blow from the west-southwest on the highlands and northern slopes. The maximum temperature at an altitude of 1200 metres will be about 14°, at 2000 metres, about 9°.

Over the Black Sea coast, the cloudiness will be variable. In the morning, mainly along the southern coast, there will be low layered clouds and reduced visibility. There will be a strong to stormy southwest wind. Maximum temperatures will be 21°-23°, the meteorological bureau said.

World.title: Bulgaria’s government proposes complete ban on advertising gambling games
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Cabinet approved on November 11 proposed amendments to the Gambling Act that, if approved by Parliament, will see a complete ban on the advertising of gambling games.

“The aim is to strengthen the prevention of the development or deepening of addiction, as well as to have a positive impact on the most vulnerable groups of people,” the government information service said.

A limited presence of trademarks of organisers of gambling would be allowed only in sponsorships of sports clubs, federations, associations and organisations, as well as in support of activities in the fields of culture, healthcare and education, the statement said.

The amendments propose that the activities of affiliate operators be suspended. This ensures consistency between the ban on advertising gambling games and the regime applicable to persons who promote them.

A one-time state fee is introduced for maintaining a licence for organising the activities of production, distribution and service of gaming equipment and import, distribution and service of gaming equipment.

A five-year licence would cost 50 000 euro and a 10-year licence would cost 100 000 euro.

The alternative tax under the Corporate Income Tax Act (CITA) for land-based casinos and gaming halls is increasing in 2027. From 2028, this tax will be eliminated from the CITA and will be replaced by a two-component state tax provided for in the Gambling Act.

A minimum of 100 000 euro per month will be the variable part of the two-component state fee for issuing and maintaining an online betting licence.

The amendments are also related to an increase in the one-time fees for maintaining a licence to organise gambling games, the amount of contributions for socially responsible behaviour, and fines and property sanctions.

Activities are also planned to expand the prevention of gambling addiction among individuals in the education system, including through the implementation of information campaigns, preventive programmes and the development of appropriate teaching materials, the government information service said.

The amendments introduce a new requirement, that a foreign legal entity organising online betting must have a place of business in Bulgaria.

“This creates an additional mechanism for tracking financial flows, helping to detect discrepancies between the declared activity, the amount of bets, the paid out winnings, the income and expenses, and the corporate tax due,” the statement said.

A mandatory cash contribution is also introduced for payment institutions, banks and electronic money companies that carry out payment transactions related to participation in gambling games and the payment of winnings.

The bill also proposes a complete ban on cash payments between construction companies, contractors and subcontractors under contracts, construction activities, supplies of materials and provision of services.

It is envisaged that payments will be made by bank transfer or through other traceable electronic payment instruments.

“The measure will contribute to limiting the shadow economy, increasing financial discipline and creating a level playing field for construction companies that comply with the legislation,” the statement said.

(Photo: Daniel Alther/ freeimages.com)

World.title: European Parliament demands that Russia returns deported Ukrainian children
World.content:
In a resolution adopted on November 13, members of the European Parliament said that perpetrators responsible for the deportation or forced transfer of Ukrainian children during the war must be held to account.

Strongly condemning Russia’s systematic deportation, forcible transfer, illegal adoption, forced Russification, indoctrination and militarisation of Ukrainian children during the war, the text – adopted by 536 votes in favour, eight against and 37 abstentions – demands the immediate cessation of these practices and reiterates Russia’s full responsibility for respecting the rights of children under its control.

MEPs are calling on Russia to immediately, safely and unconditionally return all deported and forcibly transferred Ukrainian children back from Russian-controlled territory to unoccupied Ukraine.

They are insisting that the return of children is an obligation under international law and must never be used as a bargaining instrument or made conditional upon territorial concessions, prisoner exchanges, or other political agreements.

According to the resolution, as of September 2026, a total of 20 651 cases of the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children by Russia have been verified, whereas approximately 1.6 million Ukrainian children are estimated to remain under Russian occupation.

It also states that, as of October 28 2026, a total of 2752 Ukrainian children deported, forcibly transported or rescued from Russian-occupied territories have so far been returned.

MEPs firmly insist that the safe and unconditional return of all unlawfully deported and forcibly transferred Ukrainian children constitutes not only an urgent humanitarian necessity but also remains a centrepiece of international efforts to establish accountability for Russian crimes committed during the war.

It must, they argue, be a central priority in all diplomatic initiatives and negotiations concerning any genuine peace agreement ending Russia’s war of aggression.

MEPs emphasise that no lasting peace can disregard the rights of these children or the accountability of those responsible for violating their rights.

The European Parliament also calls on EU member states to strengthen their practical cooperation with Ukraine, international partners, and organisations to accelerate the identification, documentation, tracing and return of all missing and deported Ukrainian children, as well as to further expand existing EU sanctions against officials and entities identified as being responsible for child deportations.

The European Parliament reiterated its full support for the International Criminal Court, the court’s unhindered activity, and its arrest warrants issued against Russian President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Children’s Rights Commissioner for the President of Russia, for the war crime of the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children.

MEPs emphasise, however, that accountability must extend beyond Russia’s upper leadership to encompass the entire chain of perpetrators and enablers responsible for the execution of these crimes .

The resolution also supports the close collaboration between different stakeholders, including Europol and Eurojust, and the Ukrainian Ombudsman, for information gathering and locating illegally transferred children.

World.title: Bulgaria’s Cabinet approves large-scale military joint acquisition deals with Italy, France and Spain
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Cabinet approved on November 11 agreements and memoranda with France, Italy and Spain on the joint acquisition of artillery ammunition, military vehicles and anti-drone systems under the EU’s SAFE programme

The largest of the projects by declared value is for the acquisition of up to 1040 military transport vehicles from Italy. The maximum budget envisaged is 410 million euro, with deliveries to be carried out in two stages.

The first covers the period from 2027 to 2030 and envisages the purchase of up to 700 vehicles worth up to 290 million euro. The financing will be provided through SAFE, and the amount also includes training of military personnel, technical support and spare parts.

The second stage should be completed by the end of 2032 and provides for the delivery of the remaining machines, up to a total of 1040. This will require additional funds of up to 120 million euro.

The project aims to improve the transport provision and operational readiness of the army. Opportunities for industrial cooperation are also envisaged, including the assembly of part of the equipment in Bulgaria with the participation of Bulgarian industry.

Bulgaria will prepare a framework agreement with France for the joint acquisition of 155-mm ammunition for the Caesar self-propelled howitzers.

This is the next step in the implementation of the project for the development of the artillery capabilities of the Bulgarian Army.

In 2025, the two countries signed a framework agreement for the acquisition of the howitzers themselves. The National Assembly is yet to approve the investment expenditure project, after which the individual orders with the specific financial parameters and deadlines will be signed.

Bulgaria will cooperate with Spain in the acquisition of systems to counter unmanned aerial vehicles. The approved memorandum provides for the joint purchase of up to 10 mobile systems and up to 10 container-type systems. Spain is the lead country in the project.

The next steps are for the National Assembly to approve the relevant investment expenditure project and for Bulgaria to join Spain’s contract for the acquisition of the systems.

All three projects are part of the efforts to develop Bulgaria’s defense capabilities through joint European procurement under SAFE. The documents approved by the government mark the beginning of the next stages, but the acquisitions will require additional decisions and the conclusion of specific contracts.

World.title: Sofia signs 282M euro contract on EU grant funding to modernise urban transport, infrastructure
World.content:
Sofia mayor Vasil Terziev signed a contract for 282 million euro in European grant funding for the modernisation of public transport and the construction and renovation of streets and boulevards in Bulgaria’s capital city, the municipality said on November 12.

The contract was signed with Regional Development and Public Works Minister Ivan Shishkov.

The funds are provided under the procedure Support for Integrated Urban Transport and Sustainable Urban Mobility of Sofia Municipality, Priority 1 Integrated Urban Development of the Regional Development programme 2021 – 2027.

“We expect the metro line from the centre to Tsarigradsko Shose, the connection with Obelya and the connection that will provide contact with the railway station, as well as the extension of the Ring Road from the Lyulin metro stations to the Sofia Ring Road, to be built and put into operation soon,” Shishkov said.

The programme envisages large-scale investments in the development of transport.

Among these are the extension of the Third Metro Line through the Slatina district, the construction of a metro station next to the Obelya railway station on the Sofia – Kyustendil railway line, with a tunnel connection to the Obelya metro depot, as well as the acquisition of new metro trains for lines No. 1, 2 and 4.

With the signing of an additional agreement on October 27 for the delivery of eight more metro trains, the total number of new trains planned under the programme for lines No. 1, 2 and 4 will reach 16.

All of them should be delivered by autumn 2028. The new metro trains will provide greater comfort with quieter movement and air-conditioned cabins, as well as higher energy efficiency through an energy recovery system during braking, the municipality said.

The secured financing will contribute to covering part of the investments already made and will support the further development of the metro as the main backbone of public transport in Sofia.

In land transport, the funds will ensure the delivery of 75 low-floor trolleybuses with batteries for autonomous movement – 40 articulated with a length of 18 metres and 35 single ones with a length of 12 metres. 50 low-floor fast-charging electric buses and the necessary charging stations will also be delivered. Of these, 35 will be 12 metres long and 15 will be 18 metres long.

The new trolleybuses will allow for the expansion of the route network. It is planned to extend line No. 3 to Mladost-4 and provide a connection with Vrazhdebna, as well as line No. 8 to Orlandovtsi. New trolleybus connections are also planned between Lyulin and Gotse Delchev and between Nadezhda and Mladost-1.

The electric buses will serve two new ring lines – No. 71 between Levski G and Gotse Delchev and No. 75 between Geo Milev and Pavlovo. The routes will pass through key directions, including G. M. Dimitrov Blvd. and Todor Kableshkov Blvd.

With this European funding, combined with the long-term loan that the Sofia municipality will procure, the aim is for all ground public transport vehicles to be low-floor and air-conditioned by 2030, the municpality said.

This will improve accessibility and travel comfort, as well as connections between neighbourhoods, it said.

Investments for which construction activities have already been completed are also included. They are for the construction of Todor Kableshkov Blvd. between Louis Ayer St. and Cherni Vrah Blvd., which was completed this year, as well as Rozhen Blvd. from the overpass over the railway line to the Northern Expressway. Rozhen Blvd. was completed at the end of last year, and now the municipality is preparing the repair of the section from the railway overpass to the Nadezhda overpass, which will be financed through a long-term loan.

According to data from the Management and Monitoring Information System (MIS), the contract is the largest in terms of value for a project under this programmeme, under which Sofia municipality is a beneficiary, since the first programmeming period 2007-2013.

(Photo: Sofia municipality)

World.title: Croatia is Facing a Waste Crisis: Waste Could End Up in Forests
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Croatia is currently facing a serious waste crisis, in which waste could end up in the streets and forests. In some cases, it often already is.

The Ekologija grada (City Ecology) association recently warned of the growing problem of waste acceptance at landfills in Croatia, assessing that due to insufficient capacities and the refusal to accept waste from other areas, regular waste collection could be interrupted in part of the country. Poslovni reports that because of what they describe as a crisis of trust in the waste management system after scandals involving illegally disposed waste, a number of landfills have limited or stopped accepting waste from other cities and municipalities. Among them are Karepovac, Ploče’s Lovornik, Bjelovar’s Doline, Diklo, and Sodol.

The consequences of the lack of available capacities, they emphasise, are particularly felt by Makarska and the municipalities of the Makarska Riviera, Omiš, Kaštela, Dugi Rat, Zadvarje and Šestanovac, which have been forced to look for alternative landfills, conclude temporary agreements or organise the transport of waste to more distant counties.

Similar difficulties, they note, have also been experienced by Varaždin, Samobor, Jastrebarsko, Josipdol and Plaški, while Otočac, after the closure of the Podum landfill, redirected its waste to the Babina Gora Waste Management Centre.

The association warns that the problem does not affect only municipal waste but also industrial waste, and that public service providers and authorised companies could be left without space for its disposal and treatment. “If public service providers and authorised companies are left without a place for disposal, the waste will not disappear,” they warn, noting that it could end up on the streets, in forests and by rivers, or in overcrowded warehouses where the risk of fire increases.

They are calling on the Ministry and the Environmental Protection and Energy Efficiency Fund to adopt a binding decision on the acceptance of municipal waste from municipalities that have been left without landfills, and to draw up an urgent plan for the disposal of non-hazardous industrial and hazardous waste.

They are also requesting a check of the contractual obligations of landfills that received Fund resources, with the application of contractual measures, including the return of funds, if it is established that they are refusing to accept waste contrary to the contracts.

They further demand the public disclosure of data on landfills that have free capacities, on the extent of those capacities, and on those that refuse to accept waste. “It is time for decisions, not for politics. Every week in which parties, ministries, counties and cities accuse each other is a week closer to waste on the streets,” said the association’s president, Josip Pavlović.

World.title: Split Port Opens Brand New International Passenger Terminal
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Split Port opened its brand new international passenger terminal this week, concluding a 20+ million euro project.

Split Port officially opened its new international passenger terminal this week, formally marking the completion of a project worth over 20 million euros. Poslovni reports that the extensive project was co-financed with non-repayable EU funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan.

a ground floor passenger reception

The former ugly, totally dilapidated building has finally been renovated into a modern passenger terminal, the construction of which has upgraded the port infrastructure and reorganised domestic and international traffic. The terminal was built due to the increase in capacity of the city port, where passenger traffic is almost four times higher and vehicle traffic three times higher than 25 years ago, the Split Port Authority pointed out. The new terminal covers more than 12,000 square metres, while the building itself has almost 3,000 square metres. On the ground floor there is space for receiving passengers, while the upper floor houses operational services, including the police, customs, and the security and port authority departments.

Vice Mihanović, director of the Split Port Authority, announced that the roof of the building will be opened to citizens and will contain public amenities such as a children’s playroom, an outdoor gym and a telescope.

“The facility is intended for international traffic, while domestic liner traffic will remain at the previous locations. With the construction of the terminal, we are relocating international traffic to the port breakwater, and we have repurposed the entire St. Duje Quay for domestic liner traffic,” Mihanović stated. St. Duje Quay spans over 10,000 square metres and six berths, and the re-purposing will improve travel conditions for islanders and domestic passengers and bring them closer to the city after disembarking from the ferry. The old terminal building has also been put into use for domestic traffic only.

the viewpoint and lungomare

Mihanović also announced four major projects of the Port Authority with a total value of almost 60 million euros, including the expansion of St. Peter’s Quay by more than 5,000 square metres and the construction of two new berths. Split Mayor Tomislav Šuta said that the construction of the terminal is a major step forward for the city and passengers, and announced the arrangement of a lungomare and viewpoint in that area.

World.title: Croatia Introduces Tougher Rules and Surveillance for Short-Term Rentals
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Croatia is set to introduce much stricter rules and heightened surveillance for short-term rentals, with around 60,000 units in particular being under the state’s magnifying glass.

Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina stated recently that the Hospitality Activity Act, which has been sent for a second reading in Parliament, is one of the most important for tourism and a major step forward in its development. “With this law we want to achieve three fundamental goals: a strong step forward in suppressing unregistered activity, the complete digitalisation of all administrative procedures in tourism, and the introduction of order, transparency and an increase in the quality of the offer, especially in the category of short-term rental accommodation,” Glavina said after the government session.

Poslovni reports that he further explained that the most important goal – suppressing unregistered activity – is achieved through the law in several ways, one of which is the transposition into Croatian legislation of the European Commission regulation and the introduction of a digital registration number whose aim is to prevent service providers who do not have it from appearing and advertising on online platforms.

He assessed these platforms as very important because the largest tourist traffic comes from them, so among the goals is the introduction of more order into the ways they operate, because until now short-term rental and accommodation could be advertised and sold through them without a decision in the member state.

“The penalties for platforms that would ignore this are draconian and they will certainly make an effort across Europe, including in Croatia, to ensure that this does not happen,” Glavina said. He recalled that the new law expands the powers for supervising providers of this accommodation, in addition to the State Inspectorate, to the Customs Administration, cities and municipalities through the activities of municipal wardens, and it has also been agreed that all eventual revenues from fines will go entirely to the budgets of local and regional self-government units.

The State Inspectorate has also been given the possibility of secret supervision of classifieds, groups on social networks and similar, so that it can react and control the facilities. “This year we have significantly strengthened the activities of inspectors against unregistered activity, and when it enters into force, the law will contribute to this even more,” Glavina said. He repeated that private landlords and family accommodation are very important and that they have been accommodated.

When asked whether he knows how many registered apartments for rent to tourists there are in buildings, he said that he does not have exact data because until now no records have been kept of the type of facilities in which the apartments are located, which will change with the new law and digitalisation.

According to our estimate, that is around 60,000 facilities-apartments, Glavina said, noting that other EU countries are also struggling in various ways with short-term rental to tourists because it reduces the available housing stock.

Regarding the objections and complaints of small landlords and entrepreneurs to the draft law, he said that from 2016 until about a year and a half ago, the number of newly registered beds in short-term accommodation for tourists grew by around 25,000 every year, which led to the fact that, despite the growth of overall tourism, growth in that accommodation was smaller. That is why the steps forward with the law and responsible tourism policy were important, and that is why in the last two years we have not had growth in the number of those beds but even a slight decrease, and those beds have gone into long-term rental, which is also the goal of housing policy, Glavina concluded.

World.title: Croatia Will Need 100,000 New Hotel Beds Over the Next Decade
World.content:
November the 13th, 2026 – Croatia is going to need anywhere between 80,000 and 100,000 new hotel beds over the next decade, according to hotelier reps warn.

Croatia will need between 80,000 and 100,000 new hotel beds over the next ten years, hoteliers’ representatives warned at a recently held congress in Poreč. There’s an issue, however, as building new hotels is becoming increasingly difficult due to high land prices, expensive construction work, slow administration and shrinking opportunities for profit. Index reports that in Croatia currently, hotels currently account for only 9.2 percent of total accommodation capacity in Croatia, yet generate approximately a quarter of all tourist overnight stays. Hoteliers are therefore calling for the continuation of state incentives, better conditions for investment and measures that would attract more tourists outside the summer months.

croatia’s accommodation capacity poses an issue

Veljko Ostojić, president of the Association of Entrepreneurs in Croatian Hospitality and director of the Croatian Tourism Association, said that the hotel sector achieved good results this year, but that Croatia must change the structure of its tourist accommodation. “Croatian hospitality is the winner of this tourist year, not only according to physical indicators but also according to everything it does to raise the quality of Croatian tourism. However, the structure of our accommodation capacity is currently the biggest challenge,” Ostojić said. According to his estimate, Croatia should increase the number of hotel beds by 80,000 to 100,000 over the next decade. The problem, he warns, is that most investments relate to the renovation and reconstruction of existing hotels, while completely new hotel complexes on previously undeveloped land are almost not being built at all.

why are so few hotels being constructed in croatia?

Ostojić believes that investors are deterred by a combination of several problems, from the price of land and construction to slow administrative procedures and legal uncertainty. “The question is why there are practically no significant greenfield investments in Croatia. The reasons are numerous: the price of land, the slowness of administration, legal uncertainty, the cost of construction and the hotel business model itself. We must be open and realistic,” he said. He added that the space for new investments is getting smaller, which he considers bad for the long-term development of Croatian tourism. Hoteliers also warn of rising operating costs and declining profitability, which makes it increasingly difficult to find financially viable projects.

the interest in the height of summer is waning…

Ostojić also warned that tourist habits are changing. According to him, some guests are increasingly avoiding the busiest summer months because of the heat, high prices and excessive crowds in certain destinations. He believes Croatia must develop new tourist facilities, events and manifestations that would attract guests during spring and autumn. This would extend the tourist season, increase the occupancy of hotel capacities and reduce dependence on July and August alone, which many are now avoiding due to extreme temperatures and crowds.

Robert Pende, director of the Directorate for Entrepreneurship Development, Investments and Competitiveness at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport, said that the state has been encouraging investments in the hotel sector for years. The aim of these incentives is not only the construction of higher-quality accommodation but also the reduction of seasonality in Croatian tourism. Pende warned that Croatia still has one of the most pronounced seasonalities of tourism in the European Union.

“We want to change that, and investments are key to this,” he said, noting that 34 applications for projects with a total value of approximately 500 million euros have been received through the investment incentive system. This refers to the value of planned investments, not the amount of state support.

has croatia managed to retain its competitiveness?

Kristijan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board, assessed that Croatia, despite global challenges and unpredictable circumstances on the tourist market, has retained its competitiveness among Mediterranean destinations. “The tourist year that is slowly coming to an end has shown that Croatia has retained its competitiveness. The results we have achieved confirm positive trends in tourist traffic, and a great deal of credit for this belongs precisely to hoteliers,” Staničić said. He added that new investments, raising the quality of service and the development of tourist destinations play an important role in the further development of Croatian tourism.
