World.title: Nations League: Croatia Fall 2-1 to England at Wembley
World.content:
Croatia were beaten 2-1 by England at Wembley on Thursday night, with Morgan Rogers’ opener and a VAR-awarded penalty cancelling out Petar Sučić’s equalizer, but Slaven Bilić’s depleted side showed the fight and organization that had been so badly missing in Rijeka a month earlier.

Croatia faced England at Wembley on Thursday night in the fifth round of the Nations League, a month after the 7-0 defeat in Rijeka that Slaven Bilić and his players have since called a “collective blackout”.

Croatia went into the match on three straight defeats, though the 2-1 loss to Spain at Poljud had restored some pride. Bilić arrived in London with a depleted squad. Josip Šutalo, Marin Pongračić, Kristijan Jakić, Andrej Kramarić and Franjo Ivanović were all ruled out through injury; Luka Sučić was struggling with a virus, and Ivan Perišić was suspended after his red card against Spain.

England, without the injured Djed Spence and Ezri Konsa, marked a special night for Harry Kane, who presented his Ballon d’Or to the Wembley crowd before kick-off and was set to become England’s most-capped player.

Lineups

England (4-2-3-1): Pickford; Quansah, Burn, Hall, Alexander-Arnold; Rice, Anderson; Gordon, Rogers, Bellingham; Kane

Croatia (3-4-2-1): Livaković; Gvardiol, Vušković, Stanišić; Vlašić, Mišić, Kovačić, Smolčić; Baturina, Sučić; Matanović

Bilić switched to a back three, with Vlašić and Smolčić as wing-backs, and left Luka Modrić on the bench.

Match report

Before kick-off, Wembley celebrated a landmark night for England captain Harry Kane. He showed his recently won Ballon d’Or to the home crowd, and Sir Peter Shilton, whose record he was about to break, honored him on his 126th appearance, making Kane England’s most-capped player. Croatia captain Luka Modrić joined the ceremony to present him with a replica of the Croatian first football.

The match then got underway in front of more than 80,000 spectators.

Croatia started with real purpose, pressing England on both flanks and keeping the hosts from settling on the ball in Croatia’s half. By the 13th minute, though, England were gradually taking control of possession, even if neither side had yet created anything clear.

The first moment of danger came in the 16th minute. Trent Alexander-Arnold crossed, Croatia failed to clear properly, and Elliot Anderson hit a fierce shot from the edge of the box that flew over the bar. England threatened again two minutes later, when Alexander-Arnold tried his luck himself, but Mišić was quick to block.

Morgan Rogers sent another ball into the box in the 20th minute, but Vušković cleared. Croatia responded two minutes later with a long spell of possession that ended in a speculative shot from distance by Mišić.

England took the lead in the 24th minute. Kane switched the play to the right, Bellingham crossed into the middle, and after a poor reaction from Gvardiol, Rogers managed to bundle the ball into the net for 1-0.

England kept pushing. In the 29th minute, Lewis Hall broke forward and shot, but Mišić got across to block it behind for a corner, his second important block of the night. The hosts were proving especially dangerous from set pieces, with every corner causing alarm in the Croatian box.

Croatia finally tested Pickford in the 33rd minute, when Kovačić tried his luck from distance. Baturina also shot straight at Pickford a few minutes later.

Croatia went into the break 1-0 down. They had started the match well, and apart from the Gvardiol slip that led to Rogers’ goal, their performance looked much closer to the display against Spain at Poljud than to the collapse in Rijeka.

Neither coach made a change at the break.

England started the half on the front foot. Anthony Gordon aimed for the far corner from the inside-left channel in the 48th minute but missed the target, and two minutes later Rice arrived from deep and cut the ball back for Kane, only for Vušković to react and clear.

In the 55th minute England broke quickly, cutting through Croatia in a few passes, and Bellingham’s shot was saved by Livaković. Gordon then fired wide again from the left. At the other end, Croatia were finding out once more how hard it was to get through the England defense, with every route to goal closed off so far.

Croatia then hit back. Pushing England back as the second half went on, they equalized from a corner in the 59th minute. Quansah’s headed clearance went straight to the feet of Petar Sučić, who made it 1-1.

The lead was not level for long. Smolčić was penalized for pulling back Quansah in the Croatian box, and after a VAR review, England were awarded a penalty, with Smolčić booked. Kane scored for 2-1 in the 64th minute.

Bilić then made a double change in the 70th minute, bringing on Ante Budimir and Mario Pašalić for goalscorer Petar Sučić and Matanović.



In the 74th minute, Bilić turned to Luka Modrić and Marco Pašalić, replacing Mišić and Smolčić. A minute later, Baturina’s cross for Budimir was claimed by Pickford. Tuchel then made a triple change in the 77th minute, sending on Garner, White and Ngumoha for Rice, Gordon and Alexander-Arnold.

Croatia created their best chance of the half in the 82nd minute. Modrić found Vlašić, who turned and sent his shot just wide of the right-hand post. Two minutes later, Vlašić was involved again, crossing for Budimir, whose header went off target.

England had the ball in the net in the 86th minute through Garner, but the flag was already up for offside. It was again a Gvardiol error.

Croatia pushed for a winner in the closing minutes. In the 87th minute, Marco Pašalić played Budimir through, but Pickford made an excellent save. A minute later, there was a scramble in front of the England goal. Budimir, using Gvardiol to lift himself higher in the air, could not direct his header from close range.

In the 90th minute, Majer came on for Kovačić. A corner for Croatia came in the 90th minute, which found Budimir’s head and went just above the crossbar. After a last effort from England, the game ended 2-1.

The result went England’s way, but a month on from the humiliation in Rijeka, this was a far braver and more convincing Croatia, one that matched the hosts for long spells and gave Bilić real reason for optimism before Sunday’s game against Czechia in Osijek.

World.title: Vis Archipelago Retains Status as UNESCO Global Geopark
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – The Vis archipelago has successfully retained its status as a UNESCO Global Geopark for another four years as all 10 recommendations from the previous evaluation have been fulfilled.

The above was confirmed on the 4th of November at the 11th session of the UNESCO Global Geoparks Council, held at UNESCO headquarters in Paris. The Geopark Vis Archipelago has been part of the UNESCO Global Geoparks Network since 2019.

Morski reports that the re-validation, which is carried out every four years, included a review of documentation and a field mission by international evaluators from the 22nd to the 27th of June 2026.

During their stay on the Vis archipelago, the evaluators visited numerous geological sites, geotrails and visitor centres, and held talks with representatives of the local community, institutions, scientific organisations and partner organisations.

The international evaluators praised the way the sites are presented to visitors, the cooperation with schools and scientists, and the support given to local producers. They also highlighted how the geopark has connected Vis and Komiža in caring for the heritage of the entire archipelago.

World.title: New Dawn for Luxury Tourism in Kaštela With High-End Hotel Brand
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – A new dawn for luxury tourism in Kaštela is beginning with the arrival of one of the world’s most recognisable brands in the high-end hotel segment.

It’s genuinely no exaggeration to say that a new tourism dawn of sorts in Kaštela is now beginning. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the international Odien Group, headquartered in Prague, is bringing Sofitel, one of the world’s most recognisable brands in the luxury hotel segment, to Kaštela and Croatia. The contract with Accor, one of the world’s leading hotel groups that includes the Sofitel brand in its portfolio, was formally signed at the Renaissance Vitturi Castle in Kaštel Lukšić.

high-end tourism

Sofitel Kaštela, which will be constructed on the site of the former Zeničko resort in Kaštel Stari, is expected to open its doors in 2029 and will be managed by Odien Hotels, the hotel division of the Odien Group. The hotel will have 137 rooms and apartments, including spacious junior suites and higher-category accommodation units with private balconies or terraces overlooking the sea. Guests will have access to several restaurants and bars, a spa centre, indoor and outdoor pools, a beach club, and spaces for business meetings and various events. It goes without saying that this is an important milestone for Croatian tourism, and especially for Kaštela, which with this project is positioning itself on the international map of luxury hospitality. For the Odien Group, Sofitel represents much more than a new hotel project. It is an important part of the group’s long-term investment strategy aimed at developing Kaštela into an internationally recognisable tourist destination.

a luxury hotel brand blends with heritage

Kaštela will get an internationally recognisable luxury hotel brand, as well as an intimate heritage hotel located in a Renaissance building.

“Our ambitions go beyond the mere construction of luxury hotel facilities. We want to contribute to creating a destination with a strong international identity, recognised for quality, authenticity and the experiences it offers. Kaštela has exceptional potential: a rich history, valuable architectural heritage, an authentic Mediterranean character and an ideal location between Split and Trogir. Combining all these qualities with the international recognition and reputation of the Sofitel brand, which is synonymous with quality, will undoubtedly open a new chapter in the city’s tourism development,” said Mike Saran, owner of the Odien Group.

“Croatia has become one of the most attractive European tourist destinations, recognised for its unique combination of natural beauty, rich culture and authenticity. We are proud that, through this exceptional project with the Odien Group, we are bringing Sofitel to the Croatian market as the first international luxury hotel brand in the country. Sofitel Kaštela will embody the elegance of French luxury while embracing the spirit, heritage and lifestyle of the Adriatic coast, creating a unique destination for travellers from around the world,” said Maud Bailly, CEO of the Sofitel, Sofitel Legend, MGallery and Emblems brands. The arrival of this prestigious hotel brand is part of the Odien Group’s long-term development strategy and commitment to Kaštela. As part of that strategy, the group will, through its companies Odien Hotels and Odien Real Estate, invest more than 100 million euros over the next five years. In addition to the new Sofitel Kaštela hotel project, the company this year also purchased the historic Štafileo Castle in Kaštel Štafilić, which it plans to renovate and convert into a luxury heritage hotel.

These two projects bring two different but harmoniously connected hotel concepts: an internationally recognisable luxury hotel brand and an intimate heritage hotel located in a historic Renaissance building, which will offer guests an authentic experience of local heritage. Together with the group’s existing hotel operations in Croatia, these projects are part of its long-term vision of creating new tourism content and value in Kaštela and throughout Dalmatia.

international luxury tourism for Kaštela

“These projects give the Kaštela the opportunity for a significant step forward in the segment of international luxury tourism. The city’s growing recognition as a tourist destination, its rich cultural and historical heritage and its geographical location form solid foundations for the development of a tourism offer that goes beyond the framework of traditional seasonal tourism,” said Denis Ivanović, Mayor of Kaštela.

“This is an extremely important moment for Kaštela. The arrival of an international luxury hotel brand and the Odien Group’s investments in our city confirm that Kaštela has the potential to become a recognisable high-end tourism destination. It is particularly important to emphasise that this is not just about one hotel project, but about a series of investments that can contribute to the development of the city, open new jobs, strengthen the local economy and extend the tourist season. For us, it is of key importance that this development takes place in parallel with the preservation of Kaštela’s identity and in close cooperation with the local community,” the mayor added. The Odien Group has otherwise been present in Croatia since 2015, when it took over the Le Méridien Lav Split resort in Podstrana.

World.title: Zagreb-Podgorica Direct Flights Coming on November the 26th
World.content:
November the 12th, 2026 – New Zagreb-Podgorica direct flights are coming on November the 26th, with the two capitals being linked in this way after several years.

Travel between Croatia and Montenegro will soon become significantly faster and simpler. Index reports that Montenegro’s national airline Air Montenegro has announced the introduction of a new direct route between Zagreb and Podgorica, with the first flight scheduled for the 26th of November this year.

The flight between the two capital cities will last only 50 minutes, allowing passengers faster and simpler travel without transfers. The new route will operate three times a week, and the flights will be operated by Embraer E195 aircraft, which can accommodate 118 passengers. The introduction of this route is part of Montenegro’s Public Service Obligation (PSO) programme, whose aim is to improve Montenegro’s international transport connectivity and enable more regular air links with important European destinations.

the upcoming flight schedule

According to the announced timetable, aircraft will operate between Zagreb and Podgorica on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays. From Zagreb, these flights will depart at 08:50 and are expected to arrive in Podgorica at 09:40. In the opposite direction, departure from Podgorica is planned at 07:20, with arrival in Zagreb scheduled for 08:10. All departure and arrival times are given in local time, and the schedule is of course subject to change.

the price

One-way ticket prices start at around 50 euros, depending on the direction of travel and the chosen date. On the official Air Montenegro website, the currently listed price for the first flight from Zagreb on the 26th of November is 58.30 euros. The ticket price includes all mandatory fees, as well as one piece of hand luggage weighing up to eight kilograms and one piece of checked luggage weighing up to 23 kilograms. The final price will depend on the travel date, seat availability and the time of booking.

The new air route could also be interesting for travellers who want to get better acquainted with Podgorica, the capital and largest city of Montenegro. Located in the area where the Morača and Ribnica rivers meet, Podgorica combines modern city life, historical sights and natural beauty. One of the places worth visiting is Stara Varoš, the historic city quarter that preserves traces of the Ottoman past. There you will also find the Clock Tower (Sahat-kula), one of Podgorica’s recognisable landmarks. A walk through this part of the city is an opportunity to get to know traditional architecture and local culture.

Among the best-known modern symbols of the city is the Millennium Bridge, which stretches across the Morača River. Visitors can also walk to the place where the Ribnica flows into the Morača and view the old stone bridge on the Ribnica. Nature lovers can head to Gorica hill, after which the city is named, which is a popular place for walking and recreation. Near Podgorica there are also waterfalls on the Cijevna River, known as the Montenegrin Niagara, which are especially impressive when the water level is high. For those who want to explore the surroundings of the city as well, an interesting choice can be Lake Skadar, known for its rich plant and animal life, picturesque landscapes and opportunities for boat trips.

World.title: Estonia's NATO envoy Kristjan Prikk: Europe has undergone a mental shift
World.content:
Estonia's permanent representative to NATO, Kristjan Prikk, said in an interview that Europe has undergone a mental shift and that countries increasingly understand the need to act differently and more quickly.

There can hardly be a more exciting time to work at NATO. But when I look at public opinion and comments from some analysts, the more diplomatic observers say NATO is changing, while the more skeptical say the alliance is in deep crisis and will eventually fall apart. Which view is closer to reality?

First, it is certainly true that there are few more exciting times. I will not try to compete with the experiences of the 1950s and 1960s, when Estonia was not in NATO, but compared with the period since Estonia became a member, these are undoubtedly, for unfortunate reasons, particularly interesting times.

As for NATO's health, there have always been people predicting its demise. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte recently told me that whenever NATO summits take place, a large proportion of the people milling around are busy forecasting how soon NATO will disappear.

What we actually see is that NATO is more relevant and necessary for its allies today than it has been for decades.

Today, together with the other members of the North Atlantic Council, meaning representatives of all member states, we are visiting SHAPE, NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe, where we will discuss practical matters: how Europe is defended and how the alliance has adapted and responded to changing circumstances.

When we look at the changes NATO is clearly undergoing, is the "Europeanization" of NATO, an interesting concept, inevitable to some extent?

Many slogans and terms have been used lately. Having spent the last year and a half observing European security from here in Europe, and before that serving as Estonia's ambassador in Washington, I saw how there were initially voices in the United States talking about the Europeanization of NATO.

Quite quickly, however, the prevailing view became that while Europe's role within NATO must grow, it remains in the United States' own interest to maintain a strong American role in the alliance.

Personally, I do not particularly like the term "Europeanization of NATO" because it does not accurately reflect the sentiment inside this building.

It is actually quite interesting that many of the passionate and often contradictory political statements made in public do not really penetrate these walls.

As you saw when entering, this is an architectural marvel in its own right: a huge building where all allies are brought together equally under one roof. It is not as though the larger allies have some separate NATO facility somewhere else.

That also means the working environment here, not only physically but politically, is somewhat calmer. There is a very strong understanding of the common purpose we share. Day-to-day political rhetoric does not necessarily affect processes here in the way one might assume based on public statements.

The United States has clearly changed in recent years and may continue to change. For us, however, the key question is whether Europe has changed enough. From NATO headquarters, what does it look like?

I would say definitely not enough, at least not yet.

In practical terms, we all know that most allies remain quite far from reaching the 5 percent defense spending target agreed upon in The Hague. That is the practical measure of whether the agreed changes are actually happening.

I do believe that a mental shift has taken place, both across governments and within individual countries, not only in defense and foreign ministries. People understand that certain things must be done differently and more quickly.

Ultimately, however, results are measured through practical action. We must stay on our own course while continually encouraging our allies to move in the necessary direction and at the necessary pace.

Estonia has always said that a strong NATO is clearly in our interest. But what are the main topics dominating NATO discussions today? The issue is not only America's role.

Put simply, NATO's focus has returned to something very close to its original mission.

Collective defense is the highest of priorities. It is the standard by which NATO's necessity and success have always been judged. That is the common thread running through many current discussions.

The current U.S. ambassador to NATO, Matt Whitaker, has said that what NATO is doing today amounts to restoring the alliance's factory settings.

Of course, we neither can nor want to go back to 1949 or the early 1950s when those original settings were established.

But even people who have been here much longer say that practical defense issues dominate discussions: how NATO's defense plans are structured, how to provide the capabilities needed to implement those plans, and how to help countries procure equipment and develop military units more quickly.

Developing those capabilities will be a tremendous challenge because Europe still lacks strength in areas such as space-based intelligence and early warning systems, aerial refueling and long-range strike capabilities. One could write an entire book about it. How can Europe overcome these shortcomings? We know increasing defense spending is not politically popular in many countries.

Of course it is not.

We all remember what happened in the early 1990s when it became possible to collect the so-called peace dividend. At that point many Western countries believed they could redirect defense spending toward other priorities that were both important and politically more popular.

That era is over?

Very much so.

What is interesting now is that people increasingly talk about a "defense dividend" that benefits society. Not only because people feel properly protected and NATO's deterrence works, but because industry and innovation ecosystems can also develop.

We know that defense industries have often served as engines of innovation and economic development.

Certainly, we understand the challenges posed by interest rates and budget pressures. But when reports emerge about incidents in NATO countries that turn out to be sabotage attempts, assassination plots or similar provocations, governments and societies begin asking what they can do to better protect themselves. That is one reason defense spending is rising.

You mentioned incidents. We were going to get to that topic anyway. At what point does NATO lose patience when it comes to cyberattacks, drone incidents, bomb threats and the provocations you mentioned? At what point does NATO say, "Enough"?

NATO has already said and done certain things in response to some of these incidents.

At the same time, we cannot treat such incidents as though they are all planned, executed and intended in exactly the same way.

For example, we know that the Baltic Sentry maritime operation was launched in response to incidents in the Baltic Sea. Surveillance and patrol capabilities have also been strengthened in areas such as the Black Sea region.

It is often difficult to determine with certainty whether a particular operation achieved exactly the intended effect or prevented something from happening. Nevertheless, I believe NATO's actions have had a positive and sobering influence.

It is also true that NATO, as a military-political organization, cannot be the solution to every such incident. In most cases, national police and security agencies must carry the main responsibility. NATO can provide a platform, and indeed it does, where countries share information about incidents and about the measures they have taken to prevent them.

Sometimes that involves practical police and security measures. Often it also involves legal reforms to adapt legislation to current circumstances. In some countries, an act of vandalism that is actually sabotage intended to create fear and undermine public confidence is still treated no more seriously than juvenile hooliganism.

We believe such incidents must be assessed according to the forces behind them and their intended purpose. That, too, contributes to deterrence.

Let's talk about the U.S. military presence in Europe. A political decision is expected by the end of the year or beginning of next year. Has NATO been officially informed about what it will mean in practice?

No, it has not.

Various consultations have taken place, and discussions have been held about the background to the ongoing U.S. force posture review in Europe, why it is being conducted and the main considerations behind it. But we still do not know for certain what conclusions will emerge.

With President Donald Trump, one might say that an official decision could be made and then another official decision could follow the very next day.

Since you previously served as ambassador to the United States, what do you think? After his party's poor showing in the midterm elections, where might Trump's attention turn? Could he focus more on foreign and security policy, and could that prove problematic for us?

The U.S. Constitution creates a situation where a president who lacks strong congressional support often finds it easier to focus on foreign and security policy. Presidents frequently do so, sometimes out of practical necessity and sometimes to secure their legacy.

During his second term, even before losing his congressional majority, President Trump was certainly not restrained in foreign policy matters. I see no reason to believe that would fundamentally change during the second half of his second term.

The developments of the past week suggest that Trump sees a need to strengthen his position quickly and prevent the administration from becoming a domestic political punching bag. At the moment, his focus appears to be on securing the strongest possible position ahead of the new Congress through personnel changes and public statements.

So he is fighting to the end, then, if you look at his choice for personnel chief as well?

Without a doubt, yes, he is fighting to the end.

Winston Churchill is said to have once remarked that America does the right thing after it has tried everything else. Does that still apply to today's United States?

There are countless Churchill quotes, or alleged Churchill quotes. Most of them, whether he actually said them or not, are witty and insightful. I have to say, however, that I have heard this particular line repeated by Americans themselves over the past few years almost to the point of irritation.

That said, I still believe that in certain situations patience is required when dealing with the United States, and that one must present one's own arguments as convincingly as possible rather than remain silent when there is both room and opportunity to make them. I believe the United States will ultimately help us achieve the right goals.

The U.S., Ukrainian and Russian delegations have just met in Abu Dhabi and agreed on a prisoner exchange. But a political storm followed reports that Russia and the United States want to revisit Europe's security architecture. Why does it seem that people at NATO's political headquarters did not like that at all?

Looking back at the Abu Dhabi talks, it appears that the only truly concrete outcome, one that can hopefully be verified and actually lead to people returning home, is the prisoner exchange. We are relatively confident that this is a tangible result that will hopefully be completed in the coming days.

As for everything else, there has honestly been a great deal of information noise and selective leaks into the public sphere. In some cases, we can guess what Russia's objectives are. For example, when Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky spoke after the talks yesterday, or when the Russians discussed their proposals at a meeting of the Collective Security Treaty Organization. All of this is intended to influence the other side, throw it off balance and create divisions within this building and within this organization.

That includes bluffing about how much control Russia has over Ukraine.

About how much control it has over Ukraine, and probably also about how much agreement there is between Russia and the United States. I think it is very important to look at what the U.S. negotiators themselves have written publicly. Their statements mention NATO as the cornerstone of European and transatlantic security, and they mention territorial integrity. These are the right issues, and they are the issues we discuss with allies here.

It is clear that when it comes to Europe's security architecture, European countries must have the central role in making decisions.

And from the European perspective, the issue is not so much whether Europe is at the table during negotiations on Ukraine, but that discussing Europe's security architecture without Europe present sounds like a bad history lesson.

Yes, and I can confirm that this is not a case of Estonia standing in one corner and Portugal or some other more distant country standing in another. On this issue there is a very clear and shared understanding across Europe. I deliberately said Europe, not just NATO, because European countries more broadly, including those outside NATO, are largely in agreement.

Could Russian President Vladimir Putin be reckless enough to test NATO's unity?

In a sense, he already does through his statements, and indeed he has tested it throughout his aggression against Ukraine. But if you are referring to a practical test, such as putting NATO's Article 5 commitment to the test, then I have sufficient reason to believe that Vladimir Putin understands, takes into account and respects Article 5 and is not looking to challenge it directly.

The threat assessment has not really changed in that respect because there is less Russian military activity near Estonia's borders than there has been in years?

Exactly.

A few days ago, the war became visible in Estonia again when fires could be seen in Ida-Viru County and a Russian warship was struck in the Gulf of Finland. How seriously are such incidents analyzed and discussed within NATO? On the one hand, it is a legitimate military target for Ukraine, but on the other hand, it is happening on NATO's border.

Unfortunately, we live in a time when warfare is taking place very close to us. A few years ago, many of these scenes would have seemed more suited to movies or military exercises. Five years ago, few would have imagined this.

Everyone in this building understands that incidents such as the fire at the Ust-Luga port or drones entering our airspace are consequences of Russia's war against Ukraine and Ukraine's actions in self-defense. I would not speculate on exactly how those drones got here or from where. In the most recent case, we know they entered Estonian airspace from Russia, but I do not want to speculate on the precise circumstances.

On some occasions, Ukrainian drones have reached this area as well. But yesterday's events certainly did not cause anyone here to panic. There are people and structures responsible for monitoring such developments in real time. They are not learning about them after the fact.

It is absolutely clear that neither Estonia nor NATO has opened its airspace to anyone. We also discussed the matter yesterday with Ukraine's ambassador to Estonia. We want to make it very clear that misuse of Estonian airspace in this manner is not something we would accept.

And even NATO aircraft sometimes miss their targets.

Sometimes things are missed. But it is important to remember that every situation has its own risk assessment, and the final decision remains with the pilot. The pilot must evaluate various risks, including where the drone is heading and where any missile fired to intercept it could end up.

One more question to test your expertise. Will the arrangements continue under which Europe and Canada provide the funding while the United States supplies military equipment to Ukraine? At times, President Trump has cast doubt on that model.

Yes, those arrangements continue.

It is important to understand that throughout periods of political tension, the United States has continued assembling and transferring equipment packages to Ukraine. During the entire period in which this arrangement has existed, the United States has continued deliveries.

In certain cases, payments from Europe and Canada have come afterward, meaning that the United States effectively extended credit.

Ukraine is now facing what is literally a winter of survival because its energy infrastructure has been severely damaged. Can Ukraine hold out?

I can only judge based on what Ukrainians themselves tell me and on what people who know Ukraine and the Ukrainian fighting spirit better than I do are saying. So far, I have not heard a single note of doubt.

It is certainly important that on the battlefield Ukraine has made Russian advances virtually impossible. The extent to which Ukraine has managed to control Russian troop movements is impressive. In recent months, Ukraine has even regained more territory, albeit mostly through tactical advances, than Russia has captured.

That should help Ukrainian society endure as well, even though the winter will be extremely difficult.

That is why I would say that anyone watching this interview and supporting Ukraine should try in 2026 to find some way to contribute personally to Ukraine's survival and resilience. I certainly will. I have done so throughout the past five years, and I will continue to do so.

--

World.title: Weeks of temperature swings, black ice ahead as Estonia heads toward winter
World.content:
Black ice and temperature swings are in the forecast for Estonia in the coming weeks, bringing slippery roads now and the prospect of a colder, snowier spell later this month.

Tallinn is unlikely to see snow on Friday, said Estonian geoecologist Hannes Tõnisson. While some areas already saw a light dusting of snow in the morning, including in Central Estonia, roads remain too warm for anything to stick yet.

Farther east, and around Lake Peipus, snowfall was expected to be much heavier, with a cloud band moving directly over the region forecast to bring several centimeters of snow.

The bigger concern over the next few weeks, however, is black ice, as temperatures repeatedly hover around freezing.

"Temperatures are so close to freezing that whenever the skies clear, roads can turn icy in no time," Tõnisson explained.

Colder by St. Catherine's Day

Rain is expected in most parts of the country on Friday, but colder air moving in from the north and northwest could bring heavy coastal snow overnight.

Snow could also reach the Tallinn area by Saturday morning, Tõnisson noted, although most of the cloud band is expected to pass east of the capital and rising daytime temperatures are likely to bring rain instead.

He warned that another round of icy roads is possible early Sunday before temperatures climb again next week.

Roads can be slippery when too warm for snow to stick. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"Along the coast, particularly on the islands and in Tallinn, temps are more likely to stay above freezing," he said. However, the risk of slippery road conditions is expected to persist, especially during brief clear spells.

Inland, temperatures are expected to dip below freezing and stay there the following week, with the arrival of sharper cold and potential for heavier snowfall more likely starting around St. Catherine's Day on November 25.

"We could easily see temps drop to 10 degrees below zero Celsius, and locally dip briefly even below that," Tõnisson said.

Why Estonia's weather is so hard to predict

Tõnisson explained that long-range forecasts are particularly difficult to pin down for Estonia because it lies on the boundary between warm and cold air masses.

"That means we could get either very cold or very changeable conditions," he said. "This happens here all the time: snow on the ground in the morning, it's gone by noon and almost warm enough to go swimming, then the snow is back again by evening."

Weather systems moving in from the Atlantic and circling over Latvia can also have a major impact on the weather in Estonia, depending on their precise position.

"If a system moves directly over us, its southern edge is more likely to bring rain while the northern part brings snow," the geoecologist explained. "But if it passes north of us, you can bet we'll get rain."

World.title: Health Board greens Tallinn's 2-member ambulance crews
World.content:
The Health Board has authorized Tallinn Ambulance to operate two reduced-staff nursing ambulance crews during daytime hours in 2027.

Birgit Lao, director general of the Health Board, signed a decision this week allowing Tallinn Ambulance to operate two reduced-staff nursing ambulance crews from January 1 through the end of 2027. One crew will be based in Haabersti and the other in Lasnamäe.

The reduced-staff crews may operate only during daytime hours, from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m.

The main reason the Health Board granted Tallinn the authorization is the city's population growth over the past 15 years. Between 2012 and this year, the capital's population has increased by nearly 50,000 people, or 12 percent, while growth has been even faster in percentage terms in the municipalities surrounding Tallinn.

"Population growth and aging are expected to increase demand for ambulance services and the likelihood of simultaneous emergency calls. It is therefore justified to expand Tallinn's ambulance resources to ensure that emergency medical services remain accessible and capable of responding even as demand grows," Lao said.

According to the Health Board, the data collected provides sufficient evidence that the increased workload in Tallinn is neither isolated nor temporary, but reflects a persistent gap between the region's ambulance resources and actual demand.

The Health Board noted that authorizing additional reduced-staff crews is also consistent with the findings of its analysis of ambulance network planning.

Under a regulation dating from 2016, the Health Board may authorize an ambulance service provider to operate a reduced-staff crew if doing so improves the quality, accessibility and efficiency of ambulance services.

The Health Board's decision has also been approved by the Estonian Health Insurance Fund.

According to the Health Board's 2025 analysis of ambulance utilization, Tallinn's ambulance crews had a utilization rate of 53 percent during the day, between 9 a.m. and 8:59 p.m., compared with 28 percent at night, between 9 p.m. and 8:59 a.m. This indicates an excessive workload, with utilization rates nearly twice as high as in other counties.

The decision noted that Tallinn has experienced situations in which its regular ambulance resources were insufficient to handle the volume of emergency calls. As a result, additional crews have repeatedly had to be deployed in Tallinn, approximately 10 times a year, with the approval of the Health Board's on-call operations staff.

World.title: Vocational schools get half the funding of academic education, hindering progress
World.content:
This lack of funds is blocking them from updating aging equipment with modern robots, drones and simulators needed to prepare students for work.

Vocational schools (Kutsekool) take on students who have finished mandatory education (Põhikool) and the age ranges are the same as for high school (Gümnaasium).

Aulika Riisenberg, an adviser at the Ministry of Education and Research's department of secondary and vocational education, said the sector accounts for around 5.5 percent of Estonia's total education spending, a share that has declined over time.

Tartu Rakenduslik Kolledž (VOCO) is one such vocational school. Its director, Raini Jõks, said modernization was necessary to prepare students for the world of work and ensure they have at least acquired the skills needed to begin a work placement. "We don't need to build a factory in every school," he said. Jõks added that the main needs were modern robots, drones and simulators.

The Tartu college has had to reduce classroom teaching hours and increase the amount of independent study to stay within its budget for teachers' salaries. According to Jõks, the funding shortage has already affected how teaching is organized, and efforts were being made to ensure that independent study was also as well supervised as possible.

"We are certainly in a good position in terms of the quality of vocational education, but we are approaching a critical point where it is no longer sustainable," Jõks acknowledged. He explained that vocational students receive the lowest funding per student in Estonia's education system, and that taking the next step forward was no longer possible under current conditions.

Jõks said this was the last opportunity to begin developing policy solutions and making decisions to secure funding for vocational education reform, and stressed that reforms should not be shelved because of funding shortages — political decisions and the necessary funding were needed to implement them.

Drone training (photo is illustrative). Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

Jõks added funding shortages and the inability to upgrade technology had not yet reduced student numbers at the college, which this year are at their highest in a decade. However, students have expressed dissatisfaction at having to cover part of the cost of some clothing or learning materials required for school. "We are trying to resolve this so that secondary education — both general and vocational — is free everywhere," he said. Without additional investment, the current quality of teaching might not be sustainable in the longer term.

Riisenberg said the world of work was evolving at pace, with new tech, including artificial intelligence, being introduced, and the knowledge and skills expected of employees changing along with it. Both the content of vocational programs and the way teaching is organized therefore need to keep pace.

She noted that people employed in traditional occupations, such as sewing, construction and car repair, increasingly needed digital skills and knowledge of new technologies. Energy-efficient solutions and digital tools are becoming more important in construction, automation and smart systems in electrical work, and skills related to electric and hybrid vehicles in vehicle maintenance.

When demand for a particular occupation declines or the nature of the work changes significantly, Riisenberg said it was necessary to consider whether to continue the existing training, update it or combine it with another program. She added this did not necessarily mean traditional occupations would disappear, but rather that the way they were taught would be modernized.

Ott Pärna, head of Tallinna Tehnoloogiakolledž (Techno TLN) said artificial intelligence (AI) had impacted various occupations, and noted that young people's and adults' learning preferences had changed in line with this. "To support this change at the college of technology, we need to develop our teaching facilities and hire more teachers, particularly in math, science and technology," Pärna went on.

Pärna said that in today's world, where AI is taking over more complex office work and young people are facing high unemployment and considerable uncertainty about the future, most young people need to study technological subjects.

He said around 70 percent of basic school graduates in Estonia went on to general upper secondary schools, while too few chose vocational education with a practical and technological focus. Pärna said applied education should account for a larger share, approaching the levels seen in the Nordic countries and other wealthy European countries.

Although general high school remains the most popular choice among basic school graduates, the number entering vocational and vocational secondary education rose somewhat this year.

Pärna also said applied colleges and vocational education centers needed substantial additional investment to modernize teaching. He said vocational institutions taught subjects as complex as those taught at universities, requiring similar teaching facilities and qualified teachers.

World.title: Polar scientist: Antarctica's solitude isn't for everyone
World.content:
Estonian polar scientist Priit Tisler is heading to Antarctica for the 13th time, and says the isolation there does not suit everyone, with storms which last up to ten days.

He told "Ringvaade" that his worst storm ran ten days, followed by a two-day break and then another eight-day storm, and that constant daylight makes sleep difficult.

"What could be better than a person being able to do work they enjoy?"Tisler inquired ahead of the next trip.

Priit Tisler during a previous trip to Antarctica. Source: Private library

Whereas his first trips were entirely scientific research."Now the work has shifted somewhat towards logistics," he went on. Tisler is deputy head of a Finnish research station, responsible for setting up the station, getting it running, and checking and maintaining the scientific equipment.

Research at the station covers lichens, mosses, meteorology and ice, with everything governed by the Antarctic Treaty of 1959."All the countries work together amicably, sit at a long table and discuss," Tisler explained.

There are nowadays more than 70 bases in Antarctica. The Estonian scientist's current mission will last three months, with a planned return in the second half of February next year. "That kind of solitude does not suit everyone," he noted.

Priit Tisler in Antarctica. Source: ERR

That said, the advent of Starlink satellite internet service provider has transformed life in Antarctica enormously in just two years — he can now talk via WhatsApp, and video calls work perfectly. In their free time people read books and listen to music, and he noted that people there can be very resourceful.

The hardest part is the storms." he said. "The worst is during a storm, when everything vibrates — you feel like you're on a tram doing 60 km/h with square wheels." His only thought then is that no pump breaks down, as repairs would be challenging to say the least.

Food is calculated precisely per person. This consists of: "Mainly dry goods and frozen meat, fish and sausages, which we buy in Cape Town." Small aircraft can only carry a limited number of kilos, meaning every choice counts.

World.title: Political scientist: Vseviov's rise pushes Reinsalu into the background
World.content:
Political scientist Tõnis Leht said that the emergence of Social Democratic Party prime ministerial candidate Jonatan Vseviov has altered the dynamics among the parties' candidates for prime minister and pushed Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu into the background.

According to the latest prime minister preference poll conducted by Norstat and NGO Ühiskonnauuringute Instituut, 28 percent of respondents would like to see Center Party chairman Mihhail Kõlvart as prime minister, 21 percent support Social Democrat Jonatan Vseviov and 19 percent favor Isamaa chairman Urmas Reinsalu.

"Urmas Reinsalu's drop to third place in the prime minister poll is directly linked to Jonatan Vseviov entering the race as the Social Democrats' prime ministerial candidate," Leht said.

He pointed out that some Isamaa supporters appear to have shifted their support to Vseviov.

Urmas Reinsalu. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"When comparing the November and October surveys, we see that support for Urmas Reinsalu among Isamaa's own voters has fallen by 13 percentage points. In other words, some of Isamaa's own supporters no longer consider Reinsalu the best candidate for prime minister," Leht said.

Leht added that Vseviov's candidacy has also attracted potential supporters away from the Reform Party and Parempoolsed.

If the Social Democrats had nominated party chairman Lauri Läänemets instead, he would not have achieved such popularity in prime minister preference polls, Leht noted.

"Läänemets' support as a prime ministerial candidate has been around 10 to 11 percent. Neither Social Democratic voters nor the broader electorate have viewed him as a particularly strong or credible prime ministerial candidate," Leht said.

According to Leht, neither the Center Party nor Mihhail Kõlvart has been hurt by Vseviov's arrival.

"It appears that the rise in Mihhail Kõlvart's popularity as a prime ministerial candidate is moving in parallel with the growth of the Center Party's broader support. This may be linked to increased support for the Center Party among Estonian-speaking voters," Leht said.

Center Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

"EKRE voters may also be willing to look at Center Party candidates if they feel their own candidates are not strong enough. EKRE voters see considerable common ground with Center Party candidates, particularly meaning that EKRE's Estonian-speaking voters may also look favorably on Estonian-speaking Center Party candidates," he said.

Only eight percent of respondents said they would prefer Prime Minister and Reform Party chairman Kristen Michal as prime minister.

"The Reform Party is clearly not in an easy position today. Prime Minister Michal's ratings in prime minister preference polls have remained relatively low for quite some time. That reflects the generally low level of trust in both the Reform Party and the government," Leht said.

Tõnis Leht Autor/allikas: ERR

World.title: State wants €1.33 million back from Estonian Business and Innovation Agency
World.content:
The Estonian Business and Innovation Agency (EIS) has been ordered to repay more than €1.3 million in awarded EU funds amid conflict-of-interest concerns.

The Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications (MKM) is seeking to recover €1.33 million, which was paid to the Estonian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (EKTK) in 2023 for hiring international experts.

Minister of the Economy and Industry Liina Vahtras (Reform) has ordered EIS to repay the money.

EKTK director general Mait Palts submitted successful bids for the contracts while simultaneously serving on EIS' supervisory board, which oversaw the procurement. He also signed the resulting agreements.

EIS board chair Ursel Velve disputed the finding of a conflict of interest, point out that the European Union had identified only the appearance of one.

Palts has also argued that the arrangement was not a grant but a procurement of services by EIS to help Estonian companies enter foreign markets.

He resigned from the agency's supervisory board this spring, after the issue came to light.

While the MKM found the risk was indirect because the money went to a business association rather than directly to companies, however, an audit by the Finance Ministry disagreed that there had been no conflict of interest.

'The rules are strict'

The MKM's foreign funds chief, Rando Härginen, said Finance Ministry audit could not establish whether the perceived risk had materialized. But EU funding rules are strict, he acknowledged, leaving little room for a different outcome.

"Unfortunately, the rules governing this funding source are so strict that this process simply has to end this way," Härginen said.

Various officials resigning from public positions, he added, are a matter of each individual's personal ethics and conscience.

The EIS will not appeal the decision and has agreed to repay the €1.33 million. Velve said the agency would cover the cost using savings from efficiency measures introduced this year.

World.title: Estonia expands police right to confiscate illegal electric scooters
World.content:
Proposed amendments to Estonia's Traffic Act would expand police powers to confiscate noncompliant electric scooters and allow drivers with category B licenses to operate heavier electric vans.

"The current bill would allow police, as a last resort, to confiscate electric scooters that exceed the permitted speed or power limits according to the manufacturer's specifications. Under the amendments now proposed, police would also be able to confiscate vehicles equipped with a hidden higher-speed mode installed by the manufacturer or modified by the user to exceed the permitted speed. The amendment would also apply to light mopeds and bicycles converted into motor vehicles," Ministry of Climate communications adviser Martin-Erich Torjus told ERR.

According to the ministry, the bill also currently fails to specify what happens to confiscated vehicles. As a result, they would be sold under the general rules governing state property and could end up back on the roads.

"Without the proposed amendments, the provision would therefore fail to achieve its objective. The amendments aim to ensure that the power to confiscate vehicles covers all situations encountered in practice and that confiscated vehicles do not return to the roads," the ministry said in its document outlining the proposed amendments.

"We emphasize that confiscation is not an automatic consequence of a violation. The provision gives the authority conducting extrajudicial proceedings the right, but not the obligation, to confiscate a vehicle. According to Supreme Court case law, the possibility of confiscation does not mean that a vehicle must always be confiscated. Confiscation is justified only when there are sufficient grounds to believe that the person will commit similar violations in the future and that less severe measures have failed to have an effect," the ministry noted.

In Estonia, electric scooters are permitted on public roads if their maximum design speed does not exceed 25 kilometers per hour and their motor power does not exceed 1 kilowatt.

The corresponding amendments to the Traffic Act, which would also give police the authority to confiscate noncompliant electric scooters without court authorization, are currently awaiting their second reading in the Riigikogu.

B category license enough to drive vans weighing up top 4.25 metric tons

Under another proposal from the Ministry of Climate, the Traffic Act would also be amended to allow holders of category B driver's licenses to operate heavier vans powered by electricity and other alternative fuels. The change would reduce the need for an additional category C1 driver's license.

"Until now, the rule has been that a category B driver's license allows you to drive vehicles weighing up to 3.5 metric tons. But because of the weight of their batteries, electric vans exceeded that 3.5-ton limit, meaning drivers would have needed a category C1 license. We're changing that. The amendment is heading for its second reading and will hopefully be adopted, allowing electric vans weighing up to 4.25 metric tons to be driven with a category B license," Minister of Infrastructure Kuldar Leis said at a government press conference.
