Chit Swe, an Upper House lawmaker representing Ayeyarwady Region’s Constituency No. 11 and first deputy chair of the Joint Public Accounts Committee, urged parliament on November 5 to approve the regime’s proposed budgets, including the record-high military budget.

He said the committee had only eight days to verify the budget, with some items requiring ground observation, and that at least two weeks would be needed for verification.

If the supplementary allocations are approved, the budget deficit is projected to surge from 8.98 trillion kyats to 11.41 trillion kyats, he stated.

The military budget has surged continuously since the coup.

Under the last civilian government, led by ousted democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, defense expenditure for the 2020-21 fiscal year stood at just 3.4 trillion kyats.

In the 2023-24 fiscal year, it increased to over 5.6 trillion kyats. Although defense expenditures for the remaining years were not officially released, the current budget figures show that spending has nearly doubled compared to 2023-24.

Meanwhile, approximately 17.9 million people are “multidimensionally poor”, while two-thirds of the population are either poor or at risk, according to a UN Development Programme (UNDP) report published on October 8.

After five years of military regime rule, Myanmar people continue to suffer from soaring prices of basic goods and living costs amid the civil war, and face personal safety and security concerns.

Although the budget is still in draft form, the proposed military expenditure has drawn widespread criticism from the public.

“The budgets that should be spent on the country’s education, health, social welfare and nation-building are instead being used to kill the people,” said Naung Yoe, a military defector who now works with the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute.

According to the MDSI, the Directorate of Defense Industries, which manufactures ammunition and aerial bombs used in the regime’s indiscriminate attacks, has consumed the largest share of the military’s budget since the coup.

“It is deeply tragic and unfortunate,” he said.

World.title: Mideast Crisis Fuels Oil Conflict in Myanmar’s Heartland
World.content:
Myanmar’s small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry that is becoming increasingly lucrative amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

“As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us,” said Htun Aung, a worker on an oil well in Myanmar’s arid heartlands.

“But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder,” said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.

Myanmar imports 90 percent of its fuel oil, official figures show, making it particularly vulnerable to supply issues caused by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

But the central region of Magwe hosts a hardscrabble industry of domestic prospectors manning grimy derricks that squelch up crude oil in humble quantities.

The area is dubbed “Anyar Dubai,” associating the Anyar or central dry zone landscape with the oil boom emirate, despite the pitiable US$50 per week earned by workers like Htun Aung who spend their days drenched in foul crude run-off.

With prices at Myanmar’s petrol pumps nearly double what they were in late February, the underground “black gold” is a coveted prize.

“We just want to live in peace,” said Htun Aung. “But now they strike from one side and the others strike from the other—they keep attacking each other.”

“We’ve had to flee three, four, five times already,” he added. “We run here, we run there. We fill up our motorbikes with fuel and run again.”

Digging in

Pro-democracy rebels claim to have controlled oil fields in Magwe’s Myaing Township since 2023.

They patrol the dusty territory in a westward crook of the Irrawaddy River in ragtag columns and outfitted with rocket-propelled grenades, flak jackets, tote bags and flip-flops.

Air and drone strikes in Myaing so far this year have already exceeded 2025’s total, according to ACLED, a monitor that estimates more than 100,000 people have died since the 2021 putsch.

Rebels shelter in foxholes, camouflaged among thousands of oil wells dug in an unregulated practice dating back centuries.

Engine winches chug day and night, plunging plumbing tubes dozens of meters down boreholes before dragging them up filled with crude oil slurry.

Prospectors pay landowners up to $3,500 to lease a spot to drill, one veteran said, with no guarantee they will hit oil.

Some wells yield dribbles while others gush, filling tarpaulin-lined pits and barrels with oil hauled off to improvised refineries for processing into petrol and diesel.

“Anyar Dubai” has been “going viral” for its plentiful supply, said rebel spokesman Pyae Phyo Kyaw, at a time when regime-held areas are rationing petrol.

He touted recent offensives fending off military advances but admitted being battered by counter-attacks.

“We see it primarily as an attempt to destroy what has been a strong supply route and source of revenue for us,” said the 35-year-old.

Myanmar’s military could not be reached for comment.

In September, the military claimed a month-long military operation captured over 130 wells in Myaing and 735 more in neighboring Pakokku Township.

Black market

Scores of pro-democracy factions and ethnic armed groups are fighting the military.

As the war grinds on, all sides battle to fill their war chests with the tax or trade of natural resources: gem mines, rare earth mineral deposits, gold or teak.

Oil projects are not generally contested.

The major ones are under staunch military guard, and on-the-books output is tiny by international standards at around 6,000 barrels a day last year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

But the artisanal fields are coveted by rebels precisely because of their modest size, according to Thomas Kean, a Myanmar consultant for the International Crisis Group.

“Part of the reason why they’re significant is because they’re not globally significant,” he said, explaining that they are small enough to thrive under the radar yet big enough to fund guerrillas.

Spiking oil prices may not directly drive conflict, said Kean, highlighting a broader military campaign to evict rebels from heartland footholds by squeezing revenue sources.

But as the spoils of war become more profitable, the stakes get higher.

“We’re talking about millions of barrels a year coming out of these oil fields,” he added. “With global prices what they are, that’s a significant amount of money.”

World.title: Shan State’s Scam Industry Expands Under Protection of Regime-Aligned Militias
World.content:
More than two years after high-profile anti-regime military offensives shattered many of Myanmar’s most notorious scam enclaves near the Chinese border, cyber-fraud syndicates have metastasized across the interior of Shan State, the country’s largest state.

Rather than wiping out the illicit multi-billion-dollar industry, the fall of Kokang’s capital, Laukkai, in January 2024 triggered an influx of scammers deeper into Myanmar—chiefly into Shan State’s interior and Karen State in the country’s south.

By mid-2026, cyber-scam syndicates had expanded across more than 63 percent of Shan State’s 55 townships, establishing footholds in at least 35 of them. This assessment is based on official enforcement and crackdown data published by the military regime’s Ministry of Information, alongside reports from four ethnic armed organizations (EAOs)—the United Wa State Army (UWSA), the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA), the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA).

The entrenchment of telecom fraud comes as Shan State continues to bear the brunt of decades of civil war. Observers point out that these conditions have fostered an acute crisis in which the unchecked proliferation of scam syndicates not only expands organized crime networks, but also threatens local socioeconomic stability and lures local young people into the illicit economy.

Operation 1027, an anti-regime offensive launched by the Three Brotherhood Alliance on October 27, 2023, toppled the cross-border empires run by Kokang’s notorious “Big Four” families—the Bai, Wei, Ming and Liu clans. The alliance comprised the TNLA, MNDAA and Arakan Army. Parallel crackdowns were launched in areas controlled by the UWSA and NDAA. Yet far from marking the demise of the scam industry, the dismantling of those border scam complexes simply scattered the surviving networks, driving them deep into Shan State’s interior.

From the border to the interior

According to local residents, hundreds of Chinese nationals arrived in southern Shan State’s Laihka Township around November 2023, approximately a month after Operation 1027 began. Locals said the newcomers first erected compounds near Manpang Village before launching scam operations.

Instead of operating out of massive, conspicuous complexes housing huge numbers of people as they previously did, they rented homes dispersed throughout residential neighborhoods to fragment their workforce, and even set up makeshift tent encampments in rural villages and forests.

Starting in February 2026, the regime began conducting raids against online scam compounds in Laihka. According to official releases, as of the end of October, 129 Chinese nationals had been arrested, comprising the majority of those detained.

According to statements given by detainees, they crossed into Myanmar from Xishuangbanna, in the far south of China’s Yunnan Province, entering UWSA-controlled Panghsang and the NDAA-controlled Mong La area. From there, coordinated networks facilitated their phased, step-by-step relocation across northern, southern and eastern Shan State.

Similarly, in northern Shan, residents noted that telecom fraud operators began trickling into Tangyan town in early 2024.

According to UWSA statements, during crackdowns on scam operations in Tangyan in November 2024 and July 2025, Wa forces arrested over 1,000 people, 829 of whom were Chinese nationals.

The military junta likewise launched its own raids and arrests in Tangyan across 2024 and 2025.

Despite raids conducted by both the junta and the UWSA, a military sweep proved that these criminal syndicates were still operating in Tangyan in April 2026. During a raid on an online scam camp near Kaung San Village, the military reported arresting 123 individuals, 103 of whom were Chinese nationals.

“Local youths worked at the scam centers. Usually, whenever there’s a raid, those who can run simply flee. Some get away, some don’t. But we’ve never heard of the actual bosses being caught,” a Tangyan resident said.

Throughout 2025, these fraud networks spread rapidly into numerous townships in Shan State: Mongyai and Hsipaw in northern Shan; Nansang and Mongpan in southern Shan; and Kengtung and Mong Hsat in eastern Shan.

In October 2026, the regime announced the arrest of 75 Chinese nationals and 12 Myanmar citizens involved in online scams in southern Shan State’s Hopong Township, along with the seizure of related equipment. This indicates that scam operations have spread to the doorstep of Taunggyi, the capital of Shan State.

Ko Michael, an analyst who tracks cyber-scam activities, said the crackdowns by both the regime and local armed groups have stalled because they consistently fail to net the masterminds.

“They aren’t shooting the birds; they’re just shaking the trees. So the birds simply fly from one tree to another. Everything gets scattered around. That’s why this problem has become so difficult to contain,” he said.

At the same time, while scam operations have proliferated into the interior, they have by no means vanished from the borderlands. None of the ethnic armed groups conducting anti-scam crackdowns have declared their regions entirely free of fraud hubs. Operations persist in the border town of Muse, and recruitment s seeking workers for scam centers in Tachileik on the Thai border continue to appear daily on social media. The fact that cyber-scam operations continue to operate on Shan State’s borders while simultaneously spreading inland raises a key question. Who is enabling this aggressive proliferation?

Who is providing protection?

The vast majority of individuals arrested in Shan State’s scam hubs are Chinese nationals; in some locations, nearly every person detained was from China. Yet it would be utterly impossible for foreign nationals to arrive in large groups and establish, let alone operate, these telecom fraud enterprises without local assistance.

Crucially, armed organizations and security outfits controlling the territory in these areas are the linchpins ensuring the survival of these organized crime syndicates. When cyber-scams first proliferated across the Kokang, Wa and Mong La borderlands, they took root strictly under the control of local armed actors.

In many parts of Shan State, regime-aligned armed factions have turned these operations into lucrative revenue streams, according to local residents and individuals formerly involved in the trade.

“The total proliferation of scams across Shan State didn’t happen because of just one group. But I want to stress this: it would be completely impossible to run without the military’s involvement,” said Ko Michael, the scam-operation monitor.

In December 2025, after the military raided an online scam compound in Hsipaw Township, state media reported the arrest of three members of the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), one of the major Shan armed groups. Concurrently, residents point out that in Muse, Laihka and several other areas, local militia outfits—including the Namhkam Myoma, Pansay, Kaungkha, Manpang and Wanpang militias—receive payoffs in exchange for facilitating relocations, providing physical security and protection, and transporting workers to scam centers.

“The scam business and armed groups are inseparable. Without an armed group, you simply cannot run a scam operation. It’s the armed groups that provide the protection,” said a resident of Muse.

The nexus between armed actors and telecom fraud extends to Myanmar’s most powerful ethnic armed organization, the UWSA, which has been heavily implicated in the scam industry despite its current anti-scam crackdowns.

“The ones who really laid the solid groundwork and operated these scam rings at scale were the Wa. Top Wa leaders were directly involved,” said Dr. Hla Kyaw Zaw, a veteran analyst of China-Myanmar affairs.

The Chinese state-produced documentary “The Demise of Telecom Fraud in Northern Myanmar,” which covered the anti-scam crackdowns and was aired last month, identifies UWSA-controlled territory as the incubator for northern Myanmar’s scam economy. It claimed that Bao Yanban, chief of Mong Pawk, a town in the Wa region, amassed so much wealth from the scams that he would sun-dry banknotes on rooftops to prevent mold.

Protection for scam operators has come not only from local militias, but directly from the regime itself.

In late 2023, as the Three Brotherhood Alliance was attempting to capture Laukkai during Operation 1027, the military regime sheltered top Kokang scam kingpins from the Big Four families in Naypyitaw. Among them was Bai Suocheng, the former leader of the Kokang Self-Administered Zone and head of the regime-aligned Border Guard Force.

It was only under immense pressure from Beijing in January 2024 that the regime finally handed these high-profile suspects over to Chinese security forces in Naypyitaw. They were subsequently tried in Chinese courts, where harsh penalties—including death sentences—were handed down.

What is the impact?

Despite the crackdowns and legal cases, online scam syndicates have continued to fan out from the northern Shan-China border across the entirety of Shan State, causing severe social harm in every community they penetrate.

With legitimate employment opportunities devastated by the country’s ongoing military conflict, cyber-scam compounds have emerged as places where local youth can make quick money.

A northern Shan resident who previously worked in a scam compound explained that the prospect of “easy money” causes those who have worked in the industry to lose interest in conventional jobs.

“When you return from there [working at a scam center], you come back with a lot of money. You just don’t want to do outside manual work anymore. Once that money runs out, you don’t go looking for decent, ordinary jobs. That’s true for about 80 percent of the people who go to work there,” the northern Shan resident explained.

As the industry has expanded, training courses designed to teach people how to run telecom scams have begun popping up in Shan State, according to sources close to the industry.

“There are training courses opened by people who worked inside scam compounds. They teach combined computer and communication skills. They teach basic things like how to defraud people out of money. How many words per minute you need to type—that’s something only people who worked there can teach,” said a resident of Kyaukme in northern Shan State. Citing security concerns, the resident declined to disclose the exact locations or other details of the training centers.

Scam operations also serve as a seemingly safe and profitable haven for young people trying to escape military conscription by the regime. The conscription law, which has been on the books for years but only enforced since 2024, requires men aged 18 to 35 and women aged 18 to 27 to serve up to two years in the military.

A Kyaukme resident who sought to evade conscription by working in a scam compound said he did so for his own safety. “My name came up on the conscription list. A lot of people from our area worked there. They said things were going well there, inviting us to come over,” he said.

“Quite a lot of young people ended up going,” he added.

World.title: Regime Summons German Envoy Over Call for Coup Releases
World.content:
YANGON—The Myanmar regime’s Foreign Ministry said it summoned Germany’s top resident diplomat on Tuesday over a Facebook video calling for authorities to “unconditionally release” ousted politicians, including Aung San Suu Kyi.

Germany’s mission head Mathias Licharz posted the video on Sunday, standing outside the former Yangon residence of Win Myint, the president of Aung San Suu Kyi’s government that was removed in a 2021 coup.

The junta behind the coup organized elections installing a nominally civilian government this spring, although analysts regard it as a fig leaf for ongoing military rule.

Licharz said in his message, scheduled for Win Myint’s 75th birthday, that the United Nations still regards him as the “legitimate president” of Myanmar.

Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry said Licharz was summoned for a meeting with deputy minister Ko Ko Kyaw, “warned against the video” and handed an aide-memoire.

“Should the Chargé d’Affaires choose to recognize U Win Myint as President and wish to discontinue his service in Myanmar, the Ministry would have no objection,” a statement said.

Myanmar has been riven by civil war since the 2021 coup, as pro-democracy guerrillas rose up and long-simmering ethnic minority insurgencies challenging central rule boiled over.

The ministry statement accused Licharz of “intentional conduct” that “appeared to fuel opposition to the host country and its Government, thereby inciting internal unrest.”

“The Deputy Minister strongly warned against recurrence of such act and informed him that any similar conduct would be treated with utmost seriousness and would take appropriate actions,” it said.

Germany’s embassy in Myanmar did not respond immediately to a request for comment.

Win Myint was jailed in the February 2021 coup, which ended Myanmar’s decade-long democratic experiment.

Authorities said in April he had been pardoned of his post-coup convictions—charges that supporters and analysts say were confected to oust the government.

However, Licharz said in his video message his efforts to meet Win Myint had been unfruitful.

“There is only one conclusion,” he said. “U Wint Myint is not a free man. He’s not allowed to meet with whom he would like to meet and he’s not allowed to communicate independently.”

Aung San Suu Kyi remains detained but was moved to house arrest in the capital Naypyitaw this year, authorities say, where access to the 81-year-old Nobel Peace Prize laureate remains tightly controlled.

Licharz called for authorities to “unconditionally release all those who are arbitrarily detained including U Win Myint and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi.”

World.title: Tokayev Orders Measures to Curb Corruption in Kazakhstan’s State-Owned Companies
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has ordered the government and oversight bodies to submit proposals to reduce corruption in state-owned companies by Nov. 24, following the detention of senior executives at Samruk-Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund and Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the national railway company.

Speaking at an operational meeting of the Security Council on Nov. 13, Tokayev described the detentions as “an extremely serious signal” indicating widespread corruption in state-owned companies.

He stressed that the Constitution is the country’s supreme law and that violations of its provisions would be addressed under the Law and Order principle.

“The Constitution is the Basic Law of our state, the legal passport of the people. Disregarding the Constitution and its fundamental provisions is tantamount to discriminating against the people. Such actions will be suppressed in accordance with the Law and Order principle. No one is allowed to violate the Constitution or even mock this, one could say, sacred document,” Tokayev said.

He also emphasized that officials entrusted with public authority must act decisively to protect national interests, particularly when the country’s reputation, public trust in national institutions and international standing are at stake.

He noted that Samruk Kazyna manages Kazakhstan’s strategic assets, implements major investment projects and cooperates with leading foreign companies and international financial institutions.

“Behind each such agreement and partnership are numerous years of negotiations, Kazakhstan’s commitments and the trust of the international community in our country,” he said.

State-owned companies continue operations

Tokayev stressed that the detention of executives would not affect the operations of Samruk Kazyna or state-owned companies, including KTZ. All institutions and enterprises under their management continue to operate as usual.

“This serious incident is not a reason for disruptions in the operations of the Fund and state-owned companies. Moreover, I am confident that the fight against corruption should, on the contrary, increase the confidence of investors and creditors in this institution, and its work will become more efficient, transparent and productive,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted the recovery of illegally acquired assets, noting that the Prosecutor General’s Office had secured the return of more than 1.3 trillion tenge (US$2.9 billion). The funds were allocated to building 466 social and infrastructure facilities, including medical institutions, water supply systems, schools and sports complexes. Of these, 383 have been completed.

He said the quality of completed facilities should also be assessed, pointing to recurring problems with infrastructure quality, particularly roads.

Corruption statistics and investigations

According to Tokayev, authorities identified 3,168 corruption offenses between 2023 and 2025. Of these, 2,165 were committed by civil servants, while the remaining cases involved other individuals, including employees of the quasi-public sector. The total amount involved exceeded 248 billion tenge (US$550 million).

In the first 10 months of 2026, authorities recorded 751 corruption-related offenses, including 546 committed by civil servants and 205 by other individuals, including employees of quasi-public sector entities.

Tokayev acknowledged that the corruption situation remained challenging and said the authorities would continue to report publicly on the situation and measures being taken to address it. He said all reports of corruption offenses involving officials at different levels would be promptly and thoroughly investigated by the National Security Committee’s Anti-Corruption Service, with the participation of the Prosecutor General’s Office.

“Naturally, there will be no division into ‘our own,’ ‘not quite our own’ and, even more so, ‘outsiders.’ Our Constitution has established the principle of equality of all citizens before the law. We must comply with this requirement,” Tokayev said.

He added that no one, regardless of their position, achievements or personal connections, should expect exemptions from the law.

President Tokayev instructed the government and oversight bodies to submit concrete proposals by Nov. 24 to reduce corruption offenses and improve the performance of quasi-public sector companies and their staff.

World.title: IMF, Development Partners Support Early Pension Reform Work in Uzbekistan
World.content:
ASTANA – The International Monetary Fund (IMF), together with the Asian Development Bank (ADB), International Labour Organization (ILO) and World Bank, is working with Uzbekistan’s authorities on an early-stage concept for pension reform, IMF Resident Representative in Uzbekistan Koba Gvenetadze said Nov. 13.

Speaking at a roundtable at the Central Bank of Uzbekistan in Tashkent, Gvenetadze said the reform remains at an early stage, with authorities examining international experience and assessing different approaches to pension system management. He stressed that any future reform should be financially sustainable and avoid creating additional or unforeseen pressure on the state budget.

Responding to a question about the management of pension savings, including the possibility of involving external investment companies, Gvenetadze said the authorities had not yet developed a detailed reform plan. He added that the development of domestic capital markets could also be relevant to pension reform, as pension funds and capital markets often develop alongside each other.

The IMF will continue working with the authorities as the reform process advances, he said.

World.title: Three Almaty Destinations Rank Among World’s Top 100 Tourist Attractions
World.content:
ASTANA – Three tourist attractions in Almaty have been included in the 2026 edition of the international Worldworthy 100 editorial ranking, earning places among the world’s top 100 in their respective categories.

Two hiking destinations associated with Ile-Alatau State National Park received international recognition. Kimasar Gorge ranked 56th worldwide among the best hiking trails, while Butakovka Gorge placed 79th in the global ranking and second in its category. The Shymbulak cable car ranked ninth worldwide among the best cable cars.All three attractions received Worldworthy 100 award certificates for 2026.

The ranking is compiled based on visitor reviews and ratings, journalistic research and information from open sources. The recognition is expected to raise international interest in the natural attractions of the Ile-Alatau area and promote Kazakhstan’s ecotourism potential.

World.title: Kazakhstan Plans to Issue Tokenized Government Bonds in First Quarter of 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan plans to issue tokenized government bonds in the first quarter of 2027, National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov said at the 14th Congress of Financiers of Kazakhstan on Nov. 13 in Almaty.

“We plan to issue tokenized government bonds jointly with the Ministry of Finance in the near future. This will probably take place in the first quarter of next year,” he said.

Kazakhstan is also expanding tokenization for financial and real-world assets. On Oct. 27, the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE) platform hosted the first issuance of digital financial assets by private issuers. On Nov. 9, the National Bank issued its own notes in tokenized form for the first time.

“The successful conduct of these trades means that we have tested the full readiness of the infrastructure, all institutional arrangements and so on, to expand this mechanism,” Suleimenov said.

The National Bank’s tokenized notes were issued for 10 billion tenge (US$21.5 million) through KASE’s digital financial assets platform. The notes were placed through an auction in both traditional and tokenized forms, with a maturity of 91 days. Their weighted average yield stood at 15.72% per annum.

Suleimenov said the next area of development would be tokenizing real-world assets, including real estate, precious metals and mineral resources.

“Tokenization transforms a financial asset into any type of asset. In this way, it democratizes access to finance and reduces its cost,” he said.

Regulators discuss unified financial market strategy

The congress’s plenary session also addressed the development of a unified strategy for Kazakhstan’s capital market and coordination among financial regulators.

Suleimenov said closer cooperation was needed to ensure that investors could navigate the country’s regulatory environment, which includes the National Bank, the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market, the Astana International Financial Center and, potentially, Alatau City.

“In our view, it is extremely important to ensure synergy, mutual recognition and mutual circulation, so that these markets can develop. We are not going to prescribe or dictate exactly what each one should do. This is simply about defining a kind of specialization for each market. At the same time, it is important to ensure that each market does not remain confined within its own jurisdiction. Money is fluid by nature; it cannot be locked in,” Suleimenov said.

He stressed the importance of effective cooperation and information exchange among regulators to ensure the financial system operates as a unified whole, distinguishing the strategy from day-to-day regulatory measures.

Madina Abylkassymova, chair of the Agency for Regulation and Development of the Financial Market, said the existing financial market development concept, adopted in 2020, needed to be updated in light of changes over the past five years.

“The profound changes that have taken place in the financial market over the past five years require this concept to be updated. Last year, we conducted an assessment, and approximately 80% of the concept had already been implemented,” she said.

Some changes are already reflected in the new banking law, while further measures are expected to be included in programs to develop the capital and insurance markets. Abylkassymova identified the rapid development of artificial intelligence and tokenization as key trends the new strategy should address.

“I think that by 2030 we will see very significant changes in the financial system, both globally and in Kazakhstan,” she said.

World.title: Kazakhstan Develops Medical Tourism Packages for International Patients
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has developed packages combining medical treatment, rehabilitation and wellness services to attract international patients, as part of broader efforts to establish the country as a regional medical tourism hub.

The initiative was outlined in Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov’s response to a parliamentary inquiry from members of the Kurultai. The government has also drafted an interagency plan for developing medical tourism between 2027 and 2030.

The packages include assistance with selecting medical and sanatorium-resort facilities, transfers, accommodation, meals and interpreter services for patients and accompanying persons. They also include price lists.

“We plan to promote them through travel agencies and embassies, with the possibility of obtaining a medical visa. We also intend to establish a unified service chain, from the patient’s initial inquiry to post-treatment support. Medical organizations, tour operators and service companies will be involved in this work,” Bektenov wrote in a statement.

Medical tourism development plan

The government has prepared legislative amendments to establish a framework for medical tourism. They are intended to define key terms, clarify the responsibilities of authorized bodies and market participants, and improve coordination among them.

The draft interagency plan for 2027–2030 provides improvements to the regulatory framework, statistical reporting, service standards and cooperation mechanisms. According to Bektenov, it also includes measures to develop medical tourism through the country’s research-based medical centers and institutes.

The government has identified several medical fields in demand among foreign patients, including cardiac surgery, oncology, transplantation, reproductive medicine, orthopedics, ophthalmology, dentistry and medical rehabilitation.

According to the prime minister, Kazakhstan’s medical specialists and clinical facilities in several fields are comparable to leading international centers, while treatment costs are significantly lower than in Europe, North America, South Korea and the Gulf countries.

Kazakhstan seeks to become a regional medical hub

The government is working to establish a unified Central Asian medical hub based on the country’s existing system of high-tech medical care.

“The hub will allow Kazakhstan to position itself as a regional center of advanced medical services and innovation for neighboring countries. Kazakhstan has significant potential in medical tourism, and among Central Asian countries, only our country provides a number of modern and unique medical services, including proton therapy, Gamma Knife treatment and complex cardiac surgery,” Bektenov said.

According to information attached to the prime minister’s response, 10 medical organizations in Kazakhstan currently hold international Joint Commission International (JCI) accreditation. Seven are located in Astana and three in Almaty.

In 2025, medical services in Kazakhstan were provided to 4,488 foreign patients. Almaty received the largest number, with 2,685 patients, followed by Astana with 1,396 and Shymkent with 300.

World.title: Kazakhstan Showcases Women’s Role in Preserving Cultural Heritage at UNESCO Event in Paris
World.content:
ASTANA – UNESCO Headquarters hosted an exhibition on Nov. 11 highlighting the role of women in safeguarding living heritage, along with a gala concert organized as part of the Planet of Art 2026 International Youth Festival under UNESCO patronage, with support from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Organized by the Kazakhstan National Federation of Clubs for UNESCO, the festival has developed over nearly two decades into an international platform for young artists under the age of 18. It brings together children and young people from more than 5,000 UNESCO clubs and associations in 95 countries, including 198 in Kazakhstan.

This year, the Paris exhibition features paintings by winners of the festival’s fine arts competition from 54 countries. Winners of the music competition were invited to perform on UNESCO’s main stage. Kazakhstan also holds the presidency of the World Federation of Clubs and Associations for UNESCO for 2023–2027.

Women’s role in preserving living heritage

Speaking at the exhibition’s opening ceremony, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador and Permanent Delegate to UNESCO Askar Abdrakhmanov highlighted the country’s contribution to the international network of UNESCO clubs and associations.

“Kazakhstan takes pride in its contribution to the progress of the global network of clubs and associations for UNESCO, which plays its meaningful role in international cooperation for developing the creative potential of young people – a contribution recognized in a decision of the UNESCO Executive Board in April 2026,” he said.

UNESCO Assistant Director-General for Culture Nayef Al-Fayez welcomed the festival’s focus on women’s role in preserving and passing on traditional knowledge, crafts, performing arts, rituals and customs to future generations.

“Cultural diversity is not only something to preserve. It is something to experience, share and continually reimagine. I would like to express our sincere congratulations to the World and Kazakhstan Federations of Clubs and Associations for UNESCO, to the authorities and institutions of Kazakhstan, and to all partners, educators and artists who made this evening possible,” he said.

The exhibition also features works by contemporary Kazakh artists Bakyt Shuketayev and Aigerim Karibayeva, an Envoy of Clubs for UNESCO. Their paintings explore Kazakhstan’s living heritage and that of other countries, reinterpreting traditional images and symbols in contemporary contexts to highlight women’s role in preserving collective memory and connecting generations.

The gala concert brought together young performers aged 12 to 18 from 10 countries. They performed alongside the Student Symphony Orchestra of the Kurmangazy Kazakh National Conservatory and students from the Alexander Seleznev Almaty Choreographic School.

The Planet of Art 2026 festival was held with the support of Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and corporate partners, including BI Group, Tengizchevroil, TotalEnergies and the Freedom Shapagat Foundation.

World.title: Kazakhstan Tightens Physical Security Requirements for Radioactive Waste
World.content:
ASTANA – Enterprises handling radioactive waste in Kazakhstan must protect it against unauthorized access, theft and sabotage under new physical security rules approved by the country’s Agency for Atomic Energy.

The order, signed by the agency’s chair on Nov. 5, establishes requirements for the physical protection of radioactive waste, storage and processing facilities, and waste during transportation. It applies to both individuals and legal entities involved in radioactive waste management.

Under the rules, organizations must establish a physical protection system combining organizational, engineering and technical measures. The system must prevent security breaches, identify threats promptly, restrict unauthorized access and ensure a prompt response to incidents.

Three levels of physical protection

The rules establish three levels of physical protection based on the activity of the radioactive waste.

Level A applies to high-level radioactive waste and is intended to prevent unauthorized access, theft, seizure and sabotage, while reducing potential radiological consequences.

Level B covers intermediate-level waste and aims to minimize the likelihood of unauthorized access, removal, theft and sabotage.

Level C applies to low-level waste and provides measures to reduce the risk of unauthorized access, removal and theft.

Separate requirements apply to the transportation of radioactive waste. The required level of physical protection will be determined by the highest category of waste being transported, taking into account the combined activity of all waste in the shipment. This applies whether the waste is transported in a single vehicle, a convoy, a train or separate compartments of a vessel.

Staff checks and incident reporting

Organizations must also establish procedures governing personnel access to radioactive waste, conduct background checks on employees, control the use of keys and locks, maintain security equipment and regularly test its functionality.

They must develop separate physical protection plans for facilities and for radioactive waste transportation. Employees responsible for security must receive relevant training and regularly upgrade their qualifications.

The rules also specify procedures for responding to incidents. In cases involving lost radioactive waste, attempted or actual unauthorized access, theft, seizure or sabotage, organizations must take immediate measures to address the situation.

The order will enter into force on Nov. 22.

World.title: Scientists Warn of Water Risks as Tuyuksu Glacier Records Warmest Summer Since 1972
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s Tuyuksu Glacier recorded its warmest summer since meteorological observations began in 1972, losing an estimated 5.6 million cubic meters of water during the warm season and raising concerns about the long-term water security of southeastern Kazakhstan.

Researchers at the Central Asian Regional Glaciological Center under UNESCO completed processing data from the 2025-2026 summer observation season in early November. The findings point to accelerated glacier retreat driven by unusually high temperatures and prolonged warm weather, Khabar TV reported on Nov. 11.

Located approximately 30 kilometers south of Almaty, Tuyuksu is among the world’s most extensively studied glaciers.

According to Nikolai Kasatkin, a researcher at the center, the average high-altitude temperature during the summer reached 6.17 degrees Celsius, nearly two degrees above the seasonal norm. Above-freezing temperatures lasted 150 days.

The glacier retreated by 42 meters over the summer, while its surface area decreased by 108,000 square meters.

Although snowfall last winter exceeded usual levels, it was insufficient to offset the ice lost during the unusually warm season.

Long-term water security concerns

Despite the significant glacier losses, water volumes in mountain rivers remained largely unchanged during the observation period. However, scientists warn that continued glacier retreat could disrupt the Zhetysu Region’s long-term water balance.

Vassily Kapitsa, head of the Laboratory of High-Mountain Geocryology, stressed the need for adaptation measures and more responsible water consumption, notably in major urban centers.

He highlighted Almaty, whose population has exceeded three million according to some estimates, as an example of a city that must prioritize efficient water use.

“Without rational and careful use of water resources, particularly drinking water, we may face a severe shortage of drinking water in the future,” he said.

Scientists warn that accelerated glacier degradation in the Zailiysky Alatau mountain range could gradually undermine an important source of freshwater for southeastern Kazakhstan, making sustainable water management increasingly urgent.

World.title: Can electronic salary monitoring eliminate under-the-table payments in Azerbaijan?
World.content:
Electronic salary monitoring in Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan plans to pay salaries through an electronic payment system selected by the Central Bank, based on data from the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population. Employees will still be able to choose which bank receives their salary. Deputy Labour and Social Protection Minister Zaur Aliyev announced the plans on 11 November at a meeting of the Milli Majlis Committee on Labour and Social Policy.

Aliyev said the aim of the new system was to monitor not only the salaries specified in employment contracts but also the actual amounts paid to workers.

“This will create a more effective monitoring mechanism to identify and prevent cases of delayed salary payments, underpayment or concealment of part of an employee’s earnings.”

Under proposed amendments to the Labour Code, employers will have to pay salaries in full into a bank account chosen by the employee. The Report news agency reports that the government expects the new system to strengthen oversight of timely salary payments and compliance with labour laws.

The initiative forms part of the same package of legislative amendments as the introduction of hourly pay. We have previously reported on who could benefit from such a system.

Will electronic monitoring put an end to under-the-table salary payments, or will it simply lead to new ways of concealing income?

What are under-the-table salary payments?

Under this arrangement, employers transfer part of an employee’s salary to their bank account and pay the rest in cash, unofficially. The salary stated in the employment contract is lower than the employee’s actual earnings. As a result, employers pay taxes and social security contributions only on the officially declared amount. Some workers do not have employment contracts at all.

Samed Shikhi, who has worked at various companies in Azerbaijan for around ten years, said that most of his employers had not offered him an employment contract.

“Getting an extra 50 manats (around $30) today is more beneficial for me than counting on a higher pension after the age of 65.”

He said most workers do not try to change the situation. Seeing the pensions that current retirees receive, they do not expect to get substantial payments when they grow old.

How widespread is the problem?

There are no precise figures, but official statistics offer an indication of the scale of the problem. According to the State Statistics Committee, Azerbaijan has more than 5.1 million employed people, while the number of salaried employees stands at 1,776,800. Of these, 942,600 work in the private sector.

At a parliamentary committee meeting, MP Vugar Bayramov said that 65% of employed people work without employment contracts. According to an International Monetary Fund report on Azerbaijan published this year, only 23% of private-sector workers have official employment contracts. The IMF estimates that the shadow economy accounts for around half of the country’s GDP.

Economist Rashad Hasanov believes that underreporting salaries is most common in the private sector, where it affects more than 40% of employment contracts.

“It is difficult to give an exact figure, but this is a fairly widespread phenomenon,” he said.

Independent economists consider the widespread practice of declaring minimum wages in employment contracts one indication of unofficial payments. This is particularly common in profitable industries such as construction, hospitality and retail.

For comparison, the State Statistics Committee reported that Azerbaijan’s average monthly nominal salary stood at 1,173 manats (around $690) in January–August this year. The minimum wage, meanwhile, is 400 manats (around $235).

According to figures published last year by the State Tax Service, the private non-oil sector had the highest number of registered employment contracts in retail (299,000), services (232,000) and construction (98,000).

Taxes rise as oversight tightens

The introduction of electronic salary monitoring comes alongside an increase in the tax burden. For seven years, starting in 2019, employees in Azerbaijan’s private non-oil sector were exempt from income tax on monthly earnings of up to 8,000 manats (around $4,705).

According to the State Tax Service, the number of employment contracts in the sector increased by around 470,000, or 87%, during this period. It exceeded one million in September last year. The agency attributes this growth to economic development and the tax incentives that remained in place for seven years.

The tax exemption expired at the end of 2025. Employees now pay income tax on monthly earnings of up to 2,500 manats (around $1,470) at a rate of 3% in 2026, 5% in 2027 and 7% from 2028 onwards. The first 200 manats (around $118) remain tax-free.

Last year, Bayramov wrote about how tax rules affect the number of employment contracts. He believes the decline in their number in the private sector is linked to a 2025 change that allowed micro-entrepreneurs to receive tax benefits without having to employ staff.

Hasanov warns that if the move towards official salary payments increases employers’ tax and social security costs, companies may try to pass the additional expenses on to workers:

“Given the high level of competition in the labour market, unemployment and the shortage of medium- and high-paying jobs, this could reduce the amount employees actually take home after taxes and contributions.”

What will the electronic system fail to detect?

Hasanov believes the new system will primarily monitor payments made under existing employment contracts, rather than bring undeclared salaries into the formal economy:

“This mechanism does not require employers to legalise under-the-table salaries, nor does it prevent them from declaring minimum wages in employment contracts.”

This means that if an employment contract specifies a salary of 400 manats and the employer transfers exactly that amount to the employee’s bank card, the system will not detect any violation. The remaining earnings, paid in cash, will remain outside its oversight.

Economist Akif Nasirli considers the new mechanism an “important step”. He believes that fully declaring salaries will increase workers’ pension savings. However, Nasirli also points to another practice:

“Sometimes an employer transfers the official salary to an employee’s bank card but pays the remaining amount in cash or demands that the employee return part of the money transferred.”

The economist says the authorities should compare salaries declared in employment contracts with actual pay levels, taking into account the industry, job position and workload. He also calls for an effective complaints mechanism for workers and measures to hold employers who break the law accountable.

Why don’t workers complain?

In response to a separate enquiry from Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, the State Labour Inspectorate said it could investigate violations in job s if someone filed a complaint. If it confirmed a violation, “measures would be taken against the employer in accordance with the law”. This means that oversight largely depends on workers themselves reporting abuses.

Samed Shikhi believes the main reasons workers do not complain are fear of losing their jobs and a lack of faith that their complaints will achieve anything:

“The problem is that companies often have connections with certain officials or influential people.”

The electronic system will be able to monitor only salaries officially declared by employers. Detecting cash payments will largely depend on workers themselves. As long as employees are afraid to complain, under-the-table salary payments may continue with their tacit consent. The practice is becoming an even more pressing issue as the tax burden increases.

Electronic salary monitoring in Azerbaijan

World.title: Tbilisi mayor considers restricting traffic in city
World.content:
Possible traffic restrictions in Tbilisi

Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze has outlined several possible ways to tackle traffic congestion in the capital. These include restricting vehicle traffic, introducing an alternating-day driving system based on odd and even number plates, and charging drivers to enter certain parts of the city.

He said the growing number of cars was one of Tbilisi’s main problems. Infrastructure projects, such as building flyovers, would not be enough to solve it.

Kaladze did not say that the authorities had decided to introduce any of these measures. However, he noted that restrictions might be necessary to address the problem. In that case, the public would have the final say.

On 11 November, Kaladze told the pro-government Imedi TV channel that 900,000 vehicles had been on Tbilisi’s roads during peak hours.

He rejected claims that dedicated bus lanes were the main cause of traffic congestion. As an example, he cited Agmashenebeli Avenue, where traffic becomes almost impossible at certain times despite the absence of a dedicated public transport lane.

“The biggest problem is our dependence on cars and the sheer number of vehicles, not that the city government is doing nothing. There are specific solutions, just as there are in other countries,” Kaladze said.

Asked by the presenter whether the city could restrict traffic based on whether a vehicle’s number plate ends in an even or odd digit, the mayor described this as one possible option.

“If we want to solve this problem, we could agree on measures such as allowing only cars with number plates ending in an even or odd digit on certain days. Another option would be to install cameras in specific areas and introduce congestion charges, as many European cities have done,” the mayor said.

Kaladze said that although the public might find such decisions difficult to accept, residents themselves would need to play a part in addressing the situation.

“When we make a decision, it is important that everyone understands and accepts it. Society must be ready for it. The city authorities cannot simply do nothing while the problem persists. No — we must make a decision, and we will all have to make certain sacrifices,” Kaladze said.

Traffic congestion and growing pressure on the urban environment

Traffic congestion and overcrowded public transport have remained among Tbilisi’s main transport problems for many years. Rapid urban growth, the development of new residential neighbourhoods and heavy reliance on private cars are putting additional pressure on the existing transport infrastructure.

Didi Dighomi is Tbilisi’s fastest-growing residential district, followed by Navtlughi and Varketili. A study by Danish consultancy Ramboll, commissioned by Tbilisi City Hall, forecasts that Didi Dighomi’s population will at least double between 2022 and 2042.

The study’s authors identify the development of rail transport as one possible long-term solution to the district’s transport problems.

Against this backdrop, Tbilisi City Hall is working on a tram line project. On 7 September 2026, the municipality signed a design and construction contract with a consortium of Turkish companies, EYE Group. The project envisages a tram line connecting Didi Dighomi with Didube metro station. The contract is worth 287,654,321 lari (approximately $111,089,941), and the municipality expects construction to finish by 2030.

At the same time, in recent years, City Hall has introduced dedicated bus lanes on several major streets in the capital. The aim is to speed up public transport and reduce reliance on private cars. Some categories of taxi were subsequently also allowed to use these lanes.

The possible restrictions Kaladze mentioned suggest a shift towards a stricter transport policy aimed at curbing the growth in the number of cars in Tbilisi. However, the mayor has yet to specify when the measures might take effect or how the authorities plan to implement them.



Possible traffic restrictions in Tbilisi

World.title: Why has Abkhazia been unable to resolve its waste crisis for 20 years?
World.content:
Waste crisis in Abkhazia

The history of the waste crisis in Abkhazia resembles an endless, absurdist tragicomedy: the problem is clear, experts have worked out technical solutions, yet for years the authorities have directed their efforts towards the wrong measures and on an insufficient scale.

Presidents and mayors come and go, expert commissions are convened, but each time another fire breaks out at an illegal rubbish dump or residents take to the streets to protest against the unbearable stench, the authorities are forced to revisit the issue. And each time, it emerges that the problem has only grown worse.

Timeline of waste protests

Public debate over Abkhazia’s waste problem intensified following a protest in the village of Alakhadzy, near the resort town of Pitsunda, when it became clear that the authorities’ assurances that they had the situation “under control” were far from reality.

On 27 October, residents of Alakhadzy blocked access to a rubbish dump. They were driven to take action by persistent smoke from burning waste, an unbearable stench and the risk of a major fire. Nearly 1,000 people signed a petition calling for the dump to be closed.

The head of the district administration, Yury Khagush, arrived at the scene, along with members of the district assembly, local officials, police officers and even representatives of the State Security Service. The protesters dispersed after being promised that the issue would be resolved.

This was far from the first such incident. The history of “waste protests” in Abkhazia dates back to July 2007, when residents of the Mayak neighbourhood in Sukhum first blocked rubbish trucks from entering a municipal landfill located within the city limits.

In the years that followed, the landfill continued to catch fire repeatedly, engulfing Sukhum in toxic smoke. In August 2011, city authorities promised to bring the site up to an “acceptable standard” by November that year.

However, nothing had changed by November, and in December, then-President Alexander Ankvab openly acknowledged that the republic was facing a waste crisis.

“We need to find the courage either to reach agreements with investors or to make savings elsewhere and build at least two large waste-processing plants ourselves,” Ankvab said at the time.

Two years later, he described purchasing Italian equipment as the most cost-effective option. However, the plans never materialised.

From one landfill to another

In 2018, the landfill in the Mayak neighbourhood was finally closed. However, the problem did not disappear – it was simply relocated. Waste from the capital began to be transported daily to a landfill in the village of Shashakuara, in Gali district, 72km away, resulting in significant costs and wear and tear on vehicles.

“The Sukhum landfill contains hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of waste. But most of that volume is air. Only 15% consists of solid and liquid waste, while 85% is air. So these trucks keep driving back and forth, transporting air and burning fuel,” Russian hydraulic engineer Alexander Tsekhovoy explained to specialists in Sukhum in 2019.

According to his calculations, rather than endlessly transporting waste between landfills, each district should establish special compaction stations capable of compressing waste four- to fivefold. This would reduce the number of trips to the central landfill to just four truckloads a day.

However, instead of introducing these technologies, the authorities have continued simply transporting waste from one district to another.

Costly and pointless landfill in Katsikyt

A new waste management complex in the village of Katsikyt, in Gulripshi district, was supposed to provide a breakthrough solution to the waste problem.

The 5.5-hectare site was equipped with a waste disposal pit featuring a multilayer insulating base, treatment facilities and a conveyor belt for sorting waste. Construction proved extremely challenging, both technically and financially, with the project costing more than 150m roubles [$1.81m].

However, by the time the facility was nearly complete, it turned out that nobody wanted it.

Sukhum refused to use the complex, while the authorities in Gulripshi district were also reluctant to take responsibility for it. Security personnel were soon withdrawn from the site, which has since been effectively abandoned and remains unused.

Waste processing complex in the village of Katsikyt

The landfill in the village of Katsikyt was intended to be a financially sustainable facility. During its construction, Timur Agrba, then head of the Capital Construction Department and now mayor of Sukhum, said the facility could become self-financing by sorting, compacting and selling recyclable materials, including plastic, paper and metal.

According to Agrba, if properly managed, the facility could not only cover its operating costs but also generate revenue for further development.

However, in practice, the main obstacle is the tariff for household waste disposal.

“The current tariff policy does not reflect the realities or the costs incurred by our companies. International practice shows that waste collection and transportation should be funded through payments made by the residents who generate that waste,” Beslan Eshba, then head of the Sukhum city administration, explained back in 2014.

He promised that city authorities would seek to introduce relevant amendments to a new housing code. However, 12 years later, the new code has still not been adopted.

The current waste collection fee in Abkhazia is 27 roubles [$0.33] per person per month, a relatively modest amount. Yet most urban residents do not even pay this, as there is no clearly established system for collecting utility payments.

To obtain an objective assessment of the situation, Abkhazia’s Public Chamber held a series of meetings with Russian specialists, local environmental experts and representatives of district administrations.

As a result, an expert report was drawn up, providing a comprehensive assessment of the entire household waste management system. The report has already been submitted to the president, parliament, executive authorities and the Institute of Ecology.

For now, however, it represents little more than another faint glimmer of hope on the horizon. No tangible progress has been made towards resolving the problem.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Проблема мусора в Абхази

World.title: Special forces officers convicted of assaulting protesters jailed for five years each
World.content:
Special forces officers jailed for assaults

A court has sentenced special forces officers convicted of physically assaulting journalist Guram Rogava and protester Zviad Maisashvili during demonstrations in November and December 2024 to five years in prison each.

The special forces officer convicted of assaulting Guram Rogava, a journalist with Formula TV, was also banned from professional duties for three years. Lasha Gamkrelidze, the new prosecutor in the case, informed the journalist of the verdict by telephone.

According to Formula, Rogava had expected to testify as a victim during the trial. However, the prosecutor explained that his testimony was unnecessary because the court and the defence had accepted the charges as undisputed. Rogava himself believes that the person who directly assaulted him remains at large.

Two other special forces officers arrested in connection with the assault on Zviad Maisashvili were each sentenced to five years in prison. Lawyer Dimitri Mchedlishvili confirmed the information to Tabula.

On 30 November 2024, at around 06:30, special forces officers kicked Zviad Maisashvili in the face during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, causing him to lose consciousness. Footage of the assault circulated on social media.

On 7 May 2026, Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office announced that it had identified and detained five people in connection with assaults on Rogava, Maisashvili and opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, four of those detained were current or former special forces officers, while the fifth was a serving officer with the Interior Ministry’s Security Police Department. Two of the suspects were already serving prison sentences at the time of their arrest.

Prosecutors said that on 29 November 2024, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Special Tasks Department assaulted Guram Rogava while the journalist was carrying out his professional duties.

The detainees were charged under Article 333(3) of the Criminal Code with abuse of official powers involving violence. The officer detained in connection with the assault on Rogava also faced an additional charge of unlawfully obstructing a journalist’s professional activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office’s initial statement, the charges carried prison sentences of five to eight years.

Maisashvili said both special forces officers detained over the assault on him had admitted their guilt and apologised to him.

Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili

Background

The assaults on Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili were among several high-profile incidents of police violence during pro-European protests in Tbilisi in November and December 2024.

The protests began on 28 November 2024, after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the government would take the issue of opening EU accession talks off the agenda until the end of 2028.

In the following days, law enforcement officers used water cannon, tear gas and other crowd-control measures against protesters on Rustaveli Avenue and near the parliament building. Numerous incidents of physical violence against demonstrators, journalists and human rights defenders were documented.

Both protesters and members of the media sustained injuries during the demonstrations. The assault on journalist Guram Rogava attracted particular attention. On 29 November 2024, a special forces officer attacked Rogava while he was reporting live from Rustaveli Avenue, leaving him seriously injured.

Media representatives and human rights organisations called for investigations into these incidents. On 30 November 2024, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said the police’s use of water cannon, pepper spray and batons, including against peaceful demonstrators and journalists, had been disproportionate.

According to Georgia’s Public Defender’s 2024 report, the ombudsman and his representatives visited 624 people who had been detained or injured during protests between 15 April 2024 and 1 March 2025. Of those, 360 reported ill-treatment.

The report also noted that no police officers had been held accountable for violence committed by law enforcement personnel during that period.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office statement of 7 May 2026, more than 550 witnesses were questioned and thousands of investigative and procedural actions were carried out as part of the investigations into the cases involving Zviad Maisashvili, Levan Khabeishvili and Guram Rogava.

The Prosecutor’s Office said the investigations would continue to identify other possible perpetrators and bring them to justice.

World.title: Strategic partnership signed in Dublin: What does London want from Baku, and what does Baku gain?
World.content:
Azerbaijan-UK partnership

Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed a joint declaration on strategic partnership on 12 November at the European Political Community summit in Dublin. The British government published the text of the document on the same day.

The declaration covers three main areas: defence and security; trade, investment and economic growth; and education and innovation. The two countries agreed to hold annual strategic partnership meetings to assess progress in these areas.

The document builds on a 1994 friendship and cooperation agreement and a 1998 declaration on friendly relations and partnership between the two countries.

Six months earlier, the UK signed a similar declaration with Armenia. A comparison of the two documents raises the question:

What does the UK prioritise in its strategic partnership with Azerbaijan, and which issues does it leave unaddressed?

What does the document entail?

Defence and security. The two countries intend to expand defence cooperation in training, capacity building and interoperability, as well as explore opportunities for cooperation in the defence industry. The document also provides for cooperation between law enforcement agencies, collaboration on border control and judicial and legal cooperation aimed at strengthening the rule of law and institutional resilience.

Trade and energy. The UK will support the development of the Middle Corridor, a transport route linking China to Europe via Central Asia, the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus. The two countries also intend to cooperate on renewable energy, green finance and low-carbon technologies. The main platform for cooperation in these areas will be the bilateral Intergovernmental Commission on Trade and Economic Cooperation.

Education and innovation. The document provides for cooperation in higher and vocational education, digital skills development, civil servant training, artificial intelligence and digital governance.

In the declaration, the UK welcomes steps towards normalising relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia and expresses support for efforts to achieve a “lasting peace”.

However, the implementation of all commitments is subject to the availability of resources and the domestic laws of each country.

How does the declaration signed with Armenia differ?

The declaration, signed on 5 May by then UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, also identifies three main areas of cooperation. The first two are similar to those outlined in the declaration with Azerbaijan: defence and security, and economic growth and development.

However, the third area differs. In the declaration with Armenia, it is titled “Governance and Democratic Resilience”, while the document with Azerbaijan focuses on “Education and Innovation”.

In the declaration with Armenia, the two countries commit to protecting democracy, human rights and the rule of law. The document also provides for creating an enabling environment for independent media and civil society.

By contrast, the declaration with Azerbaijan makes no mention of democracy, human rights or the media. The term “civil society” appears only once, in the context of strengthening people-to-people ties between the two countries.

Furthermore, the declaration with Armenia provides for the development of a joint “Results Framework” to monitor the implementation of the agreements. No equivalent mechanism is included in the declaration with Azerbaijan, with the two countries agreeing only to hold annual meetings.

The declaration with Armenia also explicitly states that it does not constitute an international treaty and that either party may terminate cooperation by giving six months’ written notice.

What is the wider context behind these differences?

The declaration was signed amid continuing international criticism over the arrests of journalists in Azerbaijan. According to Amnesty International, 12 people detained in connection with the Meydan TV case are being persecuted for their journalistic work. The human rights organisation has also reported serious health problems among some of those detained.

In February this year, the detained journalists appealed to diplomatic missions in Baku, including the British embassy, asking them to monitor the court proceedings.

In response to calls for the journalists’ release, Azerbaijani officials have said that the legal proceedings are ongoing and that a fair decision will be reached.

The British government’s statement announcing the signing of the declaration makes no mention of the issue.

What do the two countries expect from each other?

The UK has long been one of the largest foreign investors in Azerbaijan, largely through BP, which operates the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli and Shah Deniz oil and gas fields. According to Azerbaijani officials, British investment in the country’s economy has exceeded $39bn.

However, the two countries’ figures for bilateral trade differ. According to Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee, trade turnover between the two countries reached $3.72bn in the first nine months of this year.

According to official UK government statistics, trade in goods and services totalled £1.2bn in the 12 months to June, making Azerbaijan the UK’s 89th-largest trading partner.

British exports to Azerbaijan amounted to £724m, down 2.9% from the previous year. Imports from Azerbaijan, meanwhile, increased more than 2.6-fold to £453m.

Preparations for the declaration began well before its signing. In August 2025, UK Minister for Europe Stephen Doughty announced during a visit to Baku that the two countries had agreed to upgrade bilateral relations to a strategic partnership.

In December, UK Minister of State for Defence Lord Coaker visited Baku. In October this year, UK Trade Minister Lord Anas Sarwar announced at a meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission in Baku that the text of the declaration had been agreed.

The two countries also signed a roadmap for developing transport and digital infrastructure. Sarwar outlined the areas the partnership would cover:

“Of course, it will include energy and port infrastructure, investment, education and other areas.”

The UK government’s statement on Doughty’s 2025 visit also mentioned the peace process, the Russia-Ukraine war, the Middle Corridor, energy, defence, cybersecurity and education.

Human rights and media freedom were not mentioned on that occasion either.

What meetings took place in Dublin?

The signing of the declaration was one of several events on Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s busy schedule in Dublin. On the same day, he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and the prime ministers of Bulgaria, Greece and the Czech Republic. His meeting with the Bulgarian prime minister focused on a proposed electricity corridor between the two countries.

According to the Azerbaijani side, Aliyev and Pashinyan discussed the peace agenda under the joint declaration signed in Washington in August 2025, border delimitation, transport links and the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).

The two leaders also welcomed the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and in the opposite direction.

The UK signed strategic partnership declarations with Armenia and Azerbaijan six months apart. Both documents provide for support for the peace process in the South Caucasus. However, the third area of cooperation differs: the declaration with Armenia focuses on democracy, while the one with Azerbaijan emphasises education.

Azerbaijani human rights activists and opposition figures have yet to comment on the signing of the declaration.

World.title: Zelensky goes public on drone deals as Baku keeps quiet: how Azerbaijan balances its cooperation with Ukraine
World.content:
Azerbaijan and Ukraine: drone cooperation

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Dublin on November 12, on the sidelines of the ninth European Political Community summit.

Aliyev attended the summit at the invitation of Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin and European Council President António Costa.

Zelensky said on Telegram that his first engagement at the summit was a meeting with Aliyev.

He also noted that relations between the two countries were developing. According to the Ukrainian president, the main topic of their talks was cooperation under Ukraine’s drone production programme.

“First and foremost, the Drone Deal. Contracts have already been signed, and we are working to expand orders,” Zelensky said.

However, Azerbaijan’s official statement on the meeting made no mention of drones, defence or military cooperation. It focused on economic and trade ties, exchanges of delegations and Zelensky’s gratitude for electrical equipment supplied by Azerbaijan.

Azerbaijani media also reported on the drone contracts, citing the Ukrainian president’s statement.

In April, we reported on Zelensky’s visit to Gabala.

What role does Azerbaijan play in Ukraine’s drone production programme, and why does Baku prefer not to discuss it publicly?

What is the Drone Deal?

The Drone Deal is a framework of intergovernmental agreements developed by Ukraine to share military technologies with partner countries, primarily drones and counter-drone systems. In addition to arms supplies, the agreements provide for joint production, technology transfers and the sharing of Ukraine’s battlefield experience.

For Ukraine, the initiative offers a way to secure long-term foreign orders and funding for its defence industry during the war. Partner countries, in turn, gain access to technologies tested in combat.

Since spring this year, Kyiv has been signing similar agreements with countries in the Gulf, particularly those facing attacks by Iranian drones.

In July, the Ukrainian government cut the approval period for transferring technologies and weapons under the programme to 30 days. Under the rules, the purchasing country must provide state guarantees.

Technologies are transferred for use only, while intellectual property rights remain with Ukraine. If products made using Ukrainian technologies are sold to a third country, 20% of their value is transferred to Ukraine’s state budget.

Organisations under sanctions or controlled by an “aggressor state” are not eligible to take part. According to a list published by Ukrainian media, countries that have signed Drone Deal agreements include Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, the Netherlands, Denmark, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and Azerbaijan.

At the Dublin meeting, Zelensky did not specify the types or number of drones covered by the contracts, their value or which companies would be responsible for fulfilling them.

From Gabala to Dublin

Military cooperation between Baku and Kyiv first came to light in April. On April 25, the presidents of the two countries signed six documents in Gabala. Their full contents were not made public.

Zelensky described security as the main area of cooperation and called the signing of documents on joint defence production “a very serious step”. He also said Ukrainian drone specialists were already working in Azerbaijan.

During the same visit, Zelensky proposed holding talks with Russia in Azerbaijan, with the participation of the United States. In response, Russian Federation Council member Vladimir Dzhabarov described Azerbaijan as a “normal place” for such a meeting.

Aliyev, in turn, confirmed that military cooperation had been discussed and said there were “excellent opportunities” for joint production.

He also noted that trade between the two countries had exceeded $500 million.

A month earlier, in March, Azerbaijan’s Nakhchivan exclave came under a drone attack. Aliyev blamed Iran, but Tehran rejected the accusation. The incident heightened interest in Ukraine’s experience in countering drones.

In August, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov became the first head of the country’s foreign ministry to visit Kyiv since 2022. During the visit, he met Zelensky, presidential chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov and National Security and Defence Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko.

According to Interfax-Ukraine, Bayramov and Zelensky also discussed defence cooperation and implementation of the Drone Deal. Bayramov raised the issue of gas supplies to Ukraine:

“If necessary, we will be ready to supply gas to friendly Ukraine as well.”

Why does Baku prefer to remain silent?

Baku’s caution is likely shaped by its relations with Russia.



The crash of an Azerbaijani AZAL passenger plane in December 2024, after it was hit by Russian air defences, killing 38 people, caused tensions between the two countries.

In April this year, the leaders acknowledged in a joint statement that the aircraft had been unintentionally shot down by a Russian air defence system. In July, following a meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in Moscow, Bayramov said the “difficult period” in bilateral relations was over.

Thus, Baku has only recently begun to repair relations with Moscow.

Political analyst Elkhan Shahinoglu said during Bayramov’s visit to Kyiv that the Kremlin would be closely watching the trip.

Baku’s cautious approach was also evident in another incident. On June 5, two cargo ships bound for the Russian port of Rostov were hit by drones in the Sea of Azov. According to updated figures from Azerbaijan’s foreign ministry, four Azerbaijani citizens aboard the vessels were killed.
