World.title: Victorian election hot seats: Kylie worked in coal, gas and mining. Now she’s running for the Greens
World.content:
By her own admission, Greens candidate Kylie Rocha has worked in all the “bad things”.

Raised in Wheelers Hill, the self-described “maths and science nerd” studied mechanical engineering and economics at university before landing a job at one of Australia’s dirtiest power stations in Yallourn.

Kylie Rocha is the Greens candidate in the seat of Hawthorn. Jason South

She has also had a stint in mining, worked on gas projects and spent time at other coal-fired power stations.

Now she’s trying her hand at politics. In this month’s state election, Rocha is standing in Hawthorn for the Greens, the party that is campaigning to phase out the fossil fuel industries where she cut her teeth.

Rocha doesn’t have any regrets, insisting her experience in the fossil fuel industry only strengthened her conviction that Australia needs an energy transition that supports workers and their communities.

After graduating from Monash University in 2008, Rocha entered the workforce as Kevin Rudd’s government was promising to tackle climate change.

“At that point I was naïve about politics. I thought the politicians would sort it out,” Rocha told The Age at a cafe in Glenferrie Road.

“It [Yallourn] was a great place to work for me as an engineer out of university … all of the things you learn at university at the one place.

“I loved it there.”

Rocha’s political awakening came almost a decade later, when she was headhunted by Tesla and moved to California. Working on automated systems controlling Tesla robots that build Elon Musk’s electric vehicles, she said she finally felt like she could use “her skills for good”.

Living in San Jose, she found herself at the centre of the clean energy transition. At the same time, Donald Trump’s polarising presidency was in its infancy.

“They were so much further ahead, there were charging stations and infrastructure and solar panels everywhere,” she said.

“You start asking questions like, why are we so far behind in Australia? What’s holding us back?

“When I came back I wanted to answer that question fully.”

Struck by wealth inequality and privatised healthcare in California, as well as Australia’s comparatively sluggish uptake of renewables, Rocha began searching for her “political home” back in Melbourne.

By 2019, she was inspired to join the Greens, attracted to the party by its refusal to accept corporate donations.

At the last state election, the Greens received 11 per cent of the primary vote. The latest Resolve Political Monitor surveys suggest that this time around, the Greens are on track to land a primary vote between 13 and 15 per cent.

Rocha is campaigning on rent controls, free public transport and returning energy infrastructure to public ownership. And she supports the planned closure of the Yallourn coal-fired power station in 2028.

“For me, the climate transition isn’t just a technical thing, it’s a people thing,” she said.

“We need to look at what places like the Latrobe Valley have provided the people of Victoria for so many years and is so crucial to where this state is. That strong, stable supply has been crucial to what we have been able to achieve.

“I think we have to recognise that and support people as we transition.”

While she doesn’t support opening up any more coal and gas mines, she doesn’t describe herself as “anti-mining” and insists critical minerals – such as lithium, nickel, cobalt – are essential to the clean energy transition.

“We need critical minerals,” she said. “I think we need to be honest about that.”

She said the Greens wanted mining companies to take more responsibility for the environmental impacts and minimise damage done to the land.

“I think with mining … we need to work with traditional owners, local groups to see if it is the correct place ... but let’s talk about a local industry that can support Australian growth, productivity and supply the critical minerals we need to transition.”

“I know what it’s like to live near large industrial sites like mines and power stations, and proper environmental controls are required and should be as stringent as possible to protect residents and our precious natural environment.”

World.title: They sang about honouring their club’s name then ordered strippers ‘asap’
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Swans players linked arms in the bowels of the MCG after a professional but workmanlike victory over a struggling Essendon. “Cheer, cheer the red and the white,” they sang. “Honour the name by day and by night.” With the club bound for finals, and on trajectory to seriously contest for the 2026 premiership cup, coach Dean Cox was on a high. However, within hours the private choices of key members of the group – including star players Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner – would drag their 152-year-old club’s name through the mud for the next three months and heap pressure on the chairmanship of millionaire investment banker Andrew Pridham and his rookie chief executive Matthew Pavlich. Cox, a former West Coast premiership ruckman, decided to give his men the night off to celebrate, telling them to enjoy themselves, within reason. The players and staff were not set to fly home until the next morning, thanks to Sydney Airport’s 11pm curfew and the players seven-day break before their last home and away match.



The short story is that beers at the MCG, turned into dinner, which became a pre-dawn August 17 party with three strippers at the Pullman East Melbourne and the now infamous group of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice, former teammate Taylor Adams and a mystery seventh man. Swans players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Artwork: Marija Ercegovac A distressed woman, a call to police and suddenly the group were part of one of the biggest scandals in AFL history. Four of the Swans players were informed on Friday they had been cleared over the incident, while Riley Bice, Taylor Adams and the unknown man, had already been told by police they were only being treated as witnesses. The club is now amid what can only be described as a period of profound reckoning. The famous “Bloods Culture”, shaped in the early 2000s under then-coach Paul Roos around high standards, a team-first mentality and accountability has come under intense public and internal scrutiny. Sydney’s pain was compounded last week by the foolish actions of star forward Tom Papley, who was busted driving with a suspended licence and subsequently failed a roadside drug test for methamphetamine. Results from a second test are still pending.



Season 2026 will be one for the Swans and their fans to remember for all the wrong reasons. Wanted: ‘Topless waitresses. Asap arrival’ The Swans’ playing group, coaching and other support staff had splintered across Melbourne for their sanctioned night off. Cox and other members of his coaching staff went out for drinks at a planned get-together at Harlow Bar on Church Street in Richmond, leaving just after midnight. Swans teammates attended various venues before returning at different times to their Wellington Parade hotel, where players and staff occupied a secure floor. The accommodation had been paid for by the Andrew Dillon-led AFL. Loading It’s history now how the clutch of five players, Adams and the mystery man ultimately found themselves partying in one room.



Deciding to up the ante on proceedings, one of the group engaged two exotic dancers as “topless waitresses” for an “asap arrival” via an agency called Party Girls Melbourne. After some mix-up in logistics, three women journeyed to the Pullman for the job, with the trio ending up in a player’s room between 4am and 5am. The players let the women believe they were carpenters and attempted to negotiate a discount. Drugs were also believed to be in the suite as the party unfolded. However, the Swans teammates have denied being responsible for the drugs being there or taking them. Amid the high jinks, one of dancers began to experience what has been described as a medical episode, including shortness of breath and anxiety over the close confines of the hotel room, which by that time was filled with 10 people. She left the room to find some space and fresh air, while her fellow dancers continued on with the players booking. The woman was outside the room for an extended period, during which time none of the group checked on her welfare.



She found her way downstairs to the hotel lobby, still scantily clad – effectively in her work gear – seeking assistance. Meantime, the other two women finished their time with the players, got dressed, gathered their things and went downstairs, where they found their companion. The pair sought to regain access to the secure floor where the Swans were staying to help the woman retrieve her belongings, left in the party suite. Without a hotel swipe card or any authority from a hotel guest, the women were denied re-entry. By this time, about 7.30am, the lobby of the Pullman was coming to life with guests heading to the dining room for breakfast and Swans officials and players packing up and preparing to board a bus bound for their flight home. The increasingly distressed woman began confronting Swans staff in their red club shirts. Photographs later emerged of Cox talking to one of the women in the lobby, while the Swans head of media, Tom Chadwick, and the club’s head of football, Leon Cameron, were among club officials on the scene seeking to triage the fast-moving events.

World.title: Seven takeaways from one of Australian sport’s most memorable press conferences
World.content:
Analysis SportCricketAustralian cricket Seven takeaways from one of Australian sport’s most memorable press conferences Tom Decent November 13, 2026 — 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Pat Cummins walked into Cricket NSW headquarters in Sydney on Friday morning with Australian cricket in turmoil and his integrity under question. He walked out 69 minutes later having delivered one of the most memorable and absorbing press conferences in Australian sporting history. Loading The Australian Test captain came armed with a pre-prepared statement (via notes typed out on sheets of paper), a few sharp bouncers up his sleeve directed at Usman Khawaja and a determination to defend himself against allegations, aired by Khawaja, stemming from the 2018 “Sandpapergate” scandal. There were moments of humour, flashes of frustration and some honest admissions about the culture of the Australian cricket team eight years ago.



But while Cummins may have won-over plenty of people with his performance, the fallout from Khawaja’s explosive new book, Sabr, is far from over. Here are seven takeaways from an absorbing morning. Pat Cummins answered questions from reporters for more than an hour. Sam Mooy 1. That was one of Australian sport’s great press conferences Before getting into the detail of what Cummins said, it is worth reflecting on the event itself. This reporter has covered plenty of press conferences over the years, including the tearful appearances of Steve Smith and David Warner after that fateful 2018 tour of South Africa, but this was probably the most extraordinary of the lot.



Perhaps it was the anticipation. Cummins had announced the press conference on his own social media accounts on Thursday, rather than leaving it to Cricket Australia media managers to arrange through its usual channels. Close to one hundred onlookers – journalists, photographers, camera operators and cricket officials – were crammed into the indoor nets area waiting for the Test captain to appear at 9.30am. Breakfast television cameras were parked outside at first light. However, Cummins was quietly and deliberately ushered into Cricket NSW headquarters through a back entrance, away from the cameras. He had been instructed to wear a Cricket Australia polo shirt and had spent considerable time discussing what he would say with his wife, Becky, and his manager, Neil Maxwell. Afterwards, Cummins went out and bowled some balls alongside Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood before popping into the public cafe to get a sandwich and pose for photographs with fans. Pat Cummins (centre) training with fellow bowlers Mitchell Starc (right) and Josh Hazlewood (left). Sam Mooy 2. It was a tremendous display of leadership



There was no hiding. No interventions from a media manager, and no attempts to shut down difficult questions. It was as compelling as it gets. From a journalist’s perspective, it yielded almost too much material. This was arguably Cummins’ finest hour, and it was leadership personified – no matter whether you believe his version of events. This is why he is the captain of the Australian men’s cricket team. Cummins leaves after his press conference. Sam Mooy Cummins is renowned as one of Australia’s greatest fast bowlers, but on Friday he was belting fours and sixes to all corners. It was reminiscent of his memorable 2022 press conference following Justin Langer’s departure as Australian coach amid player unrest, when Cummins declared: “To all past players, I want to say this: just as you have always stuck up for your mates, I’m sticking up for mine.”



Cummins had been pressured to respond to Khawaja’s claims since they were first reported in this masthead on Saturday. But he took his time, worked through the allegations methodically and established precisely what he wanted to address. It was worth the wait. Related Article Analysis

Ball tampering Generation of Australian cricketers at war as sandpaper scars ripped open Cummins was clear and concise in his recollections. When he couldn’t remember something, he said so. He had even gone to the trouble of contacting former teammates to check their versions of events. But when it came to having no knowledge of a plot to use sandpaper on the ball, he was unequivocal. An accomplished public speaker, Cummins was confident and charismatic under the pressure. But his masterstroke was allowing journalists to ask questions for as long as necessary. Now, nobody can accuse Cummins of failing to front up. The longer the press conference went, the more the mood in the room – which had been combative at first – appeared to shift in his favour.



Cummins spoke for so long that at one point an SBS journalist retrieved their microphone from the collection and left. It was jokingly suggested a “drinks break” should be taken at the hour mark, but Cummins kept his pads on and kept facing up to the next delivery. 3. Cummins is very annoyed For all his composure, Cummins was clearly angry that his integrity had been questioned and annoyed that he had been dragged back into a scandal he believed was behind him. One of the more revealing moments came when Cummins disclosed that his wife, Becky, had also been angry with Khawaja. The controversy had even reached the couple’s doorstep, with The Australian publishing footage of the couple in a heated conversation outside their Sydney home after arriving there by chance. The newspaper did not purchase the images. Cummins still found room for humour. At one point, he looked towards the Sheffield Shield match between NSW and South Australia playing out on the adjacent field before him (journalists had their back turned to it) and jokingly called “not out” in response to an lbw appeal. He also made light of suggestions he and Becky had been arguing, joking that he’d put the wrong bin out.



But his words about Khawaja were far more cutting. Cummins referred to Khawaja as a friend, before conceding the future of their relationship was now uncertain. 4. Australia’s cricket team was out of control in 2018 We already knew there was something amiss within the culture of Australian cricket in the years leading up to Sandpapergate, such was the win-at-all-costs mentality and the aggression. But Cummins offered one of his most candid assessments yet of the environment in which the scandal unfolded. Admittedly, injuries meant Cummins missed considerable international cricket in the years before 2018. Nonetheless, his description of the dressing room offered an insight into the circumstances that may have encouraged Bancroft, Smith and Warner to cross the line in South Africa.



“I think we had a win-at-all-costs mentality, had an ugly underbelly, and there were too many silos within the team,” Cummins said. “They were traits that I hope that everyone’s seen and I tried very hard to eradicate for the last six years as captain.” 5. Sandpaper, superglue and the tricks of the trade One of the more fascinating elements was Cummins’ discussion of the methods cricketers have used to alter the condition of a ball. Lost in much of the coverage this week has been the distinction between legally maintaining a cricket ball and illegally changing its condition. Just because someone is “working” on a ball doesn’t mean it is ball-tampering. Cummins explained that Australia had even used sandpaper during training sessions to rough up balls and practise facing reverse swing. But his description of the tricks discussed in cricket dressing rooms was particularly revealing. He opened up on other “dark arts” he’d heard about when it came to illegal alterations to cricket equipment.



“I’d heard zippers,” Cummins began. “I’d heard superglue on wicketkeepers’ gloves. I’d heard layers and layers of nail polish. I bite my fingers, so I’d be terrible. Obviously, Murray Mints is one, too. I’d heard … from a long time ago that sandpaper was actually taped in between fingers. Related Article ODI Debutant fires Aussies to huge win over England after Warner slams Cummins comments “These are all discussions that I’m sure every suburban change-room has. It’s one thing to talk about it but then it’s another thing to go ahead and do it.” 6. The actual cricket has become a sideshow Imagine telling someone two years ago that NSW prodigy Sam Konstas would blast 173 in a Sheffield Shield match less than a month before Australia’s first Test of the summer – and it would barely rate a mention in the national sports news agenda.



Yet that is where Australian cricket finds itself today. Some outstanding performances are being overshadowed. Konstas’ innings is one example. Young fast bowler Mahli Beardman’s six-wicket haul on ODI debut against England is another. Khawaja had said his words no longer affected the Australian team, now that he had retired. Perhaps not in the dressing room, but their impact on the wider game has been enormous, and Cummins alluded to that frustration on Friday. Funnily enough, Cummins copped one cricket-related question. It was about Beardman. So spooked were Cricket NSW about the Khawaja situation that they pulled Konstas from media duties on Thursday after he reached triple figures. However, he came out on Friday after play and laughed about the nearby circus. “It was a bit hectic,” Konstas said. “Obviously there was a lot of media today with Pat. We’ve got a massive job to do [in this game].”



Could he get a car park on Friday morning? “I thought they were all coming for me,” Konstas said with a laugh. “They were all here for Pat.” 7. Two versions of events – and a scandal that refuses to die Cummins insists Khawaja was wrong, while Khawaja and Warner are disputing the version of events put forward by Cummins and the bowlers.



As the Test captain pointed out, international cricket dressing rooms are big places. Conversations can take place between different groups of players, often without everyone knowing what has been said. Tellingly, Cummins said Khawaja had not asked him for his version of events in 2018. Several key figures from the 2018 tour are yet to publicly address Khawaja’s latest allegations in detail. Steve Smith, Cameron Bancroft, Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood and Tim Paine are among them. So, too, is Brad Haddin, an assistant coach at the time and now coach of NSW. As long as Warner continues his public campaign to challenge the established account of Sandpapergate, as he did during Fox Cricket’s coverage, the controversy will linger.



Khawaja, meanwhile, has endured a bruising week. His awkward appearance on the ABC’s 7.30 program, where veteran journalist Sarah Ferguson pressed him on further details in his book account, was uncomfortable viewing. He is scheduled to appear on popular cricket podcast The Grade Cricketer later this week, although whether that interview proceeds after Cummins’ extraordinary intervention remains to be seen. Friday may have been a significant victory for Cummins in the court of public opinion. At the time of writing, a poll on this masthead, with more than 18,000 respondents, showed that 46 per cent of readers believe “everyone” knew about the use of sandpaper in South Africa. Meanwhile, 44 per cent don’t think every Australian player knew, while 10 per cent were yet to make up their mind. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: Albanese and Bowen caught in hot mic gaffe
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAnthony Albanese Albanese and Bowen caught in hot mic gaffe Natassia Chrysanthos November 13, 2026 — 10:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen have been recorded making small talk about phone radiation and “dicks” in a candid moment caught on camera at this year’s global climate conference. The exchange was picked up with a hot mic on Friday as the pair chatted while waiting to start a roundtable discussion about business investment at this year’s COP31 climate conference in the Turkish town of Antalya. The prime minister and Chris Bowen in the moment when the conversation was captured by a TV microphone. Seven News The prime minister’s office brushed off the incident after Channel Seven was first to broadcast the clip on Friday evening (AEDT), having picked up on the conversation during the production process. According to the footage, which started recording before Albanese and Bowen made their official remarks, the prime minister put his phone in his jacket pocket and asked Bowen whether he was right-handed. He then told Bowen that he should store his phone away from his heart because “it can interfere with your rhythm”.



Bowen jokingly asked whether it was because it was “a little bit radioactive?” to which Albanese said yes, “it makes absolute sense”. Related Article Updated

Climate policy ‘She’s entitled to her views’: Albanese defends himself after Thunberg’s ‘snail’ jibe The climate change minister said he was more conscious of putting his phone in his pants pocket. The prime minister asked: “Because of your dick?” Bowen agreed. “Arguably more important than the heart,” he said. A spokesman for the prime minister said: “They were having a joke in between meetings.”



Friday’s event was held to discuss business opportunities with Australian agencies and both current and potential investors in the country’s renewable energy transition. “Trade and investment components of these annual climate meetings are absolutely critical,” Albanese said in his opening remarks. “It’s how we turn the commitments that we want to make into actions and outcomes, and capitalise on the opportunity which is before us.” Anthony Albanese (left) with Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen (right) greeting Andrew “Twiggy” Forrest at COP31. AAP Australia’s involvement in this year’s COP has attracted heightened scrutiny because the federal government is co-hosting the event with Turkey. Bowen has taken on a new role as president of negotiations – a position he secured after Australia lost its bid to host the event in Adelaide. Albanese arrived in Antalya on Wednesday for the conference leaders summit. He left Turkey shortly after Friday’s business roundtable, and will head straight to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit. Bowen will stay in Antalya and lead negotiations between 190 countries until the end of next week.



Hot mic moments involving the Australian prime minister have drawn attention since former prime minister Tony Abbott and then home affairs minister Peter Dutton were caught in 2015 joking about “water lapping” at Pacific islands threatened by rising sea levels. While the pair didn’t know they were being recorded, the comments were damaging to Australia’s reputation in the Pacific. World.title: Microsoft’s attempts to resolve major outage ‘not working as expected’
World.content:
Updated TechnologyNetwork outage Microsoft’s attempts to resolve major outage ‘not working as expected’ Elias Visontay, Jack Gramenz and Emily Kaine Updated November 13, 2026 — 9:01pm ,first published November 13, 2026 — 7:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tech giant Microsoft scrambled for solutions and prioritised restoring government services in Australia during its global outage on Friday, conceding its attempt at a broad fix for users around the world hadn’t worked as expected. The widespread server-related outage – which Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has insisted is not the result of a cyberattack – hit Microsoft Outlook, Teams and Copilot early on Friday morning in Australia, causing users to have issues accessing or sending emails, while other errors affected the tech giant’s apps. Microsoft users were hit with a widespread outage overnight. AP Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook and other Microsoft services, beginning just before 5am (AEDT). At one point, reports to the platform reached almost 20,000 per minute, stemming from outages across five Microsoft services in 74 countries. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they still couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes.



Related Article Exclusive

Telecommunications ‘Didn’t foot the bill’: Telstra outage cost the economy half a billion dollars, modelling finds By afternoon, Microsoft email access was still patchy, while other Microsoft platforms such as Teams appeared functional – prompting memes on social media from frustrated workers lamenting the split-level of functionality. A swath of corporate Australia and government departments and agencies were among those affected. They included the Australian Federal Police and the ABC. While they were still able to function, email issues also plagued national supermarket chain Coles as well as government agencies in NSW, Victoria, Queensland, Tasmania and Western Australia. Australia Post suspended its phone payment system and suppliers were unable to send delivery notices to supermarket distribution centres. The cost to Australia would be billions of dollars, said Ashwin Pal, of accounting firm RSM Australia.



Related Article Exclusive

Telecommunications ‘Didn’t foot the bill’: Telstra outage cost the economy half a billion dollars, modelling finds “That’s not just direct, but indirect costs as well,” he said. “But a protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities.” The Australian Computer Society renewed its call for a national review of sovereign risk in Australian IT. “Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service are entitled to be worried,” chief executive Prins Ralston said. “Where were the direct updates to Australian customers and media - and who will answer for the lost productivity and the cost to the economy?”



Such a widespread and prolonged global outage highlighted the dangers of reliance on a very small number of tech firms, University of Melbourne professor Toby Murray said. “And to find ourselves many hours later still in the same position that we were when we got up this morning, it really is surprising,” he said. The US tech company was reported to be focusing on restoring services to government first given its large user base. In a statement on Friday afternoon, Microsoft said: “We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed that change is not taking as expected. “We’re identifying alternate workstreams that can be applied to increase capacity in the face of sustained traffic management imbalances.”



Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services. Loading To fix the issue, Microsoft said it had so far attempted to restart its servers, and validate a change. But initial efforts to fully restore services proved unsuccessful. “We’re continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service, as our actions taken thus far have not provided the anticipated relief,” the company said. “Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss.” An update issued on Friday morning said the company had “observed limited recovery in some regions”, but its efforts for a quick fix proved unsuccessful. Microsoft later said it was implementing “protective traffic management measures” region by region to test if it helped with restoring its services.



“[We are] fully isolating a portion of our service infrastructure, restarting the affected components, and gradually reintroducing traffic to confirm our services remain stable before applying this approach more broadly. “We’re also analysing traffic patterns across our entire service infrastructure and evaluating whether isolating traffic within each region may allow affected regions to recover independently.” At a press conference in Sydney on Friday morning, Burke said he had been briefed by Australia’s cybersecurity coordinator and the head of Microsoft Australia and that they did not believe they were dealing with a cyber threat. “The perspective of Microsoft at this stage … they believe in some ways [similar] to what we saw with CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke said. View post on X



Microsoft said it was “also investigating why affected servers are experiencing elevated processor usage while handling requests”. In updates posted earlier, it said it was aware of users “experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes”. Microsoft later explained that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load”, which it said was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors”. The company determined several servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” due to a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks. “We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X. The company earlier said it had “successfully restored” problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

World.title: Debutant fires Aussies to huge win over England after Warner slams Cummins comments
World.content:
Mahli Beardman has stamped his reputation as the next big thing in Australian cricket by producing a sizzling ODI debut in his team’s crushing seven-wicket victory over England in Perth.

On a day when Australian cricket was still knee-deep dealing with the ghosts of sandpapergate 2018, Beardman snared 6-24 as the tourists were skittled for 131 in 33.4 overs at Optus Stadium.

In reply, Mitch Marsh smashed 50 off 30 balls as Australia reached the victory target with a whopping 159 balls to spare. Matt Renshaw (26 not out) and Josh Inglis (23 not out) finished the job.

The result gave Australia a 1-0 lead in the three-match series before game two in Adelaide on Sunday.

While Marsh provided the fireworks with four sixes and four fours before holing out in the deep, it was Beardman’s performance that will live long in the memories of the 27,313 fans at the stadium on Friday.

Mahli Beardman walks off after a six-wicket haul. Getty Images

The 21-year-old was near unplayable at times, with England collapsing from 2-38 to 7-60 on the back of Beardman’s devastating burst.

It marked just the second time an Australian has produced a five-wicket haul in their ODI debut, following Tony Dodemaide’s 5-21 against Sri Lanka at the WACA Ground in 1988.

Only some late handy runs from Gus Atkinson (29 not out off 32 balls) and Will Jacks (25) ensured England made it to triple figures, with the visitors 8-65 at one stage.

“It all happened very quickly,” Beardman told Fox Cricket when asked about his big haul.

“It’s just a great privilege and honour to be able to represent my country. And to go out and take a few wickets as well is the cherry on top.

“Harry Brook was a nice wicket to get off the mark. Anytime you get your first one it’s a weight off your shoulders, so that was awesome.”

Loading

Beardman, who was handed his ODI cap by Test legend Mike Hussey, received a big cheer from his home town crowd when he was introduced into the attack for the 10th over – a maiden.

The right-arm paceman snared his maiden ODI wicket in his next over when he found the edge of England captain Brook (1).

That was just a taste of things to come.

Hitting speeds of up to 145.4km/h, Beardman was able to entice 200-game milestone man Joe Root (17 off 36 balls) to drive on the up to gift wicketkeeper Josh Inglis his third catch of the innings.

And Beardman was on a hat trick when he collected the scalp of Jordan Cox at the start of his fourth over – again with another pearler of a delivery that caught the edge.

Beardman’s hat-trick ball was anticlimactic – a wide down the leg side.

But while his first three wickets came courtesy of fuller deliveries that featured swing and seam, Beardman’s next wicket proved his pace and bounce is also a major weapon.

Sam Curran’s attempted pull off Beardman’s bouncer gave Adam Zampa a catch on the boundary rope.

Spencer Johnson (3-42) ensured the party continued by jumping high in the air to pull off a one-handed catch off his own bowling to send Jamie Overton packing.

Atkinson and Jofra Archer (11) struck a series of boundaries in a 29-run last-wicket stand before Beardman completed the demolition job by having Archer caught at gully.

Beardman’s figures were the fourth best by a debutant in ODI world cricket, with Charlie Cassell’s effort of 7-21 for Scotland against Oman in 2024 still the best.

Mitch Marsh of Australia and Harry Brook of England at the coin toss in Perth. Getty Images

And Beardman’s five-wicket haul was complete when Liam Dawson was caught at gully, giving the West Australian figures of 5-13 off 4.4 overs at that point.

To mark the special moment, the Australian team formed a circle around Beardman as the rising star raised the ball in the air.

World.title: Liberals would be irresponsible to preference Labor
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Liberals would be irresponsible to preference Labor November 13, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Several correspondents are disappointed, even disgusted, by the Liberal Party’s decision to preference One Nation ahead of Labor (Letters, 12/11). However, given the extent of the maladministration of recent Labor governments, it would be irresponsible for the Liberal Party to give Labor any electoral assistance at all. Their first priority must be to get rid of Labor. It can then deal with One Nation in the event it has any significant power in the new parliament. It could be a case of the Liberals supporting the devil they don’t really know ahead of the devil they definitely do.

Rod Wise, Surrey Hills Torn by the choices

I have always been a left-leaning Labor party supporter, but I recognise and realise that the government has run out of steam and we need a change. However, I cannot vote for the Liberal Party now that they have put One Nation above Labor. I will not support One Nation in any way. What to do?

Malcolm I Fraser, Oakleigh South Independents, where are you?

Victoria urgently needs improved governance, yet the upcoming election is like “Morton’s Fork” where both likely paths of travel are unsatisfactory – the conservatives and an apparently chaotic One Nation alliance with a few “back to the future” policies or the continuation of Labor and its apparent fiscal mismanagement. Where are the strong independents?

Ian Gibb, St Kilda



Forced into ‘donkey vote’ and not happy

Jess Wilson, you had our vote. It’s way past time for the government to go. Sadly, you then announced the Liberal Party is giving its preferences to One Nation. I now can’t vote for you. I can’t vote for Labor or the Greens either and I don’t know if we have an independent running in our electorate or if they are even worth voting for. Your best move politically would have been to say to voters, “Vote 1 for the Coalition. We aren’t going to tell you how to number the rest of the ballot. That is up to you.” Had you said that your candidate would have had my vote in a heartbeat. It’s not too late to change your mind. If you can’t then perhaps for the first time in my decades-long voting life I will be forced into a “donkey vote”.

Irene Wyld, Cape Schanck Treaty decision factor in selection

I refuse to give my votes to either the Liberal Party or to One Nation. The Liberals partly because they want to take away the Treaty with our First Nations people. Nor to One Nation because of Pauline Hanson herself as well as all her policies. Who am I left with? Ben Carroll, who needs to be given a go partly because he is neither Dan Andrews or Jacinta Allan, or to the minor parties, or an informal vote.

Lesley Taskis, Kingsbury THE FORUM Home a human right

I don’t see the boulevard of broken dreams and routes of regret Shane Wright speaks of (“Record plunge in loans as tax overhaul hits the property market”, 12/11). If there is a problem it is that debt has become the engine of housing, and that housing has become an avenue for financial speculation over what it truly is, a human right. The ill-effect of credit-fuelled growth, the basis of the Australian economy, starts to show when the government refuses to fund public goods directly and looks to budgetary savings elsewhere.

Anders Ross, Heidelberg Aged care grief

It was good of your correspondent (Letters, 13/11) to at least say something in response to an article on aged care (″⁣Aged care homes guarded amid fears of attacks″⁣, 11/11). The inconvenient truth is not old age itself, but the deregulated, privatised system this country so shamefully operates.

I still call Australia home, but its aged care ″⁣homes″⁣ grieve me deeply.

Ruth Farr, Blackburn South



Boot the bosses

It was sad to read Dee Madigan’s article on why Qantas would want to get rid of its own staff in Australia (Comment, 12/11). I think big business is using AI all wrong. If a company was looking to save money, AI would be best suited replacing CEOs and senior executives, instead of replacing staff who are the everyday talent and service providers of a company.

AI could easily analyse commercial prospects, long-term strategic directions, global markets and financial risks to successfully steer a company. All without the need for multimillion dollar salaries and exorbitant annual bonuses.

Customers could train the AI CEO through all the surveys, feedback and reviews we are asked to provide about a company’s performance to make decisions in the best interests of staff, customers and shareholders. Company staff could provide logical solutions to improve productivity and performance directly to the AI entity, providing a more rapid response to everyday customer concerns. CEOs and executives would not be missed by customers, but the staff at ″⁣front and back of house″⁣ would be sorely missed.

The industrial revolution replaced workers on the shop floor. The AI revolution should replace executives on the top floor.

Elizabeth Balogh, Heathmont Ban fossil fuel exports

It was embarrassing to listen to the Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at COP31. Following António Guterres’s focused and consummate speech reiterating the major source of global heating, the PM’s response consisted of prevarication,and a total lack of self-awareness and awareness of the problem at hand.

Especially when at the same time he trumpets Australia as the ″⁣saviour″⁣ of the Pacific.

We should stop all fossil fuel exports. This would be extremely costly, some will say. Think of it in these terms: we have just commemorated the armistice following the Great War, which was hugely more costly than ceasing the use of poisonous forms of energy. And it will not cost any lives. The very opposite, in fact.

Ruben Buttigieg, Mount Martha PM’s climate failure

The Prime Minister Anthony Albanese travelled to COP31 as a person of little credibility when it comes to effective climate change mitigation and it is unsurprising that he failed to mention fossil fuels.

It was he, in response to pressure from WA Premier, Roger Cook, who immediately after the last federal election installed Murray Watt into the environment portfolio with a brief to approve the extension of Woodside’s NW Shelf gas project to 2070. This was effectively an Albanese-Watt green light for Woodside to pour copious amounts of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere for more than another four decades.

A decision to accept or reject Woodside’s enormous and controversial Browse gas project is due by the end of this year.

Once again, this project would run until 2070 and produce an estimated 6.4-6.8 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year. Albanese tried to convey the impression at COP31 that he is serious about climate change mitigation but if a few weeks after his return he announces his government’s approval of the Browse project, his credibility will be zero.

Ian Bayly, Upwey Questions for voters

Gay Alcorn’s profile captures Opposition Leader Jess Wilson as a young but capable, relatable, decent leader (“How a daggy Millennial came to hold a party’s hope in her hands”, 13/11).

Many of her Coalition’s policies, particularly those on climate, energy and reconciliation, however, raise questions for voters. As Alcorn reports, in 2022 Wilson said we must “accelerate the transition” to clean energy and modernise transmission; now her Coalition would scrap the VNI West transmission line and “throw open the doors” to gas.

Where is the evidence these choices will lower bills or improve reliability? And how do they align with climate targets?

Her party has made a similar reversal on Treaty, from bipartisan support to promising repeal.

Decency is welcome in politics; consistency and evidence-based, fair policy matter too.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Election ripple effects

It’s disappointing that so many seem to view the election as no more than an opportunity to punish the government for past albeit significant mistakes, though the extent to which there is corruption rather than mismanagement and overreach is yet to be determined.

However, government is a job to be done into the future not a trophy to be awarded or denied based on past performance. The campaigns are effectively the equivalent of a job application.

As a state we have to live for years with the consequences of our decision at the end of this month. The two credible options for government offer many similar commitments as they always do but one also takes away things like a pathway to sustainable, low emissions energy, significant revenue necessary to fund services without increasing debt and sadly one of the most significant steps toward constructive reconciliation, Treaty with First Nations peoples of Victoria

As the old saying goes “marry in haste, repent at leisure”.

Richard Jamonts, Williamstown



One Nation, one party

Warren Pickering, One Nation leader in Victoria, blames “a bit of a hole” in vetting candidates (“One Nation leader Pickering blames ‘bit of a hole’ in vetting for pro-Nazi candidate”, 13/11). It seems that Pickering has not realised that people with extremist views are going to be attracted to One Nation as the party openly espouses similar views that candidates have been criticised for.

It’s even more astonishing that Jess Wilson seems to have a view that she can distinguish between One Nation candidates with “offensive views” to whom she won’t direct preferences, and the rest of the candidates, as if the One Nation party itself is completely acceptable in its leaders’ policy statements and are therefore deserving of Liberal Party preferences.

Heather D’Cruz, Geelong West Leave green spaces

I read with dismay articles (High-rise horizons) referring to high-rise activity centres and the need to jam more people into areas near transportation, which I support in principle. However, what is lost in this argument is that I see and hear absolutely no mention of providing balance with green open space where one can walk a dog or simply sit on a park bench and get a little sunshine. Charge ahead by all means – and create overcrowded ghettos of the future.

Vince Vozzo, Elwood Not all unions bad

The behaviour of the CFMEU should not distract us from the fact that the majority of trade unions act honestly and fairly to uphold the rights of working men and women. Without them children would probably still be working down coal mines.

Rob Willis, Newlands Arm Photo: Matt Golding



AND ANOTHER THING Politics

Time for a royal commission into redacting (″⁣Redacted notes spur fierce rebuke at royal commission″⁣, 13/11).

Peter Randles, Pascoe Vale South The Liberals’ decision to preference One Nation is in cricket parlance a reverse sweep. It seemed like a good idea at the time but can go horribly wrong.

Dan Drummond, Leongatha Perhaps it’s time to ban parties’ how-to-vote cards. Not only should voters make their own decisions but think of the paper that will be saved.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick Labor is really on the nose when voters are preferring parties that refuse to support the generation of electricity by the cheapest means.

John Groom, Bentleigh



“Bring back David Jones” sounds like another great back-to-the-future policy for One Nation.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton Furthermore

If we keep outsourcing to other countries, not only will brands suffer, but what will become of the Australian workforce? Are we to be just a country of cafes and couriers? Big business is selling out the Australian identity.

Catherine Leos, Brunswick West If the homeless can be accommodated during lockdown, why not now?

Katriona Fahey, Alphington Give AI the task of working out the best way to reach world peace, end poverty, solve climate change and find how Essendon can win an AFL flag (″⁣AI could be utopian, or destroy humanity″⁣, 13/11).

John Hughes, Mentone Could we please have some debate before it is too late on this mad rush to build data centres. I am no expert but the many downsides on the environment and abuse of power and water resources plus loss of jobs just doesn’t make sense.

Tony Jackson, Fitzroy I chuckled when Pat Cummins said while describing his appraisal of the Australian team when he first came on board: “I thought that the way we acted on the field was quite abrasive.” Pure gold.

Nick Brennan, Rowville

World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Five of the best Sydney homes with facades we love Shona Hendley November 13, 2026 — 7:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

Whether it’s a modern or period home, a standout facade can include features such as textural contrast, visual anchors, dramatic rooflines and architectural lighting, leaving a striking impression and setting the home apart. These Sydney homes not only have great street appeal, but their interiors back it up, making them standouts both inside and out. Here are five of the best Sydney homes with facades we love. 72 Oxford Street, Woollahra NSW



This terrace has a width of 8.2 metres with a striking facade featuring a lacework balcony. Inside, the home is just as impressive, with interiors by Phoebe Nicol featuring oak, natural stone and a textural palette. The open-plan living, dining and kitchen areas feature high ceilings and engineered flooring, opening onto an undercover al fresco with an integrated barbecue and landscaped gardens. With two bedrooms, 2½ bathrooms and basement car parking with an internal lift, there is plenty to enjoy. 92 Balfour Road, Bellevue Hill NSW



Featuring curves, an arched window and contrasting materials, the facade of this home makes a statement. This design continues inside with high ceilings, sculptural curves, skylights and an interplay of oak, glass and Arabescato Corchia marble. Highlights include the central atrium, all-weather al fresco, lower-level media room and considered design features such as brushed gold tapware, rainwater showers, underfloor heating in the bathrooms, an integrated Bose sound system and an AV security intercom with keypad and swipe entry. 207 Bridge Road, Glebe NSW



With a jasmine-framed filigree facade, this Victorian terrace features an iron lacework balcony and plenty of period charm. This continues inside with the timber floors, high ceilings and archways. Modern updates include skylights, glazing and a bistro-style kitchen with a servery bar that connects to a wraparound deck. The home is set over three levels, with an additional attic.



The dual-access block offers double garaging, while the terrace itself is one of a historic row of four. 29 Pacific Parade, Manly NSW This c.1922 bungalow’s tuck-pointed brick facade, high gables and covered north-facing porch with tessellated-tile floors have been beautifully preserved. There are modern updates including the fence and undercover carport. One family has owned the home for 62 years, and it was renovated in 2015.



The home features abundant natural light, a stone-crafted kitchen, a formal lounge with a gas log fireplace, and a rear entertainer’s terrace with a landscaped garden. Only a short walk from Manly Beach, in leafy “Manly Flat”, the location is a definite drawcard. 9 O’Connor Street, Haberfield NSW This Federation home located in the inner west has an elegant facade framed by jacaranda and immaculate landscape gardens, with level lawns and established greenery.



Sitting on a prized 720-square metre corner position on a tree-lined street, the home features ornate ceilings, leadlight windows, original fireplaces and a wraparound verandah. Alongside its period craftsmanship, the four-bedroom, three-bathroom home has had a contemporary extension with a covered al fresco terrace overlooking its gardens and pool. Other features include generous attic storage, ducted reverse-cycle air-conditioning and an elegant lounge with floor to ceiling bookshelves.

World.title: Victorian election hot seats: Kylie worked in coal, gas and mining. Now she’s running for the Greens
World.content:
By her own admission, Greens candidate Kylie Rocha has worked in all the “bad things”.

Raised in Wheelers Hill, the self-described “maths and science nerd” studied mechanical engineering and economics at university before landing a job at one of Australia’s dirtiest power stations in Yallourn.

Kylie Rocha is the Greens candidate in the seat of Hawthorn. Jason South

She has also had a stint in mining, worked on gas projects and spent time at other coal-fired power stations.

Now she’s trying her hand at politics. In this month’s state election, Rocha is standing in Hawthorn for the Greens, the party that is campaigning to phase out the fossil fuel industries where she cut her teeth.

Rocha doesn’t have any regrets, insisting her experience in the fossil fuel industry only strengthened her conviction that Australia needs an energy transition that supports workers and their communities.

After graduating from Monash University in 2008, Rocha entered the workforce as Kevin Rudd’s government was promising to tackle climate change.

“At that point I was naïve about politics. I thought the politicians would sort it out,” Rocha told The Age at a cafe in Glenferrie Road.

“It [Yallourn] was a great place to work for me as an engineer out of university … all of the things you learn at university at the one place.

“I loved it there.”

Rocha’s political awakening came almost a decade later, when she was headhunted by Tesla and moved to California. Working on automated systems controlling Tesla robots that build Elon Musk’s electric vehicles, she said she finally felt like she could use “her skills for good”.

Living in San Jose, she found herself at the centre of the clean energy transition. At the same time, Donald Trump’s polarising presidency was in its infancy.

“They were so much further ahead, there were charging stations and infrastructure and solar panels everywhere,” she said.

“You start asking questions like, why are we so far behind in Australia? What’s holding us back?

“When I came back I wanted to answer that question fully.”

Struck by wealth inequality and privatised healthcare in California, as well as Australia’s comparatively sluggish uptake of renewables, Rocha began searching for her “political home” back in Melbourne.

By 2019, she was inspired to join the Greens, attracted to the party by its refusal to accept corporate donations.

At the last state election, the Greens received 11 per cent of the primary vote. The latest Resolve Political Monitor surveys suggest that this time around, the Greens are on track to land a primary vote between 13 and 15 per cent.

Rocha is campaigning on rent controls, free public transport and returning energy infrastructure to public ownership. And she supports the planned closure of the Yallourn coal-fired power station in 2028.

“For me, the climate transition isn’t just a technical thing, it’s a people thing,” she said.

“We need to look at what places like the Latrobe Valley have provided the people of Victoria for so many years and is so crucial to where this state is. That strong, stable supply has been crucial to what we have been able to achieve.

“I think we have to recognise that and support people as we transition.”

While she doesn’t support opening up any more coal and gas mines, she doesn’t describe herself as “anti-mining” and insists critical minerals – such as lithium, nickel, cobalt – are essential to the clean energy transition.

“We need critical minerals,” she said. “I think we need to be honest about that.”

She said the Greens wanted mining companies to take more responsibility for the environmental impacts and minimise damage done to the land.

“I think with mining … we need to work with traditional owners, local groups to see if it is the correct place ... but let’s talk about a local industry that can support Australian growth, productivity and supply the critical minerals we need to transition.”

“I know what it’s like to live near large industrial sites like mines and power stations, and proper environmental controls are required and should be as stringent as possible to protect residents and our precious natural environment.”

World.title: They sang about honouring their club’s name then ordered strippers ‘asap’
World.content:

Swans players linked arms in the bowels of the MCG after a professional but workmanlike victory over a struggling Essendon. “Cheer, cheer the red and the white,” they sang. “Honour the name by day and by night.” With the club bound for finals, and on trajectory to seriously contest for the 2026 premiership cup, coach Dean Cox was on a high. However, within hours the private choices of key members of the group – including star players Isaac Heeney and Chad Warner – would drag their 152-year-old club’s name through the mud for the next three months and heap pressure on the chairmanship of millionaire investment banker Andrew Pridham and his rookie chief executive Matthew Pavlich. Cox, a former West Coast premiership ruckman, decided to give his men the night off to celebrate, telling them to enjoy themselves, within reason. The players and staff were not set to fly home until the next morning, thanks to Sydney Airport’s 11pm curfew and the players seven-day break before their last home and away match.



The short story is that beers at the MCG, turned into dinner, which became a pre-dawn August 17 party with three strippers at the Pullman East Melbourne and the now infamous group of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice, former teammate Taylor Adams and a mystery seventh man. Swans players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Artwork: Marija Ercegovac A distressed woman, a call to police and suddenly the group were part of one of the biggest scandals in AFL history. Four of the Swans players were informed on Friday they had been cleared over the incident, while Riley Bice, Taylor Adams and the unknown man, had already been told by police they were only being treated as witnesses. The club is now amid what can only be described as a period of profound reckoning. The famous “Bloods Culture”, shaped in the early 2000s under then-coach Paul Roos around high standards, a team-first mentality and accountability has come under intense public and internal scrutiny. Sydney’s pain was compounded last week by the foolish actions of star forward Tom Papley, who was busted driving with a suspended licence and subsequently failed a roadside drug test for methamphetamine. Results from a second test are still pending.



Season 2026 will be one for the Swans and their fans to remember for all the wrong reasons. Wanted: ‘Topless waitresses. Asap arrival’ The Swans’ playing group, coaching and other support staff had splintered across Melbourne for their sanctioned night off. Cox and other members of his coaching staff went out for drinks at a planned get-together at Harlow Bar on Church Street in Richmond, leaving just after midnight. Swans teammates attended various venues before returning at different times to their Wellington Parade hotel, where players and staff occupied a secure floor. The accommodation had been paid for by the Andrew Dillon-led AFL. Loading It’s history now how the clutch of five players, Adams and the mystery man ultimately found themselves partying in one room.



Deciding to up the ante on proceedings, one of the group engaged two exotic dancers as “topless waitresses” for an “asap arrival” via an agency called Party Girls Melbourne. After some mix-up in logistics, three women journeyed to the Pullman for the job, with the trio ending up in a player’s room between 4am and 5am. The players let the women believe they were carpenters and attempted to negotiate a discount. Drugs were also believed to be in the suite as the party unfolded. However, the Swans teammates have denied being responsible for the drugs being there or taking them. Amid the high jinks, one of dancers began to experience what has been described as a medical episode, including shortness of breath and anxiety over the close confines of the hotel room, which by that time was filled with 10 people. She left the room to find some space and fresh air, while her fellow dancers continued on with the players booking. The woman was outside the room for an extended period, during which time none of the group checked on her welfare.



She found her way downstairs to the hotel lobby, still scantily clad – effectively in her work gear – seeking assistance. Meantime, the other two women finished their time with the players, got dressed, gathered their things and went downstairs, where they found their companion. The pair sought to regain access to the secure floor where the Swans were staying to help the woman retrieve her belongings, left in the party suite. Without a hotel swipe card or any authority from a hotel guest, the women were denied re-entry. By this time, about 7.30am, the lobby of the Pullman was coming to life with guests heading to the dining room for breakfast and Swans officials and players packing up and preparing to board a bus bound for their flight home. The increasingly distressed woman began confronting Swans staff in their red club shirts. Photographs later emerged of Cox talking to one of the women in the lobby, while the Swans head of media, Tom Chadwick, and the club’s head of football, Leon Cameron, were among club officials on the scene seeking to triage the fast-moving events.

World.title: Young smashes ton, Henry takes six as Black Caps crush India in fourth ODI
World.content:
Will Young hit a century and Matt Henry took six wickets as New Zealand sealed a dominant 244-run victory by bowling India out for 89 in the fourth one-day international in Mount Maunganui on Friday to remain afloat in the series.

The hosts trail India 2-1 and can no longer win the five-match series, but they can avoid defeat if they win the final match at the same venue on Sunday. The third match was abandoned due to rain.

Chasing 334 for victory, India got off to a disastrous start as paceman Henry ripped through their top order in a lethal first over, taking the wickets of Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer to leave the visitors reeling on 0-3.

Ruturaj Gaikwad also departed shortly afterwards, but a steely 44-run partnership between Ishan Kishan (27) and Axar Patel (21), and a quickfire 21 from Naman Dhir helped ensure they did not lose by a record margin in terms of runs.

Henry took three more wickets as India were bundled out for their sixth-lowest ODI total.

Earlier on Friday, New Zealand opener Young made up for his single-digit scores of 9 and 6 in the opening two matches of the series with an assured knock of 125 from 108 balls - his best-ever ODI score and his fifth century in the format.

The 33-year-old profited from some lax fielding by India, with Rohit and Kishan dropping him on consecutive deliveries in the second over of New Zealand's innings.

Young was supported by Tim Seifert (58) and Finn Allen (41), while India's Patel, Gurnoor Brar and Auqib Nabi each picked up two wickets.

India were without captain Shubman Gill and batter KL Rahul, who will also miss the final ODI as they prepare for the upcoming two-test series against New Zealand beginning on Wednesday. - Reuters
