World.title: 'Always helpful': Close friend pays tribute to BurgerFuel crash victim
World.content:
A longtime friend of one of the trio killed in the BurgerFuel crash in South Auckland has remembered him as a kind and charming man who was always willing to help others.

The trio killed in Sunday night's crash in Takanini have been named as Sukhdeep Singh, 33; his wife, Sukhvir Kaur, 29; and their brother-in-law, Gurpreet Singh, 38.

Mandeep Singh said Sukhdeep Singh had lived in New Zealand for seven years and operated an NZ Post courier business, while his wife had arrived just six months earlier.

Gurpreet Singh, who had lived in New Zealand for three years, worked as an NZ Post courier driver, he said.

His wife and young son had remained in India, according to the Supreme Sikh Society.

Three people died after a car crashed into a BurgerFuel outlet in South Auckland on Sunday. RNZ / Nick Monro

The newlywed couple and their brother-in-law died after the car they were travelling in lost control at a roundabout on Great South Road, left the road and crashed through a BurgerFuel restaurant in Takanini.

RNZ understands the vehicle is believed to have been travelling at more than 150 km/h.

Mandeep Singh said he had known Sukhdeep Singh since 2015 and the two had been close friends for more than a decade.

He described his friend as "not too extroverted, but always helpful".

"I lost my job back in 2023," he said. "He asked me, 'If you want to come with me, we can deliver parcels together. I'll help you'."

Mandeep Singh said Sukhdeep had married in February this year, and the two had travelled to India on the same flight.

"When he came back, he was really happy because he got married," he said.

He recalled the newlyweds visiting his home, where they spent time watching movies and enjoying each other's company.

Mandeep Singh described Sukhdeep's wife as "lovely and nice".

When Mandeep Singh saw news of the crash on Sunday night, he thought the car involved looked familiar.

"We [had] bought the car together," he said.

"Then I thought,'Why does the car look so similar to the one we bought?'"

Mandeep Singh said he later confirmed with a local temple that Sukhdeep and his family had attended Diwali celebrations on Sunday night.

He then learned that his friend was among those killed in the crash.

"I was terrified because my hands were shaking," he said.

Mandeep Singh urged the public not to speculate whether his friend had been speeding or was responsible for the crash, while the investigation was ongoing.

"He did not use to drink alcohol," he said.

"Police are doing their best to investigate what happened, and we have to wait until the results comes."

Emergency services were called to the crash just after 10:15pm on Sunday night.

All three occupants were pronounced dead at the scene, police said.

No one inside the building was injured.

World.title: Former RNZ board member says she knew ministerial approval was needed for overdraft
World.content:
A former RNZ board member says she was aware ministerial approval was required for a $5 million overdraft and is questioning why it wasn't sought.

On Monday, the public broadcaster revealed a shock $11.8 million budget blow-out, after a litany of financial blunders that included the overdraft that allegedly breached the Crown Entities Act.

By law, RNZ requires ministerial sign-off to set up such an overdraft.

In an email sent to media, former board member Jane Wrightson said she knew the approval was required under law, however, she did not know why it wasn't sought, adding, "it should have been".

She said she had stipulated to RNZ's board that ministerial sign-off would be required, adding the full board was aware of this.

Wrightson said that as her term was ending, she wasn't involved in any subsequent correspondence.

On Thursday board chair Brent Impey told Checkpoint a director did ask RNZ chief financial officer Hilary Parker in writing whether ministerial approval was required.

The query came after the board signed off on the overdraft, but before it was formally entered into.

"The assurance given at that time was that RNZ did not require approval from either the minister of finance or the shareholding ministers to establish the facility," Impey said.

"This matter will form part of what the independent review needs to consider and it is important that this process is undertaken with consideration of all relevant information in due course.

World.title: Students face 'derived grades' process after online glitch disrupts NCEA English exam
World.content:
The NZ Qualifications Authority (NZQA) will use a 'derived grades at scale' process to assess students affected during this week's online exam glitch.

About 40,000 students were sitting NCEA level 2 English on Thursday - many of them online - when the malfunction disrupted the exam, forcing many to revert to using paper exams.

While many students were given additional time to complete their exams, others will now be judged on internal work or assessments throughout the year.

NZQA has posted on social media to reassure these students about the process.

"You don't need to apply like with an individual derived grade," it said.

"Your school will submit this on your behalf.

"Your school will handle the evidence. This will come from the recent practice/mock exams or other stand-specific work.

"Your best result will count. If you complete the exam, we will compare your exam result with your school-assessed grade and award whichever is higher."

NZQA said Friday's Microsoft email outage had slowed communication, but assured students the process was underway with their schools.

Derived grades at scale are designed for "extraordinary circumstances" like earthquakes, flooding, blocked roads, medical emergencies or power cuts.

NZQA deputy chief executive Jann Marshall said, despite extensive testing, the online assessment platform used didn't perform as it should have.

"We are sorry for the disruption and the stress that students, as well as teachers and parents, experienced," she said.

"It's unacceptable.

"Students have worked hard for the examination and recently expected the platform to perform well."

She said their vendor had assured them that glitches that "slowed" and "locked people out" of the system would not happen again.

Secondary Principals' Association president Louise Ānaru told Morning Report that students had shown amazing resilience in the face of this setback.

"The good news is, of course, there are systems in place to make sure they're not disadvantaged," she said.

World.title: Tokomaru Bay landowner fumes at $14.5m council bridge pitch
World.content:
Audio player for " Pitch to replace bridge destroyed by Cyclone Gabrielle knocked back by NZTA " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/regions/2581618%2Ftokomaru-bay-landowner-fumes-at-14-point-5m-council-bridge-pitch

Pitch to replace bridge destroyed by Cyclone Gabrielle knocked back by NZTA Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

A Tokomaru Bay landowner with limited access to its property since Cyclone Gabrielle took out a bridge is fuming at an unrealistic Gisborne District Council pitch for a $14.5 million replacement.

The New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) has refused to fund the project. The Pourau Incorporation has now put up a $3.8m alternative and is demanding to see the council engineering reports.

First erected in the 1930s, woody debris swept away the Pauariki Bridge in February 2023.

For three years kai mahi at Māori landowner - Pourau Incorporation - and local orchardists - the Mackenzie family - have had to ford the Hikuwai River or use a flying fox to bring in supplies. Pourau chair Philip Hope said at times getting to the property was perilous.

"Access for the Mackenzie whānau became very difficult, very dangerous because you're at the whim of the weather. Some years you haven't been able to cross the Hikuwai River more than 60 days of the year."

Hope was still in the dark about the Gisborne District Council's replacement proposal.

"We've never been consulted about the business case so much as the finalised design nor the price and to date we are still struggling to really understand how they came up with a figure of $14.5m."

Philip Hope on the western abutment of the failed Pauariki Bridge. Supplied

Hope said the incorporation, which operated over two farm stations affected by the lack of a bridge, had since commissioned its own design, which came in at $3.8m - although he admitted that didn't include groundworks.

Rob Mackenzie had run a small orchard and honey operation in the area with his wife Anne for about 30 years. He said losing the bridge was a nuisance.

"It's more of a restriction than a danger because we are very careful about when we cross. You know there are times when it would be absolutely suicidal, like, there's times when that river is 10 or 15 metres deep.

"It's just very limiting. It means for instance that Anne, my wife, can't just jump in the car and go down to the Four Square or go to a tangi or whatever. We have to arrange things and go together."

It had also meant extended family of the couple - who were in their 70s - had had to leave.

"We did have three school aged kids here for a bit, but I mean there were times when we just couldn't get them to school.

"And when we could get them to school you couldn't sort of let them just jump off the bus at the end of the road and walk home, which is what my kids used to do. It's sort of a mile - or bike home - because they've got to go through a river.

"So, that means there's got to be someone there night and morning to get them across."

Mackenzie would like to sit down with the council - who he said had once promised a replacement bridge - and work something out.

Philip Hope and his son Ormond at Pauariki Bridge. Supplied

Federated Farmers board member Mark Hooper said the issue of rural bridges not being replaced was something it was watching.

"The major concern for farmers about council performance was around access, so that includes the roads, maintenance and of course where there is a critical bridge that becomes a vital access route.

"It can have really significant economic implications and where access is potentially lost or limited then viability becomes a significant issue for some farms."

In a statement, NZTA said it funded the replacement of East Coast bridges damaged during Cyclone Gabrielle at up to 100 percent.

"In December 2024 [we] approved funding for the investigation, design and professional services regarding the possible co-funding arrangement for the Pauariki Bridge.

"We received the final requested documentation from Gisborne District Council in late March 2026 after subsequent consideration the application for funding was declined."

NZTA said it understood the outcomes of its uneconomic roading policy could be disappointing for those affected, but that such decisions were not taken lightly.

World.title: Riders Supporting Kids: The motorcycle club on a mission to raise money for children's toys
World.content:
Audio player for " Motorcycle club on mission to raise money for children's toys " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/community/2580887%2Friders-supporting-kids-the-motorcycle-club-on-a-mission-to-raise-money-for-children-s-toys

Motorcycle club on mission to raise money for children's toys Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

They're born to be wild, but philanthropy is the force behind a lower North Island motorcycle club on a mission to raise money for children's toys, and support tamariki.

The patches displayed by this club's riders proudly carry their club name - RiSK. It stands for Riders Supporting Kids, and its founder says his own upbringing is behind his determined drive.

"Growing up I saw that there was a real hole for some kids in the community and there was just nobody there for them," said president Steve Curtis.

"That was something I wanted to pick up so they don't go down the roads to the gangs and that sort of thing."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408314859112

The 54-year-old spent time in state care, in Epuni Boys' Home, and said he knew what it was like to feel let down.

So, he and his late wife, Jolene, took action - founding the motorcycle club and an annual toy run where people donate gifts for children who need them.

"Jolene and I founded this club five years ago in February and the toy run was an idea that she and I came up with together.

"She passed away in July last year, so since then I've just put my nose down and dedicated carrying this toy run on and RiSK on as far as I can, to see where we can go with it," Curtis said.

Jolene died of heart failure, but even then made a difference as an organ donor.

Part of the club's work is partnering with children's charity Barnardos Aotearoa, which distributes toys from the toy run and has also matched the club with a young man who's become a member.

"We do a bit of mentoring at the moment with a young local boy, Carter. He's been the first. He's come on and helped with sausage sizzles and all that sort of thing.

"His attitude at school has changed and he's doing really well, so we're looking at extending that."

Steve Curtis started the club and the toy run with his late wife, Jolene. Supplied

New friendship 'means a lot'

When RNZ met 9-year-old Carter Harbers at his Palmerston North home, he was keen to show off his club patches, including one marking the $1000 he's raised for the club's efforts.

"My mum really got me in it. Barnardos came with Steve and we talked about me getting in the club," Carter said.

"I love riding motorbikes. At my dad's we've got go karts and motorbikes, and I'm really good at riding."

Carter's been riding bikes since he was three - an interest he shares with club members such as Curtis.

"He's really really kind. He's a good leader for the club... They came to my birthday and took all my friends on their bikes."

Carter's mum Brooke said she appreciated the club's values and what they could teach her son.

"They all make it very clear that if he needs them then they're there as well. That's quite beautiful for us to know," she said.

"Just randomly we'll get a message for them checking in on us. It means a lot to know there's people out there thinking of Carter and us as well."

That includes watching Carter play football and do kapa haka.

Carter Harbers is a junior member of the RiSK club. Jimmy Ellingham

Barnardos' regional operations manager for early learning, Hayley Vinten, said its connection with RiSK began when the club asked for help to find homes for toys leftover after its first toy run.

"When we met with Steve it was quite clear we shared the same mission," she said.

"When we worked with Steve and RiSK, as our relationship built, we realised there's more than the toy run here. Steve has a real focus on tamariki and rangatahi. He really believes that they should be supported."

This year toys will go to families around New Zealand.

Club offers support

Curtis said some of the club's work was just about being there for a young person.

"We also have a 'get out of jail free card' that we give out to kids as well. That's basically if you get into trouble then you can give us a call and we'll work as an advocate to talk with your parents, or with you with the police, just so you've got somebody there who's backing you up.

"That's open to any child who gives us a call."

Those cards get cashed in, too.

"I actually had a 17-year-old involved in a police chase in Palmerston North. I run the holiday park. They actually led the police straight to my gate because they knew I'd look after them."

It's an approach that's attracted more than 20 members to the club.

Brooke and Carter Harbers. Jimmy Ellingham

"It just strikes a chord. It's the right thing to do. I picked up the name Rabbi 45 years ago with my long hair and long beard, but I've grown into that terminology too," said club member Keith "Rabbi" Klein.

"I like the RiSK traditions and their morals and values, and what they try to achieve - just riding for the course and still getting that brotherhood and MC tradition," said Logan Kennedy.

Dan Drummond added that he remembered the guilt he felt as a child when he received a toy that he didn't like, but he didn't want to say anything, so he was determined to make sure others didn't face that.

And the club's focus is now on its toy run on Sunday, 22 November.

That's the final drive for toys, but the club's been collecting them all year, filling a lock up with donations that will soon make their way out as presents to children who otherwise might miss out.

These include push bikes to give away on the day and a couple of dirt bikes that are prizes. Curtis was keen to thank The Warehouse, Toyworld, Bisset Honda in Pahīatua and Honda Horowhenua for their donations.

"We've got nearly $20,000 worth of toys sitting in the storage shed, plus we've got another $12,000 to $13,000 sitting in the bank so we can go shopping, plus we'll probably collect up to another $10,000 worth of toys on the day.

"We're aiming for $50,000 worth of toys."

The toy run leaves from The Warehouse Palmerston North at 10am and travels down the Kāpiti Coast to Mana and back.

World.title: Pacific MPs across political spectrum pledge to work hard for 'our communities'
World.content:
A senior Green MP says Pasifika voters have rewarded those with a track record of dealing with their issues.

Teanau Tuiono, a Cook Islander, will return to Parliament on the list after the Green Party achieved another record high in the polls.

He said the Green's message has resonated with Pasifika voters nationwide.

"They see the work that we've been doing over the last three years, whether that's sheparding through the restoration of Samoan citizenship bill, whether it's supporting Pacific visa waiver access into Aotearoa or New Zealand, and all those other things as well.

"My message to our Pasifika communities is, regardless of who is in government, to continue to hold us all to account to make sure that we all work hard to do the best for our Pasifika communities."

New Zealand Green MP and Cook Islander Teanau Tuiono in Rarotonga, collecting his scooter license Caleb Fotheringham

Labour's MP for Māngere Auckland, Lemauga Lydia Sosene, said she never took the result for granted.

Following the preliminary results from Saturday night, Lemauga received 14,815 votes - almost twelve-thousand more than the next best placed candidate.

She said Labour is still very strong in South Auckland.

"In South Auckland you'll still see quite a vote for Labour between Mangere, Manurewa and Otahuhu and so what that means is - while it's wonderful to have our community support - we've got to work really hard for our people."

Alfred Ngaro, centre, with Michael Tuffery and Tuaine-Nurse Tamarua Robati (L-R). Dominic Godfrey / RNZ Pacific

New Zealand First's Alfred Ngaro said his return to parliament has been six years in the making.

New Zealand First won no electorates, but secured a party vote increase and will have 12 MPs in Parliament, with 9.8 percent of the vote, if preliminary results hold.

Ngaro - a former Pacific Peoples minister in a National government - said everyone gave it their all and he expects the special votes to only increase his party's vote.

"The most important poll is what's we're seeing on the ground, and I believe there will be a growing number of support and we're looking forward to NZ First getting to double digits in the party vote."

He added that he's heard from many Pacific voters on the campaign trail who have switched their votes to NZ First, from Labour.

"Traditional voters for Labour have told me they believe it's time for change and we've seen that at the public meetings - our Pacific community are saying, actions always speak louder than words."

Following the preliminary results from Saturday night, Labour's Barbara Edmonds received 17,294 votes for her Kenepuru electorate which she looks well set to retain.

Edmonds, who is Labour's Finance spokesperson, has emphasised the life journeys of Pacific people who migrated to New Zealand seeking better opportunities for future generations.

"They worked incredibly hard on the shop floors and admin roles to ensure that the next generation could get ahead. If I can become the first Pacific Minister of Finance for Aotearoa, New Zealand, that is a reflection of all our generations of Pacific workers and their hard work to get our generation ahead."

World.title: Senior Wellington City Council leaders facing restructure, two jobs to go
World.content:
Senior leaders at Wellington City Council (WCC) are facing a restructure.

RNZ understands two roles will ultimately be cut. It's understood four roles are being disestablished and two roles are being created, meaning four people will compete for two jobs.

There are currently eight people in the council's executive team.

Chief executive Matt Prosser said the leadership team had a new set of priorities from the mayor and councillors through the Triennium Plan, Annual Plan and 2027-2037 Long Term Plan, and it needed to focus on delivering those.

"On top of this, there still lies the possibility of amalgamation and the introduction of rates-capping measures.

"Against this backdrop, I do not believe that standing still is the right option for WCC."

Matt Prosser. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Prosser said a consultation was underway on the changes, and people would be informed of the outcome at the appropriate time.

"Right now, my focus is on ensuring WCC kaimahi are supported, heard, and their feedback reflected in any final change decisions."

The council cut 47 staff roles in September, in a drive to save over $4 million.

World.title: The Rugby League World Cup final should have solved the Golden Boot battle
World.content:
The Golden Boot hasn't gone to the best player in the world for many years now but if it did you can still make the case it should have ended up in Reece Walsh's hands.

The Australian fullback is not always the best, but when he is at his best there's nobody better and his performances for the Kangaroos has been a scorching reminder that nobody in rugby league is as made for the fast lane.

These days the Golden Boot goes to the best player in Test matches for the year and by giving it to Kalyn Ponga after just 150 minutes in international football, the credibility of the award is on the line in Sunday's World Cup final.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

If New Zealand wins and Ponga plays well, two things that feel inextricably linked, it retroactively becomes a better decision. The outcome will be correct even if the process was flawed.

If Australia wins and Walsh plays well, it highlights the farce of giving out an accolade for international player of the year before the biggest international game of the year.

In a perfect world, or even an imperfect one given it just makes sense, the Golden Boot wouldn't be awarded until after full-time on Sunday, by which time Ponga could be a worthy winner, but as it stands Walsh should have won the trophy.

He has as many man-of-the-match awards in this tournament than Ponga has completed games and after a premiership hangover with Brisbane that could have killed a brown dog, the Australian jersey has banished the demons and brought Walsh roaring back to life.

Reece Walsh has been in brilliant form through the World Cup. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Sometimes he spins out of control, such as when he lost sight of a Samoa bomb in the semifinal, leading to a Stephen Crichton try, but when he stays on the road it's an exhilarating sight.

From his length-of-the-field try in the tournament opener against New Zealand to his five try assists against Cook Islands and a hat-trick against Samoa, Walsh's football over the past month has been reminiscent of the form he showed in leading Brisbane to the 2025 premiership.

It has served as a reminder of his game-bending abilities for anyone who needed it after a title defence to forget, and it's all the more impressive given his initial selection in this squad was far from guaranteed.

The loyalty of coach Kevin Walters played a major part and if James Tedesco had not played in the grand final, there's every chance he would have started against New Zealand in the tournament opener.

But right from the beginning, where Walsh won a brilliant duel with Ponga, he has made the spot his own and shaped Australia's fortunes along the way.

Ponga's win on awards night is just the prelude, with both men shaping as their country's best and most important players in Sunday's World Cup final.

It caps a year that has pulled back and forth between two of the biggest names and best players in the sport, and this last battle will determine who wins the war.

Ponga got the early running when he beat Walsh to the Queensland fullback job only for Walsh to strike back in their showdown three weeks ago that left both of them with stuffed highlight reels and Ponga with a broken arm.

The return from that injury has no doubt played a part in Ponga winning the award and while it's too early to be handing out Golden Boots there is no denying that his 150 minutes on the field for New Zealand has been exemplary.

Tedesco and Ponga walk different paths to grand final On Sunday, opposing fullbacks James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga will lead their teams into the NRL grand final. It's about the only thing their paths have had in common.

Ponga linking up with the Kiwis wasn't possible until the Test eligibility laws were changed earlier this year, and what he's done since fits in with the wider journey he's been on this season.

It mirrors his run to the grand final with Newcastle, where he changed from being someone who could play great into a great player and it was a transformation based on emotion more-so than any technical improvement.

That evolution has continued through the World Cup, where he has proven the black and white jersey calls to him in a way the green and gold never did or could.

When the chance to represent Australia came up in the past he opted to stay home and prepare for the next NRL season.

When finally offered a shot for New Zealand not only did he accept, he rushed back from a serious injury and threw himself in front of Tongan freight trains without fear.

That feeling has unlocked something inside Ponga, which comes out as the most whole-hearted and inspiring play of his career.

He becomes what he was always said to be when he fully committed to a cause greater than himself.

That was not always possible in Newcastle, where Ponga's star power once overpowered the entire club, but it was this year and the same has been true for New Zealand throughout this tournament even as the new guy doubles as the most famous face on the team.

Where once he was cool and impenetrable to the point of being unknowable, now Ponga is throwing himself into contests heart first which is what makes his contrast with Walsh so compelling.

The Queensland teammates will fight it out for the right to be world champion. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Bronco is all bleeding edges, all the time. What Ponga has learned to do is something Walsh does by compulsion. He could not hide his emotions if he tried and he never tries.

They come bursting out of him, as chest-beating when he rounded Ponga over the sideline against New Zealand or as acrobatics when he scored against Samoa.

He is desperate to excel, to strike fast and hard and deadly and most of all to win and sometimes Walsh wants it too much and chases it too hard, but it's one of those things you'd rather have too much of than not enough.

There will be a galaxy of stars fighting it out for the World Cup in Brisbane on Sunday, where the end of so many stories will be told.

Casey McLean, another Golden Boot nominee, is off to the fastest start for world domination since Alexander the Great and Jamayne Isaako is kicking goals from the middle of hurricanes.

Half of Isaah Yeo's chest is ripped apart and he's made 109 tackles while only missing two all tournament and he'll have to pull off a similar job if Australia is to slow New Zealand's astonishing forward pack.

Australia's old power conquers the new world Rugby league's Davids have gotten much bigger in recent times but Australia's win over Samoa in the World Cup semi-final was a reminder of Goliath's power.

Jahrome Hughes and Cameron Munster, whose playmaking genius is so often paired together with Melbourne, will fix both of their minds on the destruction of the other.

But nobody will have a greater impact on the winning and losing of it than Ponga and Walsh, two players who are so different yet have arrived in the same place as they both burn white hot.

If their meeting in Sydney was high noon, the sequel at Lang Park may as well be a one-horse town that ain't big enough for the both of them.

After they meet with guns drawn and the dust finally settles it'll prove a Golden Boot is one thing but being able to call yourself a world champion is quite another.

World.title: Cummins hopes his answers ended the sandpaper war. He is sadly mistaken
World.content:
If nothing else, nobody can ever say that Pat Cummins didn't front up and face the music.

For 70 minutes he stood there, smiling through whatever other emotion was boiling inside of him, disarming with charm and eloquence and just enough humour for the situation at hand. He took the questions until they dried up.

He lifted the lid on cricket's uncomfortable history with ball tampering, detailing specific examples he had seen within Test and Sheffield Shield cricket. He said he believed Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were punished much too harshly by Cricket Australia.

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

He spoke to the 2018 Australian team's "ugly underbelly", addressed allegations of systemic racism within the sport, and spoke about the culture of casual verbal abuse that stretched all the way to suburban club cricket.

Cummins provided a detailed floor plan of the Newlands dressing rooms, and mustered a laugh despite his obvious distaste for the cameras which captured he and his wife conversing on the street.

He pledged to be as open as possible, to dig into the game's nuances — he used that word a lot — to explain as much of what happened in that Cape Town Test match as he could.

And his verdict, repeated multiple times and with precise wording, was clear: Pat Cummins did not know sandpaper was being used to tamper with the ball, and Usman Khawaja's version of events is incorrect.

Pat Cummins rejected allegations made by Usman Khawaja in his book Sabr. (ABC News)

Was he telling the truth? Who really knows. David Warner says he wasn't.

The technicality Cummins and his fellow bowlers have relied upon since they released their first statement of denial in 2021 was that they did not know "sandpaper had been brought out onto the field". Those words have been repeated often this week, presented carefully each time.

By Khawaja's version of events, as printed in his book Sabr, that leaves some wriggle room in which perhaps there was wider knowledge sandpaper was being used on the sidelines in breaks of play when the umpire had left the ball on the boundary.

Sandpaper response plagued by error Usman Khawaja's revelations on Sandpapergate may have come eight years after the fact, but time has not changed Australia's response to the cricket scandal.

But Cummins was questioned about that too, and once again had a firm and unflinching answer.

"That was news to me this week. I had no idea," Cummins said.

"Even chatting to a couple of the guys, that was a revelation to ourselves. That was one of the things that really surprised us because that doesn't happen anymore; the umpires give the ball to you out in the middle."

The good news is that is a fact someone will be able to check.

Somewhere in the SuperSport archives there will surely be footage of the players coming onto the ground after the breaks in play during that series, and surely in that it will be clear to see precisely when the ball is exchanged between umpire and players.

The bad news is that is just about the only fact that can be checked. Everything else is hearsay, one man's word against another, a civil war whose weapons are alternate offerings of "my truth" and "my story".

Cummins suggested the past eight years have weighed on Khawaja, and hinted that may be because, as Khawaja expressed in his book, he specifically knew about the plan to bring sandpaper onto the field and even warned Cameron Bancroft to be careful.

What does Khawaja think about that pretty loaded suggestion? We will surely find out soon enough, either on Instagram or on the next stop on the book tour.

David Warner says Pat Cummins threw Usman Khawaja under the bus. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

We already know what Warner thinks. He said he believed Cummins threw Khawaja under the bus.

This just days after Khawaja had to deny he had thrown Cummins and co under the bus. At this point, there is not a member of the Australian cricket team who does not reside beneath a bus.

Warner said on Fox Cricket he would not be able to move on until the truth came out. The truth, he says, is what is written in Khawaja's book.

Warner was given the opportunity to expound on that truth in his own words, but did not take it, suggesting instead a future book of his own would eventually do that job.

It's all a total mess. Social media reaction to Cummins's conference suggests the Australian public, growing increasingly fatigued by it all, has long since made up its mind on what really went on in Cape Town and is past the point of being swayed by new information.

At some point, most likely when all of these players are comfortable in retirement and these squabbles make up part of the nostalgia tour rather than dominate the discourse, we may wonder what all the fuss was about.

The biggest error of the Cummins Q and A was his belief that his appearance would allow everyone to draw a line under the affair and move on.

That's not happening. We're dealing with hurt feelings here, fractured relationships and bruised egos and nebulous concepts of truth and justice. You better pick your side, if you haven't already, because this is never going away.

World.title: David Warner slams Pat Cummins over Sandpapergate denial
World.content:
Former Australia opener David Warner has stood by Usman Khawaja's revelations about the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal, saying Australia captain Pat Cummins threw Khawaja "under the bus" at a press conference in Sydney this morning.

Cummins had said Khawaja's claims that the entire Australian camp knew about ball tampering in Cape Town were "complete and utter nonsense", repeating that he had no prior knowledge of plans for using sandpaper to illegally alter the ball.

Warner, who was vice captain at the time of the incident and who received a year-long ban for his involvement, said he was "very disappointed" by his former captain on Fox Cricket's coverage of the opening ODI between Australia and England in Perth.

"I feel the captain today threw Ussie under the bus and I'm very, very disappointed by that," Warner said.

Warner said Cummins threw Khawaja "under the bus" at this morning's press conference. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett/Cricket Australia)

Warner also stood by his assertion that the initial investigation had been "botched", and that he, along with fellow suspended players Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft, had no choice but to bear the blame.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence. I feel like it was a botched investigation," Warner said.

"It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us and we had to move on and just accept responsibility, the three of us, and we ultimately did.

"We don't have that opportunity to go there and speak again. [Cricket Australia CEO] Todd Greenberg squashed that the other day. There probably are going to be conversations behind the scenes after this."

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

Warner, a childhood friend of Khawaja's, also said he expected the truth about the saga to come out eventually.

"It's inevitable. Everyone writes a book at the end of their career but for me it's about accepting the truth and I just don't think this will rest," Warner said.

"It's very, very difficult with the acceptance of the consequences that we live day to day in our lives."

Warner described the blame levelled at him, Smith and Bancroft a "life punishment", saying he and wife Candice experienced a miscarriage in the aftermath of the incident.

"All three of us have paid a big price in this and I hadn't spoken about it in eight years, but at the end of the day, we've got to live with these consequences daily," Warner said.

"And we've been served a life punishment. So when other people talk about that they've been affected by it, there's nothing worse than for me, Steve and Cameron, who have to walk over there every single day and we cop abuse.

"Yes, we accepted it, but at the end of the day, my wife and I as well pay the greatest price.

"We lost a baby during that time. And that's why it really hurts me the most until the truth is accepted."

Loading...

Earlier today, Cummins claimed he could not explain why Khawaja's and Warner's recollections of the incident were so different to his.

"That sounds like a pretty good question for those two," Cummins said.

"Again, there's quite a few different accounts here, so they've got two accounts.

"There's 11 players in that room, so that means there's nine other guys who I think it's appropriate you give an equal amount of weight into their story as well."

World.title: Cummins addresses Khawaja claims in passionate hour-long press conference
World.content:
Pat Cummins has labelled Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering allegations "utter nonsense", revealing he has received legal advice that the claims are "probably defamatory".

In an extraordinary 70-minute press conference on Friday, Australia's Test captain ruled out legal action against his former teammate, but was scathing in response to the bombshell revelations in Khawaja's book.

Cummins repeated he and the bowlers' stance that he had no prior knowledge of plans for illegal ball tampering, until Cameron Bancroft was caught with sandpaper during a Cape Town Test match in 2018.

Sandpapergate live updates: Cummins says Khawaja's ball-tampering claims '100 per cent wrong'

He agreed the bans handed down to Bancroft, David Warner and Steve Smith were too harsh after an investigation found they were the only players behind the plot, but rejected Khawaja's assertion that the entire team knew.

"When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins told a packed press conference in Sydney.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.

Pat Cummins has rejected Usman Khawaja's claims that everyone knew about ball tampering in 2018. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"But Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper.

"That's complete and utter nonsense."

Cummins said he did not remember any conversations around the team taking collective responsibility, as Khawaja said in his book he had pushed for.

The 33-year-old said he had exchanged some messages with Khawaja over recent days and planned to speak to him at some point.

Pat Cummins says Usman Khawaja has been "casual" with people's lives. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

But the pair's relationship is now considerably rocky.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations," Cummins said.

"In his book, Uzzy's been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket.

"I support his right to tell a story. I'm really glad that he feels like he can. But we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Cummins said it was up to Cricket Australia whether they would reopen the investigation into the matter, something the organisation has already ruled out.

Usman Khawaja's secret illness Cricket great Usman Khawaja could barely walk and thought he had a terminal illness when he was just starting out his Test career. He was soon diagnosed with a crippling disease, which he has kept secret for 17 years.

But he made it clear he wanted to move on from the scandal, declaring his willingness to take every question on Friday should make it the last time he has to speak about it.

"I did get advised this week that some of the things that were said are probably defamatory," Cummins said.

"But I won't be doing that. Like, you've got to move on. It's been eight years.

"We're moving on. You've got to draw a line at some point."

Now the Australia Test captain, Cummins pointed out that at the time of the scandal in South Africa, he was a 24-year-old just 13 Tests into his career.

Cummins said he had also not yet spoken to Warner since his backing of Khawaja's claims, and could not explain why their position was so different to his.

"That sounds like a pretty good question for those two," he said.

"Again, there's quite a few different accounts here, so they've got two accounts.

"There's 11 players in that room, so that means there's nine other guys who I think it's appropriate you give an equal amount of weight into their story as well."

World.title: 'Insufficient evidence' to charge Sydney Swans players with sexual assault
World.content:
Sydney Swans players embroiled in a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault in a Melbourne hotel will not face criminal charges.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Nick Blakey had been under a police investigation over the alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel in late August.

Several adult entertainers are understood to have joined players at the East Melbourne hotel after being hired in the hours after the Swans' win against Essendon on August 17.

The ABC understands the investigation centred on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

The police investigation centred on events at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne in August. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

Multiple police sources previously told the ABC they understood an arrangement was reached in the hotel room for players to pay extra to take drugs, believed to be cocaine, from the women's breasts and buttocks.

It is unclear how many players, or which players, had allegedly participated.

It is understood a woman was seen leaving the hotel room in a distressed state in the early hours of the morning, with a Triple Zero (000) call made to police soon after.

This morning, Victoria Police confirmed no charges would be laid over the incident.

"Following a thorough investigation and based on legal advice, Victoria Police will not proceed with criminal charges due to insufficient evidence," a police spokesperson said.

Victoria Police said due to an "ongoing civil matter", no further comment would be made.

Sydney 'stands by' decision to suspend players

Sydney Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich told a press conference today it had been a difficult period for everyone involved and affected by the hotel incident.

"We appreciate and understand that everyone has been dealing with it in their own way, and we thank them for their support during that time," he said.

Matthew Pavlich says the outcome of the police investigation marks a moment to move forward. (ABC News)

"We've been in constant contact with the players through the whole process.

"Today's a moment for them to move forward. It's a time for everyone to move forward, and at some point, they'll be back here at training, back with their teammates, and that's going to be an important step."

The players were sidelined by the Sydney Swans in the days after the incident, for staying out late drinking and inviting women back to the team hotel in breach of club standards.

Fellow Swans player Riley Bice, who was also stood down for breaching club standards, was earlier cleared in the police investigation.

Loading...

In an earlier statement today, Sydney Swans management said they stood by the decision to stand down the players "because their conduct fell short of the standards of behaviour expected at the club".

"The club was clear from the outset that this decision was separate from the police investigation, and it stands by that decision.

"The club has commenced a comprehensive examination of its AFL program and is committed to acting on the findings and implementing meaningful change to build an environment that players, staff, members, supporters and corporate partners can be proud of," the statement said.

Pavlich said that work was the club's express focus.

"This is not a day for anyone to really celebrate — we're still looking very hard at the program and understanding where we need to get better for the future and examining that in real thorough detail," he said.

"I can guarantee everyone out there that we'll be doing everything we can to restore the standards and behaviours that this club has held for a long period of time."

Blakey last month moved from the Swans to North Melbourne football club, apologising for "the events that led up to my exit from Sydney".

"I know I have to win back the trust of the broader community, football and otherwise," he said at the time.

Women to proceed with civil claims, lawyers say

The police update came as lawyers confirmed three women were still pursuing civil lawsuits related to the allegations.

Lawyers representing one of the women who alleges she was sexually assaulted said she was "devastated" by the decision.

Slater and Gordon lawyer Jackson Pannam said what had occurred had a "profound impact" on her.

"She reported the incident immediately, provides a formal statement and cooperated fully with the investigation," he said.

"She has shown enormous courage in coming forward."

Mr Pannam confirmed the woman would proceed with a civil case, which must be proved on a "balance of probabilities" rather than the higher criminal standard of "beyond reasonable doubt".

"The absence of criminal charges does not prevent a civil claim from proceeding," Mr Pannam said.

"Slater and Gordon Lawyers is continuing to prepare a civil claim against the relevant parties and will continue to support our client through this extremely difficult time."

Victoria Police said a thorough investigation into the incident concluded there was insufficient evidence to lay charges. (ABC News)

John Karantzis from Carbone Lawyers, who is acting for two of the women in a civil claim against the club, said his clients were "very disappointed and distressed" over the outcome of the police investigation.

He said the women would still forge ahead with their civil claim.

"My clients' civil claim is based on a different burden of proof, it is based on the balance of probabilities," he said.

"We will vigorously pursue this claim."

Asked about how the club might handle related civil claims, Mr Pavlich contained his comments to the outcome of the police investigation.

"Any future aspects, we'll deal with that as it comes," he said.

Isaac Heeney welcomes police update

In a statement, Heeney welcomed the police announcement.

"The past three months have been incredibly difficult for my family, Steffie and those close to me," Heeney said.

"Watching my family carry the weight of this has been heartbreaking.

"To my family and friends, your love and loyalty has meant more than words can do justice.

Swans player Isaac Heeney was among those spoken to by police during the investigation. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"To those that have never doubted me and stood by my side in solidarity — thank you. I know it has not been easy in the face of such intense public scrutiny. I will never forget your support.

"To the entire Sydney Swans Club — my teammates, coaches, the board, our sponsors, and our loyal members and fans — thank you for keeping faith in me.

"The Swans have given me an opportunity to live out a childhood dream and I am fully focused on repaying that faith by being the best person and player I can be."

World.title: Cummins says Khawaja's ball-tampering claim '100 per cent wrong'
World.content:
(Getty)

Before the questioning, Cummins read what seemed like a prepared statement and signalled his intentions for what he wanted to achieve with his address.

Here is that statement in full:

Loading...

"I've taken a bit of time this week to respond to Usman's allegations. I've been trying to understand exactly what those allegations have been, that's why it's taken me a few days.

"When he says 'we all knew', if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong. I've said that consistently for the last eight years; I did not know that was happening.

"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper; that's complete and utter nonsense.

(Getty)

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not the Usman that I know, it's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book Ussie's been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell a story, 100 per cent. I'm really glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do.

"So I'm here, I'm happy to answer all your questions. I'll stay here until you have no more questions. I don't want to talk about this again after today. So even if it takes all day — I've got to bowl at some stage — but I'll answer all of them because at some point we got to move on.

(Getty)

"Today I'll talk as Australian captain right now but I'll also talk about the 24-year-old young guy and his recollections playing my 13th Test back in 2018 in a team that at that stage I think had a win-at-all costs mentality, had an ugly underbelly, and there was too many silos within the team, traits that I hope that everyone has seen and I try very hard to eradicate for the last six years as captain.

"So I'm happy to take all your questions about sandpaper, ball tampering, changerooms, international cricket, whether my wife and I did have a spat out the front, whatever you want, hit me, I'm here."

World.title: Sixers win WBBL clash despite Ellyse Perry's strange run-out
World.content:
New Zealand captain Melie Kerr has starred with the bat and ball to keep the Sydney Sixers unbeaten in the WBBL with a victory over the Melbourne Renegades.

In the second match of a double-header at Melbourne's Junction Oval, Kerr set up the Sixers' 11-run win by top-scoring with 53 off 34 balls and finishing with tidy figures of 1-29.

It lifted the Sixers to 5-0 at the season's halfway mark and into second spot alongside the also unbeaten Perth Scorchers.

Kerr was the only batter to pass 50 in the game, sharing a crucial 56-run partnership with opener Ellyse Perry before the Australian star was undone in unusual circumstances.

In the 18th over, Kerr chipped a ball into the deep on the leg side and pushed for two with Perry, as Georgia Wareham swooped on the ball in the deep and fired it into the bowler's end.

Sophie Molineux fielded cleanly and whipped the bails off as Perry dove to make her ground, and there was only half an appeal from the Renegades to umpire Louise Broadfoot, who shook her head.

Former Australia captain Lisa Sthalekar in commentary credited Broadfoot and fellow caller Aaron Finch prophetically said: "There must be something in the back of the umpire's mind that goes 'what if I just haven't quite got it right though?'."

As the slow-motion replay on the big screen at Junction Oval showed Perry's dive bouncing over the line, rather than being grounded, the crowd and everyone on the field raised their eyebrows, with Broadfoot consulting fellow umpire Malcolm Wood before sending it to the third umpire.

Perry had already started making her way off the field before the decision was made, with her team adding 16 in the final two overs to set up the chase.

As the pitch slowed, the Renegades got off to a horror start chasing 141 to win after collapsing to 3-22 by the fifth over.

Molineux inched her way to 18 off 21 and was livid when caught trying to cut away Caoimhe Bray (1-17), but Tess Flintoff (44 off 33) breathed life back into the Renegades.

Needing 17 off the last over to win, spinner Ashleigh Gardner (3-13 off three overs) shut the door as the Renegades were bowled out for 129.

In the earlier game, a captain's knock from Georgia Redmayne propelled Brisbane past the Melbourne Stars and into the top four.

Set 166 for victory, skipper Redmayne (74 not out off 50 deliveries) and Irish young gun Orla Prendergast (52 not out off 36) put the Stars to the sword.

It was the Stars' fourth straight loss, while the Heat are sitting pretty in third with three victories on the bounce after going 706 days without a triumph.

World.title: AFLW has come a long way but this player 'doesn’t want to settle'
World.content:
When Jenna Richardson scrolls through TikTok, she's now starting to come across AFLW content — and lots of it.

To the inaugural Hawthorn defender, it's a sign of the game's evolution and how it's connecting to fans.

"There are videos of people analysing the games … It's nice because they analyse the men's game, so then to see them do it for the W, [it's good]," Richardson tells ABC Sport.

AFLW club culture AFL Players Association CEO James Gallagher says the gap between AFLW clubs getting workplace culture right is widening and the results can be seen on the field.

After securing Hawthorn's first finals win last week (against Gold Coast), the side are now gearing up for a semi-final against Carlton on Saturday at Princes Park, a ground that drew 5,000 fans for the weekend's prior qualifying finals.

This season, the overall AFLW home-and-away attendance record was broken in round 10, helped by the introduction of double-headers, with the two crowds at Docklands drawing 20,455 and 14,573, respectively.

Excluding the matches with men's games, standalone games were at an average of 2,500 per game, similar to the 2025 figures.

"I'm pretty level-headed in being able to see the games come a long way," Richardson said.

"So whilst I am so grateful for everything we get, and I feel quite spoiled at times, I also know there's a lot of room for growth — and not to settle."

The biggest change Richardson wants to see is the number of regular season rounds increase from 12 — which she really feels during finals.

Hawthorn are the only team to have beaten North Melbourne in three years. (Getty: Emily Barker)

"At least playing every team once to make a more realistic ladder at the end of the season," she said.

Every team's fixture is dependent on where they finished the year before, meaning sides that finished lower theoretically play more fellow-lower sides, and vice versa with the top sides.

It can result in some teams making finals that get caught out straight away, and some that could make a finals run with more rounds, missing out.

"Playing the top teams, we always get the most out of… the more you play the best teams, the better you becomel. We did," Richardson said, noting Hawthorn were the only team to beat North Melbourne in three years.

"We played Adelaide (not in finals) and got beat. I thought they were really good to play against.

"They have shown in the past, for however many years, that they're up for finals contention. I feel like if there were more games, I wouldn't be surprised if they were in there too."

Hawthorn are playing in its first semi-finals in AFLW history. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

Richardson said, she'd then like to see increased salaries for support staff and assistant coaches in women's programs.

Richardson notes how stretched programs can be, which adds pressure on coaches, assistant coaches and support staff.

"They [line coaches] sacrifice a lot from their other jobs, like they're usually losing money to come and help our program," she said.

"They have to do so much for us... (and) those two days a week where they're at our club, they're taking a massive pay cut from their other job."

Jenna Richardson joined Hawthorn as an expansion signing in 2022. (Getty: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

With the W awards coming up, Richardson is also not opposed to the introduction of a defender award, given the best and fairest generally goes to a midfielder and there is a medal for leading goalkicker.

"Why not?" Richardson asked.

"That'd actually be cool because we're never in those, you know, fun photos or celebrating goals that are down there — so that'd be fun."

Tech.title: Xbox announces Wolfenstein 3
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s been nearly a decade since Bethesda’s MachineGames released Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus in 2017, and now Xbox is ready to announce a sequel from the studio. Wolfenstein 3 was officially announced today, just days after Bethesda also confirmed that the next Elder Scrolls game will be called The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel.

In a post, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced the name and a photo of a script. “Looking forward to sharing more,” she said. MachineGames also announced the game in a post, saying the game is “in production” and sharing a photo from a motion-capture session. IGN reports that Brian Bloom (who plays protagonist William Joseph “BJ” Blazkowicz) and Debra Wilson (who plays Grace Walker) are reprising their roles, and they appear to be the featured actors in the photo.

The last mainline entry, Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus, launched in 2017 and continued the story of Blazkowicz in an alternate 1960s where Nazi Germany had won the Second World War. Wolfenstein: Youngblood also debuted in 2019 as a co-op spinoff, starring Blazkowicz’s twin daughters.

Tech.title: Whoop launched a social network where every user has a ‘verified heartbeat’
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Starting Thursday, Whoop members can share their data from its wearables on the app’s new Whoop Humans social network. Users can make their metrics, activities, and achievements visible to other Whoop wearers, post Story-like “Moments” with photos and captions, and add comments and reactions on other members’ posts.

Whoop claims its platform is “entirely human,” unlike other social media platforms that are “saturated with artificial intelligence, automated accounts and bots, and manufactured content.”

Whoop CEO Will Ahmed says Humans is “the most verifiably human network ever launched. Every account represents a real person with a verified heartbeat.” Whoop says its existing Teams social feature “will remain available,” allowing people to share strain, recovery, and sleep data along with group leaderboards.

In the Community tab in Whoop’s app, users can scroll through Moments from people they’re following, like tapping through your Stories feed on Instagram but with your friends’ fitness tracker data. In one of Whoop’s examples, swiping up on a user’s Moments post with a photo from their run shows a map with their route and details like their pace and distance. The Community tab also shows cards for people in your “community” with their sleep, recovery, and strain scores.

Whoop says users choose which activities, achievements, and metrics they want to share on Humans, including Recovery, Strain, Sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate. Any activities marked as sensitive aren’t shared by default. There’s also an option to keep Moments posts private and a “Stealth Mode” for temporarily hiding health and performance data without changing your sharing settings.

Tech.title: Humble Bundle redesign removes two-factor verification from settings
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Humble Bundle storefront for buying games and other software recently got a new look, but on the settings page, it no longer offers a way to add or update two-factor verification methods, as reported by Kotaku. PC Gamer also points out that there are Humble Bundle support pages discussing two-factor verification, and the writer for the publication said that they had set up two-factor verification on the old version of the site.

However, it does appear that, at least as of now, there is some form of two-factor verification. When I tried logging into my Humble Bundle account while writing this article, I was prompted to check my email for an access code before I could access my account. While logged in, I was able to update my password, but I didn’t have to enter my old password to be able to do so.

For what it’s worth, my passwords app also shows that I set up a rotating two-factor code for Humble Bundle at some point. I was not asked to input that at any part of my login process today.

Humble Bundle owner IGN Entertainment and IGN parent company Ziff Davis didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

We’ve begun returning a portion of the affected servers to service, and they’re remaining stable so far. We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions.
